title: Staring Down Superposition
description: Quantum mechanics is the foundation of physical theory, whose predictions have been consistently verified to an astounding degree of accuracy. However, the manner in which the mathematics must be formulated stands at odds with previously assumed to be unassailable truths of physical logic. The idea that a superposition (simultaneous manifestations of mutually exclusive properties) exists between measurements of quantum phenomenon is incongruent with the notion of objective realism: the idea that external objects exist irrespective of observation. To explain experimental results, researchers have postulated different interpretations of quantum mechanics. In the standard orthodoxy, often referred to as the Copenhagen Interpretation, particles exist in a state of superposition, a collection of all possible states described by Schrodinger's wave function, until the act of measurement, at which time the superposition collapses into only one of these possible states. The Copenhagen Interpretation is silent on what actually constitutes an act of measurement or on how or why it collapses the wave function. Unsatisfied with this lack of clarity, other interpretations have emerged that contest the reality of the superposition. For example, the Many Worlds interpretation (Everett, 1957) holds instead that the universe bifurcates every time a measurement is taken on a quantum system, that all the possibilities are actually realized. Other interpretations maintain that nonlocal hidden variables determine the results of each measurement (Bohm, 1980), or that the collapse of the wave function is a spontaneous yet objective process where collapse does not occur upon the interaction with a physical measurement device. (Ghirardi, Rimini, & Weber, 1986). Consciousness enters the conversation in the augmentation to the Copenhagen interpretation suggested by John von Neumann (1932) and Eugene Wigner (1961). This interpretation holds that there is no clear physical end to the superposition, and that the mathematics allows for the collapse of the wave function to be placed anywhere on the causal chain from the physical measurement device all the way to the experimenter's subjective perception. In other words, when a particle in superposition interacts with a physical measurement device, it is reasonable to conclude that both the particle under consideration along with the physical measurement device itself are existing in a state of superposition until they are observed by the experimenter. What reason is there to conclude that macrophysical objects persist objectively in time while microphysical objects exist only in superposition? The only clear place to draw the line of collapse is at the point where a physical system interacts with consciousness, something that is outside of the physical reality that is governed by quantum mechanics. This has subsequently become known as the Consciousness Causes Collapse (CCC) interpretation. Putting the CCC interpretation to an empirical test will require methods that are not limited to those of experimental physics. In cognitive psychology the term priming refers to an effect where exposure to one stimulus influences a person's response to another stimulus. For example, a positive word such as "happy" is recognized and responded to faster after the word "joy" as compared to a negative word such as "sadness" or "death". The word "up" is responded to faster following a prime such as "high" or "top" as opposed to "bottom" or "low". Psychologists have been exploiting these reliable reaction time effects for decades as a multipurpose research tool. In recent years, these methods have even been used to prime subjects subliminally (Dehaene et al, 1998; Greenwald et al, 2003; Kouider & Dehaene, 2009). In such research, subjects are shown a prime (such as a word or a symbol) on a computer screen for a length of time that is just underneath the duration that can be consciously experienced (about 50 milliseconds). Despite subjects reporting to not be aware of seeing the primes, they demonstrated shorter reaction times responding to stimulus that is congruent with the primes than to incongruent stimulus. Their brains processed the meaning of the primes and began to react to them even though they were not aware of it. The primes were processed unconsciously. This ability for humans to process information unconsciously makes it possible to measure the effects of something that is itself shielded from conscious observation. By deriving the direction of the primes from quantum events we can leverage the methodology of subliminal priming to put the CCC interpretation of quantum mechanics to an experimental test. EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURES A Geiger counter will be used to measure the radioactive decay from a small sample of uranium. Uranium (or anything radioactive for that matter) emits ions due to natural radioactive decay, and these ions create "clicks" of the Geiger counter. The time between ion emissions is called a "click interval". Radioactive decay is a "true quantum event" (creating a real quantum state), and the intervals between clicks are random within a Poisson distribution. To generate the digits for the Qtris-3 game, these click intervals are measured, and then divided by the number of digits being used in the game, and the remainder is then used as the prime. Calculating the remainder is referred to as "modulo" division. For example, if the click interval is 100ms, and we are using digits 1 - 9 for the game, then the remainder of 100 / 9 is 1, and thus a 1 is shown as the prime. This method maintains the quantum event while scaling it to the range of individual digits used in the game as well as eliminating any potential bias due to the Poisson distribution. Three single digit numbers (primes) using this method are then flashed on the screen for 50 milliseconds (too short a duration to be consciously experienced). The primes will be followed by a three digit stimulus number that was presented on the screen that subjects could experience and were asked to rapidly respond to by hitting a button to indicate whether the majority of the numbers were even or odd. The participant's reaction time, how long it took them to hit the button, was measured. Since each item contained three stimulus numbers and three primes, the majority of the primes were either congruent (odd/odd or even/even) or incongruent (odd/even, or even/odd) with the stimulus numbers. The participants' reaction times will be divided into groups along these lines. The incongruent group will be populated by the reaction times to all of the items where the majority of the primes were incongruent with the stimulus number and the congruent group will be populated with all the reaction times to the items that had majority congruent primes. Unobserved Condition (experimental condition) If the CCC were true, these primes, having been shielded from conscious observation, should still be in a state of superposition based on the state of the radioactive decay from which they were derived. However, if the CCC were false, then the collapse would have occurred upon the initial reading of the Geiger counter and these primes will already be in exact states when the participants take the reaction time test. This experimental condition will henceforth be referred to as the unobserved condition. Observed Condition (control condition) The primes in the control condition will be prepared identically to the experimental condition, with the exception that these primes will be observed on the computer screen prior to the participant's engagement in the response time task. This will henceforth be referred to as the observed condition. Each game played will be randomly assigned to either the Unobserved Condition, the Observed Condition, or a third condition whose purpose it will be to generate more observed primes for the next game. Response times from this third condition will not be posted in the results tabulation or included in the primary data analysis. HYPOTHESIS A prime in a state of superposition should not produce its full effect on response time as it will be simultaneously both congruent and incongruent with the stimulus. Therefore, if the CCC interpretation of quantum mechanics is correct, these unobserved primes will not have the expected effect on reaction time (reducing it when congruent and increasing it when incongruent), as they would in the control condition in which the primes were directly observed beforehand. It is hypothesized that the difference between congruent and incongruent primes in the observed condition will be significantly higher than it will be in the unobserved condition. DATA ANALYSIS T tests will be used to analyze the difference in mean response times between congruent and incongruent primes in both the observed and the unobserved condition. 1. Each subject will be asked to play 5 to 10 games of Qtris 3 consisting of 12 rows of 3 digits - for a total of 36 prime/stimulus pairs per game. To preserve diversity in responding we ask that any individual participant not play any more than 20 games during this data collection. 2. A time limit of 4,000 ms will exist for each individual item. Items responded to outside of the time limit will not be included in the data analysis. . 3. A time minimum of 200 ms will also exist for each individual item. Items responded to in less than that time will not be included in the data analysis. 3. Response times will only be computed for games where the participant has achieved a based score of 20 or higher. 4. Only the response times for correct responses will be included in the data analysis

Abstract Addressing the Identity Simulation Challenge in Cognitive AI The Multi-System Persona Framework (MSPF) addresses a central challenge in cognitive AI: how to construct highly synchronized digital personas without reducing identity to static trait sets or mystified typologies. MSPF proposes a layered architecture that simulates individual cognitive trajectories by converging multiple origin inputs—including immutable biographical anchors and reflexive decision schemas—within a framework of probabilistic modeling and constraint propagation. Unlike deterministic pipelines or esoteric taxonomies, MSPF introduces a reproducible, traceable, and ethically auditable alternative to identity simulation at scale. The Multi-Origin Trajectory Convergence Method At the core of MSPF lies a structured three-stage mechanism termed the Multi-Origin Trajectory Convergence Method, consisting of: (1) Basic identity modeling, grounded in both immutable and enculturated variables (L0–L1–L2–L3–Lx–L4–L5), such as birth context, socio-cultural environment, and cognitive trace history; (2) Stylometric tone calibration through the Multi-Faction Stylometry Framework (MFSF), which spans 5 macro-categories and 24 analyzers designed to modulate rhetorical surfaces without distorting underlying persona signals; (3) Semantic alignment and value modeling, achieved via structured questionnaires and logic encoded assessments to capture reasoning patterns, value conflict tolerances, and narrative framing tendencies. This pipeline is orchestrated by an audit-prior inference engine that supports counterfactual simulation and belief-trace exportability, ensuring traceable transparency and governance-readiness throughout the generative process. Scalable Simulation and Practical Applications MSPF enables scalable, real-time construction of cognitive personas applicable to both self-reflective and third-party use cases. Core applications include psycholinguistic diagnostics, stylometric profiling, OSINT-based modeling of public figures, and automated detection of internal cognitive dissonance. By supporting reversible cognition modeling and explainable simulation mechanics, MSPF offers a principled and extensible infrastructure for ethically-constrained AI persona construction—across personal, institutional, and governance contexts. Declarations • Ethics & Funding. This framework relies exclusively on synthetic identity composites and open-source data; no IRB sensitive samples are used. • Conflicts of Interest. None declared. • Data & Code Availability. Versioned documentation, Lx event-trace generator, and evaluation scripts will be released upon publication. •Deployment Note. A functional implementation of this framework is publicly available as a custom GPT under the name **"TCCS · Trinity Cognitive Construct System"**, accessible via the [Explore GPTs](https://chat.openai.com/gpts) section on ChatGPT. This deployment illustrates layered identity modeling in real-time interaction, including stylometric adaptation and inference trace exportability. 02. Introduction Modeling identity in computational systems is a central open problem in cognitive AI. Trait taxonomies, psychometric scales, and heuristic profiles offer convenient labels yet often flatten identity or hide provenance inside opaque embeddings. Large language models add fluency and responsiveness but not stable coherence or causal traceability. As AI systems simulate, interpret, or represent people in high-stakes settings, the inability to explain how beliefs form, values update, and roles shift creates epistemic, ethical, and governance risk. The Multi-System Persona Framework (MSPF) treats identity as a layered inference process rather than a static category. It models convergence across immutable anchors, cultural scaffolds, reflexive schema, and stylistic modulation, organized as L0–L5 plus an internalization trace layer Lx. MSPF integrates the Multi-Faction Stylometry Framework (MFSF) and an audit-first inference engine to support forward simulation and retrospective tracing with modular validation and bias transparency. This paper positions MSPF as both theory and architecture. Section 3 states assumptions and design rationale. Section 4 details the framework and cross-disciplinary mappings. Section 5 surveys application scenarios in digital psychometrics, tone calibration, OSINT-assisted public-figure simulation, and inconsistency detection. Section 6 presents limitations, validation strategy, and ethical considerations. Section 7 discusses open challenges and the stance that bias should be modeled as structure that can be audited. Section 8 concludes. Contributions: (1) a layered identity model with L0–L5+Lx and an audit-first engine that separates structural signals from surface modulation; (2) a stylometric module with 24 analyzers that adjusts rhetoric without erasing persona signals, plus clear governance injection points across layers; (3) a validation plan that tests temporal stability, internalization accuracy, stylometric fidelity, counterfactual robustness, and cross-layer independence; (4) a deployment-neutral specification that supports reproducible audits and code-data release. Materials that support granular modulation and measurement appear in Appendix DEF. They extend the questionnaires and stylometric analyzers referenced in the applications of Section 5. 03. Assumptions, Theoretical Foundation & Design 03.1 Assumptions Rationale: From Shared Origins to Divergent Identities A central question in cognitive modeling arises: Why do individuals born under nearly identical conditions—same geographic origin, birth period, and socio-economic bracket—nonetheless exhibit highly divergent developmental trajectories? While traditional psychological theories emphasize postnatal experience and environmental stochasticity, the Multi-System Persona Framework (MSPF) formalizes a complementary assumption: that identity trajectories are probabilistically inferable from a convergence of layered input variables. These include—but are not limited to—physiological constraints, familial norms, enculturated scripts, educational schema, media influence, reflexive agency, and temporal modulation. Importantly, MSPF neither essentializes identity nor advances a fatalistic worldview. Instead, it treats correlation-rich structures as state variables that serve as anchoring coordinates within a semantically governed simulation framework. Identity is conceptualized not as a fixed monolith but as a convergent output arising from the interplay of fixed constraints, cultural scripts, internalized narrative scaffolds, and dynamically modulated self-expressions. ________________________________________ Design Assumptions of MSPF Architecture MSPF rests on three foundational assumptions that govern the modeling process: 1. Partial Separability of Layers Identity is understood as partially decomposable. While emergent as a whole, its contributing strata—ranging from fixed biographical anchors to stylistic modulations—can be modeled semi-independently to ensure modularity of inference, analytical clarity, and extensibility. 2. Traceable Internalization Cultural exposure (Layer 3) only becomes computationally significant when internalized into reflexive schema (Layer x). The framework strictly distinguishes between contact and commitment, allowing simulations to reflect degrees of adoption rather than mere exposure. 3. Modulation Is Not Essence Momentary emotional, stylistic, or rhetorical shifts (Layer 5) affect external presentation but do not constitute structural identity. This assumption prevents overfitting to transient data, guarding against labeling bias, emotional state drift, or stylistic camouflage as core persona traits. ________________________________________ Computational Implications of Layered Modeling The layered modularity of MSPF architecture yields multiple benefits in simulation, validation, and governance: • Targeted Validation. Each layer can be independently tested and validated: e.g., L2 (schooling) with longitudinal retests; L5 (stylistic drift) via stylometric comparison. • Disentanglement of Causal Entropy. Confounds such as L3–L4 entanglement (cultural scripts vs. belief structures) can be algorithmically separated via event-trace analysis in Lx. • Governance Injection Points. Semantic flags and normative audits can be imposed at specific layers: e.g., L3 content bias detection, L4 belief consistency checks, or L5 tone calibration monitoring. ________________________________________ Conclusion: Assumptive Boundaries without Essentialism MSPF's assumptions serve not to constrain identity into rigid typologies, but to construct a flexible, inference-compatible structure that allows: • Simulation of cognitive divergence from common origins; • Preservation of cultural and narrative granularity; • Scalable modeling of dissociative or parallel persona states without reifying incidental biases. These assumptions make the framework particularly suitable for high-fidelity, semantically governed cognitive simulation across heterogeneous environments. 03.2 Theoretical Foundation From Typology to Trajectory: Reframing Personality Modeling Most historical systems for modeling personality—ranging from astrology to modern psychometrics—have relied on fixed typologies, symbolic metaphors, or statistical trait aggregates. This meta-analysis will use data from all published studies examining the effects of intravitreal corticosteroid treatment on patients with glaucoma in order to quantify the effects on intraocular pressure and progression of glaucomatous disease in the short, medium, and long term. Studies will further be examined to explore the indications for which intravitreal corticosteroid treatment is initiated with concurrent glaucoma; any prophylactic measures undertaken to mitigate the risks of corticosteroids in glaucoma; and which outcomes have been used to measure the safety of intravitreal corticosteroids in glaucoma. These results will help inform decision-making where intravitreal corticosteroid treatment is being considered for glaucoma patients, as potential benefits and risks must be weighed.

title: Introduction to Interferometry of Fiber Optic Strain Measurements
description: Distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) measures the average axial strain (strain rate) along a subset of a fiber optic cable, as opposed to the particle displacement (velocity) at a particular small point sensor. In shifting from measuring a vector field to a tensor field, DAS changes the directional sensitivity of measurements of every type of seismic wave when compared to single component geophones, particularly Love and S waves.We show this through theoretical analysis of planar Rayleigh, Love, P- and S-waves over both infinitesimally small and realistic gauge lengths. title: CI
description: For cochlear implant (CI) patients, reliable predictors of rehabilitative speech outcome are desirable. In this longitudinal study, we examined the relative contributions of temporal versus spectral auditory processing to successful speech recognition following cochlear implantation. Method. We tested N = 46 newly implanted patients shortly after CI activation (T1), six months (T2) and one year (T3) later. We assessed temporal and spectral modulation sensitivity using an adaptive ripple discrimination paradigm where dynamic ripples were modulated at the speech-relevant temporal rate of ~4 Hz and spectral scale of ~0.5 cyc/oct. At both time points, speech recognition in quiet was evaluated using the Freiburg number and monosyllabic word test. The Oldenburg speech-in-noise test (OLSA) was administered one year after implantation. Conclusions. Particularly temporal modulation sensitivity is here identified as reliable predictor of CI speech outcome, over and above established clinical speech tests. A simple ripple discrimination test could be a useful addition to the clinical rehabilitation routine to prospectively predict speech outcomes in adult CI patients.

title: Does the phaco-TIp position during clear corneal Phacoemulsification Surgery adversely affect corneal endothelium? TIPS study protocol for a randomised, triple-masked, parallel-group trial of bevel-up
description: Background: Globally, at least 30 million cataract surgeries are required annually to prevent cataract-related blindness. Corneal endothelial decompensation is one of the most common causes of poor visual outcome following cataract surgery, particularly in those with predisposing factors. The increasing ageing population and reduced visual impairment threshold for cataract surgery have resulted in rising cataract surgical rates and hence, an increase in corneal endothelial decompensation is expected. The role of phaco-tip position on corneal endothelial damage is ambiguous. Previous studies have reported contradictory results and were also underpowered to detect a significant difference due to small sample sizes. With no consensus regarding the most cornea-friendly phaco-tip position (bevel-up versus bevel-down) during phacoemulsification, we propose a randomised clinical trial with a robust design using direct chop phaco-technique. Objective: To compare the effect of phaco-tip position (bevel-up vs. bevel-down) on corneal endothelial cell count during phacoemulsification Methods: A randomised, multicentre, parallel-group, triple-masked (participant, outcome assessor, and statistician) trial with 1:1 allocation ratio is proposed. By adopting stratified randomisation (according to cataract grade), we will randomly allocate 480 patients aged >18 years with immature cataract into bevel-up and bevel-down groups at two centres. History of significant ocular trauma, previous intraocular surgery, shallow anterior chamber, low endothelial cell count, pseudoexfoliation syndrome, intraocular inflammation, and corneal endothelial dystrophy are the key exclusion criteria. Outcomes: Primary- postoperative endothelial cell count at one month. Secondary- central corneal thickness on postoperative days 1, 15, and 30, and intraoperative complications.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.

title: Image Investing
description: Despite the well-documented long-term benefits of stock market participation, participation rates among households remain low. Traditional explanations point to barriers such as limited financial literacy, cognitive biases, or perceived risk. However, recent research highlights an underexplored but potentially powerful driver: the social image costs associated with being perceived as a profit-maximizing stock market investor (c.f. Henkel & Zimpelmann, 2023, for example), which can be a particularly important factor in an era of increasing social and environmental awareness. This aversion raises the question of whether moral or reputation concerns might be a fundamental barrier to market participation – and whether tailored and carefully designed mechanisms can overcome this friction. Socially Responsible Investing (SRI) offers a potential solution. By allowing individuals to align financial decisions with ethical or prosocial values, SRI could reduce the perceived stigma of investing and increase stock market participation. However, little is known about the behavioral mechanisms through which SRI influences stock market participation, nor about the potential impact on market dynamics. This project addresses both aspects using two experiments. First, we analyze whether and under which conditions the introduction of socially responsible investment options can increase individual stock market participation. A key novelty is the role of social image concerns: we explore how visible status labels and the informativeness of these labels – assigned based on the proportion of one's portfolio invested in socially responsible assets – affect participation decisions. These labels represent easy-to implement real-world signals such as "green badges" in trading apps, making the reputational dimension of investment choices salient. Second, we analyze the market-level consequences of introducing SRI and associated social labels. While the expansion of SRI is often viewed positively, it is not obvious that this shift, in particular paired with labels, is welfare-enhancing. For example, labeling investors, depending on the informativeness of that label, may create unintended incentives and amplify mispricing and volatility in conventional assets. Using two complementary experimental paradigms – an individual decision-making task and a market experiment – we aim to uncover both micro-level behavioral responses and macro-level market dynamics. This dual perspective allows us to evaluate not just whether socially responsible investing changes who participates, but also whether it fundamentally changes how market dynamics function. To support the generalizability of our results, we also run a short vignette study that mirrors key features of the the individual task in a more naturalistic, real-world context. This research contributes to an emerging literature on the social dimensions of financial decision-making. It also offers practical implications for policymakers and financial institutions seeking to increase participation without compromising market efficiency.

title: Barriers and Enablers to Medication Adherence & Compliance in Glaucoma – A Scoping Review Protocol
description: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with increased intraocular pressure (IOP) being the primary modifiable risk factor. It is often referred to as the 'silent thief of sight' for its progressive, mostly asymptomatic disease course until advanced stages. First line treatment is to lower IOP by topical medication. However, adherence with topical medications is problematic, with approximately only 50% of patients taking their glaucoma medications one year post diagnosis. It is imperative that those commencing treatment are adherent since suboptimal adherence is related to poor clinical, social and economic outcomes. The aim of this review is to better understand factors influencing adherence and interventions trialled to improve adherence. Evidence synthesised will inform the development of an educational tool to improve adherence as part of an ongoing project. Methods and Analysis This scoping review will include searches in EMBASE, Pubmed, Psych Info, CINAHL, ProQuest and Web of Science electronic databases. Primary research studies, and peer-reviewed grey literature will be eligible for inclusion. A data extraction framework will guide the literature screening and papers will be independently reviewed by two reviewers to assess eligibility for inclusion. Titles and abstracts will be screened for inclusion, while full text screening of included articles will be carried out by two independent reviewers. A qualitative data analysis will be carried out to assess relevant literature, and data will be presented in a narrative synthesis format. Ethics and Dissemination This scoping review focuses on previously published literature and so ethical approval was not required. These findings will be relevant to patients, clinicians and stakeholders in the glaucoma care pathway. They will be distributed through publication in a peer-reviewed journal and at conference presentations.

title: Probe-Based Confocal Laser Endomicroscopy for Real-Time Optical Diagnosis Along the Correa Cascade of Gastric Carcinogenesis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Diagnostic Accuracy
description: Gastric cancer develops through a well-defined stepwise pathological sequence — the Correa cascade — progressing from Helicobacter pylori-associated gastritis through atrophic gastritis, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia to invasive carcinoma. Early detection at precancerous stages is critical, yet current surveillance relies on random biopsy protocols that are limited by sampling error and inability to provide real-time histological information. Probe-based confocal laser endomicroscopy (pCLE) enables real-time, in vivo optical biopsy at cellular resolution during standard endoscopy. Primary studies suggest high diagnostic accuracy across Correa cascade stages, but existing meta-analyses are fragmented — addressing only single stages, conflating pCLE with the discontinued eCLE platform, and omitting a large body of East Asian literature. This study is the first systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate pCLE diagnostic accuracy across the complete Correa cascade — from H. pylori gastritis to early gastric cancer — in a unified analytical framework. We will pool data using a bivariate random-effects model, assess evidence quality by GRADE, and conduct pre-specified subgroup analyses by geographic region, operator experience, and pCLE classification system. Both English and Chinese-language databases will be searched to minimise geographic bias. Findings will provide the most comprehensive evidence base to date for pCLE-guided gastric surveillance, with direct implications for clinical guideline development and targeted biopsy protocol design.

title: Mapping The Evidence On Diabetes Distress, Coping Strategies, And Glycemic Control In Adults With Diabetes: A Systematic Scoping Review
description: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic, metabolic disorder characterized by either insufficient insulin production or inefficient utilization, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels (Azeem et al., 2022). The main subtypes of DM are Type 1 (T1DM), involving inadequate insulin production, and Type 2 (T2DM), involving insulin resistance (Antar et al., 2023; Cheng et al, 2023). Globally, DM poses a significant health burden, affecting an estimated 589 million adults aged 20 to 79 years (International Diabetes Federation [IDF], 2025). Alarmingly, around 81% of these individuals reside in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), where healthcare systems face structural constraints, limited resources, and inadequate access to comprehensive DM care. The global impact of DM is further reflected in its growing mortality rate, with over 3.4 million in 2024, accounting for 9.3% of all global deaths (Ahmad et al., 2023). DM is associated with a wide range of microvascular and macrovascular complications, including retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, and diabetic foot infections, which substantially increase morbidity and mortality (Patel, 2024). Beyond physiological complications, many adults living with DM experience diabetes distress (DD), also referred to as diabetes related distress (DRD) or diabetes specific distress (DSD). DD encompasses negative emotional and psychological reactions to the complex demands of managing DM. These demands include adherence to diet and medications, fear of long term complications, monitoring blood glucose and financial and social challenges associated with chronic disease management (ADA, 2014; Collins et al., 2021; Polonsky et al., 2022; Elsayed et al., 2023). Unlike depression, DD is directly linked to the lived experiences of managing DM rather than constituting a clinical psychological disorder. Coping strategies are methods used to manage stress, resolve issues, and adjust to unstable conditions. These techniques are intended to assist people in managing their internal and external demands, which can include environmental, cultural, psychological, and physiological factors (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; Nugroho et al., 2024). Effective glycemic control, often measured by glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) or blood glucose levels, is essential to avoid DM related complications. Targets for optimum glycemic control are generally fasting blood sugar level between 70–125 mg/dl or, HbA1c < 7%, adjusted for age, comorbidities, and other individual factors (Aschner et al., 2017; ADA, 2024; Pleus et al., 2024). Despite the extensive literature on DD, coping techniques, and glycemic outcomes, the evidence remains fragmented, context-dependent, and methodologically diverse. Notably, no scoping review has systematically mapped the conceptualization, measurement, and correlation of DD and coping mechanisms with glycemic outcomes across various contexts, especially in LMICs. Therefore, this review seeks to synthesize existing information on these constructs, assess study quality, identify knowledge gaps, and guide future research and clinical practice.

title: Diagnostic Selective Nerve Root Block (SNRB) in Lumbar Nerve Root Compression
description: Background and Aim Selective nerve root blocks (SNRBs) are widely used in spine surgery for diagnostic clarification in patients with radicular pain, particularly when imaging (MRI) and clinical findings are inconclusive regarding the symptomatic nerve root or the expected benefit of surgical decompression. The purpose of the block is to clarify the diagnosis and prognosis of radiating lower limb pain, thereby supporting decision-making regarding surgical versus non-surgical treatment. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the prognostic value of selective nerve root blocks in lumbar nerve root compression. Objectives and Hypotheses Primary objective: To assess whether patients undergoing surgery after a diagnostic block with good effect demonstrate different postoperative outcomes, measured by the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at 12 months, compared with patients undergoing surgery without a prior block, adjusted for relevant confounders. Hypothesis: Patients with a positive diagnostic block who subsequently undergo surgery experience less postoperative improvement, measured by ODI, compared with patients undergoing surgery without prior diagnostic uncertainty. Study Design Retrospective cohort study based on registry data and medical records. Population and Eligibility Criteria Inclusion criteria: - Patients aged >18 years - Underwent diagnostic selective lumbar nerve root block (BAFA7) between January 1, 2018 and May 31, 2024 at Zealand University Hospital, Køge Exclusion criteria: - Therapeutic (non-diagnostic) blocks - Missing data regarding block level, side, effect, or subsequent surgery - Missing 12‐month follow-up in DaneSpine - Surgery performed at a different spinal level than the block Data Sources and Variables Primary data sources include the Health Platform, private hospital records, and DaneSpine. Collected variables include demographics, block characteristics, surgical details, and PROM data (ODI, VAS, EQ‐5D). Outcome Measures Primary outcome: - ODI at 12 months postoperatively Secondary outcomes: - Patient satisfaction - Likelihood ratios and predictive values - Avoided surgery following negative block - Re-referral to the spine clinic at any time during follow-up Statistical Analysis Mixed-effects linear regression models will be applied. Fixed effects include block status and relevant covariates, while patient ID is included as a random effect. Ethical Considerations This retrospective registry study involves no patient contact and has been approved in accordance with the Danish Health Act §46.2 and 5, EMN-2025-04765. Data handling complies with GDPR regulations and the project is registered at the institutional registry for research projects, p-2025-19418 Timeline Protocol and approvals: March–August 2025 Data extraction: September–January 2026 Analysis: February 2026 Manuscript preparation: February - June 2026 Publication Plan Results will be published open access. Authorship follows ICMJE guidelines.

title: Vision-Related Quality of Life Measured by NEI-VFQ-25 in Age-Related Macular Degeneration: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
description: Among many conditions that can lead to legal blindness, Age-related Macular Degeneration (AMD) is one of the most prevalent causes. As the world's population continue to age due to improved life expectancy in developed countries, the health and socioeconomic impact of AMD will only become more pronounced as its prevalence continues to increase. There are two different types of AMD, and both involve the Macula, a part of the eye which is integral to central vision. Dry AMD develops as the Macula gradually thins and small yellow deposits called drusen accumulate under the retina. Wet AMD develops as abnormal blood vessels grows in the retina, which frequently leak out fluids and blood. Both versions of the condition can severely disrupt one's vision and make it much harder to perform daily tasks such as reading, driving, cooking and shopping. Understanding precisely how AMD impacts the quality of life (QoL) of patients is key to providing proper care for them. To quantify this, the National Eye Institute Visual Functioning Questionnaire (NEI-VFQ-25) was developed to measure QoL in patients with disrupted vision, including those with AMD. Many individual studies exist on the subject within the literature, but there has been no systematic review that uses a meta-analysis to examine all the available evidence. A meta-analysis of this nature can elucidate the specific areas of QoL that is impacted by AMD, as well as how these can change across different subgroups within the population of AMD patients. This information will help healthcare providers understand how to best support patients with AMD based on the type of AMD they have as well as other factors, which can help save healthcare resources. This review aims to evaluate how AMD impacts the QoL of its patients, as well as how this varies across subgroups within the patient population.

title: Association Between Glaucoma and Alzheimer's Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Vascular, Genetic, and Epidemiological Risk Factors
description: This project is a systematic review and meta-analysis examining the association between glaucoma and Alzheimer's disease (AD) or dementia, with a focus on identifying shared vascular, genetic, and epidemiological risk factors. Previous studies have reported a potential link between these two chronic neurodegenerative conditions, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. While earlier meta-analyses have explored the general association, few have systematically examined how specific comorbidities (e.g., hypertension, diabetes), genetic profiles (e.g., APOE4), or demographic variables (e.g., race, sex) might influence this relationship. This review will update and expand the evidence base by analyzing observational studies published between January 2010 and December 2024. Eligible studies include cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs that report on glaucoma and Alzheimer's/dementia outcomes with effect estimates (e.g., OR, RR, HR). Subgroup and sensitivity analyses will explore whether risk factor stratification modifies the strength of association between the two conditions. The GRADE framework will be used to assess the confidence in cumulative evidence. This work aims to inform our understanding of potential shared pathophysiological pathways between glaucoma and Alzheimer's disease, clarify risk modifiers, and explore whether glaucoma could serve as a predictive marker or comorbid condition in neurodegenerative disease progression. Findings will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal in neurology, ophthalmology, or epidemiology, and may be presented at academic conferences such as ARVO or AAIC. This review is supported by the Medical Student Academic Fellowship (MSAF) at New York Medical College, which had no role in protocol design or decision to register the project. The lead author and guarantor of the review is Jade Suwanwanitch.

title: Edema-like symptoms are common in ultra-distance cyclists and driven by overdrinking, use of analgesics and female sex – a study of 919 athletes
description: Background: Ultra-endurance cyclists regularly report various extents of bodily decline during long-distance bicycle rides, including potential kidney function-related symptoms such as swelling of body parts and urine changes. This study aimed to assess the prevalence of these symptoms in a representative cohort of ultraendurance cyclists and shed light on potential predictors related to the ride, the rider and the rider's behavior. Methods: Between November 26 and December 14, 2020, 1350 people participated in an online survey investigating potential kidney-related symptoms of ultra-distance cycling. Frequency and severity of edema-like ("swelling") symptoms and perceived changes in urine output, concentration and quality were associated with ride-related factors, demographic parameters and rider behavior-related variables. Results: A total of 919 participants met the predefined inclusion criteria. The majority (N = 602, 65.5%) stated that they suffered from at least one potential kidney function-related symptom, out of which 498 (54.2%) stated one or more edema-like ("swelling") symptoms. In correlational and multiple regression analyses, female sex, intake of analgesics and drinking strategies correlated with swelling symptoms. Further analyses indicated that drinking due to thirst and/or drinking adapted to ambient sweating and temperature negatively correlated with swelling symptoms, whereas "drinking as much as possible" enhanced these. Intake of analgesics was moderately positively correlated with swelling symptoms. Conclusions: According to our survey, edema-like symptoms occur in the majority of ultra-distance cyclists and female sex, drinking strategy and intake of analgesic drugs are major predictors thereof. Studies are needed to investigate the underlying pathophysiological processes of such symptoms

Achados clínicos (antecedentes pessoais, hábitos de vida, adesão ao regime terapêutico) e angiográficos (características angiográficas prévias e resultados imediatos da angioplastia) nortearam alta precoce, de forma sistemática e segura. Conclusão: Características do paciente e achados clínicos possibilitam a seleção destes como baixo risco, e aptos a alta hospitalar precoce. Além de efetiva, esta prática beneficia tanto o paciente, com menores taxas de infecções e maior satisfação, como a instituição, promovendo melhor gestão de leitos e diminuição dos custos hospitalares.

title: Consciousness-related interactions in a double-slit optical interferometer
description: Motivated by a series of reported experiments and their controversial results, the present work investigated if volunteers could causally affect an optical double-slit system through mental efforts alone. The participants' task alternated between intending the increase of the (real-time feedback informed) amount of light diffracted through a specific single slit and relaxing any intention effort. The 160 data sessions that 127 volunteers took part in revealed a statistically significant 4.68 sigma difference between the measurements performed in the intention versus the relax conditions ($p=2.93\times10^{-6}; \, es= 0.47 \pm 0.20$ 95\% CL), while the 160 control sessions conducted without any observers present resulted in statistically equivalent samples ($z=0.35, \, p=0.73; \, es=0.04 \pm 0.20$ 95\% CL). The results could not be explained by environmental factors, hence supporting the previously claimed existence of a not yet understood form of interaction between a conscious agent and a physical system.

This variable captured the degree of overconfidence displayed across a wide range of domains and elicitations. In the third wave of data collection, we will measure additional variables and make hypotheses both about their relation to eachother, and to these two measures of core OC from extant data. Recruitment N = 447 participants from the platform MTurk completed the first two waves of data collection. All 447 of these participants will be invited back to complete the third wave. The sample size will be as many as return. Participants will be offered $2.50 to complete a 12 minute survey. Design In order to enter the survey, participants must pass a comprehension check item. If they fail this comprehension check, they will be excluded prior to random assignment and no data will be collected. Upon entering the survey, participants will be randomly assigned to an order condition. This will take one of two values ("OCT_first", "OCT_last"). In the condition OCT_first, participants will first answer the three items of the OCT, before responding to a series of individual difference measures. In condition OCT_last, participants will first answer a series of individual difference measures before later answering the items from the OCT. In both cases, the last thing participants will do is provide demographic information. All participants will provide responses to eight individual difference measures. Six of these pertain to cognitive styles; intellectual humility scale (Leary et al., 2017), need for closure decisiveness facet (Kruglanski et al., 1993), need for closure closed mindedness facet (Kruglanski et al., 1993), the Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT; Frederick, 2005), the Berlin Numeracy Test (BNT; Cokely et al., 2012), and a measure of actively open-minded thinking (Baron, 2019). Two of these pertain to self-view / personality variables; the dominance facet of extraversion (Wiggins et al., 1988), and a dark triad measure that contains narcissism, psychopathy, and Machiavellianism (Jones & Paulhus, 2014). The demographic information we will collect is participants' age, gender, education, race, and ethnicity. Measures The key measures / variables in the study are: - Core OC time 1 - Core OC time 2 - OCT time 3 (computed by averaging the three items oci1-oci3) - Scale variables time 3 (10 different measures total as Dark Triad has three facets; all aggregated according to their specified coding schemes) Hypotheses 1) OCT at time 3 will predict core OC at time 1 2) OCT at time 3 will predict core OC at time 2 3) Core OC (at time 1, 2) will be related with scales (at time 3) that capture both cognitive style and self-view 4) OCT at time 3 will be related with scales at time 3 that capture both cognitive style and self-view 5) OCT at time 3 will be related with scales at time 3 whether it is asked before or after them Analyses These analyses are merely a series of correlations. Hypotheses 1-4 can be tested with a large correlation table among the variables; core OC time 1, core OC time 2, OCT at time 3, scales at time 3. The fifth hypothesis can be investigated by inspecting the correlations between OCT and the scales separately for each order condition. If there appears to be a material difference, we can test the regression: scale ~ OCT*order. A significant interaction term would indicate that the correlation did vary by order. Interpretations If OCT is associated with core OC in time 1 and 2 we take this to convey that it measures the same, stable construct. We trialed OCT-type items in the earlier waves of data collection, but given these were administered at the end of experimental sessions that asked about overconfidence, it was possible that their validity was contaminated by the rest of the experiment. In this test, we ask no other items regarding overconfidence, and so if OCT is still related with the earlier measures of core OC, we take this as strong evidence of its validity as a measure. The reason why we counterbalance the order of presentation of OCT and the individual difference (ID) measures follows a similar rationale about contamination. Suppose answering a series of IDs might create a mindset that causes OCT to move in line with the IDs. Then administering OCT prior to the IDs might quash any relationship between the two. It is harder to argue that answering the three short items from the OCT will create a mindset that leads the IDs to follow (particularly when these are all well-established, stable, individual difference variables). One solution to this would be just to ask OCT first to everyone, but counterbalancing allows us to identify if this type of contamination is a concern at all.

title: EEG electric field topography is stable during moments of high field strength
description: Spontaneous broadband electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrates short moments of stability in the spatial distribution of the head-surface voltage topography. This phenomenon underlies the premise behind the segmentation of multichannel EEG into topographically defined brain states, known as EEG microstates. Microstate segmentation methods commonly identify representative topographical configurations based on clustering applied to a subset of voltage maps selected at the time series points of greatest strength in the neuroelectric field. These moments are well-reasoned to best represent periods of quasi-stability, and consequently, points of greatest signal relative to noise. Yet, more direct empirical evidence for these assumptions is valuable, and the consistency of this phenomenon across individuals has not been characterized. In the present investigation, the association between electric field strength and topographic dissimilarity of temporally adjacent samples of EEG was characterized in a large sample of healthy adults. Every individual demonstrated that samples of their EEG time series high in electric field strength were topographically similar relative to adjacent time series samples. The strong activity of phase-synchronized neuronal populations therefore coincide with periods of topographic stability, providing robust empirical support for the basic premise underlying segmentation of broadband EEG into microstates.

description: This is a data depository for Rich, T. & Palmer, J. (2021). Spatial and Attentional Contributions to Peripheral and Foveal Word Recognition in Patients with Neglect Dyslexia. Submitted for publication. Abstract Many patients with right hemisphere stroke fail to read words closest to the left margin of text and/or commit within-word errors on left-sided letters while correctly reporting right-sided letters, a condition known as neglect dyslexia. These patients also show non-spatial deficits of selective attention, which might be a contributing factor to these errors. The purpose of this study was to determine the relative contributions of spatial processing deficits and selective attention deficits on word recognition errors in neglect dyslexia. In Experiment 1, we replicated studies that showed poorer accuracy for target words when presented alongside a competitive distractor word than when presented solitarily. The effect of a distractor word was larger for target words on the left. In Experiment 2, we modified the paradigm so that the target word was positioned centrally at fixation in all conditions, in an effort to minimize spatial effects. Patients performed worse under conditions with a distractor word regardless of the side on which the distractor was presented. These findings are consistent with the errors in neglect dyslexia being at least partly due to a selective attention deficit.

title: The 2024 International Expert Panel's Extensive List of Potentially Inappropriate Prescribing Cascades for Older Adults
description: A prescribing cascade occurs when an individual is started on a drug therapy, which then causes an adverse drug event that is generally not recognized and mistaken for a new medical condition, and a further drug therapy is initiated to manage this new medical condition. Prescribing cascades are known to affect individuals across all age groups but can be especially problematic for older adults who are more likely to be prescribed multiple medications to manage chronic conditions. The study is focused on identifying potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades. An example of a potentially inappropriate prescribing cascade occurs when an older adult is started on a calcium-channel blockers (Drug A), then subsequently develops peripheral edema (adverse drug event) that is then misinterpreted as a new medical condition, and a diuretic (Drug B) is started to treat this adverse drug event. In this case, recognizing the peripheral edema symptoms as a side effect of the calcium-channel blockers (Drug A) and not a new medical condition, provides an opportunity for the calcium channel blockers to be re-evaluated and, in some cases, discontinued or dose modified. Further, by recognizing that the adverse drug event of peripheral edema is related to Drug A, the diuretics (Drug B) could also be re-evaluated and, in some cases, discontinued. The list, although created for research purposes, can be used to inform, and alert clinicians of potentially inappropriate prescribing cascades which can then be further explored in clinical practice and tailored the specific need of the individual.

title: Where to flee? Exploring household-level destination choices during displacement in the Kasai, DRC
description: Displacement, especially in developing countries, is on the rise. But where do displaced persons seek shelter when fleeing from violence? Based on existing literature, we develop a framework to understand household-level destination choices during forced displacement in developing countries. Conditional on being a safe location, we argue that not only the ability to gain livelihoods matters. Forcibly displaced populations also care about embeddedness in social, cultural and relational networks when choosing their host communities. Additionally, they want to politically integrate into community life and demand agency. Empirically, we study the choice of refuge for internally displaced persons, refugees and host community members in the Kasai, DRC, with a conjoint experiment. The study contributes household level evidence on destination choices in developing contexts and speaks to the literature on the integration of displaced populations in host communities. This registration presents the study's motivation and hypotheses. The survey instrument accompanies this document.

title: Novel intraoperative technologies in parathyroid identification and preservation – a scoping systematic review
description: The parathyroid glands are at risk of injury during thyroid, parathyroid and other central compartment neck surgery. Accidental removal or devascularisation of the glands can lead to hypocalcaemia and potentially a need for lifelong calcium supplementation. Traditional approaches to parathyroid preservation include meticulous surgical technique to identify, separate, and preserve the parathyroid glands. However, up to 23.5% of patients experience transient hypocalcaemia after thyroidectomy, and 3.6% remain on calcium supplements at 6 months (1). At parathyroid surgery, inability or difficulty in identifying abnormal parathyroid glands and differentiating them from thyroid nodules, lymph nodes and brown adipose tissue is a cause of failure to cure hyperparathyroidism. This may lead to extensive exploration and potentially damage to normal parathyroid glands. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in intraoperative techniques that can improve parathyroid identification and preservation. These can be divided into optical techniques, such as autofluorescence, and non-optical techniques such as intraoperative PTH sampling (2). There have been increasing numbers of observational studies, but there remain relatively few good quality comparative trials to determine which of these techniques may have the greatest potential. There are also many techniques in the early stages of development that show promise but require further investigation. References: 1. title: Artificial Intelligence and Deep Learning in Ophthalmology Education: A Scoping Review on Clinical Reasoning and Competence.
description: Ophthalmology is a medical specialty based on visual skills, where diagnosis and therapeutic planning depend on expert interpretation of multiple image modalities combined with clinical and functional data such as visual data (1,2). The core competency of medical students or residents is the coherent clinical reasoning by identifying subtle alterations in the retina, optic nerve or anterior segment, which is difficult to accomplish, largely because education continues to rely on opportunistic patient exposure, case variability, and the limited time available for specialists to supervise and provide feedback on performance (3,4,5). Moreover, population aging and the increasing incidence of vision-threatening diseases (e.g., diabetic retinopathy, age-related macular degeneration (ARMD) and glaucoma) are generating an increasing demand for ophthalmologic care and straining traditional training systems, which are already considered insufficient, particularly in resource-limited regions (3,1,6). In this context, the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) for the automated analysis of medical images is one of the most significant technological transformations in contemporary medicine, and ophthalmology is positioned among the specialties best suited to benefit from these advances (2,7,8). To date, most applications of AI and DL in ophthalmology have been oriented towards automated clinical diagnosis and risk stratification, with particular emphasis on diabetic retinopathy screening, detection of ARMD, and identification of glaucomatous optic neuropathy from fundus photographs and OCT (1,2,9). Currently, emerging studies explore these AI capabilities in educational contexts, such as AI-assisted tutoring platforms, retinopathy reading and labelling systems, and algorithms for the identification of multiple fundus diseases or myopia, which improve performance and understanding compared with traditional teaching methods, enable residents and students to train in lesion grading with immediate feedback and personalize residency training experiences according to case history (11,12,13, 14). Furthermore, virtual reality and augmented reality simulators combined with intelligent tutoring systems have shown objective improvements in microsurgical skills, whereas interactive machine learning platforms, such as fundus image interpretation systems, allow trainees to compare their markings against algorithm outputs and practice with substantial case variability (5,15,16). More recently, synthetic images have been generated through generative models of different pathologies, as well as the use of large language models (LLMs) to create clinical cases and examination questions, further expanding the repertoire of potentially available didactic resources (17,18,19,20). Against this backdrop, the development of clinical reasoning and diagnostic criteria has become a critical competency for these physicians. Clinical reasoning may be understood as the process by which the clinician integrates the clinical history, physical examination and complementary tests to generate, contrast and refine diagnostic hypotheses and therapeutic decisions (21,22). Recent literature on ophthalmology education underscores that one of the essential training objectives is to cultivate accurate and adaptive diagnostic reasoning and describes how AI-based diagnostic decision support systems and simulation platforms are beginning to be utilized as "virtual mentors" that provide visual explanations, saliency maps, step-by-step feedback, and exposure to diverse virtual cases, in order to help learners internalize expert decision-making patterns (3,21). Concurrently, the emergence of LLMs has renewed interest in modelling clinical thinking (22,23). However, this sparks a critical pedagogical debate: while AI can serve as a scaffold for reasoning, concerns persist regarding algorithmic opacity ("black box"), bias, and the risk of fostering technological dependence or "deskilling" (3,1,24,25,26). There has been clear evidence of the impact of AI in ophthalmic education (27,28); however, most studies prioritize algorithmic performance metrics or exam passages over actual pedagogical outcomes, failing to address how these tools modify learners' reasoning processes. This highlights a critical knowledge gap that justifies this review; the existing literature focuses predominantly on the technical performance of algorithms, leaving their real pedagogical impact largely unexplored. Consequently, a scoping review is needed to move beyond engineering metrics and systematically map the existing evidence regarding the implementation strategies of AI and DL aimed at enhancing medical education within the field of ophthalmology.

description: ReVis-MD is an interdisciplinary project aimed at better understanding functional adaptation following the onset of scotoma in patients with macular degeneration (MD). By combining ophthalmological, psychophysical, neural (fMRI), and neuro-computational (artificial neural networks) approaches, the project pursues two main objectives. The first is to characterize the cortical reorganizations occurring in patients and how these changes impact their visuo-cognitive abilities, such as scene processing, compared to an age-matched control group with an artificial central scotoma. The second objective is to assess whether these adaptations can be enhanced through perceptual learning and cognitive retraining strategies, potentially paving the way for future rehabilitation programs. The project is funded by the ANR (Project ANR-21-CE28-0021) and involves a partnership between the CERCO laboratory (CNRS UMR 5549, Toulouse; PI: Benoît Cottereau, CNRS Research Director) and the LPNC laboratory (CNRS UMR 5105, Grenoble; responsible: Carole Peyrin, CNRS Research Director).

description: we propose a conceptual wearable device, the Optical Sonar, which converts spatial structural information of surroundings to spatial audio. And then a prototype was made to extract key spatial information from the depth video stream and convert it to spatial sound clips in real-time, employing a carefully designed sonification scheme. This system is tested in an indoor experiment with 20 blindfolded volunteer participants, and the performance was compared with other spatial awareness aids including white cane and echolocation in terms of accuracy and efficiency. In addition, the learning curve of our method is far flatter than that of echolocation. The innovation of this study is to map the spatial information of vision to spatial sound through Head Related Transfer Function (HRTF) to help visually impaired people understand space in a more intuitive way. Our study enriches the attempts of visual-to-auditory mapping algorithms, and takes a promising step in enabling the visually impaired to perceive the space around them through hearing.

ABSTRACT It is a scope review with the purpose of analyzing the prevalence and associated factors of diabetic retinopathy in adults living with diabetes type 1 or 2 in Latin America, like some reviews done in other regions of the planet. The primary objective of this study is to identify and synthesize the scientific evidence of diabetic retinopathy and its associated factors published in Latin American countries. This review has been conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) Statement and the method of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) for quality evaluation of the included articles. The search for full articles published between the year 2000 and 2021 in English, Portuguese or Spanish was carried out in the databases: Medline/Pubmed, Biblioteca Virtual em Saúde (BVS) and EMBASE. Two reviewers independently will screen the studies and select them based on the titles and abstract. Subsequently, the reviewers will independently read the pre-selected articles in full. Two independent reviewers, using a structured instrument, designed for this study, will carry out the extraction and synthesis of the essential elements found in each study. Descriptors: Diabetic Retinopathy; Risk Factors; Latin America; South America; Central America. 4. INTRODUCTION The prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM) has been increasing worldwide, increasing the risk of its complications. Chronic hyperglycemia can result in damage to various organs, compromising quality of life, high health expenditures and increased mortality. Among the various changes that diabetes can cause to eye tissues, the best known and with the greatest potential for compromising vision is diabetic retinopathy (DR), the main cause of blindness in people of working age. Retinopathy results from complex inflammatory and immunological phenomena that lead to damage to the small vessels of the retina (1, 2). The prevalence of DR varies between studies and regions of the world. Klein (2007) estimates that 34.6% of diabetic patients over 40 years of age have diabetic retinopathy. According to the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB) Vision Atlas, 103 million people worldwide (22.3% of those living with DM) have some degree of diabetic retinopathy (3). The Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) found a DR prevalence of 17% after 5 years and 98% after 15 years of DM diagnosis in people who were diagnosed under 30 years of age and 29% and 78%, respectively, in those in which the diagnosis was made after 30 years of age (4). Early detection and treatment can prevent the progression of retinopathy and visual impairment. Treatment varies depending on the severity of the retinopathy and can prevent severe visual loss in up to 90% of cases. Values of 7% or less of glycated hemoglobin are recommended for most patients, although some may have additional benefits with a target of less than 6.5% (2, 5). Due to the possibility of reducing the rates of visual impairment caused by retinopathy in patients with DM through early detection and adequate glycemic control, associated with the increasing prevalence of diabetes worldwide, it is necessary to know about the prevalence and associated factors of diabetic retinopathy in Latin America. This scoping review with meta-analysis aims to fill a gap between public policy makers and health workers with an emphasis on preventing and reducing blindness among people with diabetes. 5. METHODS This scoping review with has been developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) Statement (6) and the method of the Joanna Briggs Institute (7) for quality evaluation of the included articles and will be registered in the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io). The review method follows five steps: 1) identification of the research question; 2) identification of relevant studies; 3) selection of studies; 4) data analysis; and, 5) grouping, synthesis and presentation of data. Observational studies published in Latin American countries between the years 2000 and 2021, in Portuguese, English or Spanish, whose participants were adults diagnosed with type I or II DM and that evaluated the prevalence and/or risk factors of diabetic retinopathy were included. Exclusion criteria were: studies that addressed non-modifiable (genetic/biochemical) risk factors for diabetic retinopathy, those whose participants were only patients already diagnosed with diabetic retinopathy, clinical studies, animal studies, and review articles. Database and search strategy The bibliographic searches were carried out in the Medline/Pubmed, Virtual Health Library (BVS) and EMBASE in June 2020, through a comprehensive search for titles and abstracts carried out by independent researchers. The terms referring to diabetic retinopathy, Latin American countries and epidemiological measures were used in the searches, combined using the Boolean operators "and" and "or". The selection of the filter for Latin American countries was applied in the search in the VHL database. More details can be found in the supplementary material (Table 1). Study selection and data extraction After excluding duplicate works within and between different bibliographic databases, the remaining titles and abstracts were independently peer-reviewed by four reviewers to identify articles potentially eligible for full reading. Qualitative and quantitative syntheses included studies that met all inclusion criteria. In cases of divergence, consensus was reached through discussion between the evaluators. Two reviewers independently extracted details from included studies using a predefined form. Extracted data include: first author, year of publication, study design (cohort or cross-sectional), country studied, sample size, mean age, race, sex (male or female), DM classification (DM1 or DM2), prevalence observed in percentage and confidence interval (95% CI), definition of significant risk factor, Odds Ratio (OR), 95% CI and p-value. Gut–spine axis hypotheses suggest that dysbiosis and microbiome-derived metabolites/inflammation may influence disc health. Individual studies report altered alpha/beta diversity and differential taxa in Intervertebral disc degeneration, but findings are inconsistent. A synthesis is needed to quantify differences and explore methodological sources of heterogeneity. Despite advances in imaging and biomechanics, the pathogenesis of IVDD remains only partially understood, with increasing attention now directed toward systemic biological factors. Emerging evidence suggests that the gut microbiome—through immune modulation, metabolic signaling, and systemic inflammation—may play a key role in musculoskeletal health, including spinal degeneration. title: Age-Specific Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Cut-Off Values for Detecting Raised Intracranial Pressure in Children: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This study aims to systematically evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and age-specific cut-off values of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measured using ultrasonography for detecting raised intracranial pressure (ICP) in pediatric populations. Raised ICP is a critical condition in children with neurological disorders, including traumatic brain injury, hydrocephalus, infections, and intracranial tumors. Non-invasive bedside techniques such as ONSD ultrasonography have gained increasing attention as potential screening tools for early ICP detection. A systematic review and diagnostic meta-analysis were conducted following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Multiple electronic databases were searched to identify relevant studies evaluating ONSD as a diagnostic marker for raised ICP in children. Eligible studies included pediatric participants aged 0–18 years and reported diagnostic accuracy data comparing ONSD measurements with reference standards such as invasive intracranial pressure monitoring, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or lumbar puncture. Data extracted from included studies comprised study characteristics, participant demographics, diagnostic thresholds, and diagnostic accuracy parameters including sensitivity, specificity, true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. A hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) model and random-effects meta-analysis were used to estimate pooled diagnostic accuracy. The study also explores age-specific variations in ONSD cut-off values across pediatric age groups. The findings aim to support clinical decision-making and provide evidence for the use of ONSD ultrasonography as a non-invasive screening tool for raised intracranial pressure in children.

title: Uncomfortable staring? Social modulation of attention in infants compared to adults
description: In non-social situations, adults are fascinated by other people and preferentially process social information (Dunbar, 1998, 2003). However, once they find themselves in a social situation (e.g. in a waiting room), people would avoid directly looking at strangers' faces (Foulsham, Walker, & Kingstone, 2011; Laidlaw, Foulsham, Kuhn, & Kingstone, 2011). This phenomenon of social inhibition of gaze has reliably been demonstrated in adults. However, it is unclear how it develops with age. In infants, control of gaze in social situations is lacking, as they still stare at objects falling within their visual field, have difficulties to disengage from faces (e.g. when two objects are competing for attention compared to non-competition) and little fine-grained control of their gaze (Atkinson, Hood, Wattam-Bell, & Braddick, 1992; Hood & Atkinson, 1993; Johnson, Posner, & Rothbart, 1991; Kulke, Atkinson, & Braddick, 2015). Comparisons of live and videotaped social stimuli show that infants still look longer at live humans at 9 months of age (Diener, Pierroutsakos, Troseth, & Roberts, 2008), while adults seem to look longer at videotaped than live humans (Laidlaw et al., 2011), inhibiting gaze at others in social situations. However, no direct comparison has been conducted of gaze in social and non-social situations in infants. The current study aims to fill this gap by investigating gaze at a life confederate compared to a video of a confederate in a waiting room paradigm in infants between 3 and 6 months of age and adults and relating it to attention shifts under competition compared to non-competition measured using the Fixation Shift Paradigm.

title: The Current Status of OCT and OCTA Imaging for the Diagnosis of Long COVID
description: This systematic review explores the potential of optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in diagnosing long COVID. Long term effects of the COVID-19 disease could impact the microvascular system, which can be visualized directly through changes in vessel density and foveal avascular zone in OCTA and indirectly in the form of retinal layer thicknesses in OCT. This review shows a summarized comparison of all 24 topic-related clinical studies of adult participants, collected in the database PubMed and, with the AI research assistant Elicit published in the period between February 2021 and March 2024. Studies with participant groups of patients with active COVID-19, recovered participants and participants with ongoing symptoms were included. During the various stages of COVID-19, retinal changes could be observed, but a comparison between long COVID and recovered cohorts was aggravated by diverse inclusion and exclusion criteria as well as small sample sizes. Changes in long COVID were seen in most OCT examinations as thinning or partial thinning of certain retinal layers, while in OCTA a consistently reduced vessel density was revealed.
