title: Scenes modulate object processing before interacting with memory templates
description: When searching for relevant objects in our environment (say, an apple) we create a memory template (a red sphere), which causes our visual system to favor template-matching visual input (apple-like objects) at the expense of template-mismatching visual input (e.g., leaves). While this principle seems straightforward in a lab-setting, it poses a problem in naturalistic viewing: Two objects that produce the same size on the retina will differ in real-world size if one is nearby and the other is far away. Using the Ponzo illusion to manipulate perceived size while keeping retinal size constant, we demonstrate (across 71 subjects) that visual objects attract attention when their perceived size matches a memory template, compared to mismatching objects that encompass the same size on the retina. This shows that memory templates impact visual selection after object representations are modulated by scene context, thus providing a working mechanism for template-based search in naturalistic vision.

title: Ocular Toxoplasmosis Reactivation Following Intraocular Interventions: A Scoping Review
description: Ocular toxoplasmosis (OT) remains a significant global health concern as the leading cause of infectious posterior uveitis, frequently resulting in permanent visual impairment due to its high and unpredictable recurrence rates. While various risk factors for reactivation are well-established, the specific role of intraocular interventions—ranging from phacoemulsification and pars plana vitrectomy to intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF or corticosteroids—as potential triggers for disease recurrence is not yet fully understood. Currently, the ophthalmic community lacks standardized evidence-based guidelines regarding the perioperative management of these patients, leading to significant variability in clinical practice, particularly concerning the use and timing of prophylactic antitoxoplasmic therapy. This clinical uncertainty is further complicated by the phenomenon of subclinical or peripheral retinochoroidal scars that may go undetected during routine pre-operative fundoscopic assessments, only to reactivate following the inflammatory stimulus or mechanical trauma associated with a procedure. The primary purpose of this research project is to conduct a scoping review, following the rigorous methodology established by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), to systematically map and characterize the available evidence surrounding OT reactivation in the context of intraocular interventions. This review defines reactivation as the development of active lesions regardless of whether the underlying scar was known prior to the intervention or identified postoperatively. By synthesizing data from both retrospective studies and a predominant body of case reports, this project seeks to define the typical clinical presentation and temporal onset of post-procedural reactivation. A key objective of this work is to explore the differences in outcomes and reporting between patients with a known history of OT and those identified as having silent scars only after a postoperative event occurs. The expected outcomes of this scoping review include a comprehensive categorization of the types of procedures most frequently associated with reactivation and a detailed analysis of both patient-related and procedure-related factors described as potential triggers. Furthermore, the review will provide a summary of the various prophylactic and therapeutic regimens currently reported in the literature, revealing the degree of heterogeneity in global practices. By identifying the limitations within the existing evidence base, this project will highlight critical knowledge gaps that prevent the formation of a clinical consensus. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a foundational evidence map that can inform better pre-operative screening protocols, guide perioperative therapeutic decisions, and establish the necessary parameters for future prospective research into the prevention of ocular toxoplasmosis reactivation.

title: Observer Physiological State as an Uncontrolled Variable in Attention-Modulated Double-Slit Experiments: A Preregistration-Ready Protocol
description: A contentious experimental literature claims correlations between observer attention and interference pattern characteristics in double-slit optical systems. Independent replication attempts have identified serious methodological concerns, including false-positive rates of 50% in sham conditions and sensitivity to undisclosed analytical choices. This preregistered protocol proposes that observer physiological state—specifically cardiac coherence indexed by heart rate variability (HRV)—represents an uncontrolled variable contributing to inconsistent outcomes across studies. The design is a 2×2 between-subjects factorial crossing coherence level (high vs. low, induced via resonant vs. non-resonant paced breathing) with mental mode (analytical vs. non-analytical attention). All analytic decisions are fully locked prior to data collection: primary spectral method (AR Burg order 16), fringe visibility algorithm (Fourier-based V = 2A1/A0), coherence thresholds (CR > 0.70 high, CR < 0.30 low), and statistical model (linear mixed-effects with Bonferroni-corrected α = 0.025). The protocol integrates the Advanced Meta-Experimental Protocol (AMP) with sham blocks evaluated via cumulative z-scores at fixed intervals, pre-registered pass/fail criteria, and explicit decision rules for calibration failures. Physical negative controls (single-slit, beam-blocked configurations) further strengthen artifact detection. This mechanism-agnostic framework explicitly proposes no physical mechanism by which cardiac activity could influence quantum systems. The win-win epistemic structure ensures valuable scientific contribution regardless of outcome: positive results identify a previously unrecognized moderating variable; null results eliminate observer physiological state as a confound and constrain future theorizing. Sample size: N = 320 (80 per cell) plus pilot N = 40 (excluded from confirmatory analysis). Primary hypothesis test: Coherence × Attention interaction (β4) at α = 0.025.

title: Uniforms Image Coding
description: In this project, we investigate how work uniforms support the recognition of people in everyday roles. To study this, we are looking at familiar occupations in the United States and how the prevalence of uniforms in those occupations is related to the need to be recognized by others. As part of that project, we've developed an image coding procedure to estimate the prevalence of uniforms for certain occupations and some features of those uniforms. We have selected 50 occupations from the Bureau of Labor Statistics occupation categories which people in the US rated highly in familiarity. For each of those 50 occupations, we selected images from the internet of people in those occupations which will be coded by research assistants for uniform prevalence and other features of uniforming. For each of the 50 occupations, 10 images were selected using Google Image search. The search was conducted from a New Haven, CT IP address on a private window of the Mozilla Firefox browser with strict search and privacy settings to minimize user-specific bias in search results. Each search includes screenshot of the date and time the search was conducted, search term, and top results yielded by that page. The first 10 photos which met the following criteria were selected: contains at least one actual person whose head and outfit are not totally occluded, is not covered in text, is not a duplicate (or near duplicate, for example same individual in the same attire), is not a collage. If a search term mostly yields irrelevant images, we will add "(occupation)" to the search term (ex. "teller" mostly returned the magician named Teller). This was done for the following terms: teller, receptionist, painter, translator. In each image, one person was selected to be coded. For any image with more than one person in the occupation, the largest of those people was selected. If more than one person are close to the largest, we used a random number generator to select one of these people ordered from left to right. Coders are instructed to rate the following features of the selected person's appearance for each image: - General Uniform: Is someone wearing a uniform? 0/1 (no/yes) - Equipment Uniform: How many of the objects or items this person is wearing are physically-necessary for doing the job? 0+ (positive integer) - Non-equipment Uniform: After you take away the equipment, are they still wearing a uniform? 0/1 (no/yes) - Social Uniform: Consider all the items/articles which make up the uniform. How much could you change these items/articles (e.g., in color, material, style, etc) without affecting their ability to do their job? This is assuming everyone in society is familiar with and recognizes the changes to the uniform. 0-10 In addition, coders rate the following feature across all 10 images for each occupation: - Standardization: How similarly are the people are dressed across those 10 images? 0-10 Two research assistants were familiarized with the full coding scheme and trained on 10 separate occupations not used in the main set. These research assistants will independently code the above measures for all 50 occupations. We will correlate coders responses along continuous measures and percentage agreement for binary measures to verify inter-rater reliability. Disagreements will then be resolved by a third researcher to create the final ratings dataset. The full coding scheme and all test images are attached in this preregistration.

title: Study 2: Neural basis of violation-of-expectation in intuitive physics and intuitive psychology
description: **IMPORTANT**: This registration constitutes one original pre-registration from Oct 2022, and then two further updates in Dec 2022. Because of an OSF technical issue, none of these registrations archived properly. OSF's support team retracted this registration and asked us to submit them again. We uploaded pre-registration documents, including the updates, to OSF storage in Oct and Dec 2022, and these documents detail the status of data collection at each stage. The most up to data version of the document can be found at https://osf.io/ktq53. 1. Background Why do babies look longer when an object floats in midair, or someone behaves inefficiently (Baillargeon et al., 1985; Needham & Baillargeon, 1993; Spelke et al., 1992; Woodward, 1998) during violation-of-expectation (VOE) studies? In this project, we test two non-mutually exclusive hypotheses: H1: VOE stimuli evoke domain-general processes, like visual prediction error and endogenous curiosity. These surprising events may have distinct visual features, either guided by top-down predictions from intuitive theories (e.g. I expected to see the ball falling, and yet I see it floating) or by virtue of bottom-up stimulus features that are not specific to agents or objects (Haith, 1998; Rivera et al., 1999; Sirois & Jackson, 2012). These events may also evoke curiosity and motivation to explore and explain the source of surprise (Perez & Feigenson, 2022; Raz & Saxe, 2020; Sim & Xu, 2018; Stahl & Feigenson, 2015). H2: VOE stimuli also evoke domain-specific responses, as violations of specific expectations related to psychology and physics. A second hypothesis is that these events violate infants' domain-specific expectations about the physical and psychological world (Carey, 2009; Gergely & Csibra, 2003; Spelke & Kinzler, 2007). These hypotheses are associated with distinct patterns of activity, in distinct neural regions. Broadly, the domain-general hypothesis (H1) predicts greater responses to unexpected than expected events, in perceptual and multiple demand regions, that generalize across domains. The domain-specific hypothesis (H2) predicts greater responses to unexpected events in different regions, depending on the domain (supramarginal gyrus for physics, superior temporal sulcus for psychology).

title: Non-invasive indices of MASLD and diabetic microvascular complications in patients with type 2 diabetes: a population-based cohort study
description: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) impacts more than 30% of the adult population and is associated with an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). Nevertheless, longitudinal data examining the association between the severity of MASLD and the occurrence of diabetic microvascular complications (DMC) are limited. The present study seeks to fill this knowledge gap by exploring the dose-response relationship between non-invasive MASLD indices and the risk of DMC among individuals with T2D, utilizing a large, population-based cohort. Methods: A total of 22,957 participants were sourced from the UK Biobank for analysis. Three non-invasive hepatic steatosis indices—Fatty Liver Index (FLI), Hepatic Steatosis Index (HSI), and Diabetes Steatosis Index (DSI)—were used to assess their dose-response relationships with DMC.DMC, defined as diabetic nephropathy, diabetic retinopathy, and diabetic neuropathy, was identified using hospital inpatient records and death registries. Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to evaluate the associations of frailty phenotype with overall DMC events and subtypes. Results: In this prospective cohort of 22,957 T2D patients followed for 13.7 years (median), 5,694 developed diabetic microvascular complications (DMC). Multivariable-adjusted analyses demonstrated robust associations between elevated MASLD indices and DMC risk, with FLI showing the strongest effects: participants in the highest FLI quintile (Q5 vs Q1) had 71% higher overall DMC risk (HR=1.71, 95% CI: 1.59–1.85; P<0.0001), specifically 106% increased nephropathy (HR=2.06, 1.74–2.44) and 239% increased neuropathy risk (HR=3.39, 2.44–4.71). Notably, no significant associations were observed between any MASLD indices and diabetic retinopathy. FLI also exhibited superior discriminative performance for DMC (C-statistics 0.68–0.71), significantly outperforming HSI and DSI. Restricted cubic splines confirmed nonlinear dose-response relationships for FLI and DSI (P-nonlinearity<0.0001). Stratified analyses showed that the associations between MASLD indices and overall DMC risk were consistent across subgroups defined by age, sex, physical activity, and most other baseline characteristics (all P for interaction > 0.05), except for modest interactions with HbA1c and Townsend deprivation index. Sensitivity analyses including competing risk models supported robustness. Conclusions: Our study reveals that non-invasive MASLD indices, such as FLI, HSI, and DSI, are strong predictors of diabetic microvascular complications (DMC) in T2D patients. These markers, reflecting hepatic steatosis, offer potential for early risk assessment. Future research combining imaging and multi-omics will help further elucidate the liver-metabolism link in DMC and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Topical diagnostic agents for identifying head and neck cancers of unknown primary: a systematic review across aerodigestive tract specialties
description: Topical contrast agents have been explored for decades as adjuncts in the detection of malignant and premalignant disease of the upper aerodigestive tract (UADT). Applied directly to the epithelium, these dyes enhance visual discrimination between normal and abnormal tissue, guide biopsy selection, and assist in delineating resection margins. Their appeal lies in their low cost, ease of application, and immediate visual feedback, making them suitable for both outpatient and intraoperative use. Agents trialled include non-fluorescent dyes such as toluidine blue (TB), Lugol's iodine (LI), methylene blue (MB), and acetic acid (AA). Fluorescent probes, most notably 5-aminolevulinic acid (5-ALA), allow fluorescence-guided assessment under specialised illumination. Despite widespread use, uptake has been uneven, with diagnostic performance varying by agent, method of application, and anatomical site. Concerns about false positives and specificity have limited broader acceptance. Newer optical imaging modalities, such as narrow-band imaging, autofluorescence, and chemiluminescence, are often promoted as alternatives. However, these require costly equipment and have shown variable accuracy, limiting uptake, particularly in low-resource settings. By contrast, topical dyes remain inexpensive, pragmatic tools that can augment mucosal assessment. The aim of this systematic review was to evaluate the diagnostic performance of topical dyes, both fluorescent and non-fluorescent, in the assessment of UADT lesions. Specifically, we examined their utility in detecting malignant and dysplastic change and in delineating surgical margins, with the goal of providing a comprehensive overview of their clinical value across subsites. To address this aim, we undertook a systematic literature search and critical appraisal of published studies, followed by quantitative and descriptive synthesis of the available evidence.

ABSTRACT It is a scope review with the purpose of analyzing the prevalence and associated factors of diabetic retinopathy in adults living with diabetes type 1 or 2 in Latin America, like some reviews done in other regions of the planet. The primary objective of this study is to identify and synthesize the scientific evidence of diabetic retinopathy and its associated factors published in Latin American countries. This review has been conducted according to Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) Statement and the method of the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) for quality evaluation of the included articles. The search for full articles published between the year 2000 and 2021 in English, Portuguese or Spanish was carried out in the databases: Medline/Pubmed, Biblioteca Virtual em Saúde (BVS) and EMBASE. Two reviewers independently will screen the studies and select them based on the titles and abstract. Subsequently, the reviewers will independently read the pre-selected articles in full. Two independent reviewers, using a structured instrument, designed for this study, will carry out the extraction and synthesis of the essential elements found in each study. Descriptors: Diabetic Retinopathy; Risk Factors; Latin America; South America; Central America. 4. INTRODUCTION The prevalence of diabetes mellitus (DM) has been increasing worldwide, increasing the risk of its complications. Chronic hyperglycemia can result in damage to various organs, compromising quality of life, high health expenditures and increased mortality. Among the various changes that diabetes can cause to eye tissues, the best known and with the greatest potential for compromising vision is diabetic retinopathy (DR), the main cause of blindness in people of working age. Retinopathy results from complex inflammatory and immunological phenomena that lead to damage to the small vessels of the retina (1, 2). The prevalence of DR varies between studies and regions of the world. Klein (2007) estimates that 34.6% of diabetic patients over 40 years of age have diabetic retinopathy. According to the International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness (IAPB) Vision Atlas, 103 million people worldwide (22.3% of those living with DM) have some degree of diabetic retinopathy (3). The Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) found a DR prevalence of 17% after 5 years and 98% after 15 years of DM diagnosis in people who were diagnosed under 30 years of age and 29% and 78%, respectively, in those in which the diagnosis was made after 30 years of age (4). Early detection and treatment can prevent the progression of retinopathy and visual impairment. Treatment varies depending on the severity of the retinopathy and can prevent severe visual loss in up to 90% of cases. Values of 7% or less of glycated hemoglobin are recommended for most patients, although some may have additional benefits with a target of less than 6.5% (2, 5). Due to the possibility of reducing the rates of visual impairment caused by retinopathy in patients with DM through early detection and adequate glycemic control, associated with the increasing prevalence of diabetes worldwide, it is necessary to know about the prevalence and associated factors of diabetic retinopathy in Latin America. This scoping review with meta-analysis aims to fill a gap between public policy makers and health workers with an emphasis on preventing and reducing blindness among people with diabetes. 5. METHODS This scoping review with meta-analysis has been developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) Statement (6) and the method of the Joanna Briggs Institute (7) for quality evaluation of the included articles and will be registered in the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io). The review method follows five steps: 1) identification of the research question; 2) identification of relevant studies; 3) selection of studies; 4) data analysis; and, 5) grouping, synthesis and presentation of data. Observational studies published in Latin American countries between the years 2000 and 2021, in Portuguese, English or Spanish, whose participants were adults diagnosed with type I or II DM and that evaluated the prevalence and/or risk factors of diabetic retinopathy were included. Exclusion criteria were: studies that addressed non-modifiable (genetic/biochemical) risk factors for diabetic retinopathy, those whose participants were only patients already diagnosed with diabetic retinopathy, clinical studies, animal studies, and review articles. Database and search strategy The bibliographic searches were carried out in the Medline/Pubmed, Virtual Health Library (BVS) and EMBASE in June 2020, through a comprehensive search for titles and abstracts carried out by independent researchers. The terms referring to diabetic retinopathy, Latin American countries and epidemiological measures were used in the searches, combined using the Boolean operators "and" and "or". The selection of the filter for Latin American countries was applied in the search in the VHL database. More details can be found in the supplementary material (Table 1). Study selection and data extraction After excluding duplicate works within and between different bibliographic databases, the remaining titles and abstracts were independently peer-reviewed by four reviewers to identify articles potentially eligible for full reading. Qualitative and quantitative syntheses included studies that met all inclusion criteria. In cases of divergence, consensus was reached through discussion between the evaluators. Two reviewers independently extracted details from included studies using a predefined form. title: Foveal sensitivities for target-congruent and target-incongruent orientation information during saccade preparation
description: The preparation of rapid eye movements (i.e. saccades) entails dynamic changes in visual sensitivity across the visual field. Pre-saccadic attention shifts and accompanying sensitivity enhancements at the saccade target have been studied extensively. At the same time, little is known about the development of visual sensitivity in the pre-saccadic center of gaze. Behavioral findings suggest that, just like at the saccade target, visual sensitivity increases at the pre-saccadic foveal location (e.g. Rolfs, Jonikaitis, Deubel, & Cavanagh, 2011; Szinte, Jonikaitis, Rangelov, & Deubel, 2018). This finding has been attributed to a predictive remapping mechanism that directs attention to the future retinal (i.e. foveal) location of the saccade target to provide a head start for post-saccadic processing. To date, however, it remains unclear if a transfer of activation between the saccade target's current and future retinal location involves a transfer of information about its features. Behavioral evidence in favor of feature remapping remains indirect (e.g. He, Fritsche, & de Lange, 2018): adaptation effects resulting from prolonged stimulus exposure have been shown to transfer between the foveal and target location during saccade preparation. Crucially however, direct behavioral evidence for a pre-saccadic transfer of feature information remains to be established. In an attempt to provide this evidence, we will measure observers' ability to detect an orientation-filtered pink noise patch (the probe; oriented -45° or 45°) in the pre-saccadic center of gaze while they are preparing an eye movement to a second orientation-filtered noise patch in the periphery (the target; oriented -45° or 45°). Probe and target will be smoothly embedded in full-screen pink noise images presented in quick alternation. If present, the orientation of the foveal probe will be either congruent or incongruent with the orientation of the saccade target. If feature information is transferred from the saccade target to the fovea during eye movement preparation, the target's orientation should interact with foveal orientation information and influence present/absent judgments.

title: Advanced Diagnostic Paradigms in Oral Oncology: A Comprehensive Scope Review of Innovations in Clinical and Technological Methodologies
description: O câncer bucal permanece um grave desafio para a saúde global, com a detecção precoce sendo essencial para melhorar as taxas de sobrevivência e a qualidade de vida dos pacientes. Métodos diagnósticos tradicionais, como a biópsia tecidual, embora sejam o padrão de referência, apresentam limitações como invasividade, alto custo e dificuldades em realizar monitoramento contínuo. Isso tem motivado a busca por alternativas rápidas, não invasivas e eficazes. Avanços tecnológicos destacam-se nesse cenário, como as técnicas ópticas (fluorescência, espectroscopia Raman e absorção no infravermelho), que oferecem rapidez, objetividade e baixo custo. Essas metodologias, viabilizadas pela acessibilidade anatômica da cavidade oral, têm o potencial de complementar ou substituir os métodos convencionais de diagnóstico. Estudos recentes demonstram que essas tecnologias podem ser aplicadas na prática clínica para detecção precoce do câncer bucal, especialmente com o uso de abordagens minimamente invasivas, como análise de soro ou saliva. Outro destaque é o papel crescente da inteligência artificial (IA) no diagnóstico de câncer bucal. Programas baseados em aprendizado de máquina conseguem integrar grandes volumes de dados de diversas fontes – incluindo imagens, genômica e registros de saúde – de forma quantificável e personalizada. Estudos demonstram que redes neurais podem atingir alta precisão na diferenciação entre lesões benignas e malignas, superando as limitações da observação humana. No entanto, a validação clínica dessa tecnologia ainda é limitada, exigindo mais estudos para sua aplicação rotineira. Adicionalmente, métodos inovadores, como biópsias líquidas, citologia por escova oral, microfluídica e a detecção de biomarcadores específicos (como RNA não codificante, DNA tumoral circulante e componentes do microbioma), têm se mostrado promissores. Esses métodos não apenas facilitam o diagnóstico precoce, mas também oferecem perspectivas para estratégias de triagem mais eficazes e menos invasivas. A Tomografia de Coerência Óptica (OCT) é outra tecnologia emergente com alta resolução e capacidade de fornecer imagens em tempo real da morfologia tecidual. Quando combinada à IA, a OCT tem demonstrado potencial significativo para a detecção precoce do câncer bucal e para orientar intervenções cirúrgicas de maneira precisa. Baseando-se no framework PCC (Problema, Conceito, Contexto), esta revisão busca sintetizar as estratégias diagnósticas para o câncer bucal, avaliando sua eficácia, aplicabilidade e limitações. Serão priorizados estudos que abordem metodologias como técnicas de imagem, biomarcadores e IA, enquanto estudos focados exclusivamente em intervenções terapêuticas serão excluídos. Além disso, a revisão analisará as lacunas existentes na literatura, propondo um direcionamento para futuras pesquisas. Ao destacar tecnologias emergentes, como aprendizado de máquina e métodos moleculares avançados, espera-se contribuir para a melhoria da acurácia diagnóstica e para a detecção precoce, reduzindo atrasos no diagnóstico e melhorando os desfechos clínicos.

title: Decoding of Peripheral Saccade Targets from Foveal Retinotopic V1
description: Visual acuity differs greatly between the fovea and the periphery. While the fovea covers only a fraction of the visual field, it accounts for over 40% of primary visual cortex processing. Studies in recent years have shown that this processing power is not only used to process visual input presented directly to the fovea, but that some input from the periphery is remapped to the foveal parts of the visual cortex. While the precise processes behind this remapping remain elusive, it is thought that foveal areas of visual cortex are recruited for peripheral tasks that require increased control. In addition, foveal remapping is associated with eye movements that require precise judgments of peripheral stimuli. In this fMRI study, we attempt to elucidate the mechanisms underlying foveal remapping and to better understand the visual features that are propagated from the periphery to the foveal parts of the visual cortex. To this end, we designed an fMRI study with two conditions: 1. In the main condition, we will present participants in the scanner with natural object images in the periphery and instruct them to make a saccade to them. However, before participants can fully execute the saccade, the object will disappear. This allows us to capture saccade preparation and early execution without the object ever appearing in the participant's fovea. 2. In the control condition, the object will appear in the participants' fovea without any eye movements. This condition will serve as a control to assess what information we can decode from the foveal retinotopic cortex when the objects are presented directly in the fovea.

title: Ocular Toxoplasmosis Reactivation Following Intraocular Interventions: A Scoping Review
description: Ocular toxoplasmosis (OT) remains a significant global health concern as the leading cause of infectious posterior uveitis, frequently resulting in permanent visual impairment due to its high and unpredictable recurrence rates. While various risk factors for reactivation are well-established, the specific role of intraocular interventions—ranging from phacoemulsification and pars plana vitrectomy to intravitreal injections of anti-VEGF or corticosteroids—as potential triggers for disease recurrence is not yet fully understood. Currently, the ophthalmic community lacks standardized evidence-based guidelines regarding the perioperative management of these patients, leading to significant variability in clinical practice, particularly concerning the use and timing of prophylactic antitoxoplasmic therapy. This clinical uncertainty is further complicated by the phenomenon of subclinical or peripheral retinochoroidal scars that may go undetected during routine pre-operative fundoscopic assessments, only to reactivate following the inflammatory stimulus or mechanical trauma associated with a procedure. The primary purpose of this research project is to conduct a scoping review, following the rigorous methodology established by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), to systematically map and characterize the available evidence surrounding OT reactivation in the context of intraocular interventions. This review defines reactivation as the development of active lesions regardless of whether the underlying scar was known prior to the intervention or identified postoperatively. By synthesizing data from both retrospective studies and a predominant body of case reports, this project seeks to define the typical clinical presentation and temporal onset of post-procedural reactivation. A key objective of this work is to explore the differences in outcomes and reporting between patients with a known history of OT and those identified as having silent scars only after a postoperative event occurs. The expected outcomes of this scoping review include a comprehensive categorization of the types of procedures most frequently associated with reactivation and a detailed analysis of both patient-related and procedure-related factors described as potential triggers. Furthermore, the review will provide a summary of the various prophylactic and therapeutic regimens currently reported in the literature, revealing the degree of heterogeneity in global practices. By identifying the limitations within the existing evidence base, this project will highlight critical knowledge gaps that prevent the formation of a clinical consensus. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a foundational evidence map that can inform better pre-operative screening protocols, guide perioperative therapeutic decisions, and establish the necessary parameters for future prospective research into the prevention of ocular toxoplasmosis reactivation.

title: Ultrasonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Measurement Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC) : Scoping Literature Review
description: The optic nerve is surrounded by the same meningeal coverings that surround the brain. This anatomic relationship allows the use of Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) as a non-invasive, bedside estimate of elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP). Despite the increasing research interest in ultrasonographic ONSD, it is not widely used clinically. This can be due to variability in ONSD measurements as identified by several meta-analyses that showed significant heterogeneity in ONSD measurement techniques. We propose that this heterogeneity is due to lack of consensus on ONSD measurement technique, which can cause variations in image acquisition and measurement. In this review, We will identify published ONSD imaging and measurement criteria through a scoping systematic review of ultrasound ONSD studies. We will use a piloted data sheet to extract ONSD imaging and measurement criteria. We will then use the output of the review to develop a checklist for ONSD Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC). This checklist will undergo further refinement in the future by using the modified Delphi method to reach expert consensus on ONSD quality criteria.

title: Consciousness-related interactions in a double-slit optical interferometer
description: Motivated by a series of reported experiments and their controversial results, the present work investigated if volunteers could causally affect an optical double-slit system through mental efforts alone. The participants' task alternated between intending the increase of the (real-time feedback informed) amount of light diffracted through a specific single slit and relaxing any intention effort. The 160 data sessions that 127 volunteers took part in revealed a statistically significant 4.68 sigma difference between the measurements performed in the intention versus the relax conditions ($p=2.93\times10^{-6}; \, es= 0.47 \pm 0.20$ 95\% CL), while the 160 control sessions conducted without any observers present resulted in statistically equivalent samples ($z=0.35, \, p=0.73; \, es=0.04 \pm 0.20$ 95\% CL). The results could not be explained by environmental factors, hence supporting the previously claimed existence of a not yet understood form of interaction between a conscious agent and a physical system.

title: Larger head displacement to optic flow presented in the lower visual field.
description: Optic flow that simulates self-motion often produces postural adjustment. Although literature suggested that human postural control considerably depends on visual inputs from the lower field in the environment, effects of the vertical location of optic flow are not well investigated on postural response. Here, we examined whether optic flow presented in the lower visual field produces a stronger postural response than optic flow in the upper visual field. Either expanding or contracting the optic flow was presented in three visual locations (upper, lower, and full visual fields) on an Oculus Rift head-mounted display. Head displacement and vection strength was measured. Results showed larger head displacement under the optic flow presentation in the lower visual field, than in the upper visual field, but only for the early period of the presentation of the contracting optic flow. Full visual field condition also produced larger head displacement than the upper visual field condition, but for contraction only. Vection was stronger for the lower visual field than the upper visual field, stronger for full visual field than upper and lower visual field. Our findings support the notion that more ecologically relevant information has a more important role in human postural control and self-motion perception.

title: Quantification of palmar and digital epidermal thickness and sweat duct density
description: Palmar digital skin, with its high density of epidermal sweat glands and unique stratum corneum, derives its autonomic innervation from peripheral nerves. Understanding the changes to these structures could serve as objective proxy markers following peripheral nerve injury and interventions to promote regeneration. There are limited data in humans for these measures and normative reference ranges are yet to be defined. Light-based imaging techniques, such as optical coherence tomography (OCT), can detect quantifiable changes in these epidermal parameters. This study aims to define the normal epidermal thickness and sweat duct density (SDD) of volar hand skin. A total of 53 healthy, non-injured participants, 21 males and 32 females were enrolled. Two-and three-dimensional images of defined 1x1mm areas of volar fingertip skin were obtained using OCT. The mean epidermal thickness and SDD were manually calculated. Results were compared across all digits and by hand-dominance, age, gender, and race and ethnicity. The 95% reference intervals for both parameters were also calculated. There was a significant (p<0.0001) progressive reduction in the epidermal thickness across the digits, from the thumb towards the little finger. Females had a significantly thinner (p=0.011) epidermal layer in comparison to males. SDD was significantly lower (p<0.030) in the thumb compared to middle, ring, or little fingers. There was a significant reduction (p=0.039) in SDD in the dominant hand and a general downward trend in number of sweat glands per mm2 with age (p<0.0001). No statistically significant differences were identified for both measures between different races and ethnicities. The reference interval for epidermal thickness was 0.37–0.79 mm, while for SDD the interval was 30–86 ducts/mm2. This study has outlined normative differences in SDD and epidermal thickness in palmar digital skin. Our results can be used as control measures for prospective studies looking into the regenerative process following peripheral nerve injuries or identifying potential trauma to digital nerves.

title: The Psychophysics of ON- Versus OFF- Pattern Recognition and Myopia
description: the prevalence of myopia was around 10%, but today nearly 90% of young adults are afflicted [1]. In the United States and Europe, the prevalence has doubled over the last half-century with half of young adults now having myopia[1]. The consequence of myopia extends beyond the inconvenience of using optical correction. Myopia is associated with increased incidence of diseases such as retinal damage, cataract, and glaucoma [1]. Increased levels of near-work have commonly been associated with the onset of myopia [2]. It is therefore important to gain a better understanding of what is happening from a functional and anatomical standpoint when subjects complete near-work tasks. There are two different types of text, texts that have positive contrast (white text on a darker background) and texts that have negative contrast (black text on a lighter background). Aleman et. al (2018) found that negative contrast texts produced a thinning effect on the choroid (-16.13土4.54 μm), and positive contrast produced a thickening effect on the choroid(9.96土 6.51μm) [3]. Aleman et. al interpreted these results in the context of ON and OFF pathways in the visual system [4]. They suggested negative contrast texts stimulate the OFF pathway, while positive contrast texts stimulate the ON pathway. Choroidal thickening and thinning in both chicks and marmosets has been observed to be a precursor to a decrease or an increase in axial growth respectively [5, 6, 7]. The latter leading to the development of myopia. Trolio et. al documented 20 μm of choroidal thinning in myopia induced marmoset eyes and 12 μm of thickening in eyes induced with hyperopia [5]. It is hypothesized that the choroid either acts as a mechanical buffer or a diffusion barrier for the sclera [5]. Qualitatively, Aleman et al's data showed the thinning effect was more pronounced in myopic individuals as compared to their emmetropic counterparts [3], but their sample size was insufficient to draw quantitative conclusions. The plasticity of the human choroid is an important link to animal models. For example, Read et. al found that among a group of 39 myopic individuals subfoveal choroidal thickness was 50 μm thinner than nonmyopic age-matched children [8]. Retinal Ganglion Cells are organized in an ON center OFF surround arrangement or vice versa [2]. ON cells become depolarized to an increment in light, while OFF depolarize in response to decrements in light. OFF retinal ganglion cells are twice as numerous and half the size of ON rental ganglion cells in the fovea. Several studies such as Mazade et. al, Lu et. al, and Tyler et. al corroborated the different spatial tuning and cortical connectivity of the ON and OFF pathway [9, 10, 11]. Mazade et al showed maximal cortical responses for small fast stimuli in the OFF pathway and maximal cortical responses for slow slow global stimuli in the ON pathway [10]. Zhong-Lin et. al found negative stimuli (or decrements in light) to be 25% more effective than equal magnitude positive stimuli (or increments in light) across eleven different types of stimuli [11]. Taken together, these studies support a distinct roles for the ON and OFF pathways in the visual system. The goal of our study is threefold. We aim to replicate the changes in choroidal thickness in response to negative and positive contrast with a larger subject group. We aim to measure the sensitivity to positive and negative contrast tasks and compare the ratio of contrast sensitivity to these two contrast types among refractive error/axial length. Finally, we will monitor the changes in sensitivity to positive and negative contrast as the session proceeds as to understand the functional implications choroidal thickness changes may have.

title: Scanning Cue Approach with Faces
description: Description: In this MRI experiment we will test the underlying neural mechanisms of non-reinforced learning, by changing preferences of face images using the Cue Approach Task (CAT). Recently, Schonberg et al.(2014) showed a preferences increase toward snack food-items following a short (less than one hour) cue-approach training in which some items were consistently associated with a neutral tone and a button press. Stimuli: Sixty colour images of unfamiliar faces taken from the Siblings database (Vieira et al., 2014) and modified for the current procedure will be used as stimuli for the current experiment. Procedure: Subject will undergo several tasks both outside and inside MRI scanner. Inside the scanner, in order to control for viewing times, and make sure participants are engaged with the task, their eye position will be recorded using a MRI-compatible eye-tracker. Outside of the scanner: 1. Baseline evaluation - Binary ranking: Subjects will be presented with a forced choice between 300 random pairs of stimuli. Each stimulus will be presented exactly 10 time, in a binary choice against 10 other random stimuli. for each choice subjects may respond within a 2.5 seconds time-window. After all choices are done, a ranking algorithm (Colley, 2008), will be applied to deduce a quantitive preference value for each item. These rankings will be used later in the probe phase to create pairs of similarly valued items. From all 60 items, a subset of 40 item in predetermined ranks will be chosen for the rest of the experiment. Inside of the scanner: 2. Passive viewing task: Subjects will passively view the subset of 40 images in order to evaluate the baseline neural activation for these stimuli prior to training. As a way of monitoring their engagement in the task, subject will be asked to count how many male or female faces they had seen. 3. Cue approach training: Subject will undergo 16 cue approach training runs; in each run, each image will be presented once. in each trial a single face will be presented on the centre of the screen. 30% of stimuli will be consistently associate with a tone, appearing ~750ms following visual stimulus onset. Subjects are asked to press a button on the response box with their index finger, before visual stimulus offset (1000 ms following the onset). Subjects are informed in advance that the stimulus-tone association is consistent. 4. Seven minutes break: during which anatomical scans are made 5. Passive viewing task: Subjects will passively view the subset of 40 images in order to evaluate the post-training neural activation for these stimuli. As a way of monitoring their engagement in the task, subject will be asked to count how many male or female faces they had seen. 6. Probe: subject will be presented with a forced choice task between two faces out of the 40 faces subset. for each choice there will be a 1500 ms time, followed by a jittered duration ITI. Three pair type are used: a) High-value (HV) pairs - stimuli ranked 7-18 - 6 Go items, and 6 NoGo item (both Go item and NoGo item have a mean rank of 12.5). In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a HV Go item and a HV NoGo item. b) Low-value (LV) pairs - stimuli ranked 43-54 - 6 Go items, and 6 NoGo item (both Go item and NoGo item have a mean rank of 48.5). In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a LV Go item and a LV NoGo item. c) Sanity check - 2 HV NoGo stimuli ranked 5-6, and 2 LV NoGo stimuli ranked 55-56. In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a HV NoGo item and a LV NoGo item. We hypothesize that in pair a and b, subjects will choose the Go item over the NoGo items, and in pair type c subjects will choose the HV items over the LV items. 7. Face localizer (1-back task): In order to functionally locate face selective brain areas, we will use a block design of dynamic videos of faces and objects. Subject will be presented with short 1000 ms videos of either faces or objects in motion (as well as blocks of fixation). In a one-back task, subjects will be asked to indicate when a video was presented two consecutive times.

title: Foveal sensitivities for target-congruent and target-incongruent orientation information during saccade preparation
description: The preparation of rapid eye movements (i.e. saccades) entails dynamic changes in visual sensitivity across the visual field. Pre-saccadic attention shifts and accompanying sensitivity enhancements at the saccade target have been studied extensively. At the same time, little is known about the development of visual sensitivity in the pre-saccadic center of gaze. Behavioral findings suggest that, just like at the saccade target, visual sensitivity increases at the pre-saccadic foveal location (e.g. Rolfs, Jonikaitis, Deubel, & Cavanagh, 2011; Szinte, Jonikaitis, Rangelov, & Deubel, 2018). This finding has been attributed to a predictive remapping mechanism that directs attention to the future retinal (i.e. foveal) location of the saccade target to provide a head start for post-saccadic processing. To date, however, it remains unclear if a transfer of activation between the saccade target's current and future retinal location involves a transfer of information about its features. Behavioral evidence for a transfer of feature information between the saccade target and foveal location remains indirect (e.g. He, Fritsche, & de Lange, 2018): visual adaptation effects resulting from prolonged stimulus exposure in the fovea have been shown to alter the perception of saccade target stimuli when they were shown during saccade preparation. Crucially however, direct behavioral evidence for a pre-saccadic remapping of feature information from the saccade target to the fovea remains to be established. In an attempt to provide this evidence, we will measure observers' ability to detect an orientation-filtered pink noise patch (the probe; oriented -45° or 45°) in the pre-saccadic center of gaze while they are preparing an eye movement to a second orientation-filtered noise patch in the periphery (the target; oriented -45° or 45°). Probe and target will be smoothly embedded in full-screen pink noise images presented in quick alternation. If present, the orientation of the foveal probe will be either congruent or incongruent with the orientation of the saccade target. If feature information is transferred from the saccade target to the fovea during eye movement preparation, the target's orientation should interact with foveal orientation information and influence present/absent judgments.

title: Ophthalmic outcomes after surgical treatment of isolated primary sphenoid sinus mucoceles: a systematic review
description: This systematic review aims to synthesize evidence on ophthalmic outcomes following surgical treatment of isolated primary sphenoid sinus mucoceles. Sphenoid sinus mucoceles are rare expansile lesions that can cause compressive optic neuropathy and cranial nerve palsies due to their proximity to the optic nerve, chiasm, and cavernous sinus. The review will evaluate the proportion and degree of visual recovery after surgical decompression, identify prognostic factors (including baseline visual acuity, symptom duration, and imaging features), and compare outcomes between different surgical approaches (endoscopic vs open vs combined). Only primary isolated sphenoid sinus mucoceles will be included; mucoceles involving Onodi cells, anterior clinoid processes, or secondary to vascular lesions, skull-base reconstruction, or systemic disease will be excluded. Primary ophthalmic outcomes include changes in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), changes in visual fields, and the proportion of eyes achieving complete recovery (return to normal or near-normal vision), partial improvement, stable deficit, or worsening vision. Secondary outcomes include the time from symptom onset to surgery and its association with visual outcomes; resolution or persistence of other neuro-ophthalmic signs (diplopia, ptosis, extra-ocular movement limitation, cranial nerve palsies); radiological outcomes (decompression of optic nerve, resolution of mucocele); surgical complications (CSF leak, meningitis, vascular injury, reoperation); recurrence of mucocele and need for revision surgery; and length of follow-up.

title: Driving person models
description: One mechanism to manage decisions efficiently is the ability to predict how a situation will unfold (sometimes referred to as 'projection'; Endsley, 1995). However, our ability to accurately predict (and, therefore, to make appropriate decisions) is dependent on our situational awareness – our awareness of critical information in the environment (Endsley, 1995). Having an accurate understanding of what is happening in a given situation is particularly crucial in high-pressure situations where errors in decision-making can have serious consequences such as within driving. This process is complicated when other people are involved. Indeed, my previous research has shown that we create 'person models' based on how our interaction partners have behaved previously, and this information is (implicitly) used to predict how they will behave in the current situation (Joyce et al., 2016; Schenke et al., 2016, 2020; see Bach & Schenke, 2017 for a review). However, there is little research to date into the impact of these predictive person models on situation awareness and decision making within driving. Thus, this research will test whether situation awareness (and subsequent decision making) is different based on who else is involved in the scenario. A second factor will involve whether having an active task (in the form of seeking out a specific location) alters situation awareness compared to just passively observing the environment.

title: Potsdam Dataset for Eye Movement On Natural Scenes (Potsdam DAEMONS)
description: In this study we will collect experimental data from participants viewing natural scenes. We want to generate a data set that is useful for both machine learning applications as well as experimental analysis. Previous data sets from the field of machine learning, such as MIT1003 (Judd et al., 2009) or CAT200 (Borji & Itti, 2015), encompass a large number of images seen by a comparatively small number of subjects for a fairly short amount of time. The eye tracking recordings are often only available only as ordered scan paths, sometimes omiting fixation durations altogether (Borji & Itti, 2015). By contrast, data sets from experimental eye movement research tend to have more subjects and longer fixation sequences but fewer images: having more data per image allows to quantify effects on a per-image bases more precisely (e.g. the SpatStat data set (Trukenbrod et al., 2019)). This leads to a comparability problem: machine learning models, such as Deepgaze III (Kümmerer et al., 2019), which need large amounts of data with many different image examples can not be trained on the same data as the procedural models such as SceneWalk (Schwetlick et al., 2020), which require longer sequences and vice versa. Additionally for evaluation purposes, it's often good to have many observers per image. Therefore, since mechanistic models need less training data, vision science traditionally chooses a different tradeoff: many subjects on fewer images. For fair comparison and insightful evaluation we propose to collect a single data set that combines both: Many images with potentially fewer subjects per image as a training set, and many subjects per image for insightful evaluations as a validation and test set. We aim to address this gap by collecting a data set which can be used by both research traditions, and which will enable us to combine and compare insights from research of the visual system with state of the art machine learning techniques. It will also be invaluable in establishing a benchmark (see Kümmerer et al., 2018 for static saliency benchmark) for scan path modelling.

title: Noninvasive Measurement of Retinal Dopamine Levels Using Electroretinography: A Novel Approach
description: Dopamine is a crucial neuromodulator in the retina, involved in various visual functions, including adaptation to light, color perception, and circadian rhythms. It is also one of the basic neuromodulators that influences the sensitivity to spatial frequencies of the visual field. Traditional methods of studying retinal dopamine levels, such as post-mortem analysis and animal models, limit the understanding of its real-time role and dynamics in vivo. Electroretinograms (ERG) provide a non-invasive means to study retinal function, but their capability to reflect dopamine levels indirectly through specific wave components is underexplored. Recent advances in vitreous analysis techniques offer a new avenue to quantify dopamine metabolites, like DOPAC and homovanillic acid, which could correlate with ERG findings. This study aims to bridge the gap in methodology by combining ERG with biochemical analysis of the vitreous humor from patients undergoing vitrectomy, potentially unveiling a novel, non-invasive biomarker for retinal dopamine activity.

title: Association Between Sleep Disturbances and the Severity and Progression of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma: A Systematic Review
description: Current management of Primary Open-Angle Glaucoma (POAG) relies almost exclusively on lowering intraocular pressure (IOP). However, a significant subset of patients continues to experience optic nerve deterioration despite well-controlled IOP, suggesting that other systemic modifiable risk factors drive disease progression. Sleep quality is a leading candidate due to its direct role in regulating ocular perfusion, oxygenation, and neuroprotective circadian rhythms. While numerous studies have linked sleep disturbances to the prevalence of glaucoma, the literature regarding disease progression is fragmented and contradictory. Some studies suggest a clear linear relationship between sleep apnea or insomnia and structural worsening, while others find no association. This systematic review is necessary to synthesize these conflicting data, clarifying whether sleep disturbances are merely a symptom of advanced disease or an active contributor to glaucomatous neurodegeneration.

title: Causal Optics
description: This paper introduces a transdisciplinary theoretical framework called Causal Optics, which reconceptualizes light, velocity, and dimensional transitions through the lens of causal mathematics and entropy dynamics. Rather than treating the speed of light as a rigid constant solely defined by relativistic postulates, this framework interprets it as the causal velocity threshold within a three-dimensional entropy-stabilized universe. Drawing parallels to the role of sound speed within atmospheric systems, we argue that light speed emerges from systemic constraints driven by entropy flow, information compression, and causal inertia. The paper outlines nine core chapters exploring the causal foundations of optics, entropy as a directional operator of time, the constraints of light as a structural limit of causality, and the potential implications for dimensional emergence and transitions. We critically examine current attempts to surpass the speed of light through energetic stacking, and instead propose a new approach grounded in causal transitions across entropy thresholds or non-material information flows. In doing so, this paper extends the epistemological boundaries between physics and metaphysics, offering a unified causal model that incorporates quantum behaviors, systemic feedback, and dimensional causality, while remaining anchored in thermodynamic reasoning.

title: Course and Branching of the Oculomotor Nerve: A Systematic Review
description: Oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) is principally responsible for somatic innervation of the extraocular muscles such as levator palpebrae superioris, superior rectus, medial rectus, inferior rectus and inferior obliqe muscles. It gives also a parasympathetic branch to the ciliary ganglion, which provides the ciliary muscles and pupillary sphincter muscles. Any variations in the branching or innervated structures may alter eye functioning. On the other hand, some pathologies on the course of the nerve may obstacle the oculomotor fibers resulting in visible symptoms of the pathology. The main purpose of this research is to collect, analyze, and synthesize published data on the anatomical features of the cranial nerve III. Our review includes nerve origin, course, branching patterns, diameters, lengths, and common variabilities, as well as the prevalence of such variations. We included articles which describe the oculomotor nerve using different imaging methods. Our intention was to provide evidence-based insights for other researchres and clinicians as well.

title: Pinocchio Paradox and the Double-Slit Experiment: A Conceptual and Javedian Analysis
description: This project develops a conceptual and interdisciplinary connection between the classical Pinocchio Paradox and the quantum-mechanical Double-Slit Experiment. Although one belongs to the domain of self-referential logic and the other to physical measurement, both illustrate the same fundamental mechanism: a system existing in multiple potential states until an act of observation forces a collapse. Building on Javed's Quantum Thought, this work argues that collapse—whether logical or physical—is not self-generated but governed by an external truth-determining authority. The Pinocchio Paradox reveals how self-reference creates a logical superposition that cannot resolve internally, while the Double-Slit Experiment shows that quantum states collapse only when observed. By integrating insights from logic, quantum physics, and metaphysical philosophy, this project proposes a unified principle explaining how intention, observation, and external governance shape the emergence of definable reality. The study aims to stimulate cross-disciplinary dialogue and provide a foundational model for further inquiry in theoretical physics, cognitive science, and philosophy of mind.

title: Independent Risk Factors for Retrograde Ejaculation after Anterior versus Posterior Lumbar Fusion in Male Patients: A Protocol for a Cox Proportional Hazards Analysis
description: Anterior lumbar fusion (ALF) as a surgical intervention for lower lumbar degenerative pathology has grown in popularity over the past few decades,1,2 potentially due to its biomechanical advantages, avoidance of posterior neural and muscle elements, and decreased blood loss as compared to traditional posterior lumbar fusion (PLF).3 As ALF is primarily for pathology involving the L4-L5 and L5-S1 segments, risk of injury to anterior lower lumbar structures is a unique concern for spine surgeons performing ALF.4 One such concern in male patients is injury to the superior hypogastric plexus (SHP),5 an autonomic plexus anterior to the L5 vertebra, L5-S1 disc space, and sacral promontory.4 Injury to the SHP during ALF can impair regional sympathetic function, causing aberrant relaxation of the internal bladder sphincter during sexual activities in males. This can lead to retrograde ejaculation (RE),3 a condition in which ejaculate undergoes retrograde flow into the bladder, potentially causing infertility.3 In a recent meta-analysis, Body et al. (2021) pooled the incidence of RE across 2,503 patients who underwent anterior lumbar surgery, including both ALF and total disc replacement, across 18 studies.3 The authors found a mean incidence of RE of 2.3% with a range of 0% to 9.8%.3 Due to this relatively high incidence of RE, some surgeons may avoid ALF when otherwise indicated. However, Body et al. (2021) acknowledged several methodological limitations among included studies, including reliance on questionnaires and/or a lack of objective measures of RE such as post-ejaculation analysis, small sample sizes, and the inclusion of female patients in many studies, hindering male-specific risk assessment.3 Importantly, several factors have been explored as the cause of RE in ALF. First of all, direct nerve injury to the SHP during surgical dissection, retraction, and/or electrocautery during anterior approaches is a key possibility.3,6 Additionally, recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is supported as a risk factor due to its neuroinflammatory properties and/or stimulation of ectopic bone formation ventral to the spine.3,7 Some evidence suggests that the relative influence of rhBMP-2 may have lessened following adoption of safer handling practices following a warning from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2008 regarding surgical complications.3,8 Unrelated to lumbar fusion, previous medical or surgical treatment for prostatic hyperplasia has been suggested as a risk factor for RE after ALF.7 Apart from these factors, general predispositions to RE after lumbar fusion including medications, comorbidities, and age have remained under-explored, hindering clinician decision-making at this time. An enhanced understanding of the incidence and independent risk factors for RE after ALF may improve surgical decision-making and preoperative patient education. Due to the limited understanding of RE after ALF, this study will utilize Cox proportional hazards modeling to assess the independence and magnitude of multiple potential risk factors associated with RE after ALF.9 Therefore, the aim of this retrospective analysis is to investigate the incidence and independent risk factors for RE in adult males after ALF versus PLF to enhance surgical decision-making as well as patient education to optimize patient care.

description: This research project focuses on exploring and summarizing the recent advancements in the use of naltrexone (NTX) a known opioid receptor antagonist as a novel therapeutic agent for ocular diseases. Due to the eye's complex anatomy and physiological barriers, delivering sufficient drug concentrations to intraocular tissues is extremely difficult. This review addresses these challenges by evaluating multiple nanocarrier systems including niosomes, hydrogels, in-situ gelling films, and polymeric matrices designed to enhance NTX's stability, precorneal retention, corneal penetration, and sustained release. These studies span from preclinical formulations to human safety trials, investigating NTX's role in treating conditions such as diabetic keratopathy, dry eye syndrome, neuropathic corneal pain, and corneal wound healing. The review identifies formulation strategies that significantly improve NTX's ocular bioavailability and therapeutic performance while minimizing systemic side effects. Additionally, the research project provides a patent landscape analysis, highlighting key innovations in NTX delivery platforms such as mucoadhesive systems, sustained-release polymers, and topical anti-inflammatory formulations. The study also applies the GRADE framework to evaluate the quality and certainty of the evidence, giving a robust assessment of NTX's potential in ocular pharmacotherapy.

title: Spontaneous ocular scanning of visual symmetry is similar during classification and evaluation tasks
description: Visual symmetry perception and symmetry preference have been studied extensively. However, little is known about how people spontaneously scan symmetrical configurations with their eyes. title: Predicting cover crop biomass by lightweight UAS-based RGB and NIR photography: an applied photogrammetric approach
description: Easy-to-capture and robust plant status indicators are important factors when implementing precision agriculture techniques on fields. In this study, aerial red, green and blue color space (RGB) photography and near-infrared (NIR) photography was performed on an experimental field site with nine different cover crops. A lightweight unmanned aerial system (UAS) served as platform, consumer cameras as sensors. Photos were photogrammetrically processed to orthophotos and digital surface models (DSMs). In a first validation step, the spatial precision of RGB orthophotos (x and y, ± 0.1 m) and DSMs (z, ± 0.1 m) was determined. Then, canopy cover (CC), plant height (PH), normalized differenced vegetation index (NDVI), red edge inflection point (REIP), and green red vegetation index (GRVI) were extracted. In a second validation step, the PHs derived from the DSMs were compared with ground truth ruler measurements. A strong linear relationship was observed (R 2 = 0.80−0.84). Finally, destructive biomass samples were taken and compared with the remotely-sensed characteristics. Biomass correlated best with plant height (PH), and good approximations with linear regressions were found (R 2 = 0.74 for four selected species, R 2 = 0.58 for all nine species). CC and the vegetation indices (VIs) showed less significant and less strong overall correlations, but performed well for certain species. It is therefore evident that the use of DSM-based PHs provides a feasible approach to a species-independent non-destructive biomass determination, where the performance of VIs is more species-dependent.

title: Examining the Role of Personalized Digital Health Solutions in Pre-Diabetes Management Among Young Adults
description: Prediabetes is a condition where blood glucose level is higher than normal but still can't be classified as diabetes. This stage represents a critical opportunity for intervention, as individuals with prediabetes have a significantly higher risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes without timely intervention. Studies have shown that prediabetic individuals have a 74% risk of developing diabetes if not treated timely (Ligthart et al., 2016). Also, it is important to intervening at the prediabetic stage to mitigate its associated complications, such as cardiovascular diseases, neuropathy, and retinopathy (Kurihara et al., 2013). Young adults aged 18-34 are particularly vulnerable due to unhealthy lifestyle choices, limited engagement with traditional healthcare models, and low health literacy. Digital health solutions, such as mobile apps, gamified interventions, and AI-powered tools, have emerged as promising platforms to address these gaps. Effective interventions during the pre-diabetic stage, such as personalized digital health solutions, have been shown to improve engagement and adherence while reducing the risk of diabetes progression. Evidence indicates that features like tailored recommendations, interactive educational modules, and gamification significantly enhance self-management practices and health literacy (Wang et al., 2023). This review aims to evaluate the role of personalized digital health solutions in pre-diabetes management, focusing on their effectiveness in improving engagement, knowledge, and self-management practices.

title: Psychosocial observations in ocular genetics consultations: from genetic diagnosis to rehabilitation
description: Individuals with genetic eye diseases (GED) experience low quality of life and high levels of anxiety and depression, in addition to frequently attending ocular genetics consultations. Therefore, the aim of this study is to investigate the psychosocial aspects experienced by patients with genetic eye diseases throughtout ocular genetics consultations. The method was a review of multidisciplinary records from observations conducted between a geneticist and a psychologist during consultations in a Ocular Genetics Clinic. Using the R statistical package, a word cloud was generated, enabling subsequent thematic analysis. The participants were 37 patients, with a mean age of 36.9, standard deviation (SD) 18.5, and 6 types of genetic ocular diseases, with an average diagnosis time of 18.5 years and SD of 11.2.The four main themes addressed by the patients were: genetic testing and its results, non-acceptance of the disease, disease acceptance and rehabilitation. Ocular genetics consultations generate various emotional reactions in patients with genetic eye diseases and their families. Therefore, to mitigate the emotional impact of the patient's journey, it is recommended to include a psychology professional as part of the ocular genetics team. Additionally, genetic eye diseases patients experience prolonged periods of non-acceptance before embracing their condition. Upon acceptance, they improve their quality of life and emotional health through rehabilitation and psychotherapy. This underscores the importance of medical referrals to these services.

title: Spelling ability reduces readers' reliance on sentence context for word recognition especially in foveal vision
description: This is a replication of an experiment that was reviewed for the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, & Cognition, which used a quasi- experimental design with individual differences measures as a predictor. The reviewers requested that we replicate the original findings; this study will replicate the prior one and will include additional individual differences measures to determine whether the effects are due to spelling ability (as we had suggested) or more general reading ability. Prior work suggests that readers use predictions about upcoming words to facilitate word recognition, particularly in parafoveal vision (Staub & Goddard, 2019) or when the reader has poor quality lexical representations (Hersch & Andrews, 2012). We tested how these factors interact by having participants perform a word recognition task (i.e., a letter probe task) on a target that was presented in the fovea or the parafovea, and which followed a sentence that constrained (1) toward the target, (2) toward an orthographic neighbor of the target, or (3) toward neither. We measured participants' spelling abilities, which are hypothesized to reflect lexical quality. We found that spelling abilities interacted with context and visual field, suggesting that worse spellers relied more on context to perform word recognition in the fovea, but all spellers rely on context to the same degree in the parafovea.

title: OCD, Metacognition, and Cognitive Deficits Following an Induced "Not Just RIght Experience"- Follow up
description: This study is a follow-up to our previous study, "OCD, Metacognition, and Cognitive Deficits Following an Induced "Not Just Right Experience." In our previous study, we aimed to examine the effect of feelings of incompleteness, or the "Not Just Right Experience," on executive function (EF) and metacognitive judgments among those with obsessive-compulsive tendencies (OCT). The purpose of our study was to provide evidence for the need for the development of more targeted treatment approaches for those who express the Not Just Right Experience (NJRE) as the main motivator for their OCD symptoms. In our study, we randomized participants into either an induction condition or a non-induction condition (both of which included a list of words to be remembered), measured their NJREs, and then measured their performance on executive function tasks. We also asked participants in each condition how many words they thought they would be able to recall from the list of words they were presented with 15 minutes from when they saw them. They were given a recall task 15 minutes later, and we compared their predicted scores to their actual recall scores to test their calibration. Here, we wanted to know if participants with obsessive-compulsive tendencies are good at determining how much the NJRE is affecting them. At the end of the study, participants took the Vancouver Obsessive Compulsive Inventory (VOCI) to determine their levels of OCT. Initially, our analysis looked at whether OCT score, induction vs non induction, or the interaction between them, were good predictors of EF score and calibration score. Our results found that OCT score had a negative relationship with cognitive flexibility, but not with working memory or response inhibition. Furthermore, neither induction vs non induction, nor the interaction had any effect on any measure of EF or calibration scores. However, when reviewing our data, we noticed that there were several outliers that may have been skewing the results. Specifically, there were 3 participants who obtained a score of 12 on the Backwards Digit Span task (the highest possible score) but had an exceptionally high OCT score, which ranged from 114 to 140. When we examined these 3 participants more closely on Qualtrics, we noticed some evidence that these participants may have been bots. Two of these participants had IP addresses that came from the same place in Africa, and these responses seemed to be almost identical in nature. They both took an unusually long time to finish the study (greater than 1 hour), and they both obtained the exact same OCT score (114). Research on Qualtrics bots has identified that bots usually take longer to complete a survey than a human participant and that responses from the same bot will appear repetitive (Hernandez, 2020). Additionally, the study was done using two Qualtrics surveys, as after participants completed Digit Symbol Substitution, they had to be redirected to an external site to complete Stroop and then redirected back to a separate Qualtrics survey after they completed Stroop. One of them did not have the same Qualtrics ID on the second Qualtrics survey as they did on the first. The third participant also had an IP address in Africa on the first Qualtrics survey, but when this same participant was redirected to the second part of the study (which was an entirely different Qualtrics survey), their IP address was then changed so that they appeared in Miami. This participant also took an unusually long amount of time to complete the survey and obtained an OCT score of 140. Therefore, we removed these three participants in the subsequent analysis. Furthermore, after defending my thesis at Kwantlen Polytechnic University, I was asked a question as to why I didn't look at the NJRE score as a predictor variable and ignore the group entirely, as the NJRE score was really the construct I was interested in. Participants in both the induction group and the non-induction group may have been induced by an NJRE, as the non-induction group did not have an absence of NJREs (M = 7.12, SD = 9.79). So, I tested the partial correlation between OCT score and all 3 measures of executive function when controlling for NJRE score. Results revealed that before controlling for NJRE, OCT score was significantly correlated with the Backwards Digit Span score and Digit Symbol Substitution score, but not the Stroop score. After controlling for NJRE score, OCT score was no longer significantly correlated with either Backwards Digit Span Score or Digit Symbol Substitution score. This provided evidence that I needed to use a different analytical approach in testing my hypothesis. With this new information, we tested whether the NJRE score mediates or moderates the relationship between OCT score and Backwards Digit Span score, and OCT score and Digit Symbol Substitution score. We did not test a mediation or moderation of NJRE on the relationship between OCT score and Stroop score or calibration score, as no significant direct effect of OCT score was observed. Our results found that the NJRE is a moderator of the relationship between OCT and working memory and a mediator of the relationship between OCT and cognitive flexibility. Therefore, in our follow-up, we are seeking to replicate these findings using a direct replication of the previous study.
