title: Association between MRI findings and retinal alterations on OCT among patients with Schizophrenia, Bipolar Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder
description: The retina, as the outermost part of the central nervous system (CNS), shares the same embryonic origin and structural characteristics as brain tissue. Retinal imaging has emerged as a valuable approach for identifying ophthalmic markers of psychiatric disorders associated with structural CNS alterations. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), a non-invasive, painless, rapid, and cost-effective technique, enables high-resolution visualisation of retinal layers. Evidence suggests that retinal structural changes may parallel cognitive decline and the onset or progression of neuropsychiatric disorders. Recent studies have investigated retinal alterations across a range of psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, major depressive disorder, personality disorders, generalised anxiety disorder, and anorexia nervosa. This systematic review aims to investigate if there is an association between MRI findings and retinal alterations, measured by Optical Coherence Tomography, in patients diagnosed with Major Psychiatric Disorders, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder.

title: Patient-Reported Barriers and Patient-Prioritized Improvements in Postoperative Ophthalmic Pain Management
description: Abstract: Effective postoperative pain management is vital for recovery, yet often undertreated in ophthalmic surgery, impacting patient comfort and satisfaction. Patient perspectives on pain management barriers and improvements are crucial for guiding quality improvement but remain underexplored. This study examined the pain experiences, treatment adequacy, satisfaction, perceived barriers, and suggested improvements of postoperative ophthalmic patients. In a cross-sectional survey conducted as part of a quality improvement initiative, 312 postoperative patients at the Tamale Teaching Hospital Ophthalmology Department (Ghana) provided data on pain intensity, analgesic use, satisfaction, and perceived barriers and improvements. The mean age was 54.8 years. Nearly all patients (98%) had heard of analgesics, but only 55% demonstrated adequate knowledge of analgesics. Postoperatively, 61% received analgesics; however, only 33% received multimodal analgesia. Pain was common (80% reported pain), though moderate-to-severe pain occurred in 40%, and pain was effectively managed in 60% by health care professionals. Slightly over half (53.5%) were satisfied with pain management, and 30.8% were very satisfied, whereas 15.7% were dissatisfied. The most frequently reported barriers to adequate pain control were inadequate information about analgesics, poor staff–patient communication, insufficient analgesia, and staff disbelief in patients' pain. Patients correspondingly prioritized improvements such as better analgesic education, ensuring adequate analgesic provision, improved staff communication, and validation of patient pain reports. These findings reveal critical gaps in ophthalmic postoperative pain management, specifically in patient education, communication, and the provision of analgesics. Incorporating patient input to address these deficits—through improved education, communication, and adequate analgesia—could significantly enhance postoperative pain outcomes and patient satisfaction. Perspective: This study highlights the vital role of patient feedback in improving postoperative pain management. Clinicians and health systems can address patient-identified gaps, such as poor communication, inadequate education, and insufficient analgesia, to enhance pain control and patient satisfaction, ultimately leading to improved quality of care in ophthalmic surgery.

title: Barriers and Enablers to Medication Adherence & Compliance in Glaucoma – A Scoping Review Protocol
description: Background Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide, with increased intraocular pressure (IOP) the primary modifiable risk factors. Lowering IOP using topical ophthalmic medications is a crucial pillar in management of disease, however, drugs don't work in patients who don't take them and adherence is key to a successful treatment of the disease. Often referred to as the 'silent thief of sight' for its progressive, mostly asymptomatic disease course until advanced stages, adherence is problematic, with approximately only 50% of patients taking their glaucoma medications one year post diagnosis. With an ageing Irish population at increased risk of developing glaucoma, it is imperative that those commencing treatment are adherent since suboptimal adherence is related to poor clinical, social and economic outcomes. The literature regarding barriers and enablers to glaucoma medication adherence is varied. The aim of this review is to better understand these factors. Here, we describe the protocol to conduct a scoping review of the literature, discussing the methods of acquiring, reviewing and analysis of the literature. Methods The review will include searches in EMBASE, PUBMED, Medline, CINAHL and Web of Science electronic databases. A three step search strategy will be used, whereby a preliminary search was carried out of two databases and keywords identified. These keywords will support the development of the search string that will be carried out across four databases. Primary research studies, as well as peer-reviewed grey literature sources, that may include dissertations and theses, reports, guidelines, case studies, and frameworks relevant to the aim of the review will be eligible for inclusion. They must be in English to be included. Non-peer reviewed grey literature sources will not be included. References from papers identified will also be searched. A data extraction framework will guide the literature screening and papers will be independently reviewed by two reviewers to assess eligibility for inclusion. Titles and abstracts will be screened for inclusion, while full text screening of included articles will be carried out by two independent reviewers. A qualitative data analysis will be carried out to assess relevant literature, and data will be presented in a narrative synthesis format comprising of charts and tabular form. Discussion This paper aims to identify enablers and barriers influencing glaucoma medication adherence which will subsequently support discussions with stakeholders to inform the development of an educational intervention in an attempt to improve adherence in the Irish healthcare setting, with the goal to improve visual outcomes for patients.

title: The Gulf of Mexico as a fallback biomass refuge for great white sharks
description: Theory proposing the presence of great white sharks using the Gulf of Mexico as biomass fallback refuge. TITLE: The Gulf of Mexico as a Fallback Biomass Refuge for Great White Sharks Author: Hayden Smith, Independent Researcher; Former Marine Biology Student, Texas A&M University–Corpus Christi, --- Abstract: This paper proposes a novel ecological hypothesis: the Gulf of Mexico may serve as a seasonal fallback biomass refuge for great white sharks (Carcharodon carcharias) during periods of reduced prey availability or increased competition in their primary migratory corridors in the western Atlantic. The Gulf's seasonal surges of blackfin tuna (Thunnus atlanticus), migratory bird fallout along the Central Flyway, and favorable thermal current systems (such as the Loop Current) create a unique, prey-rich environment with comparatively low apex predator competition. This theory integrates marine biology, oceanography, and avian ecology to present a testable model of opportunistic displacement behavior among subadult or displaced great white sharks. It further proposes that these individuals, riding favorable currents, may exploit Gulf resources until Atlantic prey stocks rebound, mirroring ecological fallback patterns seen in other apex predators. 1. Introduction Great white shark migrations have been extensively studied in the North Atlantic, with established pathways between the eastern U.S. coastline, Nova Scotia, and offshore regions near the Azores and Sargasso Sea. However, occasional tracked deviations into the Gulf of Mexico, though rare, suggest that under certain ecological pressures, white sharks may temporarily utilize nontraditional habitats. This paper explores the possibility that these movements are not random but are instead strategic responses to regional prey deficits and interspecific competition. 2. Supporting Observations Satellite tagging efforts (e.g., OCEARCH) have confirmed limited but repeated entries of great white sharks into the Gulf (e.g., individuals like "LeeBeth"). Blackfin tuna spawn seasonally throughout the Gulf and represent a major mid-level biomass surge from March to June and September to November. Migratory birds crossing the Gulf via the Central Flyway suffer significant fallout during spring and fall, contributing to surface biomass events. The Gulf current system (e.g., Loop Current and associated eddies) facilitates passive movement from the Atlantic into the Gulf, especially from Florida and the eastern seaboard. 3. Hypothesis We hypothesize that great white sharks, particularly subadults or displaced individuals, opportunistically migrate into the Gulf of Mexico in response to: Decreased seal or fish abundance in primary Atlantic feeding grounds Social displacement or intra-species competition Availability of seasonal alternative prey (e.g., tuna, migratory birds) Favorable oceanographic conditions enabling low-energy transit This behavior resembles fallback resource use seen in transient orcas, wolves, and other intelligent apex predators under ecosystem stress. 4. Proposed Research Model To evaluate this theory, we recommend: Comparative tagging data review during low Atlantic prey years eDNA or stomach content sampling near high-biomass Gulf areas (e.g., oil rigs, shelf edges) Citizen science reports from offshore oil rig workers to record sightings of sharks, bird fallout, or tuna schools Correlating sightings with Gulf current and biomass maps 5. Conclusion If validated, this theory would expand current models of great white shark behavior and establish the Gulf of Mexico as an ecologically significant secondary habitat. It may also improve our understanding of predator adaptability in the face of climate change, prey collapse, and environmental disruption. Keywords: great white shark, Gulf of Mexico, fallback biomass refuge, blackfin tuna, bird fallout, shark migration, Loop Current, apex predator behavior

title: Investigating Action Topography in Visual Cortex
description: High-level visual cortex contains category-selective areas, embedded within larger-scale topographic maps like animacy and real-world size. Here, we propose action as a key organizing factor shaping the topography and representations in visual cortex, and we assess the ability of deep artificial neural networks (DANNs) to capture this organization. Using fMRI, we examined responses to images of body parts and objects with different degrees of action-properties. In left lateral occipitotemporal cortex, we identified a topographically organized action gradient, with selective and partially overlapping activations for bodies, hands, tools, and manipulable objects. This gradient was arranged along a dorsal-posterior to ventral-anterior axis, with increasing overlap that culminates between body parts and objects that exhibit higher action properties. Multivariate analyses confirmed action as a crucial organizing principle, whereas shape and animacy dominated ventral occipitotemporal cortex and DANNs, which completely lacked an action-based organization. The proposed action dimension unifies seemingly independent regions into a coherent topographic framework, advancing our understanding of visual cortex organization and its divergence from DANN-based models.

title: Compositional Complexity in Text and Images
description: This study investigates whether the human brain uses shared mechanisms to process compositional information in language and vision. In this context, we view compositionality as the ability to derive the meaning of complex expressions based on the meaning of their individual parts and the structure used to combine them. Previous studies on compositional processing in the human brain have primarily focused on language, while a multimodal setting, particularly based on naturalistic stimuli, has been explored less so far. Here, using paired text-image stimuli from the COCO-Actions dataset, we quantify compositional complexity in both text and images with graph-based representations: abstract meaning representations (AMRs) for text and action graphs for images. We then apply both univariate analyses and multivariate pattern analyses (MVPA) to test whether brain activity patterns can decode compositional complexity within and across modalities. Specifically for the MVPA, if classifiers trained on one modality generalize to the other with above chance decoding performance, this might support a modality-independent neural basis of processing compositional complexity. Otherwise, modality-specific mechanisms may be involved.

title: Circulating Endothelin-1 as a Biomarker in Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Systematic Review
description: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by persistent hyperglycemia, insulin resistance, and progressive β-cell dysfunction, leading to widespread microvascular and macrovascular complications. Endothelial dysfunction is recognized as a central pathophysiological mechanism underlying diabetic complications, including diabetic nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy, and cardiovascular disease. Among endothelial-derived mediators, endothelin-1 (ET-1), a potent vasoconstrictor peptide produced primarily by vascular endothelial cells, has emerged as a key regulator of vascular tone, inflammation, oxidative stress, and cellular proliferation. Increasing evidence suggests that circulating ET-1 levels are elevated in individuals with T2DM and may reflect early endothelial injury prior to overt clinical complications. The primary purpose of this systematic review is to critically evaluate and synthesize existing clinical evidence on circulating ET-1 as a biomarker in adults with T2DM. Specifically, this review aims to assess differences in circulating ET-1 levels between individuals with T2DM and non-diabetic controls, examine associations between ET-1 concentrations and glycemic indices (such as fasting blood glucose and HbA1c), and explore relationships between ET-1 levels and diabetes-related complications, including nephropathy, cardiovascular disease, and microvascular dysfunction. Additionally, this review will evaluate the potential of ET-1 as a prognostic or disease-severity biomarker and its responsiveness to antidiabetic or endothelial-targeted therapies. This systematic review will include observational studies (cross-sectional, case–control, and cohort studies) and relevant interventional studies that report circulating ET-1 levels in adult T2DM populations. A comprehensive literature search will be conducted across major electronic databases using predefined search strategies, and study selection will follow the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Data extraction will focus on study characteristics, participant demographics, methods of ET-1 measurement, clinical outcomes, and reported associations. The risk of bias of included studies will be assessed using validated appraisal tools appropriate to study design. The expected outcome of this review is a consolidated and evidence-based understanding of the clinical relevance of circulating ET-1 in T2DM. By systematically summarizing current findings, this review aims to clarify whether ET-1 can serve as a reliable biomarker for endothelial dysfunction, disease progression, or complication risk in T2DM. The findings may help identify gaps in existing research, inform future longitudinal and mechanistic studies, and support the development of ET-1-targeted diagnostic or therapeutic strategies in diabetes care.

title: Anterior Cingulate Cortex for Consistency Curation
description: Control is essential in all complex systems serving any purpose, and cognitive control is claimed to fill a pivotal role for the cognition of natural agents. The Anterior Cingulate Cortex (ACC) is a neural structure, widely believed to be involved in cognitive control. In the human brain, the ACC undoubtedly takes a center position and features several peculiarities. It has been implicated in a wide range of tasks ranging from sensing pain and autonomic regulation to high-level executive functions like error monitoring and abstract control. A sketch how this seemingly irreconcilable plurality can be understood as manifestations of only one general process working in diverse contexts on different content is presented and also how this constitutes evidence for a specific cognitive architecture. Going beyond extant proposals for ACC function, the here presented one recommends an embedding into a very general overarching model of cognition. Discrepancy monitoring highlights deviations between predictions derived from memory content and current activations. A process doing this has recently been proposed as central to the 'Ouroboros Model' under the title of 'consumption analysis'. It is claimed that ONE functional account centered on consistency checking and, based thereupon, the overall minimization of discrepancies ("consistency curation and cultivation") can parsimoniously explain the plentitude of reported observations for the ACC, thus shedding new light on the neural computations, which form the foundations of cognition and, finally, consciousness. A specific "natural" reconciliation of various current conceptualizations and theoretical models is offered, which points out promising directions for future modelling efforts and attempts to harness the findings generally for artificial intelligence.

title: Do object retinal size and conceptual size interact in long-term memory? Using preferred physical sizes
description: This study follows up on the OSF project Do object retinal size and conceptual size interact in long-term memory? The results of that study replicated findings from Pilot 2, showing a main effect of physical size (better memory for physically large than small objects) and a main effect of conceptual size (better memory for conceptually small than large objects), with no interaction between physical (retinal) and conceptual size. To refine the experimental parameters and increase the likelihood of detecting an interaction between retinal and conceptual size (see previous OSF), three key modifications will be implemented. First, instead of using the arbitrary retinal sizes from previous experiments (3° and 21°), the study will adopt data-driven preferred small and large retinal sizes that correspond to the object categories used in the experiment. These preferred sizes are derived from Konkel and Oliva (2011). Second, memory will be tested using a two-alternative forced choice (2-AFC) task rather than an old/new recognition test (see Brady et al., 2023 for review). Third, encoding duration will be reduced to 500 ms to optimize conditions for detecting memory benefits when preferred retinal size aligns with conceptual size (the long durations used in previous studies may have enabled ceiling-level encoding and obscured subtle interaction effects).

title: Artificial intelligence applications in fundus photograph image analysis for diagnosis and screening of brain tumours: A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review aims to evaluate the utility and diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning algorithms applied to fundus and retinal imaging for the detection, diagnosis, and screening of brain tumours and related intracranial pathologies. Brain tumours, including gliomas, pituitary neoplasms, and other intracranial neoplasms, often present with ocular signs such as papilloedema and other optic nerve head abnormalities that can be detected through fundus photography. Early identification of these signs via non-invasive retinal imaging has the potential to facilitate timely diagnosis and improve patient outcomes. The primary purpose of this review is to synthesise current evidence on the performance of AI-based diagnostic tools in analysing retinal images to identify brain tumours and their associated ocular manifestations. Specifically, the review will assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI algorithms - measured by sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - in diverse clinical and screening settings. It will also examine the potential of these technologies to improve early detection, screening processes, and clinical decision-making compared to conventional methods, such as clinical examination and neuroimaging. The review will include original research studies, including diagnostic accuracy studies, cohort studies, case-control studies, and observational reports, that have evaluated AI/ML models applied to fundus or retinal photographs. The studies will be scrutinised for quality and bias using the QUADAS-2 tool to ensure robustness of findings. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI in this context, identification of knowledge gaps, and recommendations for future research and clinical practice. Ultimately, this review aims to inform stakeholders - including clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers - about the feasibility and accuracy of integrating AI-based retinal image analysis into routine screening and diagnostic pathways for brain tumours.

title: the role of eye contact in physiological synchrony
description: This study examines how eye contact influences physiological synchrony and lie detection in dyadic social interactions. Physiological synchrony (PS) is assessed based on the synchrony of heart rate variability (HRV) between two partners, which is continuously recorded using Polar ECG chest straps. In a laboratory setting, psychology students at the University of Konstanz participate in four rounds of interaction: twice with eye contact (visual contact) and twice separated by a barrier (no visual contact), with the order of conditions balanced between partners. During each round, participants alternately make truthful or misleading statements while their partner judges whether each statement is a lie or the truth. We test whether (1) eye contact increases HRV synchrony compared to no eye contact, (2) eye contact improves the accuracy of lie/truth assessment, and (3) higher HRV synchrony is associated with better lie detection. An exploratory mediation analysis examines whether any advantage of eye contact for lie detection can be partially explained by increased physiological synchrony. Theoretical background: Social interactions result in partners achieving temporal coordination across multiple dimensions, e.g. motor coordination, heart rates, and brain activation changes, a phenomenon often referred to as synchrony (Hoehl, Fairhurst & Schirmer, 2021). Physiological synchrony (PS) is characterized by the temporal alignment of physiological parameters, such as heart activity (measured here via Heart Rate Variability, HRV synchrony), autonomic nervous system (ANS) activity, and neural signals. This coupling is integral to successful social exchange and bonding. HRV, specifically, is a well-established quantitative marker of cardiovascular regulation by the ANS, with activation of the parasympathetic component associated with increases in HRV (Thayer & Lane, 2000; Task Force of the European Society of Cardiology and the North American Society of Pacing and Electrophysiology, 1996; Sammito et al., 2024). One of the mechanisms by which PS is achieved is the visual system. Fluctuations in pupillary diameter reflect autonomic rhythms, and are known to correlate significantly with HRV measured via cardiac monitors, suggesting that the autonomic nervous system is linked to the visual system (Parnandi & Gutierrez-Osuna, 2013). This suggests that a crucial element influencing the level of PS is visual input, particularly eye contact (Sato & Sato, 2025). This further extends from the autonomic nervous system to the central nervous system. Previous hyperscanning studies using functional near infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) paradigms have consistently demonstrated that cross-brain synchronization is significantly higher during face-to-face interactions compared to non-face-to-face or online conditions, with coherence often specifically enhanced during tasks involving mutual gaze (Sato & Sato, 2025). For example, higher brain signal synchronization was found in face-to-face scenarios, particularly within the right temporoparietal junction. The right hemisphere, which handles nonverbal information like interpreting emotions and gestures, seems central in coordinating these synchronized processes. Synchronization, which reflects a mechanism for high-level perception of rapidly streaming meaningful social cues, is consistently higher in actual face-to-face settings than in conditions involving eye contact with pre-recorded video or static pictures. Together, these findings suggest that the richness of nonverbal information exchanged through genuine eye contact is a strongly facilitating condition for PS. The importance of eye contact further extends to social cognition and interpersonal judgment (Wohltjena & Wheatley, 2021). Eye contact is thought to facilitate social interaction by signaling moments of high shared attention, an effect that can be measured using pupillary synchrony, a corollary of shared attention. Engaging in eye contact is positively correlated with increased ratings of engagement by conversation partners. Furthermore, eye contact constitutes a core element of the "social engagement system" (Niedźwiecka, 2023). From a physiological perspective, eye contact is compatible with the state warranted by the vagal brake (inhibiting the sympathetic system for social engagement), as suggested by the Polyvagal theory (Porges, 2022). Consequently, some individuals benefit from eye contact by showing enhanced cognitive performance, whereas individuals who are less well regulated may experience interference. This suggests that visual cues are not only powerful synchronizers but can also improve performance in tasks requiring social inference. Based on the established link between visual contact and heightened physiological coupling, and recognizing PS as the temporal alignment of physiological parameters like heart activity, we derive the below hypotheses for the planned study.

description: Artificial intelligence (AI) is predicted to have profound effects on the future of video capsule endoscopy (VCE) technology. The potential lies in improving anomaly detection while reducing manual labour. However, medical data is often sparse and unavailable to the research community, and qualified medical personnel rarely have time for the tedious labelling work. In this respect, we present Kvasir-Capsule, a large VCE dataset collected from examinations at Hospitals in Norway. Kvasir-Capsule consists of 117 videos which can be used to extract a total of 4,741,504 image frames. We have labelled and medically verified 47,238 frames with a bounding box around detected anomalies from 14 different classes of findings. In addition to these labelled images, there are 4,694,266 unlabelled frames included in the dataset. Initial work demonstrates the potential benefits ofAI-based computer-assisted diagnosis systems for VCE. However, they also show that there is great potential for improvements, and the Kvasir-Capsule dataset can play a valuable role in developing better algorithms in order for VCE technology to reach its true potential.

title: Comparison of Clinical and Radiological Outcomes Among Microscope-Assisted, Coaxial Endoscopic, and Non-Coaxial Endoscopic Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion for Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy:
description: Description: Background: Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) is the gold standard for treating cervical spondylotic myelopathy (CSM). While traditional microscope-assisted ACDF is highly effective, it is associated with approach-related complications, such as postoperative dysphagia. Recently, full-endoscopic ACDF has emerged as a promising minimally invasive alternative, further categorized into coaxial and non-coaxial endoscopic techniques. However, there is a lack of comprehensive studies comparing the clinical outcomes, radiological results, and surgical learning curves of these three techniques performed by a single surgeon. Purpose: This retrospective cohort study aims to systematically evaluate and compare the perioperative parameters, clinical efficacy, radiological outcomes, and approach-related complications (specifically dysphagia and dysphonia) among microscope-assisted (Group M), coaxial endoscopic (Group C), and non-coaxial endoscopic ACDF (Group NC). Additionally, this study intends to characterize the surgical learning curve for the two distinct endoscopic techniques. Methods Overview: We will retrospectively analyze the clinical data of 106 CSM patients who underwent single-level or multi-level ACDF performed by a single senior surgeon between January 2021 and December 2024. Patients will be divided into Group M (n=39), Group C (n=33), and Group NC (n=34). Perioperative data (operative time, blood loss, complications) will be collected. Radiological parameters (Cervical Cobb angle, C2-C7 ROM, and adjacent segment height) will be evaluated preoperatively, at 3 months, and 1 year postoperatively. Clinical outcomes, including NDI, JOA, VAS, and the HSS-Dysphagia and Dysphonia Inventory (HSS-DDI), will be assessed at preoperative and multiple postoperative time points (5 days, 3, 6, and 12 months). Statistical analysis will include repeated measures ANOVA, multiple regression analysis to identify independent predictors of clinical improvement, and cumulative sum (CUSUM) analysis to define the learning curve. Expected Outcomes: It is expected that both coaxial and non-coaxial endoscopic groups will demonstrate non-inferior neurological recovery (JOA, NDI) compared to the microscopic group, but with significantly less early postoperative pain (VAS) and lower incidence/severity of early dysphagia (HSS-DDI). The radiological outcomes are expected to be comparable across all three groups, maintaining optimal cervical lordosis and disc height. The learning curve analysis is expected to identify a specific case-number threshold (e.g., 15-20 cases) required for a surgeon to achieve surgical proficiency (stabilized operative time and reduced complication rates) in coaxial and non-coaxial endoscopic ACDF. Ultimately, this study will provide high-quality, real-world evidence to guide spine surgeons in selecting the most appropriate minimally invasive ACDF technique and establishing safe training protocols.

description: This paper demonstrates that the interference patterns observed in double-slit experiments are not the result of wave-particle duality—where particles transform into waves—but are rather phenomena arising from the structural commands imposed upon energy by space. The point of departure for this study is that electrons or photons do not oscillate between being particles and waves; instead, the same solitonic energy simply appears differently depending on whether it is sealed within or released from the spatial structure. In this paper, mass is not an independent entity. Mass is a state that manifests only when solitonic energy vibrations are maintained as standing waves within a cubic spatial structure. When energy is stably confined within this structure, we refer to it as a "particle." When this seal is broken, the energy ceases to be a particle and becomes an informational state propagating over the spatial medium. The rule of space that seals this energy is defined by 6π5. 6π5 is not an arbitrarily adjusted figure but a structural sealing specification that arises inevitably from the convergence of three factors: The 6 degrees of freedom (±x, ±y, ±z) inherent in a hexahedron (cube). The final dimensional closure (L5) required for information to be transmuted into mass, by adding the core axes of the spatial medium—ε (dielectric response) and μ (magnetic response)—to the 3D volume (L3). The rotational phase condition π necessary to maintain a standing wave. In simpler terms, 6π5 is a command issued by space to solitonic vibrations, instructing them to "vibrate only within this range," and it is an informational structure that exists because only then can a standing wave be maintained. title: Frailty discrimination: a scoping review
description: Frailty, a concept which defies consensus definition is nevertheless widely acknowledged to be an important and growing public health issue facing our ageing population [1]. It has become the focus of much research aiming to mitigate its costly adverse outcomes; falls and increased fracture risk, hospitalisation, institutionalisation, dependency and death [2]. Individuals living with frailty are living in an increasingly precarious situation, where insults or shocks (events such as an infection or a sudden bereavement) become harder for their bodies' physiology and social support networks to withstand. In the UK, the 2010 Equalities Act enshrines in law the right to protection from discrimination because of certain protected characteristics, including age and disability [3]. Frailty is not specified as a protected characteristic. However, frailty can be thought of as aligned with disability; given that physical dependency is a common outcome, and overlapping with age; given that frailty, while not an inevitable consequence, becomes more common as we age [4]. In our attempt to offer appropriate healthcare for older people, frailty screening has become the norm in UK primary and secondary healthcare [5, 6]. Particularly ubiquitous is Rockwood's Clinical Frailty scale, a pictorial and vignette grading system developed from the Canadian Study of Health and Aging's frailty index [7]. Guidelines now recommend screening based on our electronic healthcare records and for unplanned hospital admissions [8-10]. This recognition of frailty, suggests a recognition of differential care needs, based on frailty's association with increased risk. However, balancing an assessment of population risk with individualised care is challenging, and frailty-based discrimination could result from both system-level or individual-level problems getting this right. Objectives The aim of this scoping review is to explore frailty-based discrimination, or 'frailism', in order to better characterise the phenomenon and its effects, to examine the extent of its inclusion in any text, and identify gaps for future investigation [10]. title: 2COD: Ocular Dominance Measure
description: It is simple to determine which is a person's more dominant eye. However, outside clinical settings it is currently difficult to assign a reliable objective magnitude to the degree of dominance. For this reason, it is difficult to determine the relation between ocular dominance (O.D.) and cognitive functions that may share a common basis. Here we evaluate a mathematical model of O.D from which we derive a quantitative Index of O.D. The Index is produced by having participants reproduce, on a computer monitor, the outline of a solid disk positioned between themselves and said monitor under three conditions: with both eyes open and with only one of the eyes open. From these drawings we derive a new ocular dominance measure which we call two-camera-ocular-dominance (2COD). We quantify the test-retest reliability of 2COD, and also evaluate whether it is possible to experimentally control it by varying the amount of light arriving at the dominant and non-dominant eye

title: Migration related stress, health and integration in refugees from Syria resettled in Norway (REFUGeXpand)
description: REFUGeXpand is an extension of the 2018 REFUGE-study, a cross-sectional, nationwide, survey-study focusing on migration related stress and mental health among Syrian refugees resettled in Norway. The study's sample frame was defined by the following three criteria: 1) age over 18 years; 2) refugee from Syria; 3) granted residency rights in Norway between 1st Jan 2015 and 31st Dec 2017. Of the roughly 14,200 individuals who met these criteria in the Norwegian population registry, 10,000 were selected to receive study invitations via simple random sampling, of which 902 ultimately participated. Three waves of data-collections were initially planned, however, due to a low response rate at wave 1, the second and third waves were cancelled. Important open-access publications from the REFUGE-study, including a cohort profile paper which describes design, participants and other methodological elements of the study, are uploaded in the "Files" section below. The study was preregistered in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03742128, link provided under Wiki). REFUGeXpand builds on this initial study in several ways, extending the sample and types of data available. A mixed-methods, cohort-based project, it comprises several sub-studies and study populations: -- REFUGE-cohort, n=902: all participants from the 2018 survey-based REFUGE-study -- RBMI-cohort, n=14,200: the sampling frame for the REFUGE-study, i.e., all Syrian refugees being resettled in Norway between January 1st, 2015 and December 31st, 2017 -- NORpop, n=10,000; a control population randomly drawn from the Norwegian population registry -- Smaller qualitative samples comprised of both Syrian and Ukrainian refugees The project will use multiple data sources, including longitudinal registry data on demographic factors, primary and specialist healthcare service utilization, drug prescription and work participation/marginalization, all of which will be linked for the overall study sample consisting of Syrian refugees and the Norwegian control population (n=24,200). We will also link these registry data to survey data from the REUFGE-study (n=902) to allow more detailed investigations. In addition, qualitative interviews will be conducted separately. The overall aim of the project is to explore how pre- and peri-migration stressful experiences (e.g., exposure to torture or other potentially traumatic experiences) intersect with post-migration factors/stressors (e.g., financial difficulties) and intra-individual risk- and protective factors to shape long-term health and integration trajectories. Multiple publications are planned for the REFUGeXpand project and they are/will be pre-registered as "Components" of this main registration (please see "Components" section for details). NOTE: Since some of the planned projects have been embargoed as per OSFs' policies, making the components not visible to the public, please consult the document "Pre-registered papers" under the "Files" section for a full list of currently pre-registered analyses. The project will generate valuable evidence of relevance to policymakers, healthcare providers and other stakeholders, which may ultimately positively impact health and integration in resettled refugees in Norway and beyond.

title: Predicting Anti–VEGF Treatment Demands and Outcomes for Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration (nAMD), Diabetic Macular Oedema (DMO), and Retinal Vein Occlusion (RVO)-Associated Macular Oedema U
description: Objective: To map the evidence concerning the use of machine learning (ML) to predict treatment burden and outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema in order to understand the current state of the art and the gaps. Introduction: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD), diabetic macular oedema (DMO), and retinal vein occlusion (RVO) associated macular oedema are some of the leading causes of visual loss globally.1 Intravitreal anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) injections are currently used to treat such diseases.1 The treatment course and outcomes for each patient is variable and thus individualised treatment techniques are needed.2 Two of the most pressing issues are estimating treatment burden (e.g., patients who need fewer vs. more intravitreal injections) and visual prognosis (e.g., good vs. poor responders) in individual patients.2 This research aims to assess the potential of ML to predict treatment burden and outcomes to personalise anti-VEGF treatment in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO. We seek to understand the types of ML approaches that have been explored, their maturity, reported outcomes, and real-world applicability. Eligibility criteria: Studies will be included if they focus on ML algorithms that predict anti-VEGF treatment burden and/or outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema. The included studies will consist of full-length original research journal articles written or translated into English. We will exclude other types of literature (i.e., not full-length journal articles, not a report of original research and not centred on ML algorithms that predict anti-VEGF treatment burden and/or outcomes in patients with nAMD, DMO, and RVO-associated macular oedema). Publication dates of included studies will be from January 2000 onwards. Methods: Five academic databases will be searched (Ovid Medline, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, IEEE, and ACM Digital Library). Search strings for each database were formulated in conjunction with a Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School librarian. Studies will be uploaded to Covidence (literature management software), and duplicates will be removed. Studies will be screened by two independent screeners (SG & AYO). Disagreements will be resolved with a discussion with a third author (DM). SG will conduct a descriptive analysis of the data. We will use the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) for reporting our study, and we will publish our protocol on the Open Science Framework (OSF).3 Results: We will report the number and type of included evidence, as well as any pertinent study characteristics. Main topics of interest and significant outcomes will also be presented. Inferences will be presented in an appropriate diagrammatic or tabular format. Conclusions: Based on the key concepts and topics extrapolated from the selected studies, the scoping review will aim to explore the breadth and depth of the current literature and address any knowledge gaps that can hold the potential to inform future research and future algorithm development. Keywords: Intravitreal injections, ophthalmology, artificial intelligence, systematic scoping review

title: The impact of dance movement therapy on traumatized refugee women - A randomized controlled trial
description: Research Question: Can an eight session dance movement therapy program improve the health of traumatized refugee women? Specifically, we examine: 1. What is the effect of DMT on the reduction of trauma symptoms (depression, anxiety, stress and trauma proper), and the increase in coping compared to waiting list controls [data from standardized questionnaires (here RHS-15), in form of an individual interview; H1 (H1.1-H1.5)]; 2. What is the effect of DMT on physical, cognitive, emotional, and social, spiritual and cultural outcomes? (data from focus groups; H2: Changes will be reported on at least three out of six outcomes of the Dunphy Outcomes Framework, DOF); 3. Which live circumstances and demographic variables influence the results (control variables: age, education, income, and family status; exploratory analysis). Umbrella Project: This project is part of a wider European multi-center study (European student initiative of the efpsa) that aims to assess the benefits of dance movement therapy for traumatized refugee women. The initiative is coordinated at the University of Bourgogne, France, with five envisioned European sites of data collection. Data will be aggregated for the wider project (see study protocol / ethics approval of U Bourgogne, 24-01-2023). This study protocol describes only the trial at the node in Heidelberg, Germany, as a substudy. This substudy was conducted at SRH University Heidelberg in cooperation with University of Heidelberg and INTER-ACTIONS dance studio. Its aim is to contribute to the evidence-base of DMT for traumatized refugees. Design: This randomized controlled trial will be run in two successive intervention groups (Group A from January to March 2023, Group B from April to June 2023). For the first group 14-20 women will be randomized into two groups. All will be interviewed in January, the control group will receive the intervention from April to June. Intervention group participants of both Group A and Group B will be included. This design will likely cause more women to be in the intervention group, which we will account for in the statistical analysis.

description: We propose a novel machine learning paradigm rooted in *Genesis Calculus*, shifting from static optimization to emergent coherence maximization. Unlike traditional methods that minimize loss against labeled data, this framework evolves a relational field Rc(t, x) under the Genesis PDE G(Rc) = 0, maximizing the emergence functional J = R T 0 kρnc dt with ρc = 1 V R Ω |Rc|2 d3x. Formulated as an optimal-control problem with adjoints, it includes stability regularizers to prevent blow-ups and a coherence micro-update to boost relational alignment. We derive the adjoint equation, propose an IMEX-based algorithm, and introduce an emergent-truth criterion. Toy experiments demonstrate discovery ahead of data. The framework generalizes across neural, physical, and symbolic learning systems, enabling relational discovery beyond static datasets. This framework generalizes learning as a dynamical process, offering implications for AI, control theory, and models of emergent cognition. description: BRIEF BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE FOR THE REVIEW Incretin based drugs are a relatively new class of medications used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. They fall into two categories: dipeptidyl peptidase 4 (DPP-4) inhibitors and glucagon-like peptide 1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA) and were first approved for use in 20061, 2 with millions of prescriptions written yearly. They are typically used as second or third-line agents3 and have a favorable effect on body weight. They also pose a minimal risk of hypoglycemia. These drugs work by increasing incretin levels, which leads to increased insulin secretion, decreased gastric emptying, and decreased blood glucose levels. The 2019 guidelines from the American Diabetes Association recommend that factors such as comorbid and coexisting diseases be considered alongside clinical evidence when deciding on the most appropriate anti-glycemic agent for the management of a patient's type 2 diabetes4. There has been an evolution of the treatment goal for diabetes in recent years, with the primary objective moving from preventing imminent mortality to normalizing glucose levels with the intent of forestalling diabetic complications5. Diabetic retinopathy is the most common microvascular complication associated with diabetes. It occurs when glucose occludes the vessel supplying blood to the retina, leading to leakage or bleeding. To compensate for its presence, the eyes grow new blood vessels that may be faulty. There are usually no symptoms in the early stage of the disease, but later symptoms include blurry vision, floating spots in the vision, and blindness. Other eye conditions such as diabetic macular edema and neovascular glaucoma can also be caused by diabetic retinopathy6. Randomized controlled trials that examined this outcome among incretin-based drugs have shown mixed results. The SUSTAIN-6 trial showed an increased risk of diabetic retinopathy with semaglutide use compared to placebo7, but other trials involving other incretin based drugs showed inconclusive results8-11. These trials, however, looked at macrovascular complications (a composite endpoint of myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, and cardiovascular death) as the primary outcome and only assessed retinopathy as a secondary (and possibly underpowered) outcome. There have also been observational studies that assessed the risk of diabetic retinopathy with incretin-based drugs, but they provided conflicting results12-15. Given the heterogeneous evidence available and clinical consequences of diabetic retinopathy in this patient population, we will conduct a systematic review to examine this potential drug safety issue. The overall aim of this systematic review with meta-analysis of observational studies is to examine the risk of diabetic retinopathy with incretin-based drug use relative to the use of other anti-hyperglycemia drugs among patients with type 2 diabetes

title: Forward optic flow is prioritised in visual awareness independently of walking direction
description: Abstract: When two different images are presented separately to each eye, one experiences smooth transitions between them. Previous studies have shown that exposure to signals from other senses can enhance perceptual awareness of stimulation-congruent images. Surprisingly, despite our ability to infer perceptual consequences from bodily movements, evidence that action can have an analogous influence on visual experience is scarce and mainly limited to local (hand) movements. Here, we investigated whether one's direction of locomotion affects perceptual awareness of optic flow patterns. Participants walked forwards and backwards on a treadmill while viewing highly-realistic visualisations of self-motion in a virtual environment. We hypothesised that visualisations congruent with walking direction would predominate in visual awareness over incongruent ones, and that this effect would increase with the precision of one's active proprioception. These predictions were not confirmed: optic flow consistent with forward locomotion was prioritised in visual awareness independently of walking direction and proprioceptive abilities. Our results suggest that kinaesthetic-proprioceptive processing plays a limited role in shaping visual experience. This seems at odds with Bayesian accounts of perception but is in-line with Cancellation theories, which imply that crossmodal influences of self-generated signals are suppressed as a redundant source of information about the outside world. title: Effect of risk expression using likelihood ratios or natural frequencies in Bayesian inference tasks
description: Transparent, unbiased and evidence-based communication of risks of medical procedures is an integral component of shared decision making, empowering patients to make choices in accordance with their own values (IQWIG – Allgemeine Methoden, S. 136, 2022; Elwyn, 2012). There is ample evidence that risk communication using natural frequencies rather than conditional probabilities facilitates Bayesian Reasoning, improving participants' performance in Bayesian textbook inference tasks such as the interpretation of diagnostic or screening test results (Akl, Oxman, 2011; McDowell and Jacobs, 2017). Consequently, the German "Good-Practice"-Guideline on health communication advocates the use of natural frequencies in patient guidelines (GPGI, 2015). However, approximately 3 out of 4 people fail to correctly determine the positive predictive value of a test when sensitivity, false-positive rate and prevalence are given in the natural frequency format (McDowell and Jacobs, 2017). Alternatively, odds and likelihood ratios (LR) can be used to calculate the risk of having a disease given a positive or negative test result. The pre-test odds represent the ratio of the number of people with the disease to the number of people without the disease. To calculate the post-test odds of having the disease, the pre-test odds are multiplied by the positive or negative likelihood ratio (LR) of the diagnostic test used. The LR is a compound indicator of test accuracy, calculated by the sensitivity and specificity of a diagnostic test (Grimes & Schulz, 2005). Calculating the post-test odds requires explicit acknowledgement of the base rate. Thereby, insight into the influence of the base rate on post-test probabilities and its computation in the setting of varying base-rates might be facilitated. In contrast, in the natural frequency format, the base-rate has already been broken down into its individual components and can thus be disregarded. The evidence on the use of odds and LR as an alternative to conditional probabilities or natural frequencies remains scarce. However, some studies suggest that risk expression using odds and LR could also facilitate Bayesian reasoning compared to conditional probabilities (e.g. Juslin, 2011). It is still unclear whether odds and LR could be an alternative to the established risk communication formats, and to our knowledge, no head-to-head trial comparing natural frequencies with likelihood ratios in Bayesian inference tasks has been conducted to date. Thus, in an randomized repeated-measures trial, we assess the performance of participants in the calculation of post-test probabilities and post-test odds when presented with either natural frequencies or odds and likelihood Ratios. title: Foveal representation for briefly presented peripheral visual stimuli
description: Vision shapes our everyday experience, yet many mechanisms remain poorly understood. For example, when an object suddenly appears in the periphery – such as a car while crossing the road – it is still unclear how the brain represents it in order to make fast, accurate decisions. Prior work has suggested that peripheral objects can be remapped onto foveal primary visual cortex (V1), perhaps leveraging its high resolution to aid discrimination (Williams et al., 2008; Fan et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2024; Constantino et al., 2025). However, to date this phenomenon has only been observed using one particular task, which requires comparing two peripheral stimuli and determining whether they are exactly the same or not. This task may particularly encourage the use of explicit visual imagery and remapping to fovea as an effective strategy. Here we investigate whether this phenomenon of foveal remapping generalizes to cases when only one stimulus is presented, which would demonstrate the general principles of remapping, which apply to situations more broadly. We use novel stimuli in a categorization task, while participants undergo functional magnetic resonance imaging. Specifically, participants view briefly presented objects (for 100 ms) in the periphery while fixating centrally and making object categorization judgments. Stimuli are continuous morphs between object pairs (e.g., dog–bear, tractor–truck), while the categorization task always required binary (dog vs. bear) decisions. We investigate whether foveal parts of early visual cortex contain information about peripherally presented stimuli. Specifically, we will examine whether remapped content reflects pictorially-copied information from peripheral presentation or a task-reformatted, category-focused representation. Additionally, we will test whether foveal engagement is varied with difficulty of the categorization. The results will clarify the role of V1's foveal circuitry for peripheral vision, and more broadly expand our understanding of the visual system.

At the same time, recognizing strike-slip reactivation of normal faults in sedimentary basins is critical, as it may alter and impact basin physiography, accommodation and sediment supply and dispersal. Motivated by this, we present a study of a reactivated normal fault zone in the Liassic limestones and shales of Somerset, UK, to elucidate the effects of strike-slip reactivation of normal faults, and the inherent deformation of relay zones that separate the original normal fault segments. The fault zone, initially extensional, exhibits a series of relay zones between right-stepping segments, with the steps between the segments having subsequently become contractional due to sinistral strike-slip movement. The relay zones have therefore been steepened and are cut by a series of connecting faults with reverse and strike-slip components. The studied fault zone, and comparison with larger-scale natural examples, lead us to conclude that the relays-turned-contractional-steps are associated with (i) complex fault and fracture networks that accommodate shortening, (ii) anomalously high numbers of fractures and faults, (iii) layer parallel slip and (iv) folding and uplift. Comparison with published statistics from global relay zones shows that whereas the reactivated relay zones feature aspect ratios similar to those of unreactivated relay zones, bed dips within reactivated relay zones are significantly steeper than unreactivated relay zones. Given the potential of reactivated relay zones to form areas of local uplift, they may affect basin structure and may also form potential traps for hydrocarbon or other fluids. The elevated faulting and fracturing, on the other hand, means reactivated relays are also likely loci for enhanced up-fault flow.

title: Foveal vision contribution to peripheral object recognition
description: In this study we use a procedure introduced by Fan et al. (2016). Participants are presented with visual stimuli in the periphery. They have to identify whether the stimulus matched a learned object. At fixation a mask is presented. The main variable is the delay between stimulus onset and mask onset. A feedback signal specific to the foveal cortex has been proposed. The evidence comes from neuroimaging studies showing that when observers are presented with an object in the periphery, object category information can be decoded from the foveal retinotopic cortex (Williams et al., 2008) and that performance is affected by transcranial magnetic stimulation applied to the foveal cortex (Chambers et al., 2013). In addition to the neuroimaging studies, psychophysical experiments have manipulated the information presented in central and peripheral vision. The results show that processing of a visual object in the periphery is modulated by masking information at the fovea (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Yu & Shim, 2016). These psychophysical studies therefore support the feedback hypothesis. In the paradigm used by Fan et al. (2016) observers performed a task on peripheral stimuli, and noise was presented in fovea at different stimulus onset asynchronies (SOAs). Observers maintained fixation on a central mark, and fixation behaviour was monitored thanks to an eye-tracker. Importantly, the noise caused impairment only for SOA of 250-ms, and only for tasks that required processing of object shape. The study also included fMRI data showing shape representation in the foveal cortex. Fan et al. report several control experiments. In one of these a shape has to be memorised by the participant and the task is to detect whether the stimulus in the periphery matched the one in memory. This peripheral stimulus was presented only in the upper right field, while the noise was again in the foveal region. The stimuli were 3D rendered abstract shapes, known in the literature as spikies (de Beeck et al. 2006). Our Experiment is a conceptual replication of the control experiment reported in Fan et al. (2016). Because this experiment was only a control we were unable to locate all details of the methods. We have, however, kept as close as possible to the original design. In particular we will use a match to memory task, we will use the same class of stimuli (spikies) as Fan et al., and an increased power. The mask will also be similar and include a dynamic set of random dots changing over time. The SOA levels will be as in Fan et al.: 50, 150, 250, 350 and 450 mse plus the no-noise baseline condition.

description: 1. Camera traps have great potential for generating wildlife insights by providing high resolution site-specific data. Methods of data collection and analysis reliant on these tools for population density estimation can be relatively resource intensive, hindering their mainstream adoption. 2. The wild boar study resulted in a realistic density estimate, which can be used as a baseline when assessing future fluctuations in population density. 4. title: Modulation of visual contrast sensitivity with transcranial random noise stimulation
description: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) has been shown to significantly improve visual perception. These performance improvements manifested as both (i) after-effects of visual training combined with tRNS (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Contemori et al., 2019; Herpich et al., 2019) and (ii) acute effects during tRNS (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; Ghin et al., 2018; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). It has been postulated that the Stochastic resonance (SR) phenomenon underlie noise-induced signal enhancement in studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual processing (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). SR describes the phenomenon that the response of nonlinear systems to weak, subthreshold signals can be enhanced by adding an optimal level of random noise (Moss et al., 2004; McDonnell and Abbott, 2009). One important feature indicative of the SR phenomenon is that noise benefits are a function of noise intensity and exhibit an inverted U-shape relationship. Thus, while the optimal level of noise benefits performance, excessive noise is detrimental (van der Groen and Wenderoth 2016; van der Groen et al. 2018; Pavan et al. 2019). Previous studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual detection performance have shown that noise stimulation was particularly beneficial when the visual stimuli were presented with near-threshold intensity (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018; Battaglini et al., 2019). Currently, it is unknown whether signal enhancement via SR could be achieved separately within different neural substrates along the retino-cortical pathway. Inducing SR via tRNS offers a unique opportunity to investigate this question. Here we plan a series of three experiments which will be executed in three separate sessions. Experiment 1: TRNS over primary visual cortex (V1) has been shown previously to improve visual contrast detection (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016). Here we aim to replicate these results in a new cohort and to determine the optimal tRNS intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 2: Previous research has suggested that the retina and the optical nerve are highly susceptible to alternating currents (Schutter and Hortensius, 2010). Improvement in vision was reported after repetitive transorbital alternating current stimulation over the retina, in studies involving patients with optic neuropathy or after optic nerve lesions (Gall et al., 2010; Fedorov et al., 2011). The retina and the optic nerve are an interesting target because they can be reliably reached even with low transcranial electrical stimulation intensities since the eyeball is an excellent conductor. Here we will test whether tRNS applied to the retina and the optic nerve improves visual contrast detection in accordance with the SR mechanism. We will apply different tRNS intensities to determine the optimal intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 3: It is currently unknown whether SR effects are additive when noise is applied to connected yet anatomically remote neural populations. Here we will investigate whether simultaneous application of tRNS to the retina and V1 causes additive effects.

title: Family Support Interventions for Type 2 Diabetes Management. A Scoping Review
description: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is a growing global health crisis, characterized by insulin resistance and progressive β-cell dysfunction. It accounts for more than 90% of diabetes cases worldwide and is associated with significant morbidity and mortality due to complications such as cardiovascular disease, nephropathy, neuropathy, and retinopathy. In recent years, there has been a shift toward more holistic and patient-centred approaches to diabetes care. One area receiving increased attention is the role of family support in enhancing diabetes self-management (DSM). Family members often serve as informal caregivers, providing emotional, instrumental, and informational support. They influence dietary choices, physical activity routines, and medication-taking behaviours, particularly in collectivist cultures where family decision-making is central to daily life. Moreover, family involvement can help address barriers to DSM such as health literacy gaps, psychological distress, and social isolation. This scoping review aims to map the current landscape of research on family support interventions for Type 2 Diabetes Management (T2DM). Specifically, it seeks to: 1. Identify how family is defined and involved in DSM interventions; 2. Categorize the types and structures of family-focused strategies employed; 3. Examine the reported outcomes for both patients and family members. By synthesizing the breadth of existing studies, this review will offers insight into how family-centred care can be leveraged to improve diabetes outcomes across diverse populations and healthcare settings.

title: Investigating metamorphopsia following macula involving rhegmatogenous retinal detachment
description: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) is characterized by the intrusion of liquefied vitreous into the space between the sensory retina and retinal pigment epithelium through retinal breaks. It is one of the most common sight-threatening ophthalmic surgical emergencies. Refinements in pars plana vitrectomy (PPV), scleral buckle (SB), and pneumatic retinopexy (PnR) over the past several decades have led to excellent retinal reattachment rates. Improvements in surgical techniques have led to 90% success in the surgical repair of RRD. However, anatomical reattachment of the retina does not ensure complete recovery of visual function and despite successful retinal reattachment and anatomical improvements postoperatively, many patients report unsatisfactory functional outcomes. A common postoperative complaint is metamorphopsia. Previous studies have investigated the incidence of metamorphopsia following RRD and claim the rate to be from 24% to 88.6%. Several studies have also investigated the risk factors associated with worse metamorphopsia symptoms, and these include the presence of retinal shift, outer retinal folds, subretinal fluid, specific surgical techniques such as gas involvement or silicone in PPV, integrity of retinal layers, and retinal thickness. Despite these factors, there is limited information as to whether the duration of visual symptoms or the duration of retinal detachment impacts the rates of developing metamorphopsia and its severity. Our study aims to study these factors and its association with metamorphopsia onset and severity. Understanding the impact of delay between the duration of symptoms and surgery can help better predict outcomes and guide best practices.

title: Superposition and Interaction: A Physical-Interaction Perspective on Quantum Measurement and the Double-Slit Experiment
description: This paper proposes a physically grounded interpretation of quantum measurement in which superposition is the natural state of isolated systems, while particle-like outcomes arise from inevitable physical interactions with the environment or measuring devices. The approach retains the standard mathematical formalism of quantum mechanics but reorganizes its conceptual structure to place interaction—understood as the exchange of energy, momentum, or information—at the center of the measurement process. It offers a unified explanation of the double-slit, delayed-choice, and quantum-eraser experiments, and suggests experimentally testable ways to link interaction strength to decoherence and the emergence of classicality.

title: Implante de dexametasona biodegradável para tratamento de edema macular após oclusão do ramo da veia da retina e oclusão da veia central da retina - uma revisão sistemática
description: Resumo A oclusão da veia retiniana é considerada a segunda causa mais comum de deficiência visual por doença vascular retiniana, depois da retinopatia diabética. Estima-se que aproximadamente 28 milhões de adultos sejam acometidos por esta doença em todo o mundo. Múltiplos mecanismos estão implicados no desenvolvimento do edema macular, levando a deficiência visual que pode ser reversível (estágios agudos) ou irreversível (longo prazo). Por esse motivo, uma abordagem eficaz no tratamento do edema macular é de suma importância para evitar danos irreversíveis à função visual. Objetivo Avaliar a eficácia (alteração da acuidade visual corrigida, espessura central da retina) e segurança (efeitos adversos gerais e graves e pressão intraocular) do implante biodegradável de dexametasona em pacientes com oclusão da veia retiniana. Métodos Uma revisão sistemática da literatura foi realizada incluindo ensaios clínicos comparativos que avaliaram o implante intravítreo de dexametasona de 0,7 mg. A qualidade dos estudos foi avaliada utilizando a ferramenta RoB 2.0. E a força de recomendação da evidência foi estimada considerando o GRADE. Resultados Cinco estudos foram incluídos na síntese de dados. O acompanhamento médio dos pacientes variou de 6 a 12 meses. No sexto mês de acompanhamento foi observado melhora da acuidade visual nos pacientes tratados com implante intravítreo de dexametasona, sendo que o grupo que recebeu o implante quando necessário apresentou melhor resposta do que naqueles tratados com aplicações a cada 4 meses. Conclusão O implante de dexametasona foi eficaz em pacientes não responsivos ao tratamento com anti-VEGF, mostrando resultados melhores para acuidade visual quando administrado ao longo de 12 meses. Apresentou eficácia similar à triancinolona intravítreo e foi superior ao procedimento simulado nos desfechos de eficácia.
keywords: Revisão sistemática; implante biodegradável de dexametasona; edema macular; oclusão do ramo da veia da retina

title: Optic nerve point-of-care ultrasonography in the assessment of findings suggestive of intracranial hypertension in critically ill patients: a scoping review protocol focusing on nurses' decision-makin
description: Intracranial hypertension (ICH) is caused by various neurological conditions such as trauma, tumors, and strokes. Measuring the optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has proven to be a promising alternative for the early detection of ICH, as this diameter reflects increased intracranial pressure (ICP). The use of POCUS by nurses in critical settings such as ICUs and emergency departments can expedite triage and clinical decision-making, especially in locations with limited access to imaging exams. However, there are still gaps in practice and knowledge regarding this tool. This scoping review aims to investigate the applicability, accuracy, and impact of POCUS in nursing practice, contributing to the development of evidence-based clinical guidelines and strengthening the role of nursing in the care of critically ill patients. The research question was developed according to the PCC strategy. Therefore, the research question is: What scientific evidence is available regarding the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the optic nerve in assessing signs suggestive of intracranial hypertension in critically ill patients, with an emphasis on supporting clinical decision-making by nurses? This is a scoping review guided by the recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute and will follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols – extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The review will be conducted using the databases PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Scielo, Embase, Cochrane, and CINAHL, as well as a selection of grey literature from the CAPES database and Google Scholar. The keywords ("Intracranial Hypertension," "Ultrasonography," "Nurse," and "Optic Nerve") and indexing terms from the articles will serve as the basis for the search strategies. Studies will initially be selected based on title and abstract by independent reviewers, who will apply inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data from the articles included in the scoping review will be extracted by two independent reviewers using the JBI Template Source of Evidence Details, Characteristics and Results Extraction tool and a custom tool developed by the reviewers. The synthesis of included studies will be performed qualitatively, with results organized into tables and figures.

title: "Stare-in-the-Crowd" Effect & Anxiety
description: Eye gaze conveys crucial information for social interactions, with straight versus averted gaze triggering distinct emotional and cognitive processes. The "stare-in-the-crowd" effect exemplifies such differential visual processing of gaze direction, in more recent reports also in interaction with head orientation. title: Study 2: All in your head?
description: The findings in Study 1 showed that disclosing GenAI involvement in creative processes A) changed how creative workers approach the creative task of generating an image with the help of a GenAI tool (second-order effect) and B) affected recipients' evaluation of the generated images (first-order effect). In this follow-up study, we aim to investigate the second-order effects side in more detail and disentangle underlying theoretical mechanisms. We aim to address the following research questions: 1. Understand the design process that resulted in these images for: AI disclosed to laypersons; AI non-disclosed, AI disclosed to Expert panel, AI disclosed (no information on expert status) 2. How did the process of generating images with a GenAI change during working on the task given the designers anticipate disclosure? 3. What do the designers believe about the panel's beliefs, and how does this perception impact their process? 4. How do perceptions of recipients differ depending on whether the AI involvement is disclosed to them? Thus, we aim to conduct a two-stage experiment. In Stage 1, we will ask designers to create an image on the topic "Portrait of a Good Life" with the help of a text-to-image generative AI model (GenAI). All designers will be informed that a panel of recipients will evaluate their images in the second stage of our experiment. In a 2x2 between-subject design, we will inform the designers that a panel of experts versus laypeople (source) will evaluate their image and that the involvement of GenAI will be either disclosed or not disclosed (disclosure). In Stage 2, a panel of recipients (experts versus laypeople) will evaluate images generated in Stage 1 under two disclosure conditions (disclosed versus nondisclosed).

title: DEEP LEARNING FOR AUTOMATED DETECTION AND CLASSIFICATION OF TEMPOROMANDIBULAR JOINT DISORDERS: A SCOPING REVIEW
description: Title: Deep Learning for Automated Detection and Classification of Temporomandibular Joint Disorders: A Scoping Review Temporomandibular Joint Disorders (TMDs) are a significant clinical challenge associated with pain, functional impairment, and reduced quality of life. Traditional diagnostic approaches—such as manual interpretation of MRI, CBCT, CT, or panoramic images—can be time-consuming, subjective, and affected by inter-observer variability. With recent advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) techniques, automated detection and classification of TMDs has emerged as a promising solution to enhance diagnostic accuracy and efficiency. This scoping review systematically maps current evidence on deep learning applications for diagnosing TMDs, including anterior disc displacement (ADD), osteoarthritis, condylar degeneration, and degenerative joint disease. Using PRISMA-ScR guidelines, a comprehensive search across PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, Google Scholar, and Wiley identified 15 eligible studies published between 2015 and 2025. Across these studies, models such as Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), U-Net, ResNet, VGG16, MobileNetV2, YOLO, and ensemble architectures demonstrated high diagnostic performance—achieving accuracy levels up to 99%, sensitivity up to 98%, and significant improvements in segmentation precision. Findings indicate that deep learning can reduce diagnostic time by up to 50%, standardize interpretation, and serve as an effective decision-support tool for clinicians. Despite promising results, challenges remain related to dataset diversity, external validation, reproducibility, and clinical integration. Future research should focus on multi-center datasets, multimodal learning, standardized benchmarking, explainability methods such as Grad-CAM, and ethical frameworks for AI deployment in healthcare. This review highlights the potential of deep learning to transform TMD diagnostics, contributing to faster, more accurate, and more consistent radiologic evaluation, ultimately improving clinical outcomes for patients.

title: Preserved extra-foveal processing of object semantics in Alzheimer's disease
description: Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients underperform on a range of tasks requiring semantic processing, but it is unclear whether this impairment is due to a generalised loss of semantic knowledge or to issues in accessing and selecting such information from memory. The objective of this eye-tracking visual search study was to determine whether semantic expectancy mechanisms known to support object recognition in healthy adults are preserved in AD patients. Furthermore, as AD patients are often reported to be impaired in accessing information in extra-foveal vision, we investigated whether that was also the case in our study. Twenty AD patients and twenty age-matched controls searched for a target object among an array of distractors presented extra-foveally. The distractors could be either semantically related or unrelated to the target (e.g., a car in an array with other vehicles or kitchen items). Results showed that semantically related objects were detected with more difficulties than semantically unrelated objects by both groups, but more markedly by the AD group. Participants looked earlier and for longer at the critical objects when these were semantically unrelated to the distractors. Search responses and neuropsychological performances of AD patients did not correlate. Our findings show that AD patients can process the semantics of objects and access it in extra-foveal vision. This suggests that their impairments in semantic processing may reflect difficulties in accessing semantic information rather than a generalised loss of semantic memory.
