title: Thermodynamic Study of MWCNT Sensors: Graphene and Nitrogen Carbide Nanosheets for Drug Detection
description: This study explores the therapeutic potential of essential oils, particularly (R)-(−)-carvone and (S)-(+)-carvone, which, despite their pharmacological benefits, are hindered by low solubility and instability. The aim is to evaluate silver nanoclusters (Ag13, Ag13−, Ag13+) as carriers to enhance carvone's anticancer, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory efficacy. Using a computational framework, Density Functional Theory (DFT), Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM), Electron Localization Function (ELF), and molecular docking were applied to assess adsorption stability, electronic features, and receptor binding affinities in gas, water, and ethanol phases. Results indicate that carvone strongly adsorbs on cationic and anionic Ag13 clusters, while neutral clusters are unfavorable, with non-covalent van der Waals interactions ensuring controlled release. The complexes exhibit enhanced polarity, solubility in polar solvents, and red-shifted UV–Vis absorption, allowing optical detection. Vibrational analyses confirm structural stability, while molecular docking reveals superior receptor affinities, especially toward HER2 (anticancer) compared to Staphylococcus aureus (antibacterial) and TNF-α (anti-inflammatory). These findings confirm the thermodynamic and biological feasibility of silver–carvone nanocomplexes as multifunctional drug carriers. In conclusion, this computational work establishes Ag13 nanoclusters as promising candidates for overcoming essential oils' limitations, offering innovative strategies for nanomedicine-based cancer, antibacterial, and anti-inflammatory therapies.

title: On the scales of dynamic topography in whole-mantle convection models - preprint version
description: Mantle convection shapes Earth's surface by generating dynamic topography. Observational constraints and regional convection models suggest that surface topography could be sensitive to mantle flow for wavelengths as short as 1,000 km and 250 km, respectively. At these spatial scales, surface processes including sedimentation and relative sea-level change occur on million year timescales. However, time dependent global mantle flow models do not predict small-scale dynamic topography yet. Here, we present 2D-spherical annulus numerical models of mantle convection with large radial and lateral viscosity contrasts. We first identify the range of Rayleigh number, internal heat production rate and yield stress for which models generate plate-like behaviour, surface heat flow, surface velocities and topography distribution comparable to Earth's. These models produce both whole mantle convection and small-scale convection in the upper mantle, which results in small- (< 500 km) to large-scale (> 10^4 km) dynamic topography, with a spectral power for intermediate scales (500 to 10^4 km) comparable to estimates of present-day residual topography. Timescales of convection and the associated dynamic topography vary from five to several hundreds of millions of years. For a Rayleigh number of 10^7, we investigate how lithosphere yield stress variations (10-50 MPa) and the presence of deep thermochemical heterogeneities favour small-scale (200-500 km) and intermediate scale (500-10^4 km) dynamic topography by controlling the formation of small scale convection and the number and distribution of subduction zones, respectively. The interplay between mantle convection and lithosphere dynamics generates a complex spatial and temporal pattern of dynamic topography consistent with constraints for Earth.

title: Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Diabetes Outcomes in Adults: A Scoping Review
description: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a serious and debilitating psychiatric disorder that develops after exposure to a traumatic event, such as violence or natural disaster (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). Individuals with PTSD often experience chronic and disabling symptoms that have far-ranging effects on mental and physical health (Krantz et al., 2022). Prior research has established a clear link between PTSD and a range of physical health problems and diagnoses (Pacella, Hruska, & Delahanty, 2013; Schnurr, Wachen, Green, & Kaltman, 2021), including diabetes (Miller-Archie, 2014; Roberts et al., 2016; Vaccarino et al., 2015). A meta-analytic study of five studies found that patients with PTSD had a 49% increased risk of diabetes compared with non-PTSD controls (Vancampfort et al., 2016) across a range of populations (e.g., veterans, community-dwelling nurses, post-9/11 survivors; Miller-Archie, 2014; Roberts et al., 2016; Vaccarino et al., 2015). Despite clear associations between PTSD and diabetes, only recently has attention been given to the way in which PTSD might impact individuals once diagnosed with diabetes. Diabetes self-management is critical for minimizing adverse diabetes-related outcomes; however, individuals with PTSD may have more difficulty engaging in the required management behaviors (Lee & Park, 2018). Other related mental health conditions, namely depression, are known to impede diabetes self-management (Aikens et al., 2009; Lustman et al., 2000) and are associated with a higher risk of complications and mortality among patients with diabetes (de Groot et al., 2001; Katon et al., 2005; Nouwen et al., 2019). Yet, the impacts of other closely related psychiatric conditions with known adverse effects on health, such as PTSD, on outcomes among individuals diagnosed with diabetes are less well characterized. Thus, the purpose of this scoping review is to summarize the current literature on PTSD and outcomes among adults diagnosed with diabetes and offer recommendations and guidance for future research. This review will focus on PTSD and four categories of diabetes outcomes: (1) diabetes self-management (e.g., glycemic control); (2) living with diabetes (e.g., health-related quality of life, functioning, disability); (3) health care usage (e.g., hospitalizations), and (4) diabetes complications (e.g., cardiovascular disease, retinopathy, mortality). As the prevalence and cost of diabetes in the United States is projected to continue to rise (Lin et al., 2018), identifying and intervening on factors, such as PTSD, that may contribute to poor diabetes management and adverse long-term outcomes is imperative.

title: Aesthetic Emotions and the Drive for Knowledge
description: In this chapter I address how the arts contribute to knowledge and understanding by defending an Affective Aesthetic Cognitivism (AAC). AAC is an empirically informed theory model, concerning the role of affect and emotions in sustaining the transformative, cognitive impact of the arts. The relation of our art engagement to our drive for knowledge might at times seem rather indirect. We do not mainly engage with art for educational purposes but rather for pleasure (e.g., when we rewatch a movie or TV show we love) or for emotion regulation (e.g., when we go to an art exhibition when we are bored). Aesthetic Cognitivism in philosophy and psychology, in contrast, focuses on the epistemic outcomes of our art engagement. It provides a theory about the value of the arts not "as sources of delight, amusement, pleasure, or emotional catharsis, but as sources of understanding." (Brewer 2025, 1). The proposed AAC in this chapter goes one step further by integrating affect and cognition, arguing that the emotions are not a byproduct but a significant driver of the epistemic impact of the arts. The claim of AAC is therefore not just that the emotions accompany epistemic changes, or that they motivate cognitive engagement (they do that as well), but that specific aesthetic emotions play a constitutive role in how understanding through the arts is achieved. I first discuss the more general impact of art and cultural artifacts on our habits of perceiving and distinguish them from epistemically valuable cognitive gains; this gives me the opportunity to revisit some central claims of Aesthetic Cognitivism. I then examine how affect and cognition have been related in aesthetic psychology and, starting with Berlyne's (1960, 1970) work on curiosity that recent psychology has been amended to cover more specific emotions. The main part of the chapter analyzes two recent empirical approaches to Aesthetic Cognitivism. An attempt at a taxonomy of aesthetic impacts (Christensen et al., 2023) and an assessment of viewers' affective and cognitive experiences in a museum context (Miller et al., 2025). I propose some conditions that empirical studies must meet to speak to Aesthetic Cognitivism and AAC respectively. Overall, these studies suggest that when people actively engage with artworks their emotional involvement is not merely reactive or pleasure-based, but contains different expansive experiences that closely connect to shifts in perspective and the generation of understanding.

title: Evaluating the effects of non-specific recruitment message themes on the motivations and intention to participate in citizen science projects
description: Study summary Objective: This study aims to test whether a recruitment message focusing on scientific research or environmental/public health protection is more effective at encouraging participation in citizen science projects. Study design: This is a randomized experimental study design implemented through an online survey distributed by a survey panel provider. Prior to being able to access the survey, potential participants will be provided with an information sheet and consent form, and only participants who voluntarily agree through informed consent will be included. The survey will first ask basic demographic questions that do not contain any personal information. Then, participants will read the two recruitment messages and answer associated questions. Finally, participants will be asked about their knowledge of citizen science and history of civic engagement. The sequence of messages (the scientific research message followed by the environmental/health impacts message, or vice versa) will be randomly allocated a code of "A" or "B". The first participant will be randomly assigned one of the two codes, and thereafter the codes will alternate between surveys. The messages will be presented as "Message 1" and "Message 2" in the survey, no matter which sequence they have been allocated to, in order to reduce the risk of biased responses. Outcomes: The primary outcome will relate to the likelihood of participating in the project as described, measured through the response to the question "What is your likelihood of participating in a project that promises to achieve what is mentioned above?", with an affirmative answer (i.e., "Very likely" or "Somewhat likely") indicating intent. The secondary outcomes will relate to the likelihood of recommending the project to others, the feelings evoked by the messages, and the anticipated time commitment dedicated to the project. Finally, a tracked link to the Mosquito Alert website (https://www.mosquitoalert.de/) will be provided at the end of the survey to monitor whether intent to participate translates to interest and engagement. Statistical analysis: We will first perform descriptive data analyses. The primary outcome of intent to participate will be coded as a binary variable with the answer options "Very likely" and "Somewhat likely" indicating affirmative intent and the answer options "Neutral", "Somewhat unlikely", and "Very unlikely" indicating no intent. The main predictor will be the message theme, controlling for the experimental group (i.e., the order in which the messages were viewed). For a binary outcome, we will use generalized linear models (GLM) following a binomial distribution with a log link. Because GLMs allow the inclusion of multiple variables, we will also examine other variables that were included in the survey as potential confounders as well as interactions between covariates. Examples of potential confounding variables include gender, age, employment status, prior involvement in CS projects, and level of community engagement. Variable inclusion will be guided by the Akaike information criterion (AIC). The secondary outcomes will be analyzed by comparing the proportions of each answer between the message themes, in the whole sample as well as stratified by demographic groups (i.e., gender, age group) and experimental group. Finally, we will assess any differences in proportion of participants who access the Mosquito Alert link between those who indicated intention to participate and those who did not intend to participate, in the whole sample and stratified by the groups listed previously. All analyses will be conducted in R - The R Project for Statistical Computing (https://www.r-project.org). Ethics: The protocol and survey were approved by the ethics committee of Heidelberg University Hospital on 01 July 2024 (application number S-332/2024). title: Unconfounding the Roles of Retinotopic and Spatiotopic Coordinates in Location Suppression_V2
description: This study is designed to examine whether location-based suppression of irrelevant stimuli functions using spatiotopic or retinotopic visual coordinates. To do this, we will train participants to suppress a location in an array while fixating at a center cross. We do this using a visual search task where participants must identify a target while ignoring salient distractors. Unbeknownst to the participants, one position contains the distractor 75% of the time; this is known as the high probability location (HPL). For each other location there is a roughly 8.3% chance of the distractor appearing. These are known as the low probability locations (LPL). During training, the suppressed location will occupy the same spatiotopic and retinotopic coordinates. For baseline purposes, 1/3 of trials will contain no distractor. At test, we will shift the array and fixation in order to unconfound spatiotopic and retinotopic space. When fixation is shifted, the spatiotopic coordinates of the HPL, known as sHPL, do not change. However the coordinates of the HPL on your retina do shift. If location suppression operates within spatiotopic space, the participants should continue to suppress the sHPL at test. If, however, location suppression is retinotopic, participants will continue to suppress the high probability location on the retina (rHPL), which will now be in a different location than the sHPL. This is elaborated upon in the "design plan" section and images are included.

description: Abstract: Background: At present, laser is regarded as an effective treatment for macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion. With the breakthrough of anti-vascular endothelial growth factor drugs in ophthalmology clinical research, the intravitreal injection of ranibizumab is widely applied, but both methods have their limitations, so some clinical studies have combined and applied them together. However, the clinical results are inconsistent and controversial, and there is no relevant system evaluation for the laser combined with intravitreal injection of ranibizumab for treatment of macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion now. Objective: Meta analysis is used to analyze and evaluate the effectiveness and safety of the laser combined with intravitreal injection of ranibizumab for treatment of macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion. Two researchers conducted independent screening, quality assessment and data extraction for the literatures, and used RevMan5.3 to conduct Meta analysis for the included literatures. Result: The research has evaluated the effectiveness and safety of the laser combined with intravitreal injection of ranibizumab for treatment of macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion through the aspects of the best corrected visual acuity 6 months after operation, macular center thickness and the incidence of adverse reactions such as elevated intraocular pressure, endophthalmitis, vitreous hemorrhage and cataract. Conclusion: laser combined with intravitreal injection of ranibizumab for treatment of macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion has good effect, and the research has provided reliable evidence for the use of clinical treatment of the laser combined with intravitreal injection of ranibizumab for treatment of macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion.

title: Desempeño diagnóstico de los sistemas de inteligencia artificial en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto: una revisión sistemática exploratoria
description: El glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto (GPAA) es una neuropatía óptica crónica y progresiva caracterizada por daño del nervio óptico y pérdida de la capa de fibras nerviosas retinianas, lo que conduce a defectos irreversibles del campo visual y constituye una de las principales causas de ceguera irreversible a nivel mundial (1,2). Se estima que su prevalencia global en adultos oscila entre 2.4% y 3.0%, con variaciones importantes según edad, origen étnico y factores genéticos (3,4). El diagnóstico temprano del GPAA representa un desafío clínico importante debido a la variabilidad interobservador en la evaluación del nervio óptico y la interpretación de pruebas diagnósticas como la fotografía de fondo de ojo, la tomografía de coherencia óptica (OCT) y los campos visuales computarizados (5,6). Además, el acceso limitado a especialistas en oftalmología en muchos sistemas de salud, particularmente en regiones de ingresos medios y bajos, contribuye al subdiagnóstico de la enfermedad (7,8). En este contexto, los sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA), particularmente aquellos basados en aprendizaje automático (machine learning) y aprendizaje profundo (deep learning), han emergido como herramientas prometedoras para mejorar la precisión y eficiencia del diagnóstico del glaucoma. Diversos estudios han demostrado que algoritmos basados en redes neuronales convolucionales pueden alcanzar sensibilidades y especificidades superiores al 90% en la detección de neuropatía óptica glaucomatosa utilizando imágenes de fondo de ojo y OCT (9–12). Sin embargo, la literatura disponible presenta heterogeneidad metodológica en términos de diseños de estudio, poblaciones evaluadas, estándares de referencia y modalidades diagnósticas utilizadas, lo que dificulta la síntesis estructurada de la evidencia sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de estos sistemas (13,14). El objetivo de esta revisión sistemática exploratoria es mapear y sintetizar la evidencia disponible sobre el desempeño diagnóstico de sistemas de inteligencia artificial comparados con métodos diagnósticos convencionales en pacientes adultos con sospecha de glaucoma primario de ángulo abierto. La revisión seguirá la metodología del Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) para revisiones de alcance y las directrices PRISMA-ScR, incluyendo estudios publicados entre enero de 2020 y marzo de 2026 (15,16). Se realizará una búsqueda sistemática en las bases de datos PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science y BIREME/BVS. Dos revisores independientes realizarán la selección de estudios y la extracción de datos, y el riesgo de sesgo será evaluado mediante la herramienta QUADAS-AI (17,18). Los resultados se sintetizarán mediante análisis descriptivo y narrativo de las métricas de precisión diagnóstica reportadas, incluyendo sensibilidad, especificidad, valores predictivos, exactitud diagnóstica y área bajo la curva ROC. Esta revisión permitirá caracterizar el estado actual de la evidencia sobre la aplicación clínica de la inteligencia artificial en el diagnóstico del GPAA, así como identificar brechas de conocimiento relevantes para futuras investigaciones y estrategias de implementación clínica. title: Combined effect of topography and strontium on mineralization
description: It has been established that the osteogenic expression and mineralization of bone-forming cells at surfaces of artificial materials depends on a number of cues including elastic modulus [1], chemistry [2], pattern shape [3] as well as topography at the nanometer [4, 5] and micrometer scale [6]. At iNANO, we have developed a topographical screening assay, which has already been able to provide further insight into the interaction between surface topographies and osteogenic differentiation [6, 7]. title: Information-Geometric Degeneration in LLMs
description: Information-Geometric Degeneration in Large Language Models: Fisher Metric Collapse, Mixture Singularities, and Modular Specialization This paper develops an information-geometric framework for understanding structural degeneration in large language models (LLMs). It shows that covariance cutting, modular specialization, effective rank collapse, and curvature in empirical scaling laws arise from two core geometric processes: Fisher metric degeneration and mixture-model singularity. The study analyzes how weakening cross-module interactions produces block-structured Fisher information, reducing effective Fisher rank and constraining the number of information-geometrically active directions. It further demonstrates that modular architectures such as MoE layers induce mixture singularities analogous to classical non-identifiability, linking these phenomena to topological fragmentation in companion work on stratified topology. The framework provides a unified geometric explanation for connectivity loss, specialization, and dimensional degeneration in modern LLMs, complementing operator-theoretic, topological, and physical perspectives within Structural AI Theory.

title: Optical-photon quantum computing
description: Optical photons present many interesting aspects in the context of the research for suitable physical representations of quantum bits. Photons are chargeless particles, and do not interact strongly with each other, or even with most matter. They can be guided along long distances with low loss in optical fibers, delayed efficiently using phase shifters, and combined easily using beamsplitters. Photons exhibit typical quantum phenomena, such as the interference produced in two-slit experiments. Furthermore, in principle, photons can be made interact with each other if carefully handled. There are many practical problems with this approach; nevertheless it presents, beyond what has already been noted, an appealing conceptual simplicity. The purpose of this work is to present - at least, in its fundamental principles - a set of optical photon quantum gates that is universal for quantum computation. To do so, we begin by gathering the necessary mathematical and physical tools. We discuss canonical quantization for the electromagnetic field, and we formalize in an abstract context the characteristic properties of every realization of the Fock canonical commutation relationships (CCR). We analize the class of the spaces where it is possible to give such a realization, and that naturally lend themselves to host the physical model of our interest. Once acquired these bases, we turn ourselves to a particular optic system, the Mach-Zehnder interferometer, and we study the general properties of this system and of its essential constituents. At this point we choose a particular encoding of quantum bit and we look at the optical devices just discussed as elements of a quantum circuit. We then discuss the fundamental ideas that may guide the implementation of some important quantum gates: Hadamard gate, $\pi/8$ gate and controlled-NOT. We conclude by showing that these three quantum gates form a universal set of gates for quantum computation.

title: What can the scanning of z-strings tell paragraph reading? Evidence from eye movements.
description: In recent years there has been a proliferation in research on return-sweep saccades (Adedeji et al., 2022; Parker et al., 2017; Parker, Nikolova et al., 2019; Parker, Slattery et al., 2019; Parker & Slattery, 2019, 2021; Parker et al., 2013; Slattery & Parker, 2019; Slattery & Vasilev, 2019; Vasilev et al., 2021), i.e., the eye movement that brings a reader's gaze from the end of one line to the start of the next. One of the most consistently reported findings is that fixations preceding a return-sweep (i.e., line-final fixations) are shorter than intra-line fixations (e.g., Parker, Nikolova et al., 2019). Several explanations for shorter line-final fixations exist. For example, they may present general oculomotor programming in preparation for return-sweep execution, reduced skipping costs at line boundaries, or reduced lateral masking (Parker et al., 2023). Another robust finding is that readers' fixations following a return-sweep also differ in duration from intra-line fixations (e.g., Parker et al., 2019). Fixations following a return-sweep can be categorized as accurate line-initial fixations and under-sweep fixations. What differentiates these two populations of fixations is the direction of the following saccade with accurate line-initial fixations followed by a rightwards progressive saccade. In contrast, under-sweeps are followed by a leftwards regressive saccade that is thought to correct return-sweep undershoot errors. Accurate line-initial fixations tend to be longer than intra-line reading fixations and have been argued to reflect a reliance on foveal encoding and an absence of parafoveal preview (Parker et al., 2017; Parker & Slattery, 2019). In contrast, under-sweep fixations are much shorter than intra-line fixations and this is thought to be driven by retinal feedback and return-sweep error (Schebilske, 1976). Current arguments about the differences in fixation durations, at least for accurate line-initial fixations, are underpinned by the assumption that lexical processing is responsible for these differences in fixation duration. However, these differences may also be a consequence of low-level oculomotor control. One approach to tease these two explanations apart is to compare multiline text reading to the scanning of multiline z-strings. The scanning of z-strings has been conceptualised as an oculomotor control condition to normal reading as it approximates reading without lexical and post-lexical processing (Kuperman et al., 2010). So, eye movements during paragraph reading and multiline z-string scanning should be influenced similarly by visual and oculomotor factors. Therefore, if the line-final and line-initial fixation duration differences are not linguistic in nature, then we would assume similar reductions during paragraph reading and multiline z-string scanning. If, however, these differences are an artefact of linguistic processing, we might expect less of a reduction in durations for line-final fixations (relative to intra-line fixations) and less of an increase for line-initial fixations (relative to intra-line fixations). Previously, Kuperman et al. (2010), in a reanalysis of single-line reading and z-string data from Nuthmann et al. (2007) and Nuthmann and Engbert (2009), showed that shorter initial fixation during single-line text reading (representing "start-up" effects) and longer line0final fixations during single-line text reading (representing "wrap-up" effects) were present during sentence reading but z-string scanning. Based on these findings, Kuperman et al. reasoned that both start-up and wrap-up effects require mindful reading (i.e., lexical and post-lexical processing) and are not simply a result of a generic oculomotor programme. Following Kuperman et al.'s comparison of single sentence reading and z-string scanning, we may expect that reading time differences at line boundaries may not be present during z-string scanning; indicating that lexical and post-lexical processing are responsible for shorter line-final and longer line-initial paragraph reading fixations.

title: Visually Predictive Biomarkers on OCT & OCTA following Anti-VEGF treatment of RVO
description: Retinal vein occlusions (RVO) are the second most common retinal vascular cause of vision loss after diabetic retinopathy. They are classified as branch (BRVO) or central (CRVO), with macular edema (ME) being the leading cause of vision loss. Anti-VEGF injections are standard therapy, guided by OCT and OCTA findings such as intra-retinal fluid, sub-retinal fluid, and ME. Beyond ME, biomarkers like disorganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL), external limiting membrane (ELM) disruption, and ellipsoid zone (EZ) disruption have been linked to prognosis, though results are inconsistent. Ischemic status and vascular metrics (FAZ, SCP, DCP) may also influence recovery, but gaps remain in establishing consistent predictors. Our study will evaluate which OCT and OCTA biomarkers best correlate with visual acuity outcomes following anti-VEGF intravitreal injections (IVI) in patients with CRVO or BRVO. Eligible participants will be adults (>18 years) treated with anti-VEGF alone, with available OCT/OCTA and BCVA data. We expect to find no major differences between biomarkers in their predictive ability for visual acuity, clarifying their clinical utility.

description: During the Israel-Iran War (June, 2025), the Israeli public was exposed to a severe escalation in warfare and intensity, compared to its routine during the Israel-Hamas war, embarked on October 7th, 2023. This escalation was manifested mainly through the launching of advanced missiles and drones from Iran towards civilian targets, mainly in Israel's center. Additionally, due to the scope and sophistication of the launched missiles, the Israeli Iron Dome missile intercepting system was less effective, resulting in a higher number of strikes on Israeli cities. Our study was conducted in the following week after the announcement of cease-fire between Israel and Iran (06/24/2025). Through a cross-sectional survey, we attempted to measure levels of different types of exposure to missiles launching among the Israeli public, as well as their relationships with perceived threat from external enemies. Additional constructs that were measured included Posttraumatic Stress Syndromes (PSS), as well as identity fusion - a plausible process in times of intergroup conflicts and high exposure intensity (Swann, 2010). We further measured for public sentiments towards political violence, as well as personal endorsement of violent behavior against the political establishment. To allow for a comparative framework, we also measured for exposure to terrorism and rocket launching since the Oct. 7th terrorist attacks until the embark of the Israeli-Iran war. The main intention here was to examine whether the recentness of exposure plays a role in influencing rates of threat perceptions and violent behavior.

title: Comparative Effectiveness of Cognitive Behavioral Therapies in Schizophrenia and Schizoaffective disorder: A Systematic Review
description: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) has initially been introduced by A. Beck, as a therapy targeting on depression and anxiety disorders (Beck, A. T., 1976) Τhe limitations of traditional cognitive model of psychotherapy led to its evolution and to the development of novel techniques incorporated into the 3rd wave cognitive therapies. Τhird wave therapies, such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), Metacognitive Therapy (MT), Mindfulness Based Cognitive Therapy (MBCT), Compassiobn Focused Therapy (CFT) offer a more holistic and experiential approach, focusing on concepts such as acceptance, commitment, mindfulness, and compassion. (Hayes SC and Hofmann SG, 2017) Over the last decades, there have been efforts to adapt CBT for treatment of more severe mental disorders, including schizophrenia or chronic mood disorders. These efforts have mainly studied CBT as an adjunctive therapy, in combination with pharmacotherapy (Tai S, Turkington D, 2009;Thase ME et al,2014) The use of traditional CBT, as well as the 3rd wave therapies in psychotic disorders has been extensively studied. There is evidence supporting its efficacy in reducing symptoms, improving functionality, and enhancing overall recovery and quality of life (Heriot-Maitland C, et al, 2023; Hofmann SG et al, 2012; Lazzari C et al, 2022; Marshall M and Rathbone J, 2011; Morris EMJ, 2024; Moritz S et al, 2029) Traditional CBT model, as well as 3rd wave techniques are described to target different aspects of psychopathology (Freeman D et al, 2002; Freeman D et al, 2014; Garety P. and Freeman D., 2013; Kennedy L and Xyrichis A., 2027; Pontillo M. et al, 2020). While schizophrenia has been the primary focus of most research, schizoaffective disorder represents a subgroup with overlapping but distinct psychopathological features. However, differences in symptoms, such as the presence of mood symptoms in schizoaffective disorder or the prevalence of perceptual disorders in schizophrenia, may require specific treatment adaptations (Morrison AP and Barratt S, 2010; Spencer HM et al, 2020).On the other hand, it remains unclear whether CBT outcomes differ significantly between these diagnostic categories and if so, what are the specific appropriate treatment characteristics are required. Aims This review aims at addressing this gap by systematically synthesizing the evidence on CBT' s effectiveness in schizophrenia versus schizoaffective disorder, with an emphasis on specific outcomes, such as symptom reduction (positive, negative, affective), functional improvement and treatment compliance. Methods The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines were followed,. The review protocol was registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) platform. Eligibility Criteria: Studies that met the following criteria were included. The target population was adults that were at the time of the study diagnosed with affective or non-affective psychosis, as those are defined in commonly used diagnostic systems (DSM-IV, DSM-5, ICD-10, ICD-11) as schizophrenia spectrum disorders for the former and schizoaffective, bipolar or unipolar mood disorder with psychotic features for the latter. Of particular interest in this latter group is the psychopathological trait of mood congruency in the psychotic experiences (delusions, hallucinations) of the people that received the intervetions of interest. The intervention of interest was any CBT modalities that incorporated ACT principles, CFT, MT, or mindfulness principles, and eligible comparators were treatment as usual (TAU), waiting list, or other psychotherapies. Pharmacotherapy as a separate comparator group was excluded. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included. Case-control studies, cohort studies and case reports or case series were thus not included in order to minimise bias from design sources as much as possible. Outcomes: Primary outcomes included the changes post-treatment of positive and negative symptoms. A quantification of this change by any validated questionnaire (e.g. PANSS) was deemed eligible. Secondary outcomes included depressive symptoms, anxiety, and quality of life. Only published articles and unpublished data was not considered. The databases MEDLINE, EmBASE, clinicaltrials.gov were scanned for relevant documents from 2000 to November 15th 2024. The rationale for the date restriction is that most of these third wave CBT methods were fully fledged after 2000. The search strategy included the query of each database with the following algorithm Titles and abstracts of the retrieved results were screened independently by two reviewers and assessed for eligibility and, after identifying the most relevant articles, in a second stage full-text articles were assessed. For articles where there were disagreements, consensus was reached with the third author. The study selection process is documented using a PRISMA flow diagram (Figure X). Data Extraction: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a pre-designed extraction form. Extracted data included: Study characteristics: list of author, year of publication, country, sample size, study design. Participant details: Mean (standard deviation (SD)) age, gender (proportion of female participants), diagnosis of affective and non-affective psychosis participants, mean duration of illness. Regarding the particular intervention as well as the comparator in each study, information on the modality, frequency and number of sessions, total duration, and delivery method of CBT was gathered (in-person or from a distance through technology, inpatient setting or outpatient). For the outcomes, information was gathered on the instrument results at baseline and at each time point available, in whichever format was available (means, standard deviations, odds ratios, risk ratios or hazard ratios for binary outcomes if those were opted for). Any discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion among authors. Risk of Bias: The risk of bias was assessed with the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool (RoB 2.0) for RCTs. Information from each study was gathered on randomization, blinding, outcome measurement, and selective reporting, based on the published manuscripts and the descriptions the authors provided on their workflows. Data Synthesis: We performed a narrative synthesis of the results. Where sufficient data were available, meta-analyses with the inverse variance-weighted method were conducted using the R statistical software. Heterogeneity was assessed using the I2 statistic and Cochran's Q test, and if heterogeneity was present, a random-effects model was used to accommodate it. title: Predicting Stroke Risk Using Retinal Imaging with Artificial Intelligence: A Scoping Review of Current Evidence
description: Stroke remains a leading cause of mortality and long-term disability worldwide, with a substantial proportion of cases considered preventable through early risk identification and targeted interventions. Traditional stroke risk prediction models rely primarily on clinical and demographic variables and demonstrate only moderate predictive performance, often failing to capture subclinical vascular changes. In recent years, advances in retinal imaging and artificial intelligence (AI) have enabled the non-invasive assessment of microvascular and neurovascular alterations that may reflect underlying cerebrovascular risk. The retina shares anatomical and physiological characteristics with cerebral vasculature, making it a promising window for stroke risk assessment. As a growing body of literature explores AI-based analysis of retinal images for predicting stroke and related cerebrovascular outcomes, a comprehensive mapping of the existing evidence is needed. This scoping review protocol outlines the planned methods to systematically identify, characterize, and synthesize current research on the use of retinal imaging combined with artificial intelligence for stroke risk prediction.

description: We will conduct a discrete choice experiment (DCE) among approximately 10 Japanese drug-pricing policymakers to estimate willingness to pay (WTP) for iPSC-based retinal cell therapy. To increase design coverage under small N, we will fix an 81-profile set selected from a 9 × 5 × 9 = 405 profile universe and randomly assign 15 tasks per respondent. Preferences will be estimated using conditional logit with respondent-clustered standard errors. title: Ocular Biomarkers in Childhood Neurodevelopmental Conditions
description: Eye vergence (EV) is a fixational, binocular eye movement involved in depth perception that recently has also been linked to cognitive processing and symptoms of ADHD. More specifically, weaker EV responses to visual cues have been reported in children with ADHD compared to typically developing peers or children with a mental health condition but no ADHD diagnosis (Sole Puig et al., 2015; Varela Casal et al., 2018). This study aims to evaluate the utility of eye vergence and pupil dilation (PD), measured using computerised eye-tracking tasks, as indicators of visuo-spatial attention processing in children and adolescents. We will compare behavioural, EV and PD responses on two eye-tracking tasks (Oddball and Gap-overlap paradigms) between four groups of children: 3 neurodivergent groups (ADHD, autistic, ADHD+autistic) and a neurotypical group. The tasks are designed to measure specific attentional processes, namely sustained attention and inhibitory control (Oddball task) and orienting and disengaging attention (Gap-overlap task). The Oddball paradigm is a continuous performance test. Our version is based on the classic oddball paradigm, where subjects identify infrequent 'target' stimuli within a series of rapidly presented distractor stimuli (Huettel & McCarthy, 2004). This is a 3-stimulus task requiring participants to respond via a button press to an infrequent target presented amongst frequently and infrequently occurring distractors. Response to the infrequent target stimulus provides a measure of sustained attention and vigilance. Response to the infrequent distractor assesses executive control (inhibition of response). Our Gap-overlap task is adapted from a paradigm developed by Elsabbagh and colleagues (Elsabbagh et al., 2013; Elsabbagh et al., 2009). The participant is required to fixate on a central spinning stimulus and to shift their gaze to a peripheral stimulus as soon as it appears. There are three task conditions: gap, overlap and baseline. In the gap condition the central stimulus (CS) disappears and there is a short gap before the peripheral stimulus (PS) appears. In the overlap condition the animated PS appears while the CS remains displayed and animated. In the baseline condition the CS is extinguished, and the PS simultaneously appears. We will calculate the difference in saccadic reaction time between the gap and the overlap condition and between the baseline and the overlap condition for measures of attentional disengagement. title: The Current Status of OCT and OCTA Imaging for the Diagnosis of Long COVID
description: This systematic review explores the potential of optical coherence tomography (OCT) and optical coherence tomography angiography (OCTA) in diagnosing long COVID. Long term effects of the COVID-19 disease could impact the microvascular system, which can be visualized directly through changes in vessel density and foveal avascular zone in OCTA and indirectly in the form of retinal layer thicknesses in OCT. This review shows a summarized comparison of all 24 topic-related clinical studies of adult participants, collected in the database PubMed and, with the AI research assistant Elicit published in the period between February 2021 and March 2024. Studies with participant groups of patients with active COVID-19, recovered participants and participants with ongoing symptoms were included. During the various stages of COVID-19, retinal changes could be observed, but a comparison between long COVID and recovered cohorts was aggravated by diverse inclusion and exclusion criteria as well as small sample sizes. Changes in long COVID were seen in most OCT examinations as thinning or partial thinning of certain retinal layers, while in OCTA a consistently reduced vessel density was revealed.

title: What is the coverage of retina screening services for people with diabetes? Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision impairment globally. Vision loss from diabetic retinopathy can generally be prevented by early detection and timely treatment. The World Health Organization (WHO) included a measure of service access for diabetic retinopathy as a core indicator in the Eye Care Indicator Menu launched in 2022: Retina screening coverage for people with diabetes. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive global and regional summary of the available information on retina screening coverage for people with diabetes. Methods and analysis: A search will be conducted in Medline (Ovid) and Embase without language restrictions for studies from any country reporting retina screening coverage for adults with any type of diabetes at the national or subnational level using data collected since 1 January 2000. We will also seek reports and coverage statistics from government websites of all WHO member states. Two investigators will independently screen studies, extract relevant data and assess risk of bias of included studies. The review will be reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis guideline. We will summarise the range of coverage definitions reported across included studies and present the median retina screening coverage in WHO regions and by World Bank country income level. Depending on the availability of data, we will conduct meta-analysis to assess disparities in retina screening coverage for people with diabetes by factors in the PROGRESS framework (Place of residence, Race/ethnicity/culture/language, Occupation, Gender/sex, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status, and Social capital). Ethics and dissemination: This review will only include published data thus no ethical approval will be sought. The findings of this review will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and presented at relevant conferences.

Os cursos, em grande maioria, funcionam isoladamente, em estruturas próprias, fortalecendo e legitimando a segregação informativa, dificultando a interação entre os educandos em processo de formação inicial. Com isso, a barreira cultural ainda é compreendida como maior desafio, sendo ela inserida inicialmente pela visão epistemológica e pedagógica do docente. A proposta da Educação Interprofissional reconhece a relação de mútua influência entre atenção à saúde e educação, como estratégia de formar profissionais aptos e capazes de trabalhar em equipe, melhorando atendimento e serviço à comunidade. Este protocolo serve como norte para uma pesquisa que objetiva mapear quais os possíveis perfis docentes para educação interprofissional existente, tratando-se de um estudo descritivo, com abordagem qualitativa através de uma revisão sistemática.

title: Scanning Cue Approach with Faces
description: Description: In this MRI experiment we will test the underlying neural mechanisms of non-reinforced learning, by changing preferences of face images using the Cue Approach Task (CAT). Recently, Schonberg et al.(2014) showed a preferences increase toward snack food-items following a short (less than one hour) cue-approach training in which some items were consistently associated with a neutral tone and a button press. Stimuli: Sixty colour images of unfamiliar faces taken from the Siblings database (Vieira et al., 2014) and modified for the current procedure will be used as stimuli for the current experiment. Procedure: Subject will undergo several tasks both outside and inside MRI scanner. Inside the scanner, in order to control for viewing times, and make sure participants are engaged with the task, their eye position will be recorded using a MRI-compatible eye-tracker. Outside of the scanner: 1. Baseline evaluation - Binary ranking: Subjects will be presented with a forced choice between 300 random pairs of stimuli. Each stimulus will be presented exactly 10 time, in a binary choice against 10 other random stimuli. for each choice subjects may respond within a 2.5 seconds time-window. After all choices are done, a ranking algorithm (Colley, 2008), will be applied to deduce a quantitive preference value for each item. These rankings will be used later in the probe phase to create pairs of similarly valued items. From all 60 items, a subset of 40 item in predetermined ranks will be chosen for the rest of the experiment. Inside of the scanner: 2. Passive viewing task: Subjects will passively view the subset of 40 images in order to evaluate the baseline neural activation for these stimuli prior to training. As a way of monitoring their engagement in the task, subject will be asked to count how many male or female faces they had seen. 3. Cue approach training: Subject will undergo 16 cue approach training runs; in each run, each image will be presented once. in each trial a single face will be presented on the centre of the screen. 30% of stimuli will be consistently associate with a tone, appearing ~750ms following visual stimulus onset. Subjects are asked to press a button on the response box with their index finger, before visual stimulus offset (1000 ms following the onset). Subjects are informed in advance that the stimulus-tone association is consistent. 4. Seven minutes break: during which anatomical scans are made 5. Passive viewing task: Subjects will passively view the subset of 40 images in order to evaluate the post-training neural activation for these stimuli. As a way of monitoring their engagement in the task, subject will be asked to count how many male or female faces they had seen. 6. Probe: subject will be presented with a forced choice task between two faces out of the 40 faces subset. for each choice there will be a 1500 ms time, followed by a jittered duration ITI. Three pair type are used: a) High-value (HV) pairs - stimuli ranked 7-18 - 6 Go items, and 6 NoGo item (both Go item and NoGo item have a mean rank of 12.5). In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a HV Go item and a HV NoGo item. b) Low-value (LV) pairs - stimuli ranked 43-54 - 6 Go items, and 6 NoGo item (both Go item and NoGo item have a mean rank of 48.5). In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a LV Go item and a LV NoGo item. c) Sanity check - 2 HV NoGo stimuli ranked 5-6, and 2 LV NoGo stimuli ranked 55-56. In each pair subject will be asked to choose between a HV NoGo item and a LV NoGo item. We hypothesize that in pair a and b, subjects will choose the Go item over the NoGo items, and in pair type c subjects will choose the HV items over the LV items. 7. Face localizer (1-back task): In order to functionally locate face selective brain areas, we will use a block design of dynamic videos of faces and objects. Subject will be presented with short 1000 ms videos of either faces or objects in motion (as well as blocks of fixation). In a one-back task, subjects will be asked to indicate when a video was presented two consecutive times.

title: The effect of psychotherapy on anxiety, depression and quality of life in patients with diabetic retinopathy: A protocol for systematic review and network meta-analysis
description: Background Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the common microvascular complications in diabetic patients, which is characterized by progressive development and often leads to irreversible visual impairment. More seriously, DR patients suffer great psychological stress due to impaired visual function and reduced self-care ability like anxiety and depression, which seriously affect the quality of life of patients. In recent years, various psychological therapies have been applied to alleviate anxiety, depression and quality of life in DR patients, which have achieved positive results. However, the effectiveness and safety of different psychological therapies are unclear. This study aims to assess the effects of psychotherapy on anxiety, depression and quality of life in DR patients through a network meta-analysis. Methods All randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on the effects of psychotherapy on anxiety, depression and quality of life in patients with DR published before 30 November 2021 will be searched in the PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, Chinese Scientific Journal Database, China National Knowledge Infrastructure Database, Wanfang and China Biomedical Literature Database. There will have no restrictions on publication status and language. Two researchers will be independently responsible for RCT screening, data extraction and quality evaluation. All statistical analyses will be performed using Stata 14.0 and R 4.1.2. Results The results of this meta-analysis will be submitted to a peer-reviewed journal for publication. Conclusion This study will provide comprehensive and reliable evidence-based references for elucidating the efficacy of psychotherapy on anxiety, depression and quality of life in DR patients.

title: Foveal feedback, parvo and magno
description: In this study we use the same procedure of Fan et al. (2016). Participants are presented with visual stimuli in the periphery. They have to compare the stimuli to the left and the right side of fixation. A mask is presented at fixation. The main variable is the delay between stimulus and foveal mask presentations (SOA). A feedback signal specific to the foveal cortex has been proposed. The evidence comes from neuroimaging studies showing that when observers are presented with an object in the periphery, object category information can be decoded from the foveal retinotopic cortex (Williams et al., 2008) and that performance is affected by transcranial magnetic stimulation applied to the foveal cortex at 350-400 ms SOA (Chambers et al., 2013). In addition to the neuroimaging studies, psychophysical experiments have manipulated the information presented in central and peripheral vision. The results show that processing of a visual object in the periphery is modulated by masking information at the fovea (Fan et al., 2016; Weldon et al., 2016; Yu & Shim, 2016). These psychophysical studies therefore support the feedback hypothesis. In the paradigm used by Fan et al. (2016) the foveal mask caused impairment in performance only for SOA of around 200-ms, and only for tasks that required processing of object shape. In our Experiment the stimuli are controlled to be selective to the magnocellular or parvocellular systems. We have, however, kept as close as possible to the original design. The SOA levels will be as in Fan et al.: 0, 50, 150, 250, 350 and 450 ms plus the no-noise baseline condition. Stimuli will be 5x5° gabor patches with different spatial frequency and contrast lasting 100 ms, while the mask will be a dynamic coloured square of 7x7° displayed for 83 ms. Both stimuli will be displayed at 7° eccentricity, along a diagonal (upper right and lower left). The experiment wil be divided into two sets, with the same design. The first set will test contrast discrimination (no shape related task) and the second will test orientation discrimination (shape related task). Participants wil be asked to choose the stimulus with the more contrast or decide if the stimuli have the same or different orientation by pressing a key. Although we use the terms magno- and parvo-activating when describing our stimuli, we are aware that we will not be able to selectively activate one system without activating the other to a lesser extent. We used the literature on parvo and magnocellular systems to select stimuli that are the most likely to activate one of the two systems to a major extent and the other to a minor extent. More specifically, we will use 1 cpd spatial frequency and 30 Hz temporal frequency for the M stimuli and 7 cpd spatial frequency (static) for the P stimuli. Regarding the contrast, for the contrast discrimination task it will be 0.18 vs 0.22 (level 1 difficulty) and 0.17 vs 0.23 (level 2 difficulty) for the M stimuli. For the P stimuli, contrast will be 0.42 vs 0.58 (level 1 difficulty) and 0.41 vs 0.59 (level 2 difficulty). For the orientation discrimination task, the contrasts will be decided after conducting a pilot. Orientation will be 0° in the contrast discrimination task. In the orientation discrimination task, the orientation of one gabor will be randomly selected among all the possible orientations (0-359°); the difference in orientation between the first and the second gabor will be decided after conductiing a pilot.

We need a repeatable, gentle way to monitor small neuron clusters. --- ## Prior Art (what we stand on) * NV‐diamond magnetometry detects single‐neuron action potentials (APs) and microscopic neural signals in tissue. * On‐scalp optically pumped magnetometers (OPMs) validate non‐cryogenic quantum magnetometry for neuro. * Microwave‐free NV readout modes reduce biological interference. * Diamond nanopillar substrates can guide neuronal growth and improve coupling to sensors. * Near‐field/metamaterial lenses and time‐reversal focusing can enhance local SNR without raising in‐tissue power. --- ## MVP (buildable in a small lab) **Sensor**: Commercial NV‐diamond plate (13–50 μm NV layer); widefield ODMR microscope (low‐power 532 nm, sCMOS/CMOS camera); compact RF coil. **Prep**: Primary neurons cultured directly on diamond (standard protocols). Optional diamond nanopillar surface (v2). **Readout**: Lock‐in at ODMR modulation with **low duty cycle** illumination to suppress heating; optional PWM code on the readout for synchronous rejection. **Optional boost**: Passive near‐field concentrator (simple patterned metal/microwave lens) placed above sample; *receive‐only* triaxial array for sensitivity steering (v2+). **Deliverable**: Spatial maps of AP propagation in a few‐neuron cluster with timing correlation to patch clamp/MEA (subset validation). --- ## Milestones (12 weeks) 1. **Phantom validation (Wk 1–3)**: Micro‐wire in saline on diamond; recover known waveforms & spatial profile; SNR vs optical duty. 2. **Fixed tissue (Wk 3–5)**: Structural contrast for alignment; baseline noise & drift characterization. 3. **Live cultures (Wk 5–9)**: Spontaneous activity mapping in small clusters; cross‐validate with patch clamp/MEA. 4. **Few‐neuron demo (Wk 9–12)**: Stimulate neuron A; image magnetic transients in neighbors; show reproducible maps over days. --- ## Risks & Mitigations * **SNR too low** → average across trials; optimize NV density/ODMR contrast; use low‐noise camera; add passive concentrator (v2). * **Photothermal drift** → low‐duty illumination; frame gating; ΔT monitoring; thermal modeling. * **Motion** → short exposure windows; title: Moral Coherence
description: Some of the most significant moral problems we face involve deciding between several compelling considerations. However, despite its central importance to our lives, the process by which we form moral judgements in response to competing considerations is poorly understood. The Deontological Coherence approach (Holyoak & Powell, 2016) suggests that a constraint satisfaction model best accounts for everyday moral decision making. Under this model, moral agents hold a diversity of moral principles, rules and values that guide decision making, and these may also be in conflict. These rules are not inviolable, but rather exist as soft constraints that may be overridden by more strongly held principles or consequentialist considerations. There is evidence to suggest that constraint-based reasoning such as this may be a domain general process and has been implicated in a range of tasks including analogy, explanation and interpretation of perceptual phenomena (Holyoak & Simon, 1999). Constraint-based reasoning is also involved in evaluative decision making as well as decision making with 'hot' (i.e. affective) cognition (Simon, Stenstrom, & Read, 2015; Spellman, Ullman, & Holyoak, 1993). Importantly, constraint satisfaction in these cases is bidirectional. A judgement is made based on the relative strengths of certain considerations, and at the same time emerging judgements alter the strengths of these considerations to achieve coherent support. If bidirectional constraint satisfaction is indeed domain-general, it poses a significant challenge to the commonly held assumption that moral judgement is a unidirectional process. Moral theorists of all stripes have traditionally assumed that agents approach moral problems with a relatively static set of beliefs, values, rules or tendencies which, along with relevant factual beliefs, determine the eventual moral conclusion. Substantial attention has been given to the possibility of re-evaluation of principles between judgements, for instance the process of seeking reflective equilibrium (De Vries & Van Leeuwen, 2010; Rawls, 1971). Substantially less attention has been given to the possibility of coherence-seeking within the process of judgement formation. Hypotheses Consistent with previous work, moral judgement formation in the face of competing considerations will involve a bi-directional coherence shift. Participants with greater insight into their affective tendencies (evidenced by a higher score on self-focussed emotional intelligence) will tend to have more coherent initial values and less of a coherence shift over the course of judgement formation.

title: Investigating intraocular lens tilt in four-point scleral-sutured Akreos IOL implants
description: Cataracts are one of the leading causes of blindness around the world.[1] It was reported by 1.34 million Canadians in 2008/2009 corresponding to a prevalence of 10.2%.[2] Insertions of an intraocular lens (IOL) is a common procedure that is safe and effective in managing cataracts. The IOL is implanted in the capsular bag in most uncomplicated cases. However, when the capsular support is insufficient, the IOLs may be fixed to the sclera through sutures or sutureless techniques, fixed to the iris through sutures or haptics, exchanged for an anterior chamber (AC) IOL, or aphakic spectacle or contact lens correction may be utilized. These surgical methods may have various complications such as cystoid macular edema, intraocular hemorrhage and IOL tilting or decentration. There have been a variety of different types of lenses and techniques employed to fix the lens to the sclera and include 2 point suture fixation, 4 point suture fixation, sutureless, and glued techniques. The IOL position is a major factor that may affect the final visual acuity after cataract surgery. IOL tilt and decentration can cause defocusing, astigmatism, and wavefront aberrations postoperatively. In addition, adequate position prevents complications, such as the uveitis-glaucoma-hemorrhage syndrome, caused by prolonged contact between the haptics and uveal tissue.[3, 4] There have been studies in the past showing the utility of anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) for evaluating the postoperative position of trans scleral fixated IOLs. However, most studies focused on 2 point fixation technique with a dearth of research done on 4 point scleral sutured lenses. The aim of this study is to assess the IOL tilt and position of four-point scleral-sutured Akreos IOL implants using AS-OCT in vivo.

title: Systematic Review of Ocular Manifestations of Zika Virus
description: Introduction: Zika virus infection in newborn poses serious public health concern because of its associated complications such as microcephaly. Reports also suggest ocular complications associated with this diseases, but its findings are still limited. We therefore conduct this systematic review to summarize the ocular manifestations of Zika Virus. Methods: PubMed, OvidSP, EMBASE were searched from inception to 7th November, 2016 for reports on Zika virus related ocular findings. Case series, reports and cohorts were identified from reference list of included studies. Studies with overlapped subjects were excluded. Clinical findings data were extracted, categorized and summarized to study the spectrum of ocular findings associated with Zika virus infection. Incidence was calculated. Results: Twelve studies including a total of 51 infant cases with 84 affected eyes and 3 adult cases with 5 affected eyes were included for analysis. Macular pigment mottling (55.9%), foveal reflex loss (41.2%), chorioretinal atrophy (27.4%), optic nerve hypoplasia (20.6%) and increased cup-disc ratio (18.6%) were common ocular findings related to Zika virus in infants. Uveitis and maculopathy were seen in adult cases. Conclusions: Macular and optic nerve abnormalities are the major ocular findings in Zika virus infected infants. Eventual visual outcome is still unknown. Screening guidelines have been established. Further studies on Zika virus related ocular findings are of paramount importance for the global public health

title: Deep Learning-Based Analysis of Panoramic and CBCT Images to detect Relations and the Risk of Mandibular third and Inferior Alveolar Nerve: A Scoping Review
description: ABSTRACT Aims: The present scoping review assessed the ability of deep learning (DL) models to determine the relationship between the third mandibular molar (MM3) and the inferior alveolar nerve (IAN) using panoramic radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT). The aim was to examine the potential of these models to enhance dental diagnoses of MM3 risk to the nerve. Materials and methods: A systematic literature search encompassed studies published between January 2015 and September 2025 in PubMed, Wiley Online Library, and ScienceDirect. The review included 27 studies which used DL algorithms including the convolutional neural networks, You Only Look Once, ResNet50, AlexNet and RetinaNet to detect and analyze images. Results: The results showed that these models have high accuracy in predicting anatomical relationships with increased diagnostic efficiency compared with manual methods, reducing nerve complication risks from the MM3. The datasets included between 74 and 4,516 X-ray images. The performance metrics included accuracy, F1 score, specificity and sensitivity (Recall). Data heterogeneity including image type, DL architecture and dataset size makes, direct comparison of model performance across studies challenging. Conclusions: DL methods in panoramic radiography and CBCT analysis can improve the accuracy and the efficiency of analyzing the relationship between the MM3 and the IAN, aiding clinical diagnosis and reducing nerve compression risk from wisdom teeth. title: The role of ocular disinfectants in cataract surgery: a systematic review.
description: Cataract surgery is one of the most commonly performed surgical procedures worldwide. Postoperative endophthalmitis is a rare but serious complication of cataract surgery, potentially leading to severe and irreversible visual loss. The infectious process stems from contamination of the wound and internal eye in the perioperative environment. The most effective prophylactic measure is difficult to define due to the low incidence rate (0.014% -0.08%) and the large patient numbers needed to conduct clinical trials. A wide multicenter study from the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons on over 16.000 patients concluded that the use of intracameral cefuroxime at the end of surgery reduces the occurrence of postoperative endophthalmitis. Antibiotic drops are also routinely used in clinical practice for the preoperative disinfection of the ocular surface. However, given the exponentially increasing concerns about antibiotic resistance, there has been strong interest in developing alternative strategies for ocular surface disinfection prior to surgery. Ocular disinfectants comprise various molecules with different mechanisms of action that produce antisepsis of the ocular surface without generating resistance. In the ESCRS Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Endophthalmitis Following Cataract Surgery application of povidone-iodine 5-10%, or alternatively chlorhexidine 0.05%, to the periorbital skin, conjunctival sac and cornea before surgery is deemed mandatory. However, new molecules with different concentrations have been recently proposed and used for ocular disinfection prior to cataract surgery. Nevertheless, definite antisepsis protocols regarding which regimen is the most effective in the perioperative prophylaxis have yet to be established. Given the low incidence rate of endophthalmitis, almost all published studies considered ocular surface flora contamination as a surrogate marker to assess the disinfectant efficacy. The scope of this systematic review is to search the published evidence on peri-operative prophylaxis with antiseptics to analyze doses, regimens and antiseptic effect on ocular surface microbiome of the different agents available on the market. The proposed review will answer two questions: which type and concentrations of ocular disinfectants are used for cataract surgery prophylaxis and in which regimen? Which prophylactic regimen is more effective?

title: What Drives Risk Perception?
description: Risk is an integral part of many economic decisions, and is vitally important in finance. Despite extensive research on decision-making under risk, little is known about how risks are actually perceived by financial professionals, the key players in global financial markets. In a large-scale survey experiment with 2,213 finance professionals and 4,559 lay people in nine countries representing $\sim$50\% of the world's population and more than 60\% of the world's gross domestic product, we expose participants to return distributions with equal expected return and we systematically vary the distributions' next three higher moments. Of these, skewness is the only moment that systematically affects financial professionals' perception of financial risk. Strikingly, variance does not influence risk perception, even though return volatility is the most common risk measure in finance in both academia and the industry. When testing other, compound risk measures, the probability to experience losses is the strongest predictor of what is perceived as being risky. Analyzing professionals' propensity to invest, skewness and loss probability also have strong predictive power, while volatility and kurtosis have some additional effect. Our results are very similar for lay people, and they are robust across and within countries with different cultural backgrounds as well as for different job fields of professionals.

title: Dynamic Maps: Segmentation and Memory
description: This preregistration outlines a study on the relationship between event segmentation and memory for dynamic data visualizations. Participants (N = 275) are exposed to animated maps of insect population changes, asked to segment events, and complete order and recognition memory tasks. The study tests whether order memory differs for within- versus across-event comparisons, whether segmentation agreement predicts memory, and whether similarity in segmentation predicts similarity in memory. Analyses use mixed-effects models, with exploratory tests of segmentation grain. Power simulations suggest sufficient sensitivity to detect small effects. The goal is to characterise how segmentation processes influence memory for dynamic, non-narrative visual data. Here is a short summary, all details can be found in the attached files: Research Question: How does event segmentation relate to memory for dynamic data maps? Design: Participants view 6 animated maps of insect population changes (2 training, 4 test). Each 50s map has 10 regions grouped into 3 clusters with one global peak/minimum as an event boundary. Tasks per test map: (1) Viewing, (2) Segmentation (mark events), (3) Order Judgement (6 frame pairs), (4) Recognition (8 frames). Within-subjects design; all participants view all 4 test maps Hypotheses: 1. Event boundaries affect temporal order memory (accuracy lower for across- vs within-event frame pairs, tested with global and individual boundaries). 2. Segmentation normativity predicts memory (greater agreement with group → better order and recognition). 3. Similarity in segmentation predicts similarity in memory (pairwise). 4. Exploratory: role of segmentation grain (number of boundaries). Measures: Segmentation: keypress timings → group and pairwise agreement. Memory: 2AFC order judgements (6 trials/map) and recognition (8 trials/map). Response times. Analyses: Mixed-effects models: Logistic GLMMs for order accuracy (H1, H2A) and recognition (H2B). LMMs for similarity analyses (H3). Grain added exploratorily Sample size & power: Planned N=275. Power simulations (2,000 runs) estimate ~0.82 power to detect a small event-type effect (d≈0.2, ~5% accuracy change from baseline 50%) Exclusions: Fail comprehension check. No segmentation on >1 test map, or segmentation during "view only" task on >1 map. Exploratory re-analysis on high-performing subset (≥36/56 correct by binomial test).

title: Traditional and novel application of infrared imaging for screening of ocular disorders: a scoping review
description: Near infrared-light based imaging technology is traditionally used for the screening of uncorrected refractive errors (myopia, hypermetropia and astigmatism), amblyopia and strabismus. The technology, broadly called photoscreening, involves analysis of the the reflected luminance pattern created across the pupil from light projected onto the retina from an array of infrared LED light source situated below the aperture of an IR sensitive camera. In eyes with regular refractive error, the luminance gradient varies monotonically from brighter to darker from one edge to another edge of the pupil. Apart from these use cases, near infrared imaging techniques have also been reportedly used in the identification of ocular pathologies, such as keratoconus, spasm of near reflex, dry eye, cataract, retinoblastoma, pupillary dysfunction, etc. This technique has also been used in laboratories for measuring the eye's focusing and binocular eye alignment responses. The aim of this scoping review is to understand the traditional application of infrared imaging and the future indications of this technology for screening/detection of ocular disorders.

title: The influence of saccade target eccentricity on the spatial frequency of foveally enhanced, target-congruent feature information
description: We frequently execute large-scale eye movements (saccades) to examine peripheral visual information with foveal acuity. In several previous investigations, we demonstrated a systematic, pre-saccadic interaction between peripheral feature information and foveal visual sensitivity: right before the eye movement, foveal sensitivity for defining features of the eye movement target (in our case: its orientation) is enhanced predictively. In reverse correlation analyses, we observed that the spatial frequency (SF) of foveally enhanced orientation information mirrored the resolution of the saccade target presented at a 10 dva eccentricity. This observation motivated the question whether foveal predictions rely on instantaneous peripheral input. In other words, we ask here if saccade target features at their peripheral resolution – which is contingent on target eccentricity – are predicted in the pre-saccadic center of gaze. This would indicate that foveal predictions recruit peripheral information in a highly automatic fashion: for most target eccentricities, an image-like prediction of the peripheral target would effectively decrease the foveal resolution of target-congruent feature information. Alternatively, foveal predictions may rely on an eccentricity-invariant template of the target stimulus. This template would allow for an enhancement of the target's entire SF content irrespective of its momentary peripheral resolution. Note that both mechanisms – an enhancement of instantaneous peripheral information and the reliance on a target template – are functional, in that they correctly anticipate the target's orientation on a retinotopic scale. To investigate if foveal predictions rely on instantaneous peripheral input, we will vary the eccentricity of the saccade target (in 8 linearly spaced increments) and the SF of the foveal probe (in 10 log-spaced increments). We will determine observers' foveal sensitivity to target-congruent and target-incongruent orientation signals for different combinations of probe SF and target eccentricity.

title: Why worse detection performance in with-contour condition? : An examination
description: In a previous experiment (see pre-registration osf.io/weag6), we found that although the accuracy of memorizing four distinct discs with subjective contours (with-contour condition) was better than that of memorizing four distinct discs without subjective contours (without-contour condition), the dectection to the peripheral target was worse in with-contour condition than that in the without-contour condition. title: Mapping the Evidence on Diabetes Distress, Coping Strategies, and Glycemic Control in Adults with Diabetes: A Systematic Scoping Review
description: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a chronic, metabolic disorder characterized by either insufficient insulin production or inefficient utilization, resulting in elevated blood glucose levels (Azeem et al., 2022). The main subtypes of DM are Type 1 (T1DM), involving inadequate insulin production, and Type 2 (T2DM), involving insulin resistance (Antar et al., 2023; Cheng et al, 2023). Globally, DM poses a significant health burden, affecting an estimated 589 million adults aged 20 to 79 years (International Diabetes Federation [IDF], 2025). Alarmingly, around 81% of these individuals reside in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC), where healthcare systems face structural constraints, limited resources, and inadequate access to comprehensive DM care. The global impact of DM is further reflected in its growing mortality rate, with over 3.4 million in 2024, accounting for 9.3% of all global deaths (Ahmad et al., 2023). DM is associated with a wide range of microvascular and macrovascular complications, including retinopathy, neuropathy, nephropathy, and diabetic foot infections, which substantially increase morbidity and mortality (Patel, 2024). Beyond physiological complications, many adults living with DM experience diabetes distress (DD), also referred to as diabetes related distress (DRD) or diabetes specific distress (DSD). DD encompasses negative emotional and psychological reactions to the complex demands of managing DM. These demands include adherence to diet and medications, fear of long term complications, monitoring blood glucose and financial and social challenges associated with chronic disease management (ADA, 2014; Collins et al., 2021; Polonsky et al., 2022; Elsayed et al., 2023). Unlike depression, DD is directly linked to the lived experiences of managing DM rather than constituting a clinical psychological disorder. Coping strategies are methods used to manage stress, resolve issues, and adjust to unstable conditions. These techniques are intended to assist people in managing their internal and external demands, which can include environmental, cultural, psychological, and physiological factors (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984; Nugroho et al., 2024). Effective glycemic control, often measured by glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) or blood glucose levels, is essential to avoid DM related complications. Targets for optimum glycemic control are generally fasting blood sugar level between 70–125 mg/dl or, HbA1c < 7%, adjusted for age, comorbidities, and other individual factors (Aschner et al., 2017; ADA, 2024; Pleus et al., 2024). Despite the extensive literature on DD, coping techniques, and glycemic outcomes, the evidence remains fragmented, context-dependent, and methodologically diverse. Notably, no scoping review has systematically mapped the conceptualization, measurement, and correlation of DD and coping mechanisms with glycemic outcomes across various contexts, especially in LMICs. Therefore, this review seeks to synthesize existing information on these constructs, assess study quality, identify knowledge gaps, and guide future research and clinical practice.
