description: Cataract surgery is one of the most commonly performed surgical procedures worldwide. Postoperative endophthalmitis is a rare but serious complication of cataract surgery, potentially leading to severe and irreversible visual loss. The infectious process stems from contamination of the wound and internal eye in the perioperative environment. The most effective prophylactic measure is difficult to define due to the low incidence rate (0.014% -0.08%) and the large patient numbers needed to conduct clinical trials. A wide multicenter study from the European Society of Cataract and Refractive Surgeons on over 16.000 patients concluded that the use of intracameral cefuroxime at the end of surgery reduces the occurrence of postoperative endophthalmitis. Antibiotic drops are also routinely used in clinical practice for the preoperative disinfection of the ocular surface. However, given the exponentially increasing concerns about antibiotic resistance, there has been strong interest in developing alternative strategies for ocular surface disinfection prior to surgery. Ocular disinfectants comprise various molecules with different mechanisms of action that produce antisepsis of the ocular surface without generating resistance. In the ESCRS Guidelines for Prevention and Treatment of Endophthalmitis Following Cataract Surgery application of povidone-iodine 5-10%, or alternatively chlorhexidine 0.05%, to the periorbital skin, conjunctival sac and cornea before surgery is deemed mandatory. However, new molecules with different concentrations have been recently proposed and used for ocular disinfection prior to cataract surgery. Nevertheless, definite antisepsis protocols regarding which regimen is the most effective in the perioperative prophylaxis have yet to be established. Given the low incidence rate of endophthalmitis, almost all published studies considered ocular surface flora contamination as a surrogate marker to assess the disinfectant efficacy. The scope of this systematic review is to search the published evidence on peri-operative prophylaxis with antiseptics to analyze doses, regimens and antiseptic effect on ocular surface microbiome of the different agents available on the market. The proposed review will answer two questions: which type and concentrations of ocular disinfectants are used for cataract surgery prophylaxis and in which regimen? Which prophylactic regimen is more effective?

title: Intraocular proteomics applied to rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; a systematic review.
description: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment (RRD) is a serious ocular condition with a rising incidence. Not all cases can be repaired and vision after surgery is sometimes limited. Advancing techniques in proteomics have revealed alterations in numerous pathways and protein expression in RRD, which could be potentially used as biomarkers and inform novel therapeutics. We review the published literature of proteomics in RRD including cases associated with two important complications namely proliferative vitreoretinopathy (PVR) and choroidal detachment. A systematic search was carried using the MEDLINE, EMBASE, EMCARE AND CINAHL databases. We included 8 studies which used an unbiased proteomic approach from vitreous samples of patients with RRD with and without PVR or associated choroidal detachments (CD) in adult patients.

title: Scoping Review Protocol – Glycocalyx in Lymphatic Vessels
description: This project is a scoping review designed to systematically map and analyse the existing body of literature concerning the glycocalyx in lymphatic vessels, specifically within lymphatic endothelial cells. While the endothelial glycocalyx has been extensively studied in blood vascular systems, its structural characteristics, functional roles, and pathological alterations in the lymphatic system remain less clearly defined. This review aims to document the methodological approaches used to visualize and characterize the glycocalyx in lymphatic vessels, including histological, ultrastructural, and molecular techniques. In addition this review aims to identify, categorize, and summarize current knowledge regarding the molecular composition, physiological functions, and pathophysiological modifications of the lymphatic endothelial glycocalyx across human, animal, and in vitro studies. Particular attention will be given to its role in permeability regulation, fluid drainage, immune interactions, inflammatory processes, and tissue injury. By mapping the scope and characteristics of existing research, this study seeks to identify knowledge gaps, methodological limitations, and areas requiring further investigation.

title: Hemozoin as a Diagnostic Biomarker: A Scoping Review of Next-Generation Malaria Detection Technologies
description: Hemozoin is a biocrystal produced by Plasmodium spp. as a detoxification by-product of hemoglobin digestion. Its physical properties—paramagnetism, optical birefringence, absorption spectra, nonlinear responses, and Raman vibrational signatures—enable diverse diagnostic innovations beyond conventional light microscopy or antigen-based rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). Between 2020 and 2025, technological advances in physics, engineering, spectroscopy, and biomedical device development have led to multiple novel hemozoin-targeted diagnostic platforms, including magneto-optical devices, microfluidic magnetophoretic chips, photoacoustic Cytophone systems, Raman/SERS spectroscopy, and NMR- or hyperspectral-based methods. However, the evidence is highly fragmented across disciplines, with substantial variability in analytical performance, stage-specific sensitivity, and technology readiness levels (TRLs). To date, no scoping review has systematically mapped: (1) physical detection principles of hemozoin, (2) available diagnostic platforms and their performance, (3) technology readiness and translational barriers toward point-of-care (POC) use. This review follows PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidance to consolidate current evidence and identify research gaps.

title: Durham RIOTS club seminar: Like the layers of an onion: Transparency and reproducibility for quantitative research
description: This repository contains the slides for my seminar on 19 Oct 2022. Abstract: The successful reproducibility of research is fundamental to its reliability, usefulness and value to the research community and to society. In this talk I will describe an emerging consensus on ways of improving the computational reproducibility of social science research. I define a research result as reproducible when the same computational analysis steps performed on the same dataset consistently produces the same answer. This is possible when authors provide all the necessary data and the computer codes for another person to run the analysis again, re-creating the same results presented by the authors. I will describe an accessible 'layered reproducibility' approach to organise the various free and open source technologies available to enhance reproducibility in terms of effort to implement and payoff to the R-using researcher. This approach has five layers and I will present their corresponding tools and technologies, with reflections on my experiences using them in my research. The outer layers are relatively easy to use and share, such as a single R script file. The inner layers, such as workflow management and computational environment capture, are more complex to implement for the average researcher, and have a higher payoff in improving the long-term reproducibility of the research. My observations of how researchers are tackling reproducibility indicates that for most researchers, a compendium approach to making their work reproducible is the optimum combination of effort and reward.

title: POLYMORPHISMS IN THE VEGF GENE AND RECEPTORS IN DIABETES MELLITUS AND ASSOCIATED COMPLICATIONS: SCOPE REVIEW
description: Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a complex, chronic, and multifactorial disease that is characterized by hyperglycemia. The prevalence and incidence of DM are increasing rapidly throughout the world. There is accumulating evidence that genetic factors strongly influence the risk of DM. Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) contributes to DM pathogenesis, and genetic variations in the VEGF gene were suggested to influence VEGF secretion and DM pathogenesis. To identify studies, electronic databases, including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, will be explored. This review aimed to investigate the genotyping and allelic frequencies of the single nucleotide polymorphisms of the VEGF gene and verify their association with DM and diabetic microvascular and macrovascular complications. These possible association guided the formulation of the question: "Are polymorphisms in the VEGF gene and receptors in susceptibility to diabetes and its associated complications, including peripheral neuropathy, diabetic nephropathy, diabetic retinopathy, and cardiovascular disease?". Our proposed critical evaluation seeks to analyze the relationship between DM and VEGF polymorphisms. By identifying potential complications related to these polymorphisms, we aim to provide healthcare professionals with the necessary information to develop targeted approaches to improve patient health.

title: Geroprotective Agents and Ocular Outcomes: A Scoping Review With Emphasis on GLP-1 RAs and Glaucoma
description: Glucagon‐like peptide‐1 receptor agonists, now widely used for weight management in addition to glycemic control, have drawn increasing ophthalmic interest because emerging data suggest both potential therapeutic benefits—such as reduced glaucoma risk—and unconfirmed adverse associations, including nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Beyond GLP‐1 agents, several other pharmacologic therapies used for longevity promotion, weight reduction, or metabolic regulation are frequently encountered as concomitant medications in ophthalmic practice. Yet their ocular effects remain inconsistently characterized, with limited systematic evaluation and sparse documentation across the literature. This scoping review identifies these agents and maps their reported ocular outcomes, synthesizing both potential benefits and adverse effects to support clinical awareness and guide future investigation.

title: Non-invasive indices of MASLD and diabetic microvascular complications in patients with type 2 diabetes: a population-based cohort study
description: Background: Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) impacts more than 30% of the adult population and is associated with an elevated risk of developing type 2 diabetes (T2D). Nevertheless, longitudinal data examining the association between the severity of MASLD and the occurrence of diabetic microvascular complications (DMC) are limited. The present study seeks to fill this knowledge gap by exploring the dose-response relationship between non-invasive MASLD indices and the risk of DMC among individuals with T2D, utilizing a large, population-based cohort. Methods: A total of 22,957 participants were sourced from the UK Biobank for analysis. Three non-invasive hepatic steatosis indices—Fatty Liver Index (FLI), Hepatic Steatosis Index (HSI), and Diabetes Steatosis Index (DSI)—were used to assess their dose-response relationships with DMC.DMC, defined as diabetic nephropathy, diabetic retinopathy, and diabetic neuropathy, was identified using hospital inpatient records and death registries. Cox proportional hazard regression models were used to evaluate the associations of frailty phenotype with overall DMC events and subtypes. Results: In this prospective cohort of 22,957 T2D patients followed for 13.7 years (median), 5,694 developed diabetic microvascular complications (DMC). Multivariable-adjusted analyses demonstrated robust associations between elevated MASLD indices and DMC risk, with FLI showing the strongest effects: participants in the highest FLI quintile (Q5 vs Q1) had 71% higher overall DMC risk (HR=1.71, 95% CI: 1.59–1.85; P<0.0001), specifically 106% increased nephropathy (HR=2.06, 1.74–2.44) and 239% increased neuropathy risk (HR=3.39, 2.44–4.71). Notably, no significant associations were observed between any MASLD indices and diabetic retinopathy. FLI also exhibited superior discriminative performance for DMC (C-statistics 0.68–0.71), significantly outperforming HSI and DSI. Restricted cubic splines confirmed nonlinear dose-response relationships for FLI and DSI (P-nonlinearity<0.0001). Stratified analyses showed that the associations between MASLD indices and overall DMC risk were consistent across subgroups defined by age, sex, physical activity, and most other baseline characteristics (all P for interaction > 0.05), except for modest interactions with HbA1c and Townsend deprivation index. Sensitivity analyses including competing risk models supported robustness. Conclusions: Our study reveals that non-invasive MASLD indices, such as FLI, HSI, and DSI, are strong predictors of diabetic microvascular complications (DMC) in T2D patients. These markers, reflecting hepatic steatosis, offer potential for early risk assessment. Future research combining imaging and multi-omics will help further elucidate the liver-metabolism link in DMC and improve clinical outcomes.

title: Pupillometry for the screening and monitoring of five common eye diseases: a systematic literature review
description: According to the World Health Organization, some of the leading causes of vision impairment and blindness are; Refractive errors Cataract Diabetic retinopathy Glaucoma Age-related macular degeneration A majority of these conditions requires referrals to ophthalmologists resulting in extended waiting times, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. This can the inform the design of novel dedicated software and hardware. In summary, a systematic literature review was carried out, yielding 51 relevant studies. Among the significant variables there were constriction amplitude, velocity, duration and latency.

title: Preprint - Understanding jokes relies on the Theory of Mind system
description: Preprint of manuscript, Oct 16 2016 (NOTE: predates replication currently being conducted) To communicate successfully, we often go beyond literal meaning: we make sarcastic remarks, ask others for favors, and engage in face-saving acts. Do these abilities rely on the same mechanisms as literal sentence interpretation? Or does pragmatic reasoning draw on general social-cognitive abilities? Using a functional localization fMRI approach, we examined activity in i) the language system, ii) the Theory-of-Mind (ToM) system, and iii) the domain-general "multiple demand" system, sensitive to diverse demanding tasks, while participants processed one-liner-style jokes and non-joke controls. Only the ToM system was robustly sensitive to jokes. Further, funnier stimuli (as judged by the participants) elicited stronger responses, and the size of the jokes>non-jokes effect in ToM regions across individuals was predictive of how funny they found the jokes. Thus 'getting' jokes – and perhaps pragmatic processing more broadly – appears to stem from the same cognitive abilities that allow us to imagine what another person is thinking.

title: Relationship between homocysteine level and the risk of diabetic retinopathy: a protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Background: Previous studies have demonstrated that elevated homocysteine level represents an independent risk factor for macrovascular disease. However, the relationship between hyperhomocysteinemia and the progression of diabetic retinopathy (DR) in patients remains controversial. Therefore, the present meta-analysis was performed to summarize currently available data to provide more robust evidence on the potential relationship between homocysteine level and the risk of DR. Methods: This meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the guidelines of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols statement guidelines. The PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Library databases were independently searched by two authors to retrieve related original studies published before July 2021. The search terms used were as follows: "diabetic retinopathy", "diabetic retinopathies", "homocysteine", and "Hcy". The risk of bias assessment of the included studies was performed by two authors independently using the tool recommended in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (version 5.1.0). All calculations were carried out with Stata 11.0 (The Cochrane Collaboration, Oxford, United Kingdom). Results: The results of this systematic review and meta-analysis will be published in a peer-reviewed journal. Conclusion: The findings of this study may suggest that elevated homocysteine level was associated with an increased risk of DR, especially in type 2 diabetic patients.

title: Anatomical Variations of the Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery: A Systematic Review
description: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) is the largest and most variable branch of the vertebral artery. PICA has critical clinical relevance due to its role in supplying the medulla oblongata, cerebellum, and choroid plexus, and its variations have direct implications for cerebrovascular disease, stroke syndromes, and neurosurgical procedures. Purpose: The main goal of this research is to systematically collect, analyze, and synthesize published data on the anatomical features of the PICA. This includes its origin, course, branching pattern, diameters, lengths, and common variants, as well as the prevalence of such variations. By consolidating evidence the review aims to provide a clear and comprehensive overview of PICA morphology and its clinical significance. Expected outcomes: The systematic review is expected to: Summarize the spectrum and frequency of PICA variations. Highlight gaps and inconsistencies in the literature regarding PICA anatomy. Provide evidence-based insights to aid clinicians—particularly neurosurgeons and interventional radiologists—in anticipating anatomical variations during diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Establish a foundation for future anatomical and clinical research related to PICA and posterior circulation. Ultimately, this project will contribute to improved understanding of PICA variability, which may translate into safer surgical planning and more precise neurovascular interventions.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description: Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time. This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

title: Systematic Review of Autologous Serum Eye Drops in Dogs with Corneal Diseases
description: Autologous serum eye drops are frequently used as an adjunctive therapy in veterinary ophthalmology, particularly for dogs and cats with corneal diseases such as keratoconjunctivitis sicca (KCS) and corneal ulcers. Although their application is common in clinical practice, no systematic review has yet summarized the available veterinary evidence. The aim of this review is to systematically identify, appraise, and synthesize clinical studies evaluating the use of autologous or allogeneic serum eye drops in canine and feline patients with corneal disorders. Searches will be conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, with CAB Abstracts attempted but yielding no relevant records. Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts using Rayyan, with conflicts resolved by a third reviewer. Data extraction will include study design, number of cases, serum preparation methods, dosing regimens, comparators, and clinical outcomes such as healing rate, epithelial closure time, tear production, and complications. The level of evidence will be graded using the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine framework. The findings will provide a transparent evidence summary and highlight research gaps, thereby supporting the development of evidence-based clinical guidance in veterinary ophthalmology.

title: High Altitude Cerebral Edema - A Scoping Review
description: Introduction: High-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) is an emergency neuropathology that can occur at elevations of 2500 meters above. This review aims to highlight the pathophysiology of HACE and discuss diagnostics including non-invasive imaging modalities applicable to resource limited settings. Methods: A comprehensive search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science identified 938 records. After duplication removal and screening of 495 articles, 26 studies were included. Eligible studies included studies describing clinical, imaging, or management features of HACE. Results: 51 patients were identified across the 26 included studies, with predominantly males (86%) of 10 to 78 years. Most cases originated from Nepal (n = 10), India (n = 5), and United States (n = 3). Rapid ascent was the most common predisposing factor with symptoms occurring at 2800 to 5895 meters. Hallmark features of HACE included ataxia, altered mental status, and severe headaches. Some cases presented with stroke‐like deficits or cranial neuropathies. Neuroimaging reported vasogenic white‐matter edema, particularly involving the corpus callosum. Increased cytotoxic lesions and microhemorrhages were noted on susceptibility‐weighted MRI. Treatment emphasized prompt descent, dexamethasone, and oxygen therapy, with hyperbaric bags used when descent was delayed. Outcomes were favorable and no deaths were reported. Conclusion: This review highlights HACE occurs following rapid ascent and can present with ataxia, altered mental status, and, in severe cases, corpus callosum involvement on neuroimaging. Early recognition and descent are pivotal, while dexamethasone remains the mainstay for treatment of HACE. Keywords: high altitude cerebral edema, HACE, acute mountain sickness, dexamethasone, scoping review

title: Impact of Diabetes Mellitus on Dental Pulp Tissue Pathosis– A Scoping Review
description: Purpose and background Diabetes mellitus is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by persistent hyperglycemia and is associated with widespread microvascular and inflammatory complications affecting multiple organ systems, including the oral cavity. While there is growing evidence that diabetes alters dental pulp biology—through changes in inflammation, microvasculature, mineralization, and reparative capacity—these findings are scattered across human clinical, histological, biochemical, and animal studies. Existing reviews typically focus on broader oral or periapical disease, or on isolated mechanistic pathways, and do not comprehensively map pulp‐specific changes across both human and animal literature.​​ The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, chart, and synthesize all available evidence on how diabetes mellitus affects dental pulp tissue pathosis, across study designs and models. This approach will clarify the breadth and nature of current knowledge, reveal important gaps, and provide a conceptual framework to guide future mechanistic, translational, and clinical research. Research questions The primary question is: What are the reported effects of diabetes mellitus on dental pulp tissue pathosis (inflammatory, structural, biochemical, mineralization, and clinical changes) in humans and animal models?​ Secondary questions include: How do these pulpal changes differ between diabetes types (type 1 vs. type 2) and levels of glycemic control or disease duration?​ To what extent do diabetic vascular changes within the pulp resemble microangiopathic complications seen in other organs (e.g., retina, kidney)?​​ How is reduced pulpal reparative capacity related to reported dysfunction of dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) under diabetic conditions?​ What are the reported or plausible clinical implications of these changes for diagnosis, prognosis, and endodontic treatment outcomes in people with diabetes? Methods overview This project is a scoping review conducted in accordance with the PRISMA‐ScR extension and established methodological guidance for scoping reviews. The Population–Concept–Context (PCC) framework is used to structure the protocol:​​ Population: human participants with diabetes and experimental animal models of diabetes, as well as ex vivo/in vitro studies using dental pulp tissue or cells derived from such populations.​ Concept: diabetes‐related changes in dental pulp tissue, including inflammatory responses, microvascular and structural alterations, biochemical markers, mineralization (pulp stones, dystrophic calcification), and healing/reparative responses.​ Context: any clinical or experimental setting in which dental pulp tissue is evaluated in relation to diabetes status, with no geographic or care‐setting restriction. A comprehensive search of Medline (via PubMed), Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCOhost has been designed to capture studies up to August 2024, using controlled vocabulary and free‐text terms for diabetes and dental pulp. Additional studies will be identified through reference‐list screening and citation chasing. Two independent reviewers will screen titles/abstracts and full texts against predefined eligibility criteria; disagreements will be resolved by a third reviewer.​​ Eligible studies will include observational human studies (e.g., cross‐sectional, case‐control, retrospective), in vitro analyses of human diabetic pulp tissue or cells, and animal experiments in which diabetes is associated with defined pulpal outcomes. Data will be charted using a standardized extraction form capturing study design, sample characteristics, diabetes type and control, pulpal outcomes, and key limitations. No formal risk‐of‐bias tool will be applied (consistent with scoping review methodology), but key methodological strengths and weaknesses will be summarized narratively.​​ Findings will be synthesized descriptively and thematically, with separate presentation of human and animal data, and structured tables summarizing key features and outcomes. The synthesis will emphasize convergence and divergence between human and animal evidence, and between different diabetes phenotypes and control levels. Expected outcomes This project is expected to produce: A comprehensive map of the evidence base An overview of all published human and animal studies describing how diabetes affects dental pulp tissue, including the range of study designs, populations, and outcome measures.​​ A conceptual model of diabetic pulpal pathosis An integrated description of key pathophysiological domains—chronic inflammation, microangiopathy (thickened vessel walls, reduced lumina, endothelial loss), altered mineralization (pulp stones, dystrophic calcification), and impaired repair capacity—and how they may interact within the diabetic pulp.​​ A proposed framing of pulpal vascular changes as a potential pulp‐specific microvascular complication of diabetes, analogous (with appropriate caveats) to retinopathy and nephropathy.​​ Clarification of clinical implications and knowledge gaps Identification of how diabetic pulpal changes may influence clinical presentations (e.g., higher prevalence of pulp stones and symptomatic irreversible pulpitis), sensibility testing responses, and endodontic treatment outcomes. Highlighted gaps where evidence is sparse or inconsistent, such as direct comparisons of type 1 versus type 2 diabetes, robust stratification by glycemic control, and longitudinal endodontic outcome studies in diabetic cohorts.​​ Directions for future research and practice Specific recommendations for mechanistic studies (e.g., on DPSC dysfunction, epigenetic changes, microvascular remodeling) and for translational and clinical work (e.g., prospective endodontic outcome studies stratified by HbA1c and diabetic complications).​​ Practical suggestions for clinicians regarding risk assessment, monitoring, and treatment planning for endodontic patients with diabetes, while also outlining where evidence remains insufficient for firm guidelines.​ Significance By systematically assembling and interpreting the fragmented literature on diabetes and dental pulp, this scoping review will clarify whether diabetic pulpal changes represent a distinct microangiopathic and inflammatory complication, and how these changes may influence diagnosis and management in endodontic practice. The results will inform both clinical decision‐making and the design of future mechanistic and clinical studies, and may serve as a foundation for subsequent focused systematic reviews or meta‐analyses on specific aspects of diabetic pulp pathology.

title: Artificial Intelligence as a Surrogate for Electroretinography in Cone Dystrophy: A Feasibility Framework
description: This project registers a feasibility framework exploring whether artificial intelligence (AI) models applied to multimodal retinal imaging can predict electroretinography (ERG)–defined cone dysfunction in cone dystrophy. Full-field ERG remains the gold standard for assessing cone photoreceptor function; however, access to ERG is limited in many clinical and low-resource settings. This framework proposes the use of widely available imaging modalities—optical coherence tomography (OCT) and fundus autofluorescence (FAF)—combined with convolutional neural network–based models to infer whether cone-specific ERG parameters (photopic single-flash and 30 Hz flicker responses) fall within or outside normal limits. The project is designed as a methodological and conceptual feasibility exercise rather than a confirmatory study. It does not aim to replace ERG, predict raw ERG waveforms, or commit to a predefined dataset or sample size. Instead, it documents a structured approach for investigating structure–function relationships in inherited retinal diseases using AI, particularly in ERG-limited environments. An abstract based on this framework has been accepted into the scientific program of the 40th World Ophthalmology Congress (WOC 2026), to be held in Prague, Czech Republic, under the topic Artificial Intelligence and Telemedicine, as an E-Poster Viewing presentation (poster identifier PV-AI-033), titled "Artificial Intelligence as a Surrogate for Electroretinography in Cone Dystrophy Diagnosis: A Feasibility Framework." This registration documents the feasibility framework for academic record-keeping and research portfolio purposes.

title: What is the coverage of retina screening services for people with diabetes? Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy is a leading cause of vision impairment globally. Vision loss from diabetic retinopathy can generally be prevented by early detection and timely treatment. The World Health Organization (WHO) included a measure of service access for diabetic retinopathy as a core indicator in the Eye Care Indicator Menu launched in 2022: Retina screening coverage for people with diabetes. The aim of this review is to provide a comprehensive global and regional summary of the available information on retina screening coverage for people with diabetes. Methods and analysis: A search will be conducted in Medline (Ovid) and Embase without language restrictions for studies from any country reporting retina screening coverage for adults with any type of diabetes at the national or subnational level using data collected since 1 January 2000. We will also seek reports and coverage statistics from government websites of all WHO member states. Two investigators will independently screen studies, extract relevant data and assess risk of bias of included studies. The review will be reported using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis guideline. We will summarise the range of coverage definitions reported across included studies and present the median retina screening coverage in WHO regions and by World Bank country income level. Depending on the availability of data, we will conduct meta-analysis to assess disparities in retina screening coverage for people with diabetes by factors in the PROGRESS framework (Place of residence, Race/ethnicity/culture/language, Occupation, Gender/sex, Religion, Education, Socioeconomic status, and Social capital). Ethics and dissemination: This review will only include published data thus no ethical approval will be sought. The findings of this review will be published in a peer-reviewed journal and presented at relevant conferences.

description: Despite a wide range of preoperative anxiety-management interventions, no systematic and standardized strategy bundle tailored specifically for ophthalmic surgery exists. title: Functional topography of anger and aggression in the human cerebellum
description: New insights into the functional neuro-anatomic correlates of emotions point toward the involvement of the cerebellum in anger and aggression. To identify cerebellar regions commonly activated in tasks examining the experience of anger and threat as well as exerting an aggressive response, two coordinate-based activation likelihood estimation meta-analysis reporting a total of fifty-seven cerebellar activation foci from 819 participants were performed. For anger processing (18 studies), results showed significant clusters in the bilateral posterior cerebellum, overlapping with results from previous meta-analyses on emotion processing, and implying functional connectivity to cognitive, limbic, and social canonic networks in the cerebral cortex. By contrast, active aggression expression (10 studies) was associated with significant clusters in more anterior regions of the cerebellum, overlapping with cerebellar somatosensory and motor regions and displaying functional connectivity with the somatomotor and default mode network. This study not only strengthens the notion that the cerebellum is involved in emotion processing, but also provides the first quantitative evidence for distinct cerebellar functional activation patterns related to anger and aggression.

title: Quantifying In-Vivo Arterial Deformation from CT and MRI: A Systematic Review of Segmentation, Motion Tracking, and Kinematic Metrics
description: This project is an ongoing systematic review of methods for quantifying three-dimensional, time-resolved (3D+t) deformation and motion of human arteries using computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). We are interested in going beyond static descriptors such as vessel diameter to capture the dynamic mechanical behaviour of the arterial wall, which is strongly influenced by ageing, hypertension, genetic factors, and disease. Our goal is to map and critically appraise the current landscape of CT and MRI techniques that extract dynamic biomechanical metrics, and to clarify how these metrics relate to vascular ageing and pathology. We are conducting the review in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Our search strategy covers Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (search date: December 19, 2025), without a lower date limit. We are including peer-reviewed, patient-specific, in vivo CT or MRI studies that explicitly quantify arterial deformation or motion tracking in large human arteries, and excluding work focused on non-vascular tissues, purely experimental or in vitro setups, purely computational models, drug effects, or haemodynamics without wall deformation. After de-duplication and screening, we are selecting eligible full texts and extracting data on imaging protocols, segmentation approaches, temporal tracking methods, and reported biomechanical metrics. Methodologically, we are organizing the review around three core components of the imaging pipeline: (1) segmentation, ranging from manual and semi-automatic workflows in commercial/open-source software to more recent convolutional neural network (CNN) approaches; (2) temporal 3D motion tracking methods used; (3) biomechanical outputs, such as displacements and strains, geometric descriptors and derived stiffness indices. We expect the main outcomes of this work to be: (i) a systematic catalogue of CT and MRI pipelines for segmentation and 3D+t motion tracking of large human arteries; (ii) a structured overview of the biomechanical metrics currently reported; (iii) an integrated synthesis of dynamic findings across studies, highlighting consistent patterns such as age-related stiffening, spatially heterogeneous deformation, and differences between healthy and diseased vessels.

title: Diabetic retinopathy in primary health care: a narrative review
description: ABSTRACT Objective: This review aims to summarize the most relevant information on diabetic retinopathy (DR), a common preventable complication of diabetes, highlighting the key role of the primary care physician in its timely detection and management. Design and Methodology: A narrative review of the scientific literature published in the last decade was conducted. Study selection: original articles, reviews, clinical guidelines, consensus statements and grey literature providing current and relevant data were included; ultimately, 43 references were selected after critical analysis, compiling information on prevalence, risk factors, pathophysiological mechanisms, prevention strategies, diagnosis, and treatment. Results: DR affects more than one in five adults with diabetes, and its prevalence continues to rise. Careful control of blood glucose, blood pressure, and lipid levels, along with regular screening and patient education, are the most effective tools to prevent visual loss. Additionally, objective assessment of visual acuity (VA) and systematic fundus examination are essential for early detection and appropriate monitoring of the disease. Current therapies, such as anti-VEGF (anti-vascular endothelial growth factor) agents and laser photocoagulation, have improved the prognosis of advanced cases. Conclusions: DR can be effectively prevented and treated if detected early. The general practitioner, with a comprehensive and interdisciplinary approach, plays a fundamental role in reducing the impact of this disease and improving the quality of life of people with diabetes. Keywords: diabetic retinopathy, diabetes mellitus, primary care, microvascular complications, screening.

title: Mis-perception of motion in depth originates from an incomplete transformation of retinal signals
description: Depth perception requires the use of an internal model of the eye-head geometry to infer distance from binocular retinal images and extraretinal 3D eye-head information, particularly ocular vergence. Similarly for motion in depth perception, gaze angle is required to correctly interpret the spatial direction of motion from retinal images; however, it is unknown whether the brain can make adequate use of extraretinal version and vergence information to correctly transform binocular retinal motion into 3D spatial coordinates. Here, we tested this by asking participants to reconstruct the spatial trajectory of an isolated disparity stimulus moving in depth either peri-foveally or peripherally while participants' gaze was oriented at different vergence and version angles. We found large systematic errors in the perceived motion trajectory that reflected an intermediate reference frame between a purely retinal interpretation of binocular retinal motion (not accounting for veridical vergence and version) and the spatially correct motion. We quantify these errors with a 3D reference frame model accounting for target, eye and head position upon motion percept encoding. This model could capture the behavior well, revealing that participants tended to underestimate their version by up to 17%, overestimate their vergence by up to 22%, and underestimate the overall change in retinal disparity by up to 64%, and that the use of extraretinal information depended on retinal eccentricity. Since such large perceptual errors are not observed in everyday viewing, we suggest that both monocular retinal cues and binocular extraretinal signals are required for accurate real-world motion in depth perception.

title: Anatomical variations of the genitofemoral nerve. A systematic review.
description: The purpose of this systematic review is to comprehensively synthesize current anatomical evidence regarding the variations of the genitofemoral nerve and its branches. Although the genitofemoral nerve exhibits certain typical features of its course and branching of its divisions, there is still notable variability reported across studies. A clear understanding of these patterns is crucial for clinicians, anatomists, and surgeons — particularly those involved in urological, neurosurgical, anesthetic, and gynecological procedures of the inguinal and pelvic region. Objectives: The main purpose of this research is to systematically collect, analyze, and synthesize published data on the anatomical features of the genitofemoral nerve. This includes its origin, course, branching pattern, diameters, lengths, and common variants, as well as the prevalence of such variations. In addition, we are going to focus on its morphological data such as detailed measurements of the canals through which it passes. By consolidating evidence, this review aims to provide a clear and comprehensive overview of the morphology of the genitofemoral nerve and its clinical significance. Methods: This review will follow PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase) will be systematically searched using predefined Boolean queries focused on the genitofemoral nerve and its branches. Inclusion criteria will encompass cadaveric, radiological and intraoperative reporting detailed data on the morphology of the genitofemoral nerve. Two independent reviewers will perform screening, data extraction, and quality assessment. Expected Outcomes: Identification of common and rare anatomical variants and their prevalence. - Highlight gaps and inconsistencies in literature regarding its anatomy. - Provide evidence-based insights to aid clinicians - particularly gynecologists - in anticipating anatomical variations during diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. - Establish a foundation for future anatomical and clinical research related to the genitofemoral nerve and its area of innervation. - This project should contribute to improving understanding of genitofemoral variability, which may translate into safer surgical planning and more precise interventions within the inguinal and pelvic region. Identification of common and rare anatomical variants and their prevalence. Insights into the clinical implications of these patterns for surgical planning and peripheral nerve blockade. Recommendations for future research directions, including standardization of anatomical terminology and classification systems. Significance: By consolidating current anatomical and clinical data, this systematic review aims to enhance the understanding of the genitofemoral nerve variations, support evidence-based surgical and anesthetic practice, and provide a foundational reference for future anatomical, neurophysiological, and imaging studies.

title: The Biochemical Paradox of Combining Ozone and Platelet-Rich Fibrin for Osteoarthritis: A Critical Narrative Review
description: Abstract Background: Osteoarthritis represents a significant clinical challenge characterized by progressive hyaline cartilage degradation and limited intrinsic regenerative capacity. Platelet-rich fibrin (PRF) and ozone therapy have independently emerged as minimally invasive, biologically based interventions. Their combined intra-articular application has gained increasing clinical interest despite unresolved mechanistic contradictions. Objective: To synthesize current knowledge regarding the proposed mechanisms of ozone and PRF, critically examine the biochemical paradox underlying their interaction, and evaluate the strength of clinical evidence supporting their combined use in osteoarthritis. Methods: A narrative review was conducted through a non-systematic exploration of the literature in PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (2005–2026). Emphasis was placed on molecular mechanisms, preclinical investigations, translational rationale, and uncontrolled clinical studies. Results: Ozone (15–30 μg/mL) may modulate the joint microenvironment by activating the Nrf2 antioxidant pathway and suppressing NF-κB–mediated inflammatory signaling. PRF provides a three-dimensional fibrin scaffold that sustains the release of growth factors, including PDGF, TGF-β, and VEGF. However, a fundamental biochemical paradox exists: the oxidative properties of ozone may structurally modify or denature protein-based growth factors within PRF, potentially attenuating their biological activity. A preliminary uncontrolled clinical series reports symptomatic improvement (pain reduction and functional gains) and apparent increases in cartilage thickness on imaging. Nonetheless, these structural claims lack histological confirmation and appear to exceed biologically plausible rates of adult hyaline cartilage regeneration. Observed imaging changes may instead reflect resolution of bone marrow edema, alterations in matrix hydration, or fibrocartilaginous repair rather than true hyaline restoration. Conclusions: The combination of ozone and PRF constitutes a biologically plausible yet investigational approach that requires rigorous mechanistic and clinical validation. The identified biochemical paradox underscores the need for in vitro studies to determine whether optimized temporal sequencing (e.g., 24–72-hour interval) could mitigate oxidative antagonism. Until high-quality randomized controlled trials incorporating histological or second-look arthroscopic assessment demonstrate structural regeneration, this combined therapy should be regarded as experimental. Transparent disclosure of its preliminary evidence base and regulatory status (FDA, EMA, ANVISA) is essential during informed consent.

description: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) remains a leading cause of preventable blindness, with its global prevalence projected to rise sharply as diabetes incidence increases. Early detection and timely management are critical to reducing DR-related vision loss. Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA) now enables non-invasive, layer-specific visualization of the retinal vasculature, facilitating more precise identification of early microvascular changes. Concurrently, advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) architectures such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), attention-based models, and Vision Transformers, have revolutionized image analysis. These AI-driven tools substantially enhance the sensitivity, specificity, and interpretability of DR screening. A systematic review of PubMed, Scopus, WOS, and Embase databases, including quality assessment of published studies, investigating the result of different AI algorithms with OCTA parameters in DR patients will be conducted. The variables of interest will comprise training databases, type of image, imaging modality, number of images, outcomes, algorithm/model used, and performance metrics.

title: A qualitative study examining the health system's response to COVID-19 in Sierra Leone
description: The paper examines the health system's response to COVID-19 in Sierra Leone. It aims to explore how the pandemic affected service delivery, health workers, patient access to services, leadership, and governance. It also examines to what extent the legacy of the 2013-16 Ebola outbreak influenced the COVID-19 response and public perception. Using the WHO Health System Building Blocks Framework, we conducted a qualitative study in Sierra Leone where semi-structured interviews were conducted with health workers, policymakers, and patients between Oct-Dec 2020. We applied thematic analysis using both deductive and inductive approaches. Twelve themes emerged from the analysis: nine on the WHO building blocks, two on patients' experiences, and one on Ebola. We found that routine services were impacted by enhanced infection prevention control measures. Health workers faced additional responsibilities and training needs. Communication and decision-making within facilities were reported to be coordinated and effective, although updates cascading from the national level to facilities were lacking. In contrast with previous health emergencies which were heavily influenced by international organisations, we found that the COVID-19 response was led by the national leadership. Experiences of Ebola resulted in less fear of COVID-19 and a greater understanding of public health measures. However, these measures also negatively affected patients' livelihoods and their willingness to visit facilities. We conclude, it is important to address existing challenges in the health system such as resources that affect the capacity of health systems to respond to emergencies. Prioritising the well-being of health workers and the continued provision of essential routine health services is important. The socio-economic impact of public health measures on the population needs to be considered before measures are implemented.

title: What Drives a Jury's Deliberation
description: This study explored how pretrial publicity (PTP) exposure and jury composition affect the slant and content of jury deliberations. It compares jury deliberations (N = 63) composed of jurors (N = 333) who are exposed to the same type of PTP [pure juries: all exposed to negative-victim (NV), negative-defendant (ND), or no PTP] to juries composed of jurors exposed to different types of PTP (mixed juries, e.g., half exposed to ND PTP and half to no PTP). Jury composition was found to bias the slant of trial evidence discussion, with pure-NV juries demonstrating a pro-defense bias and pure-ND juries a pro-prosecution bias. This bias was also evident on mixed juries consisting of PTP-exposed jurors and no-PTP jurors. Importantly, biased evidence discussion mediated the effect jury composition on post-deliberation guilt assessments and was responsible for the spread of PTP bias from ND-PTP jurors to no-PTP jurors during deliberations. In addition, the deliberations of pure-NV juries showed evidence of being verdict driven by spending less time discussing trial evidence and taking more frequent straw polls than pure no-PTP juries. Finally, jury composition influenced the frequency of PTP discussion (pure ND-PTP juries discussed more frequently than pure NV-PTP juries), but not the frequency of PTP correction nor its effectiveness. Implications include that jury deliberations are not wholly effective at reducing PTP bias, regardless of jury composition. This is thought to be due to jurors' biased encoding of trial evidence and source misattributions, resulting in biased trial evidence discussion and PTP discussion during deliberations.

title: Consciousness-related interactions in a double-slit optical system
description: Motivated by a series of reported experiments and their controversial results, the present work investigated if volunteers could causally affect an optical double-slit system by mental efforts alone. The participants' task in the experimental sessions alternated between intending an increase in the (real-time feedback-informed) amount of light diffracted through a specific single slit versus relaxing their intentional effort. In total, 240 sessions contributed by 171 volunteers were recorded. The first 160 sessions were collected in an exploratory mode, and those data revealed statistically significant differences between the intention and relax conditions. The analysis method and variables of interest derived from the exploratory sessions were then pre-registered for the subsequent 80 formal sessions. The formal experiments, based on a directional hypothesis, were not statistically significant. A post hoc meta-analysis based on a bi-directional hypothesis, and applied to the same data, resulted in a 2.75 sigma outcome ($p=6.02\times10^{-3}; \, es=0.31 \pm 0.22$ 95\% CI). Directional and bi-directional analyses applied to an equal number of control sessions, all conducted without observers present, resulted in uniformly non-significant outcomes. Analysis of environmental factors did not reveal any artifactual sources that might have produced the significant bi-directional effect. While the pre-registered analysis did not support the existence of the investigated phenomenon, the post hoc findings warrant further investigation to formally test the bi-directional hypothesis.

title: Rationality, Perception, and the All-Seeing Eye
description: Seeing—perception and vision—is implicitly the fundamental building block of the literature on rationality and cognition. Herbert Simon and Daniel Kahneman's arguments against the omniscience of economic agents—and the concept of bounded rationality—depend critically on a particular view of the nature of perception and vision. We propose that this framework of rationality merely replaces economic omniscience with perceptual omniscience. We show how the cognitive and social sciences feature a pervasive but problematic meta-assumption that is characterized by an "all-seeing eye." We raise concerns about this assumption and discuss different ways in which the all-seeing eye manifests itself in existing research on (bounded) rationality. We first consider the centrality of vision and perception in Simon's pioneering work. We then point to Kahneman's work—particularly his article "Maps of Bounded Rationality"—to illustrate the pervasiveness of an all-seeing view of perception, as manifested in the extensive use of visual examples and illusions. Similar assumptions about perception can be found across a large literature in the cognitive sciences. The central problem is the present emphasis on inverse optics—the objective nature of objects and environments, e.g., size, contrast, and color. This framework ignores the nature of the organism and perceiver. We argue instead that reality is constructed and expressed, and we discuss the species-specificity of perception, as well as perception as a user interface. We draw on vision science as well as the arts to develop an alternative understanding of rationality in the cognitive and social sciences. We conclude with a discussion of the implications of our arguments for the rationality and decision-making literature in cognitive psychology and behavioral economics, along with suggesting some ways forward

title: What are the effects of different cold preservation media versus Optisol-GS on corneal quality preservation? A systematic review.
description: There are distinct cold corneal storage media used in cornea preservation. Optisol-GS (Bausch & Lomb Inc, USA) is the most commonly used corneal storage medium in the USA, and considered as the "gold standard" medium (Jeng, 2006). It contains two different antibiotics: gentamicin sulfate and streptomycin sulfate. Several studies have compared the effects of the use of distinct cold corneal storage media to the use of Optisol-GS on the quality of stored corneas. Nonetheless, there is not a single standardized protocol to assess the overall quality of the stored corneal tissue (Parek et al. 2014). Indeed, different qualitative and quantitative parameters have been used to determine their state or condition. In this sense, on the quality of stored corneas, a broad comparison between the use of distinct cold corneal media and the use of Optisol-GS, regarding the reported corneal quality parameters, would contribute to the body of knowledge on this field. The results would: shed light on the effect of media components, storage time and temperature on the quality of stored corneas; give support to the development of new corneal storage media; and contribute to the development of a standardized protocol to determine the quality of stored corneas. Therefore, the aim of this study is to systematically review the literature concerning the effects of the use of distinct cold corneal storage media compared to the use of Optisol-GS on the quality of stored corneas, aiming to answer the proposed focused question: What are the effects of different cold preservation media versus Optisol-GS on corneal quality preservation?

title: Association between cognitive dysfunction and retinal alterations on OCT among patients with Schizophrenia, Bipolar Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder
description: The retina, as the outermost part of the central nervous system (CNS), shares the same embryonic origin and structural characteristics as brain tissue. Retinal imaging has emerged as a valuable approach for identifying ophthalmic markers of psychiatric disorders associated with structural CNS alterations. Optical coherence tomography (OCT), a non-invasive, painless, rapid, and cost-effective technique, enables high-resolution visualisation of retinal layers. Evidence suggests that retinal structural changes may parallel cognitive decline and the onset or progression of neuropsychiatric disorders. Recent studies have investigated retinal alterations across a range of psychiatric conditions, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, autism spectrum disorder, major depressive disorder, personality disorders, generalised anxiety disorder, and anorexia nervosa. This systematic review aims to investigate if there is an association between cognitive dysfunction and retinal alterations, measured by Optical Coherence Tomography, in patients diagnosed with Major Psychiatric Disorders, such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder and major depressive disorder.

title: Accuracy of Intraoperative Surgical Margin Assessment Techniques in Veterinary Oncology
description: Accurate determination of surgical margin status is fundamental for detecting residual microscopic residual cancer in patients, predicting clinical outcomes, and optimizing treatment planning. Postoperative histopathology following surgical tumor resection is considered the gold standard for margin evaluation; however, this process typically takes one or two weeks to obtain results and only a limited sample of the surgical margins are assessed. Consequently, this delay results in a missed opportunity to evaluate surgical margins in real time and to utilize that information for immediate intraoperative decision-making, which could improve patient outcomes. Several techniques are available for intraoperative surgical margin assessment, each with different levels of accuracy, including frozen tissue section biopsy, imprint cytology margin, near-infrared fluorescence imaging, and optical coherence tomography (OCT) which has the potential to guide surgical-decision making in real-time. This review aims to compare the diagnostic accuracy of intraoperative surgical margin evaluation techniques as individual studies focus on the reporting of accuracy of one technique in comparison to histopathology. Only studies on canine cutaneous or subcutaneous tumors will be included in the review. The primary outcome of the review is comparison of diagnostic accuracy for detection of positive surgical margins in cutaneous and subcutaneous tumors across techniques.

description: The liquid crystal eye polarimeter measures in vivo polarimetric images of the eye in the near infrared. The polarimeter features a polarization state generator composed of a light source with a wavelength of 940nm, a linear polarizer, and two liquid crystal variable retarders to control the illuminating polarization. title: Drug-drug interactions between androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) and cardiovascular medicines in prostate cancer patients. Mapping the available evidence: a scoping review protocol
description: Patients with prostate cancer frequently have cardiovascular co-morbidities such as hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation (AF) and cancer associated thrombosis In a case control study of 12,120 patients with prostate cancer, 59% of patients had cardiovascular disease prior to prostate cancer diagnosis (1). The addition of androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) treatment to patients with advanced prostate cancer further increases their risk of cardiovascular events (2). Androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) such as enzalutamide, apalutamide, abiraterone and darolutamide are therefore frequently prescribed alongside medicines used to treat cardiovascular disease. It is known that enzalutamide is a strong inducer of the hepatic drug-metabolising enzyme cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) and a moderate inducer of CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 (3). Apalutamide is a strong inducer of CYP3A4 and CYP2C19 (4). Consequently, both drugs have the potential to significantly lower levels of cardiovascular medicines prescribed concomitantly, which rely on these enzymes for metabolism (CYP3A4, CYP2C9 and CYP2C19 substrates). These may include, but not limited to, direct acting anticoagulants (DOACs), beta blockers, angiotensin II inhibitors/antagonists, calcium channel blockers, statins and antiplatelets. Currently there is no consensus on how to manage patients on ARPIs who also require concomitant cardiovascular medicines that may interact. Prescribing information for enzalutamide advises caution or avoidance of these combinations, if dose adjustments are not easily performed based on monitoring of efficacy or plasma concentrations (5). Similarly, for apalutamide the advice is to monitor for loss of efficacy or substitute where necessary (6). It is not known whether these drug -drug interactions (DDIs) directly have an impact on cardiovascular events by way of reduced efficacy. This scoping review aims to identify and map the available research on DDIs of ARPIs and medicines used to treat common cardiovascular conditions. This will be guided by the following research questions: 1. What are the cardiovascular outcomes of patients taking concomitant ARPIs and interacting cardiovascular medicines. 2. What outcome measures were used to report the impact of drug interactions between ARPIs and cardiovascular medicines. This will identify gaps in the research to guide further work on this topic and pragmatic management of patients on these combinations. 1. Nead KT, Haas AM, Zhao J, et al. title: The cross-talk between arterial stiffness and microvascular complications in individuals with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus: a systematic review
description: Arterial stiffness (AS) is a well-established index of macrovascular damage and predicts cardiovascular complications in many diseases including diabetes mellitus (DM). DM is strongly linked with microcirculatory changes, including retinopathy, microalbuminuria and neuropathy. We aimed to review in a systematic manner the possible correlation between AS and microvascular impairment in patients with DM, type 1 or 2. We performed a literature search in PubMed, Scopus and Embase database from inception to 4 th April 2024. We included studies with adult patients diagnosed with type 1 or 2 DM, which evaluated the correlation of AS and impaired microcirculation. AS could be evaluated with pulse wave velocity (PWV), carotid-ankle vascular index (CAVI), ambulatory arterial stiffness index (AASI) and augmentation index (Aix). Impaired microcirculation was defined by the presence of one or more of the following: retinopathy, albuminuria, neuropathy, dermal capillary alterations.

title: Dynamics of attribution
description: The study generally investigates how participants' motivational/goal framings influence their Kelleyian causal attributions following goal-related failure outcomes. It also investigates the mechanisms underlying the influence of individuals' Weinerian causal attributions to a goal-related failure outcome on their subsequent behavior, beliefs, and motivation. The study was run in a second-year computer science course at the University of Toronto. Participants were students registered in the course who consented to participate in this semester-long study. The study consisted of a series of surveys, administered online through the Qualtrics survey platform. Participants received the surveys via email at pre-determined time points throughout the semester (specifically following formal evaluations). The course evaluations consisted of 1) weekly practice labs (7 in total), 2) two term tests, and 3) one project. A breakdown of the surveys is included below: T1 - Pre-survey - sept 4th T2 - Lab 2 - sept 13th T3 - Lab 4 - sept 27th T4 - Term Test 1 - oct 7th T5 - Lab 6 - Oct 25th T6 - Project Assembly - Nov 6 T7 - Lab 7 - Nov 15th T8 - Term Test 2 - Nov 18th Surveys for lab 1, 3, and 5 were skipped to avoid overwhelming students (surveys were limited to a maximum of one per week). Lab surveys were sent on the same day as the lab was completed since they were graded on the same day. However, surveys for the term test and projects were sent on the weeks that grades for the assignment were released (~2 weeks after the evaluations were completed/submitted). At the start of the study participants were asked about their goals in the course for the semester ("What % grade are you aiming to achieve in this course?") We also collected students': Demographics prior experience in computer science prior experience with the course content The value of the goal for them Their commitment, expectancy of success, commitment, willingness to exert effort, and value in relation to the goal. their motivation/self-regulation style towards their course goal (intrinsic/identified/introjected/extrinsic). Their general self-efficacy in the computer science domain Their specific self-efficacy in the course domain In the lab surveys we asked participants to rate their performance on the relevant evaluation according to the Kelleyian attributional dimensions (consensus, consistency, distinctiveness). We also ask them to identify the cause of their performance and rate the cause across the Weinerian attributional dimensions (locus, controllability, stability) and globality. We also asked participants about their study habits (times spent studying, use of course discussion board, use of office hours) that week. Finally, we asked participants for their general and specific self-efficacy ratings following the evaluation. In the term test and project surveys we asked the same questions as the lab surveys, as well as some additional measures. This is because labs had a much lower overall weight on the course grade (2% each). In comparison, term tests and the project had a greater weight (10-20%) and we anticipated greater shifts in student's beliefs, behaviors, and motivation following the major evaluations. The term test and project surveys additionally measured whether students' beliefs about what effort looks like in studying, and their own effort in the course. We also measured changes in participants' commitment, willingness to exert effort, value, and expectancy in relation to the goal. We also asked them if they wanted to retain the same % grade goal or change their goal.

title: Justice is in the Eyes of the Beholder IV: Coherence Shifts (online pilot)
description: Judges are obliged to justify the decisions they make. Judges are supposed to be impartial. One purpose of written justifications is to check for impartiality. This would be straightforward if written reasons were a faithful representation of the mental process that led the judge to her decision. A precondition for an argument brought forward by one of the parties to affect the judge's decision is the judge paying attention to the argument. Arguably the more the judge pays attention, the greater the impact of the argument. The number and the duration of fixations on items is a good proxy for attention. If there were a close mapping between mental process and the reasons expressed in the ruling, the more the judge fixates on the item representing an argument, the more importance she should give this argument in the reasons of her ruling. In an earlier study we have found that, actually, eye gaze and stated relevance are uncorrelated. The same also holds for stated difficulty in understanding the argument, stated degree of ambiguity, and stated degree of conflict with other arguments. However, eye gaze strongly predicts decisions. We take this as evidence that the mental process of discovery, and the representation of the result, are autonomous activities. As an ex post rationalisation, we propose that the decision is found by way of parallel constraint satisfaction. Decision makers are not aware of this subconscious process. A new study serves two purposes: 1. We want to put this ex post rationalisation to the test. 2. We want to gain insight into the mental process that leads to the formation of the decision. We are, in particular, interested in the importance of attention on arguments that speak against the ultimate ruling. This pre-study is confined to the first purpose. It uses the same materials that we plan to use for the main study. We however omit eye tracking. We want to test whether we do indeed find parallel constraint satisfaction. If true, we should see that participants reweight the arguments after they have made their decision.

title: Optic nerve point-of-care ultrasonography in the assessment of findings suggestive of intracranial hypertension in critically ill patients: a scoping review protocol focusing on nurses' decision-makin
description: Research Objective: Intracranial hypertension (ICH) is caused by various neurological conditions such as trauma, tumors, and strokes. Measuring the optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) using point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) has proven to be a promising alternative for the early detection of ICH, as this diameter reflects increased intracranial pressure (ICP). The use of POCUS by nurses in critical settings such as ICUs and emergency departments can expedite triage and clinical decision-making, especially in locations with limited access to imaging exams. However, there are still gaps in practice and knowledge regarding this tool. This scoping review aims to investigate the applicability, accuracy, and impact of POCUS in nursing practice, contributing to the development of evidence-based clinical guidelines and strengthening the role of nursing in the care of critically ill patients. The research question was developed according to the PCC strategy. Therefore, the research question is: What scientific evidence is available regarding the use of point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) of the optic nerve in assessing signs suggestive of intracranial hypertension in critically ill patients, with an emphasis on supporting clinical decision-making by nurses? This is a scoping review guided by the recommendations of the Joanna Briggs Institute and will follow the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols – extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The review will be conducted using the databases PubMed, Science Direct, Scopus, Scielo, Embase, Cochrane, and CINAHL, as well as a selection of grey literature from the CAPES database and Google Scholar. The keywords ("Intracranial Hypertension," "Ultrasonography," "Nurse," and "Optic Nerve") and indexing terms from the articles will serve as the basis for the search strategies. Studies will initially be selected based on title and abstract by independent reviewers, who will apply inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data from the articles included in the scoping review will be extracted by two independent reviewers using the JBI Template Source of Evidence Details, Characteristics and Results Extraction tool and a custom tool developed by the reviewers. The synthesis of included studies will be performed qualitatively, with results organized into tables and figures.

The Relational Variational Principle thus provides the unifying scaffold beneath the Kernel papers [2,3], the RFT Theory of Everything (TOE) [4], and the Seeding [5] and Subpresence [6] Theorems. It establishes the necessary mathematical foundation showing that any coherent universe must arise from self-referential geometry—and that the laws of physics are emergent consequences of coherence optimizing its own domain. This is not a model. It is the unique action whose stationary point forces domain reflexivity, fixed-point emergence, and the closure of physical law. No other variational principle is internally consistent. Provenance: Originally published on Zenodo (Oct- 2025). 10.5281/zenodo.17620253

title: Body-Image-Study
description: The use of social media platforms such as Instagram, where images and videos are primarily shared, is becoming increasingly popular. Previous studies have already shown that the use of social media can have a negative impact on mood and body image. This could be because the content shared on social media often caters to prevailing beauty ideals (e.g., slimness, fitness). Against this background, the aim of the present study is to investigate the influence of images of people who are conform to the prevailing beauty ideal on the body image of the participants. For this purpose, an online survey is conducted in a convenience sample of men and women aged 18 to 50. The participants are randomly assigned to an experimental group (EG) or a control group (CG). In the experimental group, participants see images of people who are conform to the beauty ideal of slimness and/or muscularity. In the control group, images of people of average build to overweight are shown. All participants are presented eleven images that correspond to their stated gender. In addition, participants answer questions about the images shown to ensure that they have been viewed attentively. Body image is assessed both as a stable trait and as a momentary state. The state body image is assessed using the Body Image State Scale (BISS) and a modified version of the Drive for Muscularity Scale (DMS, cognitive subscale; response scale and instructions adapted to the experience in the current moment) before and after viewing the images. To assess trait body image, subscales (shape concern, weight concern) of the Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire (EDE-Q) and the DMS in its original version are used. Furthermore, Instagram usage behavior, sports behavior, body mass index (BMI), and sociodemographic data are collected.

title: Real-World Outcomes After Switching to Faricimab in Previously Treated Neovascular Age-Related Macular Degeneration: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD) is a leading cause of irreversible visual impairment in the elderly population and requires long-term intravitreal anti–vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapy to control disease activity. Although currently available anti-VEGF agents are effective in many patients, a substantial proportion exhibit persistent or recurrent fluid despite regular treatment, often necessitating frequent injections and resulting in a high treatment burden. These challenges have led to increasing interest in alternative therapeutic strategies that may provide improved disease control and durability. Faricimab is a bispecific monoclonal antibody targeting both VEGF-A and angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2), thereby addressing two key pathways involved in vascular permeability and inflammation. In routine clinical practice, faricimab is increasingly used as a switch therapy in eyes with suboptimal response to prior anti-VEGF agents. However, the available real-world evidence on outcomes following such a switch is heterogeneous, with variability in study design, patient populations, treatment regimens, and reported endpoints. In particular, there is limited clarity regarding the temporal profile of anatomical and functional response after switching, as well as the extent to which anatomical improvements translate into visual gains. The purpose of this project is to systematically synthesize the existing real-world evidence on outcomes after switching to faricimab in previously treated nAMD. This study focuses on key functional and anatomical endpoints, including best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), central subfield thickness (CST), and pigment epithelial detachment (PED) height, assessed at predefined timepoints up to 12 months following the switch. By applying a quantitative meta-analytic approach to evaluate changes from baseline, this project aims to provide a robust estimate of treatment effects over time. In addition to quantitative synthesis, the study also explores patterns across individual studies, including differences in baseline characteristics, prior treatment exposure, and response dynamics. Particular attention is given to the relationship between anatomical improvements and functional outcomes, as well as to sources of heterogeneity across studies. Treatment interval outcomes, while clinically important, are analyzed descriptively due to substantial variability in reporting and definitions across the literature. The expected outcomes of this project include a comprehensive characterization of the real-world effectiveness of faricimab as a switch therapy in treatment-experienced nAMD. Based on existing evidence, it is anticipated that switching to faricimab will result in consistent anatomical improvements, particularly reductions in central retinal thickness and fluid compartments, while visual acuity is expected to remain largely stable in this heavily pre-treated population. The study further aims to clarify the extent to which early anatomical response may predict longer-term outcomes and to identify potential drivers of variability between studies. Overall, this project is intended to provide clinically relevant evidence to inform treatment decisions in patients with suboptimal response to prior anti-VEGF therapy. By synthesizing real-world data across multiple cohorts, the findings may help guide expectations regarding treatment response, support individualized management strategies, and identify areas where further research is needed, particularly with respect to long-term outcomes and optimization of treatment intervals.
