title: Adult-Onset Coats' Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Clinical Presentation, Imaging Characteristics, and Treatment Outcomes
description: 1. Title Adult-Onset Coats' Disease: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Clinical Presentation, Imaging Characteristics, and Treatment Outcomes 2. Background and Rationale Coats' disease is a rare, idiopathic retinal vascular disorder characterized by telangiectatic vessels, exudation, and potential retinal detachment. While predominantly described in children, a subset of cases presents in adulthood, exhibiting distinct clinical features, slower progression, and differing response to treatment. Despite increasing recognition of adult-onset Coats' disease as a separate clinical entity, the literature remains fragmented, consisting mainly of case reports and small case series. No prior systematic review or meta-analysis has comprehensively synthesized available evidence on clinical characteristics and outcomes in this population. Understanding treatment efficacy and prognostic factors in adult-onset Coats' disease is critical to inform best practices and guide management. 3. Objectives To systematically evaluate the clinical presentation, imaging findings, treatment modalities, and outcomes of adult-onset Coats' disease and to synthesize available data using descriptive and quantitative methods. Primary objectives: To estimate pooled anatomical success rates following treatment. To determine recurrence rates. To assess mean change in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) among adults. Secondary objectives: To describe the distribution of Shields stages at presentation. To compare outcomes by treatment modality (laser, anti-VEGF, corticosteroid implant, cryotherapy, vitrectomy, or combination therapy). 4. Eligibility Criteria Inclusion Criteria: Population: Adult patients aged ≥18 years diagnosed with idiopathic Coats' disease. Study types: Case reports, case series (≥1 case), observational cohort studies (retrospective or prospective). Outcomes: Must report at least one of the following: anatomical resolution, recurrence, change in visual acuity, or imaging findings. Language: English, Portuguese, Spanish, or French. Study design: Human clinical studies. Exclusion Criteria: Pediatric-onset Coats' disease without separate adult data. Secondary Coats-like vasculopathy (e.g., due to radiation, diabetic retinopathy, retinal vein occlusion, inflammation, or genetic syndromes). Reviews, editorials, conference abstracts without primary data. Animal studies or laboratory research. 5. Search Strategy Electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase) will be searched from inception to the final search date using controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and keywords including "Coats disease", "adult-onset Coats", "retinal telangiectasia", "exudative retinopathy". Boolean operators (AND/OR) and filters for human subjects and age ≥18 will be applied where possible. References of included studies will be screened manually to identify additional eligible studies. A detailed search strategy will be provided in an appendix. 6. Study Selection Process All identified records will be imported into Rayyan software for duplicate removal and screening. Two independent reviewers will screen titles and abstracts according to inclusion criteria, followed by full-text assessment. Discrepancies will be resolved by consensus or consultation with a third reviewer. Reasons for exclusion at the full-text stage will be documented. The selection process will be reported using a PRISMA 2020 flow diagram. 7. Data Extraction Data will be extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized form. Extracted variables include: Study characteristics (author, year, country, study design) Patient demographics (age, sex) Shields staging Clinical presentation and imaging features (fundoscopy, OCT, FA/OCTA) Treatment modalities and number of treatment sessions Follow-up duration Anatomical and visual outcomes Complications and recurrence Missing or unclear data will be requested from study authors when feasible. 8. Risk of Bias Assessment Methodological quality will be assessed independently by two reviewers using: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists for case reports and case series. Newcastle–Ottawa Scale (NOS) for cohort studies. Disagreements will be resolved by consensus. Studies will not be excluded based solely on quality; however, risk of bias will be considered in the interpretation of results. 9. Outcomes Primary outcomes: Anatomical resolution of exudation or retinal detachment Recurrence rate of disease after treatment Change in BCVA (logMAR) Secondary outcomes: Number of treatment sessions Complications (e.g., neovascular glaucoma, vitreoretinal fibrosis) Predictors of poor visual or anatomical outcomes 10. Data Synthesis and Statistical Analysis A narrative synthesis will be conducted to summarize clinical and imaging characteristics. When ≥3 studies report comparable data, meta-analysis will be performed using a random-effects model (DerSimonian–Laird method). Continuous outcomes will be expressed as mean differences with 95% confidence intervals (CI), and dichotomous outcomes as pooled proportions. Statistical heterogeneity will be assessed with I2 and τ2 statistics. Prespecified subgroup analyses will be performed based on disease stage and treatment modality. Sensitivity analyses will evaluate the impact of excluding studies at high risk of bias. 11. Protocol Registration Statement This protocol will be prospectively registered in the Open Science Framework (OSF) registry. Any amendments made after registration will be documented with the date, rationale, and description of changes. 12. Conflicts of Interest The authors declare no conflicts of interest. 13. Funding No external funding was received for this work.

title: The 'Neglected Art of Fundoscopy': a Scoping Review of Ophthalmic Teaching in Medical Curriculum
description: The objective of this scoping review is to investigate ophthalmological training/ophthalmoscopy training in medical schools. The Australian Curriculum Framework for Junior Doctors (ACF) provides an outline of the 'learning outcomes required of prevocational doctors, to be achieved through their clinical rotations, education programs and individual learning, in order to promote safe, quality health care'. These include ophthalmology, namely skills in visual field assessment, visual acuity assessment, direct ophthalmoscopy eye drop administration, eye bandage application, eye irrigation, eyelid eversion, corneal foreign body removal, intraocular pressure estimation and slit lamp examination. This review is focussed on direct ophthalmoscopy, as this offers the most simple route to looking at the fundus, and as direct ophthalmoscopes are more accessible and commonplace in medical care settings than slit lamps. The scoping review will aim to identify what ophthalmic training is included in university curricula, how it is taught (theoretical or practical) and the performance outcomes of using novel teaching solutions. Results will be summarised into tables. The scoping review will report on whether the training was theoretical (lectures, study notes etc) or practical (e.g. in person training using an ophthalmoscope or slit lamp) or comment if newer, more innovative technologies have been utlised. Specifically, the review question is: The 'art of fundoscopy' is being forgotten: how should the next generation of medical students be learning this essential medical skill?

title: Video-evoked neuromarkers of visual function in age-related macular degeneration
description: Neural markers of visual function in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) allow clinicians and researchers to directly evaluate the functional changes in visual processing which occur as a result of the progressive loss of afferent input from the macula. Unfortunately, few protocols exist that elicit such neural markers, and most of these are poorly adapted to AMD. Here, we propose a novel method of embedding frequency tags into full colour and motion videos by periodically manipulating the contrast of visual information of different spatial frequencies at different temporal frequencies. These videos elicit steady-state visual evoked potentials (SSVEPS) in viewers which, when measured using electrophysiological neuroimaging methods, independently represent the responses of populations of neurons tuned to the tagged spatial frequencies.

title: Studying the association between brain activation during a multisensory task and hypersensitivity to multisensory stimuli and quality of life in pediatric chronic pain patients
description: Multisensory stimulation is ubiquitous to our daily life experience. Sensory hypersensitivity can therefore compromise wellbeing and it can be particularly challenging for those experiencing chronic musculoskeletal pain. Musculoskeletal pain affects a significant proportion of adolescents, with prevalence rates ranging from 30% to 50%. For up to 20% of these adolescents, pain significantly impacts school attendance, requires medication, and hinders physical activity (Kamper et al., 2017). Evidence from epidemiological, clinical, and experimental studies suggests there are sex differences in musculoskeletal pain that emerge during adolescence (Rollman and Lautenbacher, 2001), which increase over pubertal development (LeResche et al., 2005). Most chronic pain conditions affecting adolescents are more common in girls (Unruh, 1996; Fillingim et al., 2009) and previous research has shown evidence for mechanistic differences in pain processing between males and females in health and disease (reviewed in Mogil, 2021). Also, studies have found sex differences in brain responses to unpleasant stimuli, with females exhibiting heightened brain and behavioral responses to unpleasant affective stimuli (Whittle et al., 2011). In this sense, adolescent females who suffer from chronic pain often report decreased quality of life and heightened unpleasantness in response to non-painful sensory stimuli, such as bright lights and loud sounds (Bennet et al. 2014; Kashikar-Zuck et al. 2016; Ting et al. 2016). In large samples of chronic pain patients, including adults and late adolescents, hypersensitivity to nonpainful multisensory stimulation was associated with lower quality of life (Jong-Geun and Sung-Pa, 2019; Wang and Frey-Lau, 2023). Furthermore, hypersensitivity to multisensory stimulation has been associated with greater bodily pain extensiveness across chronic pain conditions in adulthood (Wang and Frey-Lau, 2023). Here, we propose to assess the relationship between brain responses to an MRI multisensory task (Lopez-Sola et al. 2014; 2017) in youth with chronic musculoskeletal pain and self-reported (i) multisensory hypersensitivity during the task (i.e., unpleasantness ratings during exposure to controlled multisensory stimulation), (ii) quality of life (physical and psychosocial dimensions) (Gragg et al., 1996), and (iii) assess sex differences. Research Questions: RQ1: Can we identify a relationship between brain responses to multisensory stimulation and self-report ratings of multisensory unpleasantness in a large sample of youth with chronic musculoskeletal pain? RQ2: Can we identify a relationship between brain responses to multisensory stimulation and self-reported quality of life in a large sample of youth with chronic musculoskeletal pain? RQ3: In a large sample of youth with chronic musculoskeletal pain, is there a relationship between self-reported multisensory unpleasantness during the multisensory task and self-reported quality of life (physical and psychosocial dimensions)? RQ4: Are there sex-related differences in RQ 1, 2, and 3? References: Kamper SJ, Williams CM. Musculoskeletal Pain in Children and Adolescents: A Way Forward. title: Decoding of Peripheral Saccade Targets from Foveal Retinotopic Areas
description: Visual acuity differs vastly between the fovea and the periphery. While the fovea only covers a fraction of the visual field, it accounts for over 40% of primary visual cortex processing. Studies in the past years have found that this processing power is not only used to process visual input presented directly in the fovea but that some input to the periphery is remapped to the foveal parts of the visual cortex. While the precise processes behind this remapping remains elusive, it is assumed that the foveal parts of the visual cortex are recruited for peripheral tasks that require increased scrutiny. Additionally, foveal remapping is associated with eye movements. In this fMRI study, we attempt to uncover the mechanisms the underly foveal remapping and better understand the visual features that are propagated from the periphery to the foveal parts of the visual cortex. To this end, we will present participants in the scanner with natural object images in their periphery and instruct them to execute a saccade towards them. Subsequently, we will try to decode these peripheral stimuli from the perisaccadic fovea to better understand which information is being remapped.

title: Segmenting experience into generalizable predictive knowledge
description: Decisions have consequences that gradually unfold over time. For example, after choosing to drive to work instead of taking the subway, you may run into rush-hour traffic, arrive to work late, and ultimately get scolded by your boss for your tardiness. To make effective decisions, it is therefore necessary to learn not only which outcomes are beneficial (e.g., at work on time is good; reinforcement learning) but also whether these outcomes are likely to occur (predictive learning). However, learning in real-world environments is non-trivial. Human experience is complex, comprising numerous changing features. For example, each morning you consider which mode of transport to take to work, there will be differences in the weather, your mood, what you had for breakfast, and so forth. The number of permutations of these many features is astronomical, making it unlikely – if not impossible – for any to recur. In other words, almost every event is unique. If similar yet distinct events are also represented distinctly in memory, this poses a problem: learning at one point can never be applied in the future. This curse of dimensionality is particularly pronounced for predictive learning, where an agent must incorporate information not only about a given event (e.g., driving) but also the events that follow (e.g., stuck in traffic, at work late, scolded by boss, etc...). The curse of dimensionality may be overcome by learning simplified representations of this complex experience. The present research specifically considers the role of two mechanisms: selective attention and segmented learning. Selective attention gates input from the environment into memory, constraining learning to a subset of features (Leong et al., 2017). This reduces the number of feature permutations an event representation might take. Moreover, since selective attention is goal-directed, the features attended to are likely to be task-relevant. Thus, a given task may take on the same representation when performed in dissimilar contexts. Segmented learning involves learning a representation of some input as a factorized set of features. This differs to conjunctive learning, where the input is learned as a conjunction of features (e.g., as in episodic memory). Theoretically, segmented learning improves (1) speed, (2) generalizability, and (3) compositionality. (1) Learning speed is faster because features are encountered across different contexts, allowing for more opportunity for them to be learned on. In conjunctive learning, these contexts are represented distinctly despite their shared features, limiting the opportunity to learn to within contexts. (2) Generalizability is similarly greater because learning on an independent feature can be applied to any novel situation in which said feature recurs. (3) Compositionality is greater, since features are divorced from their original context, facilitating their re-composition into novel configurations. An agent can harness the power of compositionality to generate creative, goal-oriented action plans. In the domain of pure reinforcement learning, work has demonstrated the theoretical benefits (Farashahi, Rowe et al., 2017) and empirical evidence (Farashahi, Rowe et al., 2017; Ballard et al., 2019) for segmented learning in humans. However, to our knowledge, this has yet to be demonstrated for predictive learning. In all, we will investigate how humans acquire simplified predictive knowledge that is both generalizable and compositional. We will test a model of this process whereby selective attention gates input from the environment, after which either a segmented or conjunctive representation is stored in memory. This research will help elucidate the representational basis of flexible human decision-making.

title: Systematic Review of Ocular Manifestations of Zika Virus
description: Introduction: Zika virus infection in newborn poses serious public health concern because of its associated complications such as microcephaly. Reports also suggest ocular complications associated with this diseases, but its findings are still limited. We therefore conduct this systematic review to summarize the ocular manifestations of Zika Virus. Methods: PubMed, OvidSP, EMBASE were searched from inception to 7th November, 2016 for reports on Zika virus related ocular findings. Case series, reports and cohorts were identified from reference list of included studies. Studies with overlapped subjects were excluded. Clinical findings data were extracted, categorized and summarized to study the spectrum of ocular findings associated with Zika virus infection. Incidence was calculated. Results: Twelve studies including a total of 51 infant cases with 84 affected eyes and 3 adult cases with 5 affected eyes were included for analysis. Macular pigment mottling (55.9%), foveal reflex loss (41.2%), chorioretinal atrophy (27.4%), optic nerve hypoplasia (20.6%) and increased cup-disc ratio (18.6%) were common ocular findings related to Zika virus in infants. Uveitis and maculopathy were seen in adult cases. Conclusions: Macular and optic nerve abnormalities are the major ocular findings in Zika virus infected infants. Eventual visual outcome is still unknown. Screening guidelines have been established. Further studies on Zika virus related ocular findings are of paramount importance for the global public health

title: Bottleneck Layer Embedding Differences in Semantic Segmentation of Multi-Source Cardiac MRI
description: Recent research has shown advances in the analysis of cardiovascular MRI images using deep learning. However, two problems are apparent: How to measure the quality of the result of semantic segmentations and how to expose dependencies on the actual MRI apparatus used in obtaining the image data sets. The proposed method is based on traditional evaluations at the pixel level. Admittedly, it would be convenient to judge incoming samples on their fa- miliarity in relation to the training data. This would allow for filtering out inadequate samples. In order to solve this conveniently, it is proposed to compare incoming samples to prototypical centroid vectors in an embedding (sub space), by using dimensionality reduction. MRI images used for this experiment are fed through a fully connected network model trained on short-axis MRI's of left ventricles. The machine learning model was tested using two different data sets collected from two different MRI devices, one generating the UK Biobank data and another, UMCG's data. The raw MRI's and the resulting segmentations are used for investigating the problem of finding a reliable comparison method for judging whether an input sample meets the expectations that are represented by the statistics of the training data. To achieve this, a dimensionally reduced representation of the data is calculated with which centroids can be com- puted for classes. Both are then used as dimensionally reduced representations of the data and averaged to represent the centroid of their embedding. An optimal measurement is discovered among three standard distance calculations (SAD, SSD and mean correlation), that is, SAD. This was the best measurement of similarity in raw MRIs (non-segmented) as well as serving as a predictor of segmentation quality, as verified by the Dice metric.

title: Modulation of visual contrast sensitivity with transcranial random noise stimulation
description: Transcranial random noise stimulation (tRNS) has been shown to significantly improve visual perception. These performance improvements manifested as both (i) after-effects of visual training combined with tRNS (Fertonani et al., 2011; Pirulli et al., 2013; Contemori et al., 2019; Herpich et al., 2019) and (ii) acute effects during tRNS (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; Ghin et al., 2018; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). It has been postulated that the Stochastic resonance (SR) phenomenon underlie noise-induced signal enhancement in studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual processing (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018, 2019; Battaglini et al., 2019, 2020; Pavan et al., 2019). SR describes the phenomenon that the response of nonlinear systems to weak, subthreshold signals can be enhanced by adding an optimal level of random noise (Moss et al., 2004; McDonnell and Abbott, 2009). One important feature indicative of the SR phenomenon is that noise benefits are a function of noise intensity and exhibit an inverted U-shape relationship. Thus, while the optimal level of noise benefits performance, excessive noise is detrimental (van der Groen and Wenderoth 2016; van der Groen et al. 2018; Pavan et al. 2019). Previous studies investigating the acute effect of tRNS on visual detection performance have shown that noise stimulation was particularly beneficial when the visual stimuli were presented with near-threshold intensity (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016; van der Groen et al., 2018; Battaglini et al., 2019). Currently, it is unknown whether signal enhancement via SR could be achieved separately within different neural substrates along the retino-cortical pathway. Inducing SR via tRNS offers a unique opportunity to investigate this question. Here we plan a series of three experiments which will be executed in three separate sessions. Experiment 1: TRNS over primary visual cortex (V1) has been shown previously to improve visual contrast detection (van der Groen and Wenderoth, 2016). Here we aim to replicate these results in a new cohort and to determine the optimal tRNS intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 2: Previous research has suggested that the retina and the optical nerve are highly susceptible to alternating currents (Schutter and Hortensius, 2010). Improvement in vision was reported after repetitive transorbital alternating current stimulation over the retina, in studies involving patients with optic neuropathy or after optic nerve lesions (Gall et al., 2010; Fedorov et al., 2011). The retina and the optic nerve are an interesting target because they can be reliably reached even with low transcranial electrical stimulation intensities, since the eyeball is an excellent conductor. Here we will test whether tRNS applied to the retina and the optic nerve improves visual contrast detection in accordance with the SR mechanism. We will apply different tRNS intensities to determine the optimal intensity for each individual participant. Experiment 3: It is currently unknown whether SR effects are additive when noise is applied to connected yet anatomically remote neural populations. Here we will investigate whether simultaneous application of tRNS to the retina and V1 causes additive effects.

title: Visual field changes in patients receiving antitubercular therapy
description: Objective Tuberculosis is a global health challenge with one-third of the world's population infected by it. Although ocular side effects of Anti-tubercular drugs are well known, the patients generally report late in the course which can result in irreversible vision loss. The purpose of this study was to study the visual field changes during the time course of anti-tubercular therapy(ATT). Methods A total of 48 patients were studied in this prospective type of study. All patients newly diagnosed with TB and started on treatment were included in the study. Baseline examination which included visual acuity, color vision, anterior segment, IOP, Amsler grid, fundus, and visual field test were performed before starting ATT and at 6-month follow-up. Results The mean age of the study population was 35.90 ± 10.2 years. 35 (72.9%) were males and 13 (27.1%) females. 32(66.6%) had pulmonary TB and the rest 16 (33.3%) had extrapulmonary TB. MDR TB was diagnosed in 27 (56.3%) of the patients with the rest 21 (43.8%) being drug sensitive. The baseline examination was normal in all 48 patients. 3(6.3%) out of 45 patients presented with visual complaints after the treatment initiation. Altogether 7 patients out of 48, had visual field defects at the 6-month follow-up. The incidence of visual field defects in our study was 14.6% with the value being significant (0.016). 8.3% had peripheral constriction of visual fields, 2.1% with Severe generalized depression of visual fields and 2.1% with central scotoma. Out of the 45 patients with no visual complaints at 6-month follow-up, 4 (8.33%) showed peripheral field constriction. Interpretation Visual field defects caused by ATT can precede clinical symptoms. Visual field evaluation can be an important tool for the early detection of optic neuropathy in patients receiving ATT in clinical settings where Visual evoked potential testing and RNFL-OCT are not available. Keywords: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Drug toxicity, DOTS, visual field defects, toxic optic neuropathy, Ethambutol, Linezolid

title: Characteristics, licensing, and ethical considerations of openly accessible oral-maxillofacial imaging datasets: A systematic review
description: In recent years, a growing number of publicly accessible datasets have been introduced. However, the sources and characteristics of the public datasets for oral-maxillofacial imaging including annotation details, have not yet been systematically investigated. Without a thorough understanding of these datasets prior to their use in AI model training and testing, there is an increased risk of unintended biases, such as data leakage. This can occur when training and test sets contain duplicate images from various repackaged datasets, potentially leading to overly optimistic performance estimates as the model could learn from identical data in both phases. Moreover, the significance of understanding ethical considerations, specific terms, and licensing requirements for reusing these datasets is becoming more widely recognized. Using these datasets without clear understanding of ethical and licensing information may incur substantial ethical and legal risks. The issue of whether AI models trained on datasets that prohibit commercial use can be licensed for commercial purposes remains controversial. Currently, the ethical clearance and specific terms regulating their reuse in AI projects are unclear. Therefore, the primary objective of this study is to provide a comprehensive summary of openly accessible datasets containing images from the oral-maxillofacial region, including details such as the year and purpose of dataset creation, creators, country and institution of origin, imaging modality, image type and format, patient and image count, imaging device manufacturer, image annotation details, annotators' qualifications, and dataset access. The secondary objective is to investigate the ethical clearance, specific terms, and licenses for the reuse of these datasets.

title: Investigating the influence of social status on the perceived trustworthiness
description: Establishing trust in a trustworthy person is essential for establishing collective goods, cooperation and collaboration and has far-reaching consequences for the order, development and prosperity of societies. In contemporary societies, however, placing trust in the right people has become increasingly demanding. With progressing economic and political globalisation, growing mobility and increasing numbers of connections with weak ties, more and more interactions take place between strangers (Delhey & Welzel, 2012, Foddy et al., 2009; Stanley et al., 2011). Thus, in many situations, people do not have enough information on whether their interaction partners are trustworthy or not. Decisions of whom to trust might be established from a wide range of stimuli and characteristics, such as the facial expressions of the trustee, his/her vocal features, the nature of the relationship between trustor and trustee or situational aspects, such as the mood of the involved individuals (Simpson, 2007; Lu et al., 2017). title: The potential beneficial role of anti-platelet/anti-coagulant medications on diabetic retinopathy: A Scoping Review Protocol
description: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a prevalent microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus (DM, both types 1 and 2), affecting millions of individuals worldwide. DM is known to induce changes in platelet function and hemostasis, thereby elevating the risk of thrombotic incidents. The hyperglycemic environment in DM can trigger platelet hyperactivity, potentially exacerbating the onset and progression of DR. Despite the intricate pathophysiology of DR, which involves oxidative stress, inflammation, retinal neovascularization, and the disruption of the blood-retina barrier, the specific mechanisms underlying platelet hyperactivity in the microvasculature of DM patients remain inadequately explored. Antiplatelet and anticoagulation medications have proven beneficial in preventing macrothombosis events in patients with DM. Further understanding of their therapeutic and prophylactic effects on DR could improve the understanding of underlying mechanisms and the treatment of not only DR, but other microvascular complications. This study's purpose is to conduct a scoping review on the current literature surrounding the impact of antiplatelet and anticoagulant medications on patients with diabetic retinopathy.

title: The predictive accuracy of polygenic risk scores in determining the risk of developing and/or of disease progression in primary open angle glaucoma: a systematic review
description: Background: Polygenic risk scores have emerged as a new tool to predict the probability of patients developing certain conditions. One disease this has been applied to is Primary open angle glaucoma. In a polygenic condition no single gene is responsible for inheritance, with hundreds or thousands of polymorphisms instead each having a small effect on disease risk. This leads to the expectation that the analysis of the number and location of these polymorphisms could lead to the stratification of patients in terms of disease risk, with potential prognostic uses. To date screening programmes for glaucoma have not proven cost effective, however polygenic risk scores may allow for the creation of a more cost-effective screening tool. This review will evaluate the role of polygenic risk scores in predicting the development and progression of primary open angle glaucoma and evaluate its potential role in future screening initiatives. Methods: We will search for literature in Medline ALL, Web of science Core Collection, EMBASE and Google Scholar. Original studies that discuss the role of polygenic risk scores in predicting the risk of developing primary open angle glaucoma will be included. Data will first be deduplicated using Covidence before the final deduplicated search results are uploaded to Covidence software for screening by the research team. We will apply a masked screening whereby if at least one screener identifies a paper as potentially relevant it will proceed to full text screening. Full text screening will be carried out independently by at least two of the authors before consensus is reached among all authors. Studies will be assessed for bias using the QUIPS tool. Discussion: The findings from this review will document the ability of polygenic risk score to predict the development and/or progression of primary open angle glaucoma and evaluate their potential utility as a screening tool.

title: Topography and the shallow slip deficit inference
description: Images of earthquake slip serve as the foundation for understanding the distribution of coseismic energy release, theories about rupture propagation, and fault mechanics. Geodetic slip images are inferred using elastic models that link surface observations to fault activity at depth. To date, almost all elastic models used for these common calculations [10, 14, 19, 23] include the assumption that the Earth is flat [1, 6, 11], even for earthquakes in regions of extreme topographic relief like the 2008 MW=7.9 Wenchuan earthquake at the Longmenshan range-front. Here we develop three-dimensional boundary element models that explicitly include topographic relief and find that the classical flat Earth assumption may induce errors >100% in imaged coseismic slip. This topographic effect is important even in regions with small topographic gradients (1-5% , 1992 MW=7.3 Landers) and can lead to the inaccurate inference of a shallow slip deficit [9]. These results illustrate that understanding earthquake behaviors will require more accurate models not only in terms of physical processes but also in terms of geologic fidelity.

description: Loss of central vision (macular degeneration) at a later age reduces the quality of life, increases the risk of depression, shortens life expectancy, and is the most common cause of the most serious visual organ failure (legal blindness) in developed countries. There is no causal treatment for macular degeneration, but compensatory aids are mainly used - internal or external optical or electronic instruments. They aim to ensure the projection of the image on the preserved part of the retina. Because this disrupts the natural correspondence between the mapping of the external world and internal representation, visual rehabilitation is also needed to improve the quality of life. In the ending project, we demonstrated that implantation of a macular lens (Scharioth Macula Lens - SML) and subsequent visual rehabilitation in visually impaired seniors with maculopathy (EMDs) increases the recipients' quality of life. However, factors limiting the broader application of the offered intervention are the contact form of visual rehabilitation and the invasive nature of implantation. We try to address both of these factors in the proposed project. We will implement a distance form of visual rehabilitation and verify its effectiveness in a prospective study of 20 EMDs. We then relate this to data from our previous project with contact rehabilitation. At the same time, we will compare the effect of external and implanted hypercorrection on the quality of life of EMDs. For this purpose, another 20 EMDs without SML implantation will be included in the study. All EMDs in the study will also undergo the synergistic and effective form of one of the two visual stimulations, the effectiveness of which we will evaluate. We will not use a placebo to achieve the goals. Each patient enrolled in the study will take the form of an effective intervention. The project's overall impact will be an easier and more economical individual intervention to increase the quality of life of EMDs.

title: The Utility of Central versus Peripheral Visual Field Test Algorithms for Diagnosing Glaucoma: A Scoping Review
description: Glaucoma is a chronic and progressive entity of vision loss that requires detailed monitoring of visual function. In 2013, it was reported that the worldwide prevalence of glaucoma is estimated to be 64.3 million and is expected to increase to 111.8 million in 2040 (Tham YC et al., 2014). In the context of glaucoma diagnosis and management, standard automated perimetry (SAP) is the most utilised investigative technique used by eye health clinicians, with the 24-2 or the 30-2 being the mainstay (Hejil A, et al., 2003). This rationale was adopted under the premise that Glaucoma is a disease affecting the peripheral and mid-peripheral vision in early disease, with changes to central vision only occurring in advanced stages of the disease. Although, with the advent of spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT), there is emerging evidence to suggest the macula ganglion cell complex is affected in early disease processes (Hood DC et al., 2011; Hood DC et al., 2013). Hence, there is conjecture as to whether introducing the 10-2 SAP testing algorithm to Glaucoma screening may provide an added benefit in detecting perimetric changes in early Glaucoma (Kim EK et al., 2021). Therefore, in this scoping review our aim is to analyse the literature comparing the 24-2 and 10-2 SAP in the diagnosis of early glaucoma, whilst also assessing the practicability of additional perimetry testing in clinical practice.

title: ON THE VERGE OF PLAUSIBLE: UNDERSTANDING CONTRIBUTIONS OF PARAFOVEAL & FOVEAL PLAUSIBILITY EFFECTS DURING READING
description: Current controversy exists within the field of psycholinguistics regarding exactly when high-level semantic information (e.g., the plausibility of upcoming words) first becomes available to the reader. Eye tracking studies have revealed that readers rapidly extract information not only from fixated words in central foveal vision (i.e., the central 2° of visual angle where visual acuity is highest), but also from upcoming words in parafoveal vision (i.e., the central 2 -5° of visual angle) prior to fixation (Rayner, 1975; Schotter, et al., 2012). In fact, a plausibility preview benefit (e.g. shorter reading times for plausible, relative to implausible parafoveal previews) has also been shown to be irrespective of the relationship between the preview and foveal target. These findings suggest that plausible previews can be processed to a high enough level prior to fixation. However prior experiments on plausibility violations have not yet systematically examined the influence of parafoveal processing on plausibility violations. To address a current gap in the literature, the proposed study will use a gaze-contingent boundary paradigm (GCB) and orthogonally cross the (im)plausibility of the parafoveal preview and target word (i.e., similar to the frequency manipulation used in Schotter et al., 2016) as readers self-pace through sentences. We expect to replicate prior plausibility effects and to directly observe the direction of the novel interaction between parafoveal preview validity (e.g. valid identical preview versus invalid change condition) and foveal plausibility (e.g. target is plausible or implausible). In addition to addressing questions surrounding conflicts in theoretical accounts of the plausibility preview effect, our design will allow us to separate out parafoveal and foveal contributions to plausibility processing in reading.

title: Temporal perception of stimuli briefly stabilized on the retina: Voluntary saccades (TPVI)
description: This project seeks to investigate whether observers experience a feeling of agency (FoA) for microsaccades and their perceptual consequences. We will use effect binding, a phenomenon where the consequence of an action is reported earlier when FoA is experienced, to compare the perceived time of a stimulus briefly stabilized on the retina by a microsaccade (active condition) to the perceived time of a replayed retinal consequence (replay condition). In the active condition, the stimulus perception is an action-consequence, whereas the replay condition replicates this perceptual event without an action. Earlier reports of the perceptual consequence in the active condition compared to the replay condition will indicate FoA for microsaccades. Additionally, we will examine the role of movement intention in FoA by comparing intended microsaccades (following an instruction to move) and unintended microsaccades (occurring accidentally during fixation). The perceived timing of the stimulus will be assessed separately for these microsaccade types to determine if intention is necessary for FoA. Participants will adjust a clock hand to indicate the time of increased stimulus visibility, with the stimulus being a Gabor patch with internal motion visible only during microsaccades, compared to a similar stimulus with external motion visible during stable fixation. This experiment aims to reveal if FoA is experienced for microsaccades and whether intention is crucial for this experience.

title: Parafoveal and foveal N400 effects in natural sentence reading: A timeline of semantic processing from fixation-related potentials
description: The depth at which parafoveal words are processed during reading is an ongoing topic of debate. Recent studies using the RSVP-with-flanker paradigms have shown that implausible words within sentences elicit N400 components while they are still in parafoveal vision, suggesting that the semantics of parafoveal words can be accessed and used to rapidly update the sentence representation. In order to assess this effect in natural reading situations, we combined the co-registration of eye movements and EEG with the deconvolution modeling of fixation-related potentials (FRPs) to test whether semantic plausibility is processed parafoveally during natural Chinese sentence reading. For one target word per sentence, both its parafoveal and foveal plausibility were orthogonally manipulated using the boundary paradigm. Consistent with previous eye movement studies, we observed a delayed effect of parafoveal plausibility on fixation durations that only emerged on the foveal word. Crucially, in FRPs aligned to the pre-target fixation, a clear N400 effect emerged already based on parafoveal plausibility, with more negative voltages for implausible previews. Once participants fixated the target, we again observed an N400 effect of foveal plausibility. Interestingly, this foveal N400 effect was absent whenever the preview had been implausible, indicating that when a word's (im)plausibility is already processed in parafoveal vision, this information is not revised anymore upon direct fixation. Implausible words also elicited a larger late positive complex (LPC), but only when directly fixated. The present results provide convergent neural and behavioral evidence for the parafoveal processing of semantic information in natural reading.

title: Use of the Keratograph® 5M for the Diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease: A Scoping Review
description: Dry Eye Disease (DED) is a multifactorial disorder of the ocular surface characterized by tear film instability and associated ocular symptoms. Objective assessment of tear film parameters and meibomian gland function is essential for accurate diagnosis and subtype classification. In recent years, non-invasive imaging technologies have been increasingly incorporated into clinical practice to enhance diagnostic precision and reduce variability associated with traditional tests. The Keratograph® 5M (Oculus Optikgeräte GmbH, Germany) is a Placido-disc–based corneal topographer that integrates automated, non-contact measurements of tear film stability and ocular surface parameters. The device provides non-invasive break-up time (NIBUT), tear meniscus height (TMH), meibography, ocular redness quantification, and additional surface analyses. Although widely used in ophthalmology and optometry settings, the scope, consistency, and characteristics of the published evidence regarding its diagnostic application in DED have not been comprehensively mapped. The purpose of this scoping review is to systematically identify, describe, and synthesize the available scientific literature evaluating the use of the Keratograph® 5M in the diagnosis of Dry Eye Disease. Specifically, this review aims to: (1) map the clinical contexts in which the device has been studied; (2) describe the tear film and glandular parameters assessed; (3) summarize reported measurement properties (e.g., repeatability, reproducibility); and (4) identify research gaps related to diagnostic performance and clinical implementation. This review will follow established methodological guidance for scoping reviews and will include peer-reviewed primary studies evaluating the Keratograph® 5M in adult or mixed populations undergoing assessment for DED or related ocular surface conditions. Data extraction will focus on study design, population characteristics, diagnostic parameters evaluated, reference standards (when applicable), and key findings. No formal meta-analysis is planned, as the objective is evidence mapping rather than quantitative synthesis. Expected outcomes include a structured overview of the current evidence landscape, identification of methodological heterogeneity in diagnostic assessment, and clarification of how the Keratograph® 5M is positioned within the diagnostic pathway of DED. The findings may inform future diagnostic accuracy studies, health technology assessments, and clinical guideline development.

title: Assessing the Clinical Usefulness of Clinical Trials for the Treatment of Macular Degeneration
description: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are considered the gold standard for evaluating the efficacy of medical interventions. In the field of ophthalmology—particularly in the treatment of macular degeneration—a substantial number of RCTs have been published. While many of these trials are methodologically sound, their practical value for clinical decision-making remains uncertain. Conventional assessments of RCTs emphasize internal validity and risk of bias, but may overlook important factors such as clinical relevance, generalizability, patient-centeredness, and transparency. This research project aims to systematically evaluate the usefulness of RCTs investigating interventions for macular degeneration, published between January 1, 2009, and December 31, 2024. The study will apply the 13-item multidimensional framework developed by van 't Hooft et al., which encompasses eight domains: health problem relevance, contextualization, informativeness, pragmatism, patient-centeredness, economic value, feasibility, and transparency. Each RCT will be assigned a total usefulness score (0–26) based on its performance across these criteria. Eligible RCTs will be identified through structured searches in Medline and Embase. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data using a standardized Google Form. Key trial characteristics—such as intervention type, sample size, funding source, journal, and geographic location—will also be recorded. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool, with assistance from ChatGPT to facilitate the process. Descriptive statistics and regression analyses will be used to examine trends in usefulness scores over time and across different study characteristics. The aim of this study is to provide a comprehensive overview of the clinical usefulness of macular degeneration RCTs published in the last decade. We expect to observe considerable variability in usefulness, with transparency and contextualization likely emerging as common shortcomings. The results will highlight opportunities to improve trial design and reporting, offering targeted guidance for researchers, funders, and journal editors to enhance the translational impact of future research in ophthalmology. By preregistering this protocol, we aim to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor throughout the research process.

title: Foveal Feedback: The role of imagery
description: Previous neuroimaging and TMS studies (Williams et al, 2008; Chambers et al, 2013) suggest the existence of a task-dependent and temporally specific feedback signal from high-level cortex to foveal retinotopic cortex. Subsequent psychophysical studies (Fan et al, 2016; Weldon et al, 2016, 2020) also show that a foveal mask can interfere with this feedback producing a dip in performance when the mask is presented around 150-250ms after peripheral stimuli. Regarding the exact timing and size of the effect (depth of dip) there is considerable variability both between experiments and between individuals (Contemori et al, 2022). Fan et al. (2016) show that the timing of the noise-induced drop in performance varied depending on the mental operation to be performed on the target, from 250 ms (no mental rotation) up to 550 ms (mental rotation of 80°), through 450 ms (mental rotation of 40°). Currently available evidence indicates that foveal retinotopic processing is flexibly engaged only for difficult tasks requiring fine spatial processing and only when detailed information is required. These features of foveal feedback suggest an overlap (at least partial) with one of the components of Baddeley & Hitch's tripartite model (Baddeley and Hitch, 1974). Baddeley model of working memory includes a visual sketchpad that allows individuals to momentarily create and revisit a mental image that is pertinent to the task at hand. Baddeley (1988) 19 theorized that the sketchpad is the storage place in working memory that contains the necessary object and spatial information to set up and manipulate mental visual images. Although with different connotations such a construct is also present in Kosslyn's definition of surface and deep representation (Kosslyn, 1981). Assuming then that foveal feedback may be part of the neural substrate underlying the ability to mentally visualize objects in working memory, in this study we will investigate whether some of the individual variability in the delayed effect of foveal noise on peripheral discrimination (i.e., a quantitative measure of foveal feedback) can be attributed to individual differences in imagery.

title: Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter as a Diagnostic Marker for Post-Dural Puncture Headache: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic accuracy of optic nerve sheath diameter (ONSD) measurement for post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) following lumbar puncture or spinal anesthesia. The study aims to quantify the magnitude of ONSD differences between PDPH patients and controls, determine diagnostic accuracy through pooled sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC), identify optimal ONSD cut-off values, and assess evidence quality using GRADE criteria. The review follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines and includes four studies (70 PDPH patients, 285 controls) reporting ONSD measurements at 24 hours post-procedure. Primary outcome is the pooled effect size (Hedges' g) using Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman (HKSJ) random-effects meta-analysis. Secondary outcomes include pooled AUC for diagnostic accuracy with logit transformation, optimal cut-off values, and GRADE evidence assessment. Expected outcomes include quantitative estimates of ONSD discriminatory power for PDPH diagnosis and a comprehensive evidence quality rating. The findings will inform whether ONSD measurement can serve as a non-invasive surrogate marker for intracranial hypotension associated with PDPH.

title: Laminar fMRI in the human prefrontal cortex at 7T: A replication study of layer-dependent activity during working memory
description: This study aims to replicate Finn et al. 2019, specifically their "axial protocol". Briefly, Finn et al. 2019 used VASO fMRI to measure cortical layer specific cerebral blood volume (CBV) changes during different periods of a delayed-response task in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). They found that superficial layers were more active during the delay period when working memory items needed to be manipulated (alphabetization of a random letter sequence) compared to mere maintenance (remembering of the original letter sequence). In contrast, deeper layers were more active during the response period. The study by Finn et al. 2019 is the first that demonstrates the ability of high-resolution fMRI in humans to measure layer specific effects in the prefrontal cortex and thus opens the possibility to study high-level cognition layer-specifically non-invasively in human subjects. Given its importance for the field of cognitive neuroscience we think it is valuable to attempt replicating this seminal study and evaluate the robustness of its results. Moreover we want to confirm that the reported results are robust with respect to our specific slightly different experimental setup consisting of a different MRI scanner, different version and parameters of the SS-SI-VASO pulse sequence and differences in institutional constraints like maximal duration of human participant sessions. Lastly, the study by Finn et al. 2019 relied, like most layer fMRI studies to date, on a substantial amount of semi-manual or manual analysis steps including their ROI definition, gray matter segmentation and layer definition. In order to test whether less manual intervention can lead to comparable results we will limit ourselves to a more automatic analysis approach. As a consequence, our methods will follow Finn et al. 2019 closely and will only differ with respect to the above mentioned constraints. Here, we formulate and pre-register an analysis approach that automates some of the manual aspects of Finn et al. 2019. We believe this to constitute a fair attempt for replicating their results. In addition, we may explore the effects of additional analysis approaches (including manual analysis steps) on our results (see section on Exploratory analysis).

title: Anti-Angiogenic Therapeutic Techniques & Pharmacologic Agents
description: 1) Anti-VEGF Monoclonal Antibody Treatment In this anti-angiogenic therapeutic technique, anti-VEGF monoclonal antibodies are developed that bind to the VEGF molecules and prevent them from binding to the VEGF receptor tyrosine kinases, essentially preventing the growth factor signal from reaching the cell, and thus inhibiting the signaling pathway that eventually leads to angiogenesis. Bevacizumab: Clinical trials assessing the efficacy of VEGF inhibitors are currently taking place in a variety of malignancies, and recently, a humanized anti-VEGF-A monoclonal antibody called Bevacizumab (sold under the brand name, Avastin®) has been approved by the FDA as a first-line therapeutic for metastatic colorectal cancer in combination with chemotherapy (13). Bevacizumab Mechanism of Action: Bevacizumab acts by selectively and extracellularly binding to circulating VEGF-A cytokines, thereby inhibiting the binding of VEGF-A to its receptors, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, on the surface of vascular endothelial cells, and this inhibition leads to a significant reduction in the microvascular growth of tumour blood vessels, thus limiting and normalizing the blood supply to tumour tissues, allowing them to be cured more easily using more traditional methods such as chemotherapy (14). These effects also lower the interstitial pressure of solid tumour tissue by decreasing vascular permeability, may potentially increase the delivery of chemotherapeutic agents such as chemotherapy drugs to the tumour cells, promote the apoptosis of tumour cells, and most importantly, prevent metastasis from occurring (14,15). Ranibizumab: Sold under the brand name, Lucentis®, Ranibizumab is a recombinant humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody fragment that binds with high affinity to all active isoforms of VEGF-A and inhibits the cytokine from binding to its receptors on the surface of vascular endothelial cells – very similar to how Bevacizumab functions – thus preventing the neovascularization and vascular leakage that contribute to the progression of retinal diseases (16, 19). Ranibizumab is commonly used to treat visual impairments involving aberrant angiogenesis in the retina such as neovascular AMD, macular edema following retinal vein occlusion, diabetic macular edema, myopic choroidal neovascularization, and diabetic retinopathy (17). These retinal conditions occur due to the secretion of high levels of VEGF by photoreceptor cells in response to hypoxia which in turn leads to the angiogenesis of retinal blood vessels with high vascular permeability, thus causing leakage of blood in the retina or RPE, and ultimately resulting in the disruption or loss of vision. VEGF-A – which binds to the extracellular ligand-binding domains of two receptor tyrosine kinases, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 – is currently Ranibizumab's major target of inhibition for the treatment of retinal diseases by the suppression of aberrant angiogenesis (16). Each molecule of Ranibizumab has only one VEGF paratope due to the fact that it is a monoclonal antibody fragment, meaning that two Ranibizumab molecules are required to bind a VEGF dimer on the surface of a vascular endothelial cell, while each Bevacizumab molecule – which is a full-length monoclonal antibody – has two VEGF paratopes (16,18). Aflibercept: Sold under the brand names, Eylea® and Zaltrap®, Aflibercept is a soluble decoy receptor that binds to VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PlGF) with higher affinity than the cytokines' natural receptors (20,23). In one experimental model, Aflibercept's equilibrium dissociation constant, Kd (inversely related to binding affinity), for VEGF-A165 was 0.49 pM, compared with 9.33 pM and 88.8 pM for VEGFR1 and VEGFR2, respectively (20). It is called a decoy receptor because VEGF-A mistakenly binds to Aflibercept instead of binding to its natural receptors, thus suppressing their activation and preventing the subsequent development of angiogenesis (20). Structurally speaking, Aflibercept is a humanized recombinant fusion protein that consists of an IgG backbone fused to extracellular domain sequences of the receptors, VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 (20,22,23). The therapeutic is currently used to treat retinal diseases – including diabetic retinopathy, macular edema following retinal vein occlusion, diabetic macular edema, and most prominently, neovascular AMD – by preventing highly permeable blood vessels from forming underneath the retina, a condition that can leak blood and impede vision (20,21,22). Aflibercept has also been shown to be effective against metastatic colorectal cancer when combined with cytotoxic chemotherapy (24). 2) Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors Tyrosine kinases are cellular signaling proteins that mediate a variety of biological activities such as cell proliferation and migration, and in angiogenesis, multiple kinases are involved including the receptor tyrosine kinase, VEGFR (29,33). Anti-angiogenic tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are anticancer pharmacologic agents that suppress the signal transduction networks of protein kinases by several modes of inhibition (30). Three anti-angiogenic TKIs with differential binding capacities to angiogenic tyrosine kinases were recently approved for the treatment of patients with advanced cancer: Sunitinib, Sorafenib and Pazopanib (31). The inhibitors all follow the same fundamental mechanism of action: they competitively bind to the catalytic binding site of tyrosine kinases and inhibit autophosphorylation – the addition of phosphate groups after their extraction from ATP molecules to intracellular kinase domains on receptor tyrosine kinases to activate the intracellular signal transduction pathway that leads to the transcription of angiogenic factors – thereby suppressing angiogenesis (30,31,32).

title: Management of Carotid Artery Disease in Patients with Ocular Ischemic Syndrome: A Systematic Review
description: Below is a detailed project description written in the same methodological, formal, and data-driven style as your OSF registration above: --- ### **Description** Carotid artery disease is a major contributor to ocular hypoperfusion, and in its most advanced form can manifest as ocular ischaemic syndrome (OIS)—a rare but clinically severe condition associated with rapid visual decline, neovascular complications, intractable ocular pain, and a substantially elevated risk of ipsilateral stroke and cardiovascular mortality. Although restoration of carotid perfusion through endarterectomy, stenting, or transcarotid revascularisation is widely considered the cornerstone of management, the evidence base informing treatment decisions in OIS remains fragmented, consisting largely of small observational cohorts, heterogeneous case series, and variable reporting of ophthalmic and cerebrovascular outcomes. No previous systematic review has synthesised contemporary evidence on the effectiveness and safety of carotid revascularisation compared with best medical therapy in this high-risk population. This systematic review aims to provide a comprehensive and methodologically robust synthesis of all available clinical evidence on the management of carotid artery disease in adults presenting with ocular ischaemic syndrome. The review will evaluate the effects of carotid endarterectomy, carotid artery stenting, transcarotid artery revascularisation, and intensive medical therapy on visual function, ocular ischaemic signs, stroke risk, mortality, restenosis, and procedural outcomes. By applying a structured PI(E)COS framework, risk-of-bias assessment (RoB2, ROBINS-I, NOS), and both quantitative and narrative synthesis approaches, the review will examine whether revascularisation improves visual prognosis, stabilises disease progression, and reduces cerebrovascular events compared with medical therapy alone. Expected outputs include a consolidated evidence map of all published studies reporting treatment outcomes in OIS, pooled effect estimates where data permit, and a detailed summary of procedural safety across revascularisation modalities. The review will also identify gaps in current evidence—particularly regarding optimal timing of revascularisation, outcomes in complete carotid occlusion, and interactions with adjunct ophthalmic treatments such as panretinal photocoagulation or anti-VEGF therapy. By integrating ophthalmic and vascular outcome domains, the project aims to inform clinical decision-making, highlight areas requiring prospective research, and support the development of future interdisciplinary management pathways for this under-recognised but clinically significant condition.

title: In-Vivo Confocal Microscopy in the Diagnosis and Management of Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia: A Scoping Review
description: Purpose: Ocular Surface Squamous Neoplasia (OSSN) encompasses a spectrum of premalignant and malignant epithelial lesions of the conjunctiva and cornea. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective management and prevention of recurrence. In-vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) has emerged as a promising, noninvasive imaging tool that provides real-time, high-resolution visualization of the ocular surface at the cellular level. Despite growing interest, the literature on IVCM's diagnostic accuracy, characteristic imaging features, and clinical utility in OSSN remains fragmented. This scoping review aims to systematically identify, chart, and synthesize the existing evidence on the application of IVCM in OSSN. It will examine how IVCM has been used to detect, characterize, and monitor OSSN lesions; assess correlations between IVCM and histopathology; and explore its integration with complementary imaging modalities such as optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM). The review will also map methodological limitations and research gaps to inform future clinical and technological advancements in ocular oncology imaging. Expected Outcomes: The review will produce a comprehensive summary of current knowledge on the diagnostic and monitoring role of IVCM in OSSN. It will: Identify characteristic IVCM features associated with various OSSN grades. Evaluate the strengths, limitations, and diagnostic accuracy of IVCM compared to standard histopathology. Highlight how IVCM has been applied in monitoring treatment response and disease recurrence. Identify knowledge gaps and propose directions for future studies, including the potential role of artificial intelligence in automating IVCM image analysis. Overall, this review will serve as a foundational reference for clinicians and researchers, clarifying the present and potential roles of IVCM in OSSN diagnosis and management, and guiding the development of noninvasive, multimodal imaging approaches in ocular surface oncology.

title: A Dual-Layered Structure of Reality
description: This manuscript develops a dual-layered metaphysical framework, grounded in information theory and thermodynamics, to reconcile determinism with informational agency. It posits a structural stratification of reality into a deterministic lattice of potential (L1) and a finite layer of realization (I2), where agency emerges via structural compression reframing the epistemic veil as a constitutive necessity. The framework is justified by the External Reference Paradox (ERP), which employs continuous-time models and deductive arguments to demonstrate that single-layer matter-first ontologies constitute finite, informationally closed systems lacking a stable external reference for long-term error correction and are therefore structurally collapse-bound. This logical limitation is compounded by thermodynamic and dimensional deficits: closed single-layer models lack an entropy sink capable of sustaining biological and informational complexity against the Second Law, and fail to distinguish the static lattice of potential from the sequential traversal of realization. These failures are formalized through boundary conditions that distinguish thermodynamic Totality from Subsystem behavior and establish Asymmetric Persistence as the requisite test for structural viability. The dual-layered framework is therefore proposed as the structural minimum necessary to satisfy both the logical requirements for error correction and the physical requirements of an open, evolving system. Continuity is defined by conservation of information across layers rather than conservation of matter. Reality is derived as R = P(L1) ∙ N(I2), unfolding through realignment, a process by which the informational layer instantiates finite life-paths from the deterministic lattice. Constrained by informational finitude, this structure yields a Finite-Worlds framework in which agents occupy limited branches per epoch, in contrast to unrestricted multiverse interpretations. Quantum probability is reinterpreted as the geometric density of pre-encoded trajectories within the lattice. Ultimately, agency is framed not as a violation of determinism, but as the evolutionary capacity of information to navigate an exhaustive space of possibilities. Quantum theory is treated as an interpretive and modeling lens that complements this ontology, which describes reality independently of any specific microphysical formulation.

description: Abstract: BIMOD (Bodily Interferometric Magneto-Optical Discrimination) is a human-mediated polarity detection protocol that utilizes a dynamic resonance triad involving local static magnetic fields, the Earth's geomagnetic flux, and biogenic magnetic nanoparticles (BMNPs). This study demonstrates that BMNP-mediated polarity discrimination is an optically-gated, non-linear process governed by the spatial orientation relative to the geomagnetic dip angle. title: Group size and cooperation in Trinidadian guppies
description: Many theoretical studies predict that cooperativeness is reduced in larger groups (Gavrilets, 2015). Empirical tests of this prediction are primarily limited to human studies and often give mixed results. Observational evidence from Trinidadian guppies -- a fish species that performs cooperative predator inspection -- suggests that they live in smaller groups when they are under higher predation pressure (Heathcote, 2017). This could be because the benefits of cooperative predator inspection are easier to obtain in smaller groups, where individuals are more likely to be cooperative. In this study, we will directly test the effect of group size on cooperative predator inspection in Trinidadian guppies by manipulating group size and observing inspection behaviour. Further, we hypothesise that if guppies spend less time inspecting when they are in larger groups, this is because they perceive the risk posed by the predator to be lower. To test this, we will measure behaviour associated with risk perception: shoal cohesion, and the time spent in refuge areas (near plants and gravel). We predict that if guppies cooperate/inspect less because they perceive the risk to be lower in larger groups, they will also show less shoal cohesion and spend less time in refuge areas when they are in larger groups.

title: Eye-movements in Economic Games
description: This project aims at validating a model proposed in an unpublished Master's Thesis by Münich in 2019. This model is a Multinomial Mixture (MM) model that used an abstraction of eye-movement, called meta-transitions, to identify five groups of decision rules in normal-form bimatrix games (like the well-known Prisoner's Dilemma); each decision rule group with their own probability functions for four different classes of meta-transitions (MT). Here, an MT is the combination of two subsequent transition types, where a transition refers to subsequent fixations on cells of a matrix that contain potential payouts for one of the players. For example, if the row-player first looked at one of their own payouts, then at another of their payouts within the same row, and then at one of their own payouts in another row, the transitions would be "own-within" and "own-between" and the MT would be "own-within , own-between". The ultimate goal of this project is evaluating whether the model fits and where there are problems with the model, culminating in another pre-registration, this time for a confirmatory experiment optimised using all we've learned from conducting this project. The dataset used in this project was originally collected by Polonio and Coricelli (2019), and provided to us by Polonio. full reference: Polonio, L. & Coricelli, G. (2019). Testing the level of consistency between choices and beliefs in games using eye-tracking. Games and Economic Behavior, 113, 566–586.

title: Integration of Computational Modeling, Systems Biology, and Artificial Intelligence to Improve the Efficiency of Differentiation of Induced Pluripotent Stem Cells into Retinal Cells
description: Human retinal regeneration remains a major challenge due to the complexity of differentiating induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) into functional retinal cells. This paper presents an in silico proof-of-concept integrating computational modeling, systems biology, and artificial intelligence (AI) to stabilize cell proliferation and optimize iPSC differentiation into photoreceptors and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. We introduce the Proliferation Stability Index (PSI) — combining growth rate variability, temporal drift, cell-cycle heterogeneity, and a proxy for genomic risk — coupled with a closed-loop model predictive controller (CELL-MPC) with biological guardrails. As practical demonstrations, we implemented minimal prototypes: (i) a simulation/control script that estimates PSI components and applies a simplified controller; and (ii) an SBML toggle-switch gene regulatory model for CellDesigner. Results suggest reduced proliferative variability and reveal distinct regimes relevant for culture-level decisions, providing a foundation for more consistent differentiation protocols. Integrated analysis highlights the potential of this multidisciplinary approach and outlines next steps toward experimental validation with real time-series and genomic stability metrics.

title: Barriers to Accurate Epidermal Thickness Measurement Using Optical Coherence Tomography
description: Background: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique capable of measuring epidermal thickness (ET) in vivo by detecting the dermal-epidermal junction (DEJ). However, automated ET quantification does not succeed in all cases. In a prior prospective study at our institution examining OCT-derived ET across multiple anatomical regions and diverse Fitzpatrick skin types, a large portion of scans failed to yield an algorithmic ET measurement (Sonuga et al., 2026; submitted). The reasons for this high nonresponse rate are not well characterized. Objective: This scoping review aims to systematically map the existing literature to identify demographic (e.g., age, sex, skin type), anatomical (e.g., body site, skin features), pathological (e.g., skin disease), and technical/operator-related factors that influence the ability of OCT to visualize the DEJ and obtain a reliable ET measurement. Rationale: Understanding which factors impair or preserve OCT-based ET measurement is essential for guiding clinical deployment, informing study design, and identifying populations or anatomical sites where alternative imaging approaches may be necessary. No existing review has comprehensively synthesized these factors across both healthy and diseased skin. Methods: A scoping review will be conducted and reported according to the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. A systematic search of relevant databases will identify studies examining OCT-based ET measurement or DEJ visualization across varying patient demographics, anatomical sites, skin conditions, and imaging protocols.

title: The Role of the Ventrolateral Anterior Temporal Lobes in Social Cognition
description: A key challenge for neurobiological models of social cognition is to elucidate the function of brain regions and whether they are specialised for that domain, or more general in nature. In recent years, the involvement of the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) has become clearer, but discussion surrounding the nature of its function, and the relationship with conceptual-level knowledge, epitomises this debate. In the present study we used ATL-optimised fMRI to map the contribution of different ATL structures to both social cognition and semantic cognition. In doing so, we addressed hypotheses that stipulate the ATL comprises a domain-specific social function on one hand, versus a domain-general semantic function on the other. Using a set of conjunction analyses, we revealed activation of a ventrolateral region of the ATL that was common to a variety of tasks that have previously been used to probe neural correlates of theory of mind. The same region was activated by a nonverbal semantic association task. These findings support recent claims that semantic cognition is key requisite for successful social interactions and that engagement of the ventrolateral ATL in theory of mind reflects retrieval of conceptual-level representations.

title: Diagnostic Selective Nerve Root Block (SNRB) in Lumbar Nerve Root Compression
description: Background and Aim Selective nerve root blocks (SNRBs) are widely used in spine surgery for diagnostic clarification in patients with radicular pain, particularly when imaging (MRI) and clinical findings are inconclusive regarding the symptomatic nerve root or the expected benefit of surgical decompression. The purpose of the block is to clarify the diagnosis and prognosis of radiating lower limb pain, thereby supporting decision-making regarding surgical versus non-surgical treatment. The primary aim of this study is to investigate the prognostic value of selective nerve root blocks in lumbar nerve root compression. Objectives and Hypotheses Primary objective: To assess whether patients undergoing surgery after a diagnostic block with good effect demonstrate different postoperative outcomes, measured by the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at 12 months, compared with patients undergoing surgery without a prior block, adjusted for relevant confounders. Hypothesis: Patients with a positive diagnostic block who subsequently undergo surgery experience less postoperative improvement, measured by ODI, compared with patients undergoing surgery without prior diagnostic uncertainty. Study Design Retrospective cohort study based on registry data and medical records. Population and Eligibility Criteria Inclusion criteria: - Patients aged >18 years - Underwent diagnostic selective lumbar nerve root block (BAFA7) between January 1, 2018 and May 31, 2024 at Zealand University Hospital, Køge Exclusion criteria: - Therapeutic (non-diagnostic) blocks - Missing data regarding block level, side, effect, or subsequent surgery - Missing 12‐month follow-up in DaneSpine - Surgery performed at a different spinal level than the block Data Sources and Variables Primary data sources include the Health Platform, private hospital records, and DaneSpine. Collected variables include demographics, block characteristics, surgical details, and PROM data (ODI, VAS, EQ‐5D). Outcome Measures Primary outcome: - ODI at 12 months postoperatively Secondary outcomes: - Patient satisfaction - Likelihood ratios and predictive values - Avoided surgery following negative block - Re-referral to the spine clinic at any time during follow-up Statistical Analysis Mixed-effects linear regression models will be applied. Fixed effects include block status and relevant covariates, while patient ID is included as a random effect. Ethical Considerations This retrospective registry study involves no patient contact and has been approved in accordance with the Danish Health Act §46.2 and 5, EMN-2025-04765. Data handling complies with GDPR regulations and the project is registered at the institutional registry for research projects, p-2025-19418 Timeline Protocol and approvals: March–August 2025 Data extraction: September–January 2026 Analysis: February 2026 Manuscript preparation: February - June 2026 Publication Plan Results will be published open access. title: Efficacy and safety of dexamethasone intravitreal implant(Ozurdex) combined with anti-VEGF treatment for diabetic macular edema: A protocol for systematic review and meta-analysis
description: Diabetic macular edema (DME) is a leading cause of blindness in the working age population of most developed countries. The pathophysiology of DME is complex, involving vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and other inflammatory mediators. Macular laser photocoagulation, slows the rate of vision loss and helps stabilize vision, but has demonstrated only limited ability to restore lost vision. Intravitreal medications targeted toward VEGF have become first line therapy in DME patients. Anti-VEGF drugs decrease the concentration of free VEGF but do not change the concentrations of the other proinflammatory molecules that also mediate vascular permeability. Therefore, combining corticosteroids with anti-VEGF drugs may produce the greatest possible suppression of vascular permeability by both direct VEGF blockade and reducing the concentrations of other important proinflammatory and permeability enhancing chemokines. However, combination of the two medicine is also studied in the clinical treatment, and the efficacy and safety of this method is need to be proved.To prove this point, we will perform a protocal for a systematic review and meta-analysis of dexamethasone intravitreal implant(Ozurdex) combined with anti-VEGF treatment for DME.
