title: Power of Pictures? Questioning the Emotionalization and Behavioral Activation Potential of Aesthetics in War Photography
description: War photography is not only used illustratively in news media but also displayed as controversial art objects. The ethics and impact of aestheticization in war photography have long been debated. In three studies (overall N = 749), we contribute empirically to this debate by testing the impact of aesthetics in war photography (i.e., aesthetic style and context) on emotionalization and behavioral activation. While viewing war photography was, overall, emotionalizing (especially regarding negative affect and moral outrage), we did not find any behavioral activation (i.e., donation intention and behavior or general willingness to act against war). Neither aesthetic style nor aesthetic context made a difference for affective or behavioral responses. However, a salient aesthetic context (Study 3) led to higher aesthetic judgements of war photographs. Overall, these results question whether aesthetics in war photography have a particular power for evoking emotional and behavioral responses.

title: Morphological Processing of Complex Words by Foveal Split
description: What is the role of morphological analysis in word recognition? Early studies have suggested that we prefix strip complex words before they are recognized (e.g., Taft & Forster, 1975, 1976; Forster, 1976). More recent studies have also suggested that the visual word recognition system operates on the basis of morpho-orthographic analysis, which is blind to semantic processes—thus segmenting even pseudo-morphemes based on their orthographic similarity to real morphemes (e.g., -er in driv-er and *corn-er; Rastle & Davis, 2008). Other evidence for morphological analysis during the early stages of word recognition comes from studies investigating morphologically and semantically ambiguous trimorphemic words (e.g., unlockable; e.g., de Almeida & Libben, 2005; Pollatsek et al., 2010). These words constitute an important test of the nature of morphological analysis involved in word recognition. This is so because besides being ambiguous, yielding two parses (e.g., [un[lockable]], meaning 'not able to lock', and [unlock[able]], meaning 'able to unlock'), by hypotheses they require the computation of a hierarchical structure that involves computing the proper prefix-root-suffix combination to yield a proper meaning. The present study investigates the nature of morphological analysis involved in word recognition by employing a novel experimental technique. In this technique participants wear red-blue anaglyph glasses and perform a lexical decision (word/nonword) on briefly presented (initially, 133 ms) strings of letters. Letters forming morphologically complex words (the main stimuli; e.g., 'unlockable') are colored blue or red according to legal or illegal constituents. The use of anaglyphs allows for the separation of morphological constituents (or non-constituents) during early stages of word recognition, also taking into account the foveal split, thus projecting word segments to left or right hemispheres using contralateral or ipsilateral visual pathways. Response times and accuracy are predicted to be a function of morphological legality (constituents v. nonconstituent segments), visual pathway/hemisphere presentation (LH accessed via the hypothetically stronger contralateral pathway yielding faster responses). We predict faster RTs and greater accuracy for legal constituents, in particular word roots (e.g., 'lock' in unlockable) and prefix-root segments ('unlock') projected into the LH-visual world form area (VWFA) before other constituents or segment combinations (e.g., 'unlo' or 'ckable') suggesting that the word recognition system is sensitive to morphological structure in its input analysis of word strings.

title: The triglyceride-glucose index as a biomarker of diabetic retinopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
description: This project presents a systematic review and meta-analysis investigating the association between the triglyceride-glucose (TyG) index—a surrogate marker of insulin resistance—and the presence and severity of diabetic retinopathy (DR). The study aims to synthesize existing evidence from observational studies, including cross-sectional, cohort, and case–control designs, to clarify whether elevated TyG levels are associated with an increased risk of DR in individuals with diabetes mellitus. The protocol was preregistered on PROSPERO (CRD420251110467) and follows PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Comprehensive database searches were performed in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, and risk of bias was assessed using validated tools (AHRQ checklist for cross-sectional studies and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale). Meta-analytic techniques were used to pool effect sizes, evaluate heterogeneity, and assess publication bias. Subgroup analyses explored the influence of study design, diabetes type, and geographic region.The expected outcomes include pooled odds ratios or risk estimates for DR based on TyG index categories or continuous levels, identification of sources of heterogeneity, and evaluation of the predictive potential of the TyG index. This project aims to provide clinicians and researchers with a clearer understanding of the TyG index as a potential biomarker for microvascular complications, specifically diabetic retinopathy.\n\nAll data extraction forms, statistical code, risk of bias assessments, and figures are made available here to enhance reproducibility and transparency.

title: Artificial intelligence for automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy: Scoping review.
description: Introduction: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is one of the most prevalent complications of diabetes mellitus (DM) and one of the leading causes of blindness worldwide. Its high epidemiological burden emphasizes the need to improve early detection and diagnosis strategies to mitigate the onset of irreversible changes. The limitations of the current approach to DM in identifying complications such as DR in a timely manner reinforce the importance of incorporating innovative detection strategies. In this context, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool, demonstrating high levels of early diagnostic accuracy to optimize the quality of health services, mainly in developing countries. Methodology: Through a scoping review, scientific articles, reviews, technical literature, and gray literature published between 2019 and 2025 will be analyzed, covering the available evidence on artificial intelligence modalities in the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide. The PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and BIREME databases will be included, using MeSH and DeCS descriptors. Expected results: We expect to provide a comprehensive overview of the main types of artificial intelligence used for the automatic detection of diabetic retinopathy in adults worldwide, identifying benefits, limitations, and future opportunities. The findings will generate useful evidence for healthcare professionals and service planners, facilitating the design of strategies and interventions aimed at contributing scientific knowledge in this area, opening up horizons for improvement in healthcare.

title: Assessing the Clinical Usefulness of Clinical Trials for the Treatment of Age-Related Macular Degeneration
description: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are considered the gold standard for evaluating the efficacy of medical interventions. In the field of ophthalmology—particularly in the treatment of macular degeneration—a substantial number of RCTs have been published. While many of these trials are methodologically sound, their practical value for clinical decision-making remains uncertain. Conventional assessments of RCTs emphasize internal validity and risk of bias, but may overlook important factors such as clinical relevance, generalizability, patient-centeredness, and transparency. This research project aims to systematically evaluate the usefulness of RCTs investigating interventions for macular degeneration, published between January 1, 2009, and December 31, 2024. The study will apply the 13-item multidimensional framework developed by van 't Hooft et al., which encompasses eight domains: health problem relevance, contextualization, informativeness, pragmatism, patient-centeredness, economic value, feasibility, and transparency. Each RCT will be assigned a total usefulness score (0–26) based on its performance across these criteria. Eligible RCTs will be identified through structured searches in Medline and Embase. Two reviewers will independently screen studies and extract data using a standardized Google Form. Key trial characteristics—such as intervention type, sample size, funding source, journal, and geographic location—will also be recorded. Risk of bias will be assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool, with assistance from ChatGPT to facilitate the process. Descriptive statistics and regression analyses will be used to examine trends in usefulness scores over time and across different study characteristics. The aim of this study is to provide a comprehensive overview of the clinical usefulness of macular degeneration RCTs published in the last decade. We expect to observe considerable variability in usefulness, with transparency and contextualization likely emerging as common shortcomings. The results will highlight opportunities to improve trial design and reporting, offering targeted guidance for researchers, funders, and journal editors to enhance the translational impact of future research in ophthalmology. By preregistering this protocol, we aim to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor throughout the research process.

description: To maximize the potential of co-registration and build complete theories of reading, we must look beyond FRPs and account for the contingency between neuro-cognitive responses and saccadic behavior, as we aim to do in this study. We expect to observe expectancy effects and anomaly effects independently for both eye-tracking and EEG measures, as well as when coupling these outcomes together.

title: Online Control in Motor Imagery: Foveal and peripheral vision and the timing of real vs. imagined actions
description: The present experiment is designed to test the Motor-Cognitive Model (MCM) of motor imagery, as opposed to the Functional Equivalence Model (FEM). The FEM argues that motor imagery and overt action share the same internal processes, leading to a general correspondence in their timing. In contrast, the MCM argues that, although they use the same internal representation, motor imagery and overt action differ in their execution phase. Indeed, during overt action, sensory feedback allows for online control, that is one can adjust and correct the movement in flight. During motor imagery, the absence of online feedback hinders such process: the mental image is instead monitored at the cost of executive resources (Glover et al., 2020; Glover & Baran, 2017). Accordingly, one major tenet of the MCM is that motor imagery and physical actions should not be similarly affected by factors that influence online control. Specifically, we focus here on the quality of online control. For example, if a person focusses their vision in one location while reaching to another location, ongoing visual feedback will be of lower quality than had they foveated the target position throughout the movement, and the physical action will suffer from inaccuracy as a result. Thus, the quality of information available to online control may vary across different situations. For a physical movement, decreasing the quality of online control reduces its efficiency, resulting in it being more error prone and/or taking longer to execute. In contrast, during motor imagery, there is a complete lack of online control. Thus, motor imagery should not be impacted when the quality of the information used in online control is altered. To examine the above prediction, participants will either reach to grasp a small disc with their right hand, then place it into a small cylinder, or imagine doing so, a paradigm that we have used before (see Figure 1; Glover et al., 2020; Glover & Baran, 2017; Martel & Glover, Unpublished data). They will index the beginning and the end of their movement using keypresses (with their left index), allowing a comparison of the different conditions. One group of participants will perform the overt action under foveal vision and will be allowed to move their eyes freely to foveate the target and track their hand (Foveal trials) or will be required to maintain fixation on the starting position (Peripheral trials). This latter condition will require participants to conduct the vast majority of their grasping movement, and the entirety of their placing movement, in peripheral vision, changing the quality of online control. The second group will imagine grasping and placing the disc in the same two visual conditions. Participants in the motor imagery group will be instructed to imagine as rich a visual and kinesthetic image as possible. Each group will complete 12 trials per condition for a total of 24 trials, presented in two counterbalanced blocks across participants. A small number of practice trials will precede each block to familiarize participants with the task. The experimental setup consists of a 50 × 90 cm table, on which will sit a computer keyboard, a wooden box (dimensions: 15.7 × 42 × 22 cm) with a grey plastic tube inside (dimensions: 15 × 4.2 cm) and a small white plastic disc (Figure 1 in the attached document). Both the keyboard and the wooden box will be aligned on the left side of the table. The wooden box will be placed in the top left corner of the table, with 7cm being outside of the table surface, while the keyboard will be placed adjoining it. The computer keyboard will be placed in the bottom left corner of the table, so that the participant can use her left index finger to press on the 'L' key without the keyboard being in the way. The starting position will be a yellow square sticker (0.5 × 0.5 cm), positioned 52 cm away from the left side of the table, and 5 cm away from the bottom table border (close to the participants). Participants will sit with their body midline aligned to the starting position. The disc (dimensions: 1 × 4 cm) will be positioned with its centre 23.5 cm to the right and 22 cm forward of the starting position. The grey cylinder will be located inside the box, its centre being 18.5 cm forward to its bottom border. Participants in the overt action group will have their movements recorded using the Polhemus motion tracking system, with markers placed on the dorsal surface of the fingernails of the thumb and index finger of their moving hand. The Polhemus tracks the position of the markers at 120Hz, and stores data of the instantaneous x, y, and z coordinates of each marker to PC for later analysis offline.

title: Independent Risk Factors for Retrograde Ejaculation after Anterior versus Posterior Lumbar Fusion in Male Patients: A Protocol for a Cox Proportional Hazards Analysis
description: Anterior lumbar fusion (ALF) as a surgical intervention for lower lumbar degenerative pathology has grown in popularity over the past few decades,1,2 potentially due to its biomechanical advantages, avoidance of posterior neural and muscle elements, and decreased blood loss as compared to traditional posterior lumbar fusion (PLF).3 As ALF is primarily for pathology involving the L4-L5 and L5-S1 segments, risk of injury to anterior lower lumbar structures is a unique concern for spine surgeons performing ALF.4 One such concern in male patients is injury to the superior hypogastric plexus (SHP),5 an autonomic plexus anterior to the L5 vertebra, L5-S1 disc space, and sacral promontory.4 Injury to the SHP during ALF can impair regional sympathetic function, causing aberrant relaxation of the internal bladder sphincter during sexual activities in males. This can lead to retrograde ejaculation (RE),3 a condition in which ejaculate undergoes retrograde flow into the bladder, potentially causing infertility.3 In a recent meta-analysis, Body et al. (2021) pooled the incidence of RE across 2,503 patients who underwent anterior lumbar surgery, including both ALF and total disc replacement, across 18 studies.3 The authors found a mean incidence of RE of 2.3% with a range of 0% to 9.8%.3 Due to this relatively high incidence of RE, some surgeons may avoid ALF when otherwise indicated. However, Body et al. (2021) acknowledged several methodological limitations among included studies, including reliance on questionnaires and/or a lack of objective measures of RE such as post-ejaculation analysis, small sample sizes, and the inclusion of female patients in many studies, hindering male-specific risk assessment.3 Importantly, several factors have been explored as the cause of RE in ALF. First of all, direct nerve injury to the SHP during surgical dissection, retraction, and/or electrocautery during anterior approaches is a key possibility.3,6 Additionally, recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 (rhBMP-2) is supported as a risk factor due to its neuroinflammatory properties and/or stimulation of ectopic bone formation ventral to the spine.3,7 Some evidence suggests that the relative influence of rhBMP-2 may have lessened following adoption of safer handling practices following a warning from the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2008 regarding surgical complications.3,8 Unrelated to lumbar fusion, previous medical or surgical treatment for prostatic hyperplasia has been suggested as a risk factor for RE after ALF.7 Apart from these factors, general predispositions to RE after lumbar fusion including medications, comorbidities, and age have remained under-explored, hindering clinician decision-making at this time. An enhanced understanding of the incidence and independent risk factors for RE after ALF may improve surgical decision-making and preoperative patient education. Due to the limited understanding of RE after ALF, this study will utilize Cox proportional hazards modeling to assess the independence and magnitude of multiple potential risk factors associated with RE after ALF.9 Therefore, the aim of this retrospective analysis is to investigate the incidence and independent risk factors for RE in adult males after ALF versus PLF to enhance surgical decision-making as well as patient education to optimize patient care.

title: Quality evaluation indicators for Ophthalmic nursing: a scoping review
description: OBJECTIVE: To conduct a scoping review of the literature related to ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation indexes, systematically sort out the current situation of the construction of ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation indexes at home and abroad, and aim to provide theoretical basis for the establishment of a scientific, standardised ophthalmic nursing quality evaluation system with specialised characteristics. METHODS: Eleven domestic and international databases were systematically searched according to the scope review framework proposed by JBI. The search time frame was established until May 2025, and two researchers independently screened the literature and classified and analysed the content of the indicators based on the three-dimensional quality structure model. RESULTS: A total of 28 papers were included in this study. The highest frequency of ophthalmic care quality indicator application scenarios was in ophthalmic wards, the most common ophthalmic speciality care quality indicator was glaucoma, and ophthalmic speciality care quality indicators were mainly centred around forced body position. The evaluation indicators were categorised according to the three-dimensional quality structure model, and the evaluation indicators appeared 491 times cumulatively, of which 134 times (27.29%) were structural quality-related indicators, 235 times (47.86%) were process-quality-related indicators, and 122 times (24.85%) were outcome-quality-related indicators.42.2% of the tertiary-level indicators had problems such as unclear definitions. In terms of indicator content, foreign studies placed more emphasis on disease management and patient-reported outcomes. CONCLUSION: The existing ophthalmic care quality indicator system is still insufficient in terms of specialty specificity and operability. In the future, we should strengthen the clarity of the definition of the indicators and the consistency of the measurement standards, highlight the professional characteristics of ophthalmic care, and promote the establishment of a logical, scientifically rigorous, and practically valuable ophthalmic care quality evaluation system.

title: Retinal Pigment Variability and Developmental Sensory Integration: A Systems Neuroscience Hypothesis Linking Embryology, Circadian Regulation, and Predictive Coding
description: This paper proposes a developmental systems hypothesis suggesting that non-uniform retinal pigment distribution during embryogenesis may subtly influence early sensory statistics, circadian entrainment, and large-scale network integration. Because the vertebrate retina originates as an outgrowth of the forebrain and shares developmental signaling pathways with neural crest-derived pigment cells and autonomic structures, minor spectral and temporal variations in retinal filtering could theoretically shape early cortical calibration during critical periods of plasticity. Integrating predictive coding theory, circadian neurobiology, and connectomics, I outline plausible mechanisms, boundary conditions, and testable predictions. The hypothesis does not claim deterministic enhancement but instead frames pigment variability as a potential contributor to individual differences in integrative pattern sensitivity. Empirical pathways for validation are proposed.

title: The influence of saccade target contrast on predictive foveal sensitization to target features
description: We frequently execute large-scale eye movements (saccades) to examine peripheral visual information with high foveal acuity. In two previous investigations, we demonstrated a systematic, pre-saccadic interaction between peripheral feature information and foveal visual sensitivity: right before an eye movement, foveal sensitivity for defining features of the eye movement target (in our case: its orientation) is enhanced predictively. In the current investigation, we will manipulate the contrast of the saccade target, or – more specifically – its opacity against full-screen background noise. We will examine if and how a manipulation of target contrast affects the extent and time course of predictive foveal sensitization to the target's orientation.

description: The review article sought to answer the question: What are the different motivations that drive volunteering? and the objective is to determine the main motivations that people have for volunteering. The methodology used was qualitative, under the IMRyD format, of a non systematic review of the scientific literature in the closed access databases EbscoHost and ProQuest and open access Scielo with a total of 18 articles selected under an intentional non probabilistic sampling that had As i nclusion criteria, only articles in English, Spanish and Portuguese, that answered the research question, between the years 2018 to 2023 and with a DOI identifier. The results showed that the authors pointed out the existence of different motivators to car ry out volunteering, being a multi motivated activity and that, for the most part, they can be grouped into internal (intrinsic) motivators of the person such as faith, values, strong personal desire, overcoming problems, the feeling of success, the experi ences lived, etc. and external (extrinsic) such as the influence of family, friends, the community, the environment where volunteering takes place, among others. title: Ultrasonographic Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter Measurement Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC) : Scoping Literature Review
description: The optic nerve is surrounded by the same meningeal coverings that surround the brain. This anatomic relationship allows the use of Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD) as a non-invasive, bedside estimate of elevated Intracranial Pressure (ICP). Despite the increasing research interest in ultrasonographic ONSD, it is not widely used clinically. This can be due to variability in ONSD measurements as identified by several meta-analyses that showed significant heterogeneity in ONSD measurement techniques. We propose that this heterogeneity is due to lack of consensus on ONSD measurement technique, which can cause variations in image acquisition and measurement. In this review, We will identify published ONSD imaging and measurement criteria through a scoping systematic review of ultrasound ONSD studies. We will use a piloted data sheet to extract ONSD imaging and measurement criteria. We will then use the output of the review to develop a checklist for ONSD Quality Criteria Consensus (ONSD QCC). This checklist will undergo further refinement in the future by using the modified Delphi method to reach expert consensus on ONSD quality criteria.

title: Application of Wearable Devices in the Management of Diabetic Retinopathy
description: Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a major complication of diabetes and a leading cause of vision loss worldwide. Current epidemiological data from the International Diabetes Federation (IDF) indicate that approximately 550 million individuals worldwide were affected by DR in 2020, corresponding to a prevalence of 10%. Alarmingly, projections suggest a near doubling of DR cases by 2045 (1,030 million) with a forecasted prevalence increase to 14.4%. It affects approximately 30–40% of diabetic patients and is characterized by progressive damage to the retinal microvasculature. Despite advancements in laser therapy and anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) treatments, DR management remains challenging due to the difficulty of early detection, limited accessibility to ophthalmic care, and the lack of continuous disease monitoring. Traditional methods such as periodic retinal imaging and blood glucose testing fail to capture real-time disease dynamics, often leading to delayed intervention. In recent years, wearable devices have emerged as a transformative technology in healthcare, enabling continuous, real-time monitoring of physiological parameters. Originally designed for fitness tracking, these devices have evolved into sophisticated medical tools, integrating biosensors, artificial intelligence (AI), and telemedicine capabilities. Wearable technologies are now widely used for chronic disease management, including cardiovascular conditions, diabetes, and neurodegenerative disorders. Their ability to provide real-time data, enhance remote patient monitoring, and support personalized interventions makes them particularly valuable for conditions requiring long-term management. Given the close association between diabetes and DR, wearable technologies offer new opportunities to improve disease monitoring and intervention. Continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) provide real-time blood glucose data, enabling tighter glucose control and reducing the risk of DR progression. Smart contact lenses and portable retinal imaging devices enhance ocular health monitoring, allowing for early detection of retinal abnormalities. Additionally, AI-driven wearable biosensors can analyze systemic and ocular biomarkers, offering predictive insights into disease progression. The integration of wearable technology with telemedicine and cloud-based health platforms further strengthens its potential for remote DR management. This review aims to categorize and evaluate wearable devices based on their applications in DR management, focusing on their roles in monitoring, prediction, and intervention. We will explore various types of wearable technologies, including CGMs, smart contact lenses, wearable retinal imaging devices, and biosensors, highlighting their contributions to real-time disease tracking and early intervention. Furthermore, we will discuss the challenges and future directions in advancing wearable technology for DR, with the goal of improving accessibility, efficiency, and patient outcomes in diabetic eye care.

title: Event Segmentation and Memory
description: Human perceptual experience is characterized by a continuous stream of information. However, when recalling events from our past we commonly re-experience them as specific, discrete episodes. Event segmentation has proven to be a critical capacity for memory formation and subsequent recognition and/or episodes recall. For instance, previous studies have shown that items belonging to the same event (e.g. same location and/or context) tend to be better remembered than items separated by boundaries (e.g. Dubrow and Davachi, 2013; Ezzyat and Davachi, 2011). Conversely, other works have highlighted that information related to event boundaries seem to be preferentially encoded thereby facilitating retrieval (e.g. Lassiter & Slaw, 1991; Boltz, 1992; Swallow, Zacks and Abrams, 2009). While different kinds of task seem to give rise to very specific patterns of results, the underlying common rationale is that the presence of event boundaries seems to strongly influence people's memory (e.g. see Heusser, Youssef, Ezzyat, Shiff and Davachi 2018). However, despite the vast amount of literature on the topic, the specific relationship between event segmentation and construction of memory in naturalistic scenarios is still unclear. In our previous project: "Event Segmentation in Naturalistic Videos" we investigated whether events detected by segmentation models of brain activity and by deep neural networks were similar to the ones detected by humans in life-like naturalistic videos (see Conditions). In the current experiment, we will extend our findings by incorporating memory into the picture. More specifically, we will ask participants to watch a series of videos online and to estimate their duration. In a second session - after 5-8 days - we will show them a series of mini-clips that could have either being taken from the videos they saw or not. Participants will simply be requested to complete a recognition task by indicating whether each clip belongs to the videos they saw or not (Old vs New). Crucially, clips will either be taken from random portions of these videos or from specific segments centered around the event markers generated by the aforementioned computational models: either the brain-activity segmentation model and/or by a deep neural network tuned to detect perceptual changes across frames. The goal of the project is to assess whether the presence/absence of events within the subclips watched by participants will be able to affect their recognition performance. All in all, the entire project will allow us to establish and model some common determinants that underlie the ability to segment our perceptual experience, estimate its duration and store and remember (or misremember) specific details about it.

title: Unconfounding the Roles of Retinotopic and Spatiotopic Coordinates in Location Suppression
description: This study is designed to examine whether location-based suppression of irrelevant stimuli functions using spatiotopic or retinotopic visual coordinates. To do this, we will train participants to suppress a location in an array while fixating at a center cross. We do this using a visual search task where participants must identify a target while ignoring salient distractors. Unbeknownst to the participants, one position contains the distractor 75% of the time; this is known as the high probability location (HPL). For each other location there is a roughly 8.3% chance of the distractor appearing. These are known as the low probability locations (LPL). During training, the suppressed location will occupy the same spatiotopic and retinotopic coordinates. For baseline purposes, 1/3 of trials will contain no distractor. At test, we will shift the array and fixation in order to unconfound spatiotopic and retinotopic space. When fixation is shifted, the spatiotopic coordinates of the HPL, known as sHPL, do not change. However the coordinates of the HPL on your retina do shift. If location suppression operates within spatiotopic space, the participants should continue to suppress the sHPL at test. If, however, location suppression is retinotopic, participants will continue to suppress the high probability location on the retina (rHPL), which will now be in a different location than the sHPL. This is elaborated upon in the "design plan" section and images are included.

title: A head-to-head comparison of narcissism measures' ability to predict emotion dysregulation
description: Narcissism can be defined as the "ability to regulate self-esteem and manage needs for affirmation, validation, and self-enhancement from the social environment" (Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010). When this ability is impaired, individuals rely on rigid and maladaptive strategies to cope with perceived threats to self-esteem, a condition often referred as pathological narcissism (PN) (Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010). Contemporary models define at least two sub-dimensions of PN, namely, grandiosity (characterized by self-enhancement strategies such as self-overvaluation, entitlement, exploitative and exhibitionistic behaviors, absorption in idealized fantasies) and vulnerability (characterized by a depleted self-image, angry, depressed and shameful affects, hypersensitivity to criticism, emotional instability, and social withdrawal) (Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010). The diagnostic category traditionally associated with PN is narcissistic personality disorder (NPD), which primarily captures overt grandiose features (Cain et al., 2008). Furthermore, recent hierarchical models also propose a trifactorial structure underlying both grandiose and vulnerable narcissism, with three components: antagonism, agentic extraversion, and narcissistic neuroticism (Crowe et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2021). First, antagonism is shared by both grandiosity and vulnerability, and includes entitlement, arrogance, exploitation, callousness, deceitfulness, and a fundamentally adversarial orientation toward others. Second, agentic extraversion is more specific to grandiosity and encompasses dominance, assertiveness, social boldness, high self-confidence, and a strong orientation toward status and admiration. Finally, narcissistic neuroticism, more central to vulnerable narcissism, reflects emotional instability, shame, and hypersensitivity to self-esteem threats (Miller et al., 2021). Emotion dysregulation (ED) refers to a multidimensional pattern of difficulties in how individuals understand, accept, and modulate their emotional responses (Blay, Duarte, et al., 2024; McRae &Gross, 2020). Six main components of emotion regulation difficulties have been described by Gratz and Roemer and are operationalized in the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), the most commonly used scale to assess ED in clinical research (Gratz & Roemer, 2004). This model emphasizes that ED is not limited to emotional intensity but rather reflects impairments across multiple stages of emotional processing and regulation: lack of emotional awareness (i.e., difficulties to pay attention to and acknowledge one's emotions), lack of emotional clarity (i.e., difficulties in making sense out of and in labeling, identifying, or differentiating emotional experiences), non-acceptance of emotional responses (i.e., tendencies to judge emotional experiences), difficulties engaging in goal-directed behavior under emotions (i.e., problems with keeping concentration and focus, and pursuing work or purposeful goals), impulse control difficulties (i.e., reduced ability to inhibit inappropriate or harmful behaviors, feeling overwhelmed and out of control under emotional states,), and limited access to emotion regulation strategies (i.e., believing that nothing can alleviate emotional distress and lack of perceived or actual strategies to modulate emotions once they are activated). In a recent systematic review, we found that individuals presenting with higher narcissistic vulnerability tend to show greater difficulties in regulating emotions, whereas those presenting with higher grandiose narcissism show more inconsistent associations, the discordant results being often linked to the tools used to assess narcissism (Blay, Cham, et al., 2024). Regarding ED facets, results were highly inconsistent between studies for both dimensions, partly for the same psychometric reasons. For example, we found that vulnerable narcissism often showed positive associations with clarity, non-acceptance, impulse control, and strategies subdomains (when assessed with both Hypersensitive Narcissism Scale – HSNS - and the Pathological Narcissism Inventory - PNI), but also with awareness and goals (only when assessed with the PNI). Unfortunately, this high heterogeneity prevailed any conclusion regarding the association between specific facets of ED and narcissism. Moreover, these psychometric limitations were not the only one we found in the current literature on the link between PN and ED. Most studies used one-factor (narcissism) or two-factors (grandiosity vs vulnerability) tools to assess narcissism, whereas none used NPD or three-factor (agentic extraversion, antagonism, narcissistic neuroticism) measures. Finally, only two studies adjusted their analysis on comorbid borderline personality disorder (BPD) or symptomatology, a disorder that is strongly associated with narcissistic vulnerability (Euler et al., 2018) and emotional dysregulation (Glenn & Klonsky, 2009), and some who did so found a confounding effect of this comorbidity on the observed associations (Blay, Bouteloup, et al., 2024). Together, these limitations impede clarity and complicate the interpretation of findings regarding the links between PN and ED. To start addressing this issue, there is a critical need to directly compare multiple narcissism measures, including NPD and three-factor measures, on their relationship to ED, specifically the comparative predictive values of these measures. The present study aims to conduct such a head-to-head comparison, using four common narcissism measures: the DSM-5 NPD criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013), the PNI in its brief form (Diguer et al., 2020; Schoenleber et al., 2015), the Maladaptive Covert Narcissism Scale (MCNS) (Cheek et al., 2013), and the Five-Factor Narcissism Inventory (FFNI) in its super-short form (Packer West et al., 2021). These measures all capture different aspects of narcissism. NPD criteria are well-known to capture mostly overt grandiosity, with a sole focus on paradigmatic externalized manifestations that neglect vulnerability (Blay et al., 2025; Cain et al., 2008; Miller et al., 2021). On the other hand, the PNI assess both grandiosity and vulnerability, but its grandiosity subscale is considered to not grasp "pure" narcissistic grandiosity given its considerable overlap with the vulnerability subscale (Edershile et al., 2019). Furthermore, the MCNS specifically assesses covert narcissistic vulnerability, and focuses mainly on internal processes such as shame, rumination, or rage (Cheek et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2021). Finally, the FFNI is aligned with contemporary structural models of narcissism and assesses grandiosity and vulnerability, as well as antagonism, agentic extraversion, and narcissistic neuroticism (Miller et al., 2021). Using such a variety of instruments, including categorical, two-factor and three-factor conceptualizations of narcissism, allows for a more nuanced and integrative exploration of how different facets of PN may relate to ED and its components. Altogether, our primary objective is to clarify the heterogeneous associations between pathological narcissism and emotion dysregulation by directly comparing categorical, two-factor, and three-factor narcissism models in their associations with overall and domain specific emotion dysregulation in a clinical population. As a secondary aim, we will assess whether these associations remain after accounting for borderline personality disorder symptoms, given its estalished links with both narcissistic vulnerability and emotion dysregulation.

title: Methods and analysis plan for study 3b
description: Successful risk communication strategies depend upon first understanding how people process complex risk information. In the context of the coronavirus, decision-makers must take into account both the risk to themselves as well as the risk to others they may infect, if they contract the coronavirus. There are numerous cognitive issues associated with this process that at present are not well understood. In particular, how do people understand related but differing risk estimates? How do they use that information to make precautionary decisions that impact themselves as well as others? This project will conduct a series of online studies to determine how people perceive coronavirus risks, separately and in combination, as well as how risk perception impacts their precautionary decisions. Perhaps more importantly, based on preliminary surveys, understandable risk communication expressions will be developed and tested experimentally to establish causal links between information expression and risk perception, trust, and decisions. Finally, using a few relevant individual difference measures, we will determine whether specific abilities are necessary to process complex numeric risk expressions and whether simplified expressions are better in some cases. The results of this work will allow us to provide invaluable advice with the potential to save lives. This research can inform best practices in risk communication that have important implications for communicating risks in future outbreaks to avoid the overwhelming situation the world now faces. Understanding how best to communicate risks to the public and whether communication should be tailored to specific subgroups, is critical to avoiding future pandemics. This registration applies to study 3b from Oct.17, 2020.

title: Dataset of Underrepresented Languages in Eye Tracking Research
description: A number of factors come together to limit the diversity of eye-tracking research, where the majority of papers are conducted with stimuli in the English language. Studying eye movement over other languages is important considering that each language provides unique insights into human cognition. Recently, there have been valued efforts to present datasets from other languages, yet these efforts focused mostly on European languages. In this paper we highlight issues that limit diversity in eye tracking research on reading, and we present our work in collecting an open-access multilingual reading dataset of underrepresented languages. Utilizing a high-frequency research eye tracker (EyeLink 1000 Plus), we record eye tracking data of native and second language readers of English, Spanish, Chinese, Hindi, Russian, Arabic, Japanese, Kazakh, Urdu, and Vietnamese. The dataset includes demographics, language proficiency self-reporting, and answers to comprehension questions. The current version of the dataset, which we make publicly available, consists of 97 trials by 40 participants. With the goal of increasing the number of participants and included languages, we aim to make studying underrepresented languages more accessible to researchers and tool makers. title: Systematic Audit of Public Ophthalmic Imaging Datasets: Assessment of Transparency, Fairness, Usability, and Reproducibility for Machine-Learning Research
description: This project is a systematic audit of publicly available ophthalmic imaging datasets used in machine-learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) research. Its purpose is to evaluate the extent to which existing datasets support transparent, fair, reproducible, and clinically meaningful AI development. Although ophthalmology is a leading domain for clinical AI, many studies rely on datasets with inconsistent documentation, unclear licensing, limited demographic reporting, variable label quality, and data-splitting practices that may compromise reproducibility and validity. This project aims to systematically characterize these datasets and assess their readiness for clinical ML applications. Using a pre-registered protocol, the study will identify eligible datasets through bibliographic databases, preprint servers, and dataset and code repositories. The dataset will be the unit of analysis, with multiple publications or repository pages describing the same dataset consolidated into a single record. Standardized data extraction will capture information on accessibility and licensing, imaging modalities and technical specifications, annotation and labeling practices, demographic transparency, dataset structure, reproducibility features, and evidence of maintenance or versioning. Each dataset will be evaluated using a structured, multi-domain readiness scorecard designed to assess usability, transparency, fairness, and reproducibility. Scoring domains include accessibility and licensing clarity, documentation quality, label quality and inter-rater reliability, demographic reporting, technical completeness, fairness indicators, split hygiene, maintenance and versioning, and clinical and modality diversity. Domain scores will be aggregated to generate an interpretable readiness score that enables comparison across datasets and clinical tasks. Expected outcomes include a curated inventory of public ophthalmic imaging datasets, a transparent framework for evaluating dataset readiness, and descriptive analyses highlighting strengths, limitations, and gaps in the current ophthalmic AI data landscape. Findings will inform best-practice recommendations for dataset development and reporting and support more robust and equitable clinical AI research.

title: Scenes modulate object processing before interacting with memory templates
description: When searching for relevant objects in our environment (say, an apple) we create a memory template (a red sphere), which causes our visual system to favor template-matching visual input (apple-like objects) at the expense of template-mismatching visual input (e.g., leaves). While this principle seems straightforward in a lab-setting, it poses a problem in naturalistic viewing: Two objects that produce the same size on the retina will differ in real-world size if one is nearby and the other is far away. Using the Ponzo illusion to manipulate perceived size while keeping retinal size constant, we demonstrate (across 71 subjects) that visual objects attract attention when their perceived size matches a memory template, compared to mismatching objects that encompass the same size on the retina. This shows that memory templates impact visual selection after object representations are modulated by scene context, thus providing a working mechanism for template-based search in naturalistic vision.

title: Artificial intelligence applications in fundus photograph image analysis for diagnosis and screening of brain tumours: A Systematic Review
description: This systematic review aims to evaluate the utility and diagnostic accuracy of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning algorithms applied to fundus and retinal imaging for the detection, diagnosis, and screening of brain tumours and related intracranial pathologies. Brain tumours, including gliomas, pituitary neoplasms, and other intracranial neoplasms, often present with ocular signs such as papilloedema and other optic nerve head abnormalities that can be detected through fundus photography. Early identification of these signs via non-invasive retinal imaging has the potential to facilitate timely diagnosis and improve patient outcomes. The primary purpose of this review is to synthesise current evidence on the performance of AI-based diagnostic tools in analysing retinal images to identify brain tumours and their associated ocular manifestations. Specifically, the review will assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI algorithms - measured by sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve - in diverse clinical and screening settings. It will also examine the potential of these technologies to improve early detection, screening processes, and clinical decision-making compared to conventional methods, such as clinical examination and neuroimaging. The review will include original research studies, including diagnostic accuracy studies, cohort studies, case-control studies, and observational reports, that have evaluated AI/ML models applied to fundus or retinal photographs. The studies will be scrutinised for quality and bias using the QUADAS-2 tool to ensure robustness of findings. Expected outcomes include a comprehensive synthesis of evidence regarding the effectiveness of AI in this context, identification of knowledge gaps, and recommendations for future research and clinical practice. Ultimately, this review aims to inform stakeholders - including clinicians, researchers, and healthcare policymakers - about the feasibility and accuracy of integrating AI-based retinal image analysis into routine screening and diagnostic pathways for brain tumours.

title: Reference Frames in Learning of Visual Priority
description: This study is designed to examine whether location-based suppression of irrelevant stimuli functions using spatiotopic or retinotopic visual coordinates. To do this, we will train participants to suppress a location in an array of 8 shapes while fixating at a center cross. We do this using a visual search task where participants must identify a target while ignoring salient distractors. Unbeknownst to the participants, one position contains the distractor 75% of the time; this is known as the high probability location (HPL). For each other location there is a roughly 3.57% chance of the distractor appearing. These are known as the low probability locations (LPL). During training, the suppressed location will occupy the same spatiotopic and retinotopic coordinates. For baseline purposes, 1/3 of trials will contain no distractor. At test, we will shift the array and fixation in order to unconfound spatiotopic and retinotopic space. When fixation is shifted, the spatiotopic coordinates of the HPL, known as sHPL, do not change. However the coordinates of the HPL on your retina do shift. If location suppression operates within spatiotopic space, the participants should continue to suppress the sHPL at test. If, however, location suppression is retinotopic, participants will continue to suppress the high probability location on the retina (rHPL), which will now be in a different location than the sHPL. title: Blood Pressure and the Inner Retina: a Systematic Review of OCT Findings and a Call for Multidisciplinary Glaucoma Management
description: Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy causing retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thinning, retinal ganglion cell (RGC) apoptosis, and visual loss. Accumulating evidence suggests that blood pressure (BP), whether too high or too low, can predispose to negative glaucoma outcomes. Initial hypertensive or hypotensive damage to the RGCs and their axons is a likely explanation. With the constant increase in population and life expectancy, by 2040, the projected number of people with glaucoma worldwide exceeds 110 million, while hypertension already affects approximately one third of the adult population. Nevertheless, the growing disease burden related to the coexistence of glaucoma and suboptimal BP control is currently understated in clinical practice. In this regard, we conducted a systematic review on the relationship between arterial hypertension (AHT) and hypotension with inner retinal thickness, as assessed by structural optical coherence tomography. For this purpose, we searched five databases for studies reporting on BP and the RNFL or ganglion cell-inner plexiform layer thickness (GCIPL) in healthy subjects and in patients with ophthalmic or systemic disease. Findings revealed a U-shaped (or J-shaped) effect, but study design limited the conclusions drawn, especially due to the confounding role of antihypertensive medication. Last, we summarize current AHT treatment standards and call for collaborative management of patients with coexisting glaucomatous and cardiovascular risk.

title: Introduction
description: Angiogenesis is a normal and essential physiological process regulated by VEGF that occurs in all humans from embryonic development to wound healing in adults. However, VEGF is also a key mediator of angiogenesis in cancer, in which it is upregulated by oncogene expression, various growth factors, and most prominently, hypoxia (1). As a result of increased VEGF production by malignant cells, a vasculature forms around the tumour to meet the cells' oxygen and nutrient demands. Tumours at first exploit existing blood vessels within an organ for their blood supply, however, their vasculature soon destabilizes due to the release of angiopoietin-2 by vascular endothelial cells (2). This loss of vascular structural and functional integrity is caused by morphological abnormalities in the blood vessels which causes them to become leaky and hemorrhagic, meaning that the tumour vasculature is suboptimal, thus resulting in hypoxia (1,2). The resultant hypoxia leads to the selection of more aggressive tumour cells primarily due to an increase in the levels of an oxygen-sensitive transcriptional activator known as hypoxia-inducible factor-1 (HIF-1), thereby upregulating the phenotypic expression of VEGF (25). This increased VEGF production stimulates further angiogenesis and can result in an exponential growth in the tumour's size, proliferation, and metastatic potential, which is a highly concerning issue among patients who are suffering from cancer. The unique nature of the VEGF molecular signaling pathway, however, offers a plethora of opportunities for the development of novel therapeutics to treat or possibly even eradicate certain types of cancer. Therapeutics that aim to inhibit several VEGF signaling components have been developed to halt angiogenesis in diseases that involve tissue growth and inflammation, such as cancer (4). The ultimate goal with developing anti-angiogenesis treatments is essentially to deprive solid tumours of the oxygen and nutrients they require to survive and proliferate so that they die. This article discusses the VEGF signaling pathway mechanism and its role in diseases such as cancer, anti-angiogenic therapeutic techniques that have been investigated by scientists and their inhibitory mechanisms of action in the VEGF signaling pathway, as well as some effective anti-angiogenic drugs that have been developed to date. Irregular angiogenesis due to abnormal VEGF production can also contribute to the progression of retinal diseases such as wet age-related macular degeneration and macular edema, which will be further discussed in the article.

title: FOV-2: Foveal sensitivity for saccade target-congruent and saccade target-incongruent orientation information during saccade preparation
description: The preparation of rapid eye movements (i.e. saccades) entails dynamic changes in visual sensitivity across the visual field. Pre-saccadic attention shifts and accompanying sensitivity enhancements at the saccade target (ST) have been studied extensively. At the same time, little is known about the development of visual sensitivity in the pre-saccadic center of gaze. Behavioral findings suggest that, just like at the ST, visual sensitivity increases at the pre-saccadic foveal location (e.g. Rolfs, Jonikaitis, Deubel, & Cavanagh, 2011). This finding has been attributed to a predictive remapping mechanism that directs attention to the future retinal (i.e. foveal) location of the ST to provide a head start for post-saccadic processing. To date, however, it remains unclear if a transfer of activation between the ST's current and future retinal location involves a transfer of information about its features. Previous findings suggest that during saccade preparation, feature information can be transferred between two distinct locations in the visual field (motion integration: Szinte, Jonikaitis, Rolfs, Cavanagh, & Deubel, 2016; crowding: Harrison, Retell, Remington, & Mattingley, 2013; visual adaptation: Melcher, 2007 for tilt; Biber & Ilg, 2013 for motion direction). In all of these investigations, however, the discrimination target appeared midway between the pre- and post-saccadic fixation (Szinte et al; Harrison et al.) or at the ST (Melcher; Biber & Ilg). None of them inspected a transfer of feature information from the ST to the pre-saccadic center of gaze. The most direct way of investigating the latter is to i) probe visual sensitivity at the pre-saccadic fixation location and ii) determine the impact of ST features on foveal sensitivity. In the current investigation, we therefore ask observers to detect a briefly presented stimulus in the pre-saccadic center of gaze while they are preparing an eye movement to a peripheral target. The foveal probe is presented on 50% of trials. If present, the orientation of the probe can either be congruent or incongruent with the orientation of the ST. If feature information is transferred from the ST to the fovea during eye movement preparation, the target's orientation should interact with foveal orientation information and influence present/absent judgments. A transfer of feature information between separate locations in the visual field is likely facilitated by the absence of distinct stimulus borders. In consequence, we decided to smoothly embed the foveal probe and ST in full-screen pink noise images presented in quick alternation. We pre-registered and tested a previous version of this experiment (see https://osf.io/5fzda/), the results of which have informed current design choices. For ease of reference, we provide a list of all changes here. Elaborations will be provided in the respective sections. 1) ST visibility: While we intended to remove the ST during the eye movement in the previous experiment, we now include a second condition in which the ST remains visible for a brief period of time after saccade landing. 2) Predictability of probe features: We intend to determine which orientation has been perceived erroneously whenever a false alarm (FA) is generated. To achieve this goal, we previously employed a blocking manipulation that rendered the orientation of a potential probe stimulus perfectly predictable. In the current study, we decided to interleave trials with different potential probe orientations for reasons described in detail below. 3) Keyboard response: To compensate for the information loss associated with the removal of blocking, we ask observers to report the orientation of the perceived foveal probe following every 'present' response in the current investigation. 4) Minor adjustments: We added additional online eye movement criteria to reduce offline trial loss. We furthermore reduced the number of baseline trials in which the foveal probe appears prior to saccade target onset. Note that at the time of this preregistration, coronavirus cases are rising considerably in Germany in general and Berlin in particular. If lab access will be limited before data collection will have been completed, we will attempt to collect 5 instead of 7 sessions per observer and adjust our analyses accordingly (see corresponding sections). If more than 5 sessions will have been collected for some but not all observers at this point, we will only include the first 5 sessions of each observer.

title: Role of VEGF in Retinal Diseases
description: Levels of VEGF-A have been shown to be elevated in the vitreous humour of patients with angiogenesis-associated ocular disorders such as neovascular (wet) age-related macular degeneration (AMD) as a result of choroidal neovascularization (CNV), macular edema (buildup of fluid such as blood in the macula), and retinal vein occlusion (16). CNV in AMD can be induced by several factors, such as the accumulation of lipids as metabolic by-products, oxidative stress, abnormal interstitial pressure within Bruch's membrane (located between the retinal pigment epithelium [RPE] and the choroidal capillaries), and hypoxia as a result of a reduction in choriocapillaris blood flow (16,26). In response to metabolic stress, the RPE tissue produces various factors such as VEGF which induce the proliferation of CNV (27). VEGF is also a powerful agonist of vascular permeability, which causes vascular leakage and therefore macular edema (28). Proinflammatory cytokines are also secreted, which contribute to macular edema and diabetic retinopathy as they cause the breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier (35). Consequently, inhibiting VEGF activity is central to the treatment of wet AMD and macular edema, as well as the prevention of progressive capillary nonperfusion (lack of blood flow to parts of the retina which can potentially cause blindness), especially in conditions such as proliferative diabetic retinopathy and retinal vein occlusion (34).

title: Do object retinal size and conceptual size interact in long-term memory?
description: Visual objects can be represented by their retinal size (dependent on viewing distance) and their conceptual size (their canonical real-world size stored in memory). Prior research (Masarwa et al., 2022) found that scene images presented in larger retinal sizes were better remembered. Conceptual size also plays a key role in memory, as objects are represented in proportion to their real-world size relative to their surrounding context (Konkle & Oliva, 2011). This study investigates the potential interaction between retinal and conceptual size representations in long-term memory (LTM), hypothesizing that memory performance may depend on the alignment between these dimensions. Following two preliminary pilots, we hypothesize that retinal and conceptual size dimensions may interact in long-term memory (LTM), such that the advantage of large retinal sizes (Masarwa et al., 2022) will be reduced for conceptually small objects when their retinal size aligns with their canonical representation. Additionally, a general advantage of large retinal size is expected due to streamlined encoding of details, ease of recognition, and attentional factors, while conceptually small objects may show better memory performance than large ones due to inherent categorical differences.

title: Reporting Quality Assessment of Sham Acupuncture Randomized Controlled Trials for Acupuncture Intervention in Glaucoma
description: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness, yet standard treatments often have limitations, prompting interest in acupuncture as an adjuvant therapy. While acupuncture may offer neuroprotective and circulatory benefits, current research quality remains suboptimal. Existing studies are plagued by methodological flaws, including small sample sizes, inconsistent protocols, and high risks of bias, resulting in low-certainty evidence. Crucially, the adherence to international reporting standards—specifically CONSORT, STRICTA, and the recently released SHARE checklist (2023)—has not been systematically evaluated in this field. This lack of rigorous assessment obscures the true efficacy of the intervention. Consequently, there is an urgent need to re-evaluate existing randomized controlled trials against these updated standards to enhance research transparency, address methodological deficiencies, and provide reliable data for clinical practice.

title: The effect of connectives on the processing and comprehension of different types of coherence relations: An eye-tracking study with struggling readers
description: This study investigated the effect of connectives on the processing and comprehension of different types of coherence relations (Additive, Causal, and Contrastive) in struggling readers. Using a 2x3 experimental design, 110 primary school students (aged 11-13) read texts with and without connectives. Processing was measured through eight eye-tracking measures across two text segments. Comprehension was assessed through local and global true/false statements. Results revealed distinct processing patterns across coherence relations. Although no significant effects were observed in S1, connectives showed differential effects in S2. For causal relations, connectives facilitated initial processing with shorter first-pass reading times but increased subsequent regressions from the target segment. Contrastive relations showed the opposite pattern: longer initial processing times with connectives but fewer regressions from the target segment. Additive relations displayed similar patterns to contrastive relations, though not statistically significant. Despite these clear processing differences, comprehension measures showed no significant effects. These findings demonstrate that most connective effects on discourse processing, previously documented in Global North populations, extend to Global South struggling readers, though these effects do not translate into comprehension benefits.

title: OphthoEvidence Report: Baseline Structural Optical Coherence Tomography Biomarkers Predictive of Visual Acuity Following Epiretinal Membrane Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Epiretinal membrane is a common retinal condition, particularly in the elderly, than can lead to reduced visual acuity and visual distortion. Structural optical coherence tomography biomarkers have shown potential for predicting visual outcomes following surgery. We aim to evaluate the prognostic value of baseline structural optical coherence tomography biomarkers for visual outcomes following Epiretinal membrane surgery. We will assess associations between individual biomarkers and postoperative visual acuity or changes in visual acuity at 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery. We will systematically search MEDLINE, EMBASE, CENTRAL and Web of Science from inception. Eligible studies will include randomized trials and observational studies reporting the association between any baseline optical coherence tomography biomarkers and postoperative visual acuity in patients undergoing epiretinal membrane surgery. Two reviewers will independently and in duplicate perform screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. Meta-analyses using the restricted maximum likelihood random-effects model will be conducted whenever possible. The certainty of evidence for each estimate will be assessed using the GRADE approach. This review will analyze time-specific association between baseline structural optical coherence tomography biomarkers and postoperative visual acuity and change in visual acuity from baseline at 6, 12, and 24 months after surgery, quality of life measured using any validated scale, and adverse events.

title: A normative framework for selective information loss in foveal and peripheral vision
description: [Master's thesis, defended on 04.09.2023 at EPFL, Switzerland] Deep neural networks (DNNs) have reached remarkable proficiency in visual tasks, often surpassing human performance. However, their alignment with human cognitive mechanisms, especially peripheral vision, remains under debate. In humans, peripheral vision, characterized by a decrease in retinal photoreceptor density away from the fovea, is often assumed to be merely more blurry than central vision. Yet, there are reasons to believe that higher cortical processing mechanisms are involved that could explain the selective information loss observed in the periphery of the visual field. This research introduces a novel deep neural network model architecture, composed of autoencoders, as a normative framework to model human peripheral vision. By optimizing the reconstruction of visual input under a constraint on the latent bottleneck, the model aligns with the reduced processing power allocated to peripheral regions in the human visual cortex. Through psychophysical tests, including the honeycomb illusion, pop-out search, and ensemble perception tasks, the model's performance was assessed against human behavior. Results indicated that both humans and the model exhibited similar selective information loss patterns with increasing eccentricity. This work suggests that constrained optimization of a generic image representation objective is a promising approach for understanding human peripheral vision.

title: A Model for Visual Perception and Recognition of Outlines
description: Many topics in vision are still not well understood. A model for visual perception and recognition of shapes is described, by combining ideas relating to receptive fields of ganglion cells in the retina, eye movements during fixation, multiple spatial scales of precision, attention, axes and coordinates. The main objective is to provide a realistic scheme for perception of outlines, with recognition that is not prevented by changes of size and viewpoint. Outlines are detected by changes with time arising from eye movements, followed by identification of vertical and horizontal axes, and use of levels of precision that depend on the size of the area of attention. The increments of position in these levels increase in size as the size of area increases, so in an index of positions the increment numbers remain constant for all sizes. After changes of viewpoint, "attentional planes" connect changed positions on outlines to positions with a standard orientation of axes, so that shapes may be matched with stored representations. Spatial coordinates are related to positions at the retina by representations based on eye movements.

title: Scoping Review: Photoactivated Chromophore for keratitis-Corneal Cross-linking (PACK-CXL), information coming from pre-clinical studies.
description: Infectious keratitis is caused by many different pathogens and may result in vision loss if not treated appropriately. Treatment aims to eliminate pathogens and stop tissue destruction in the cornea. Current standard medical therapy routines in humans and animals are labour intensive and treatment success largely depends on the effectivity of the applied medications, including antibiotics. In the context of globally growing antibiotic resistance, increasingly reduced effectiveness of medical therapy is therefore likely, which makes non-antibiotic-based treatment alternatives desirable. Photoactivated Chromophore for keratitis-Corneal Cross-linking (PACK-CXL) is a type of photodynamic therapy that reduces enzymatic collagenolysis and damages multiple targets within microorganisms. This results in corneal tissue stabilization and non-antibiotic-based elimination of bacteria. A number of PACK-CXL protocols, with different energy sources and chromophores, has been applied in pre-clinical studies (clinical animal and experimental studies) with various experimental settings and endpoints. So far, a systematic mapping of the applied protocols is lacking but considered essential to guide future translational research. In this scoping review, we will focus on: (1) characteristics of the different PACK-CXL protocols; (2) tested infectious pathogens; (3) study designs and experimental settings (4) the spectrum of endpoints used to determine antimicrobial and tissue stabilizing effects.

title: Copyright's Topography: An Empirical Study of Copyright Litigation
description: One of the most important ways to measure the impact of copyright law is through empirical examination of actual copyright infringement cases. Yet scholars have universally overlooked this rich source of data. This study fills that gap through a comprehensive empirical analysis of copyright infringement litigation, examining the pleadings, motions, and dockets from more than nine hundred copyright lawsuits filed from 2005 through 2008. The data we collect allow us to examine a wide variety of copyright issues, such as the rate of settlements versus judgments; the incidence of litigation between major media companies, small firms, and individuals; the kinds of industries and works involved in litigation; the nature of the alleged infringement; the success rates of particular parties and claims; and the nature of remedies sought and awarded. We also analyze the data to identify ways in which copyright litigation differs from other civil suits and to show that certain plaintiff characteristics are more predictive of success.

title: Public attitudes and acceptance of screening for neurodegenerative disease by AI analysis of retinal OCT images
description: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's are a major and growing cause of disability. As the retina is essentially an outgrowth of the brain, changes in the retina are associated with changes in the brain, which can be viewed via 3D scanning Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT), increasingly available in high-street optometrists. Although these changes are often too subtle for the human eye to detect, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning allow for the possibility of screening for neurodegenerative disease as part of a routine eye test, allowing for earlier diagnosis and subsequent treatment. However, this raises the critical question of whether the public would accept such screening. The aim of this study is to determine factors which influence public attitudes to an AI-based screening tool for early signs of neurodegenerative disease, to map a route for improving acceptability and uptake of such a tool based on the results. This study utlises co-creation with a public panel to create an animation role play, simulating a visit to the optometrist. Hypothesised variables to predict uptake include socioeconomic status and uncontrollable mortality risk, whether a human or AI performs the analysis, benefits of screening, proximity to neurodegenerative disease, and demographic factors. Ordinal logistic regression will be applied as the main statistical analysis.

title: NyameriNet
description: The development of "Nyameri," a hypothetical next-generation mobile application for diabetic retinopathy (DR) image analysis, represents a synthesis of cutting-edge academic research and commercial product features into a cohesive, plausible technology. The core of the Nyameri system is its custom-designed Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), named NyameriNet. This architecture is engineered to deliver high diagnostic accuracy while operating efficiently on mobile devices without constant reliance on cloud connectivity. While specific architectural details like the exact number of layers are not provided in the source materials, the design philosophy aligns with state-of-the-art models known for their balance of performance and efficiency. For instance, NyameriNet's estimated size of approximately 40 MB is comparable to DRNet13, which was reported to be 35 MB. This suggests an architecture that may incorporate techniques such as depthwise separable convolutions or other forms of model optimization to maintain a small footprint. The primary function of NyameriNet is a five-class classification task: No DR, Mild, Moderate, Severe, and Proliferative DR. This multi-stage grading is a standard benchmark in the field, reflecting the clinical need for precise disease staging. The simulated performance of NyameriNet is projected to exceed current clinical standards, positioning it as a highly advanced tool. The model is expected to achieve an accuracy rate between 96% and 98%, a figure supported by numerous studies on complex CNN architectures. For example, a DenseNet-121 model using CLAHE and ESRGAN preprocessing on the APTOS 2019 dataset achieved 98.36% accuracy , while a hybrid Inception v3 model reached 98.7% accuracy on the same dataset. Similarly, a modified VGGNet-based transfer learning model trained on the Kaggle EyePACS dataset achieved 96.6% accuracy after extensive data augmentation. Sensitivity and specificity are critical metrics for any screening tool, and NyameriNet's projected values aim to surpass established benchmarks. An estimated sensitivity of 97-98% significantly outperforms the minimum requirements set by bodies like the British Diabetic Association (BDA) of 80%. This level of performance is consistent with top-tier models; for instance, a study on the Messidor-2 dataset achieved a sensitivity of 97.63% , and another model reached 99.21% on the Kaggle test dataset. Specificity is projected to be in the range of 95-97%, also exceeding the BDA's 95% minimum requirement. Models like DeB5-XNet have demonstrated 97.1% specificity on the DDR dataset , and a WFDLN model achieved 98.0% specificity on the Messidor dataset. These figures underscore the potential of modern deep learning to provide highly reliable screening results. The model's precision and F1-score are also projected to be very high, at 0.96-0.98, indicating a low rate of false positives and a strong balance between precision and recall.

title: Primary Bone Marrow Edema Syndrome, a prospective observational study
description: Primary bone marrow edema syndrome (pBMES) is a painful condition of unknown cause. The term edema refers to the magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings of increased interstitial fluid in the bone marrow. While bone marrow edema in it self is a common MRI finding in various conditions such as trauma, infection, joint inflammation, and tumors—what distinguishes pBMES from these other conditions is its spontaneous onset, unknown cause, and self-limiting disease course. Current knowledge about pBMES is very limited, primarily based on reports of single cases or small series, which mainly involve adult males and pregnant females. The present project is an observational study with three primary aims: a) to determine the prognosis of pBMES in terms of pain and physical functioning; b) to assess the extent of bone marrow edema over time through repeated MRIs; and c) to evaluate the incidence of BMES using the population of Østfold County and the Vestby municipality in Norway as the denominator.

title: Population-Scale Analysis of Frequency-Dependent Calcium Dynamics in Retinal Ganglion Cells Under Electric Field Stimulation
description: This OSF project contains data and code supporting the manuscript "Population-Scale Analysis of Frequency-Dependent Calcium Dynamics in Retinal Ganglion Cells Under Electric Field Stimulation." The dataset comprises large-scale ex vivo calcium imaging recordings of Thy1-GCaMP6f mouse retinas exposed to controlled horizontal electric field stimulation across a wide range of waveform frequencies and shapes, including sinusoidal, DC, and asymmetric charge-balanced (ACB) stimuli. Recordings capture single-cell and population-level intracellular calcium dynamics from thousands of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs). The repository includes processed imaging data, extracted single-cell calcium time series, and all data-processing pipelines implemented in Python. These materials enable reproduction of all figures and analyses reported in the manuscript and support future data-driven and biophysically informed modeling studies of neural responses to extracellular electric field stimulation.
